indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of a variety of songs
indicator.objective: Explain the central messages in songs

skills.description: Identify what a song is about from its lines.
State the central message of a song in own words, choosing the best one-line summary.
Tell the central message apart from a supporting detail or example in the song.
Pick the line that best supports a stated message.
Say why the song was sung or who it is meant for (to praise, to warn, to unite, to teach).
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a song and explain its central message aloud in 2-3 sentences.
Teacher-assessed performance: sing lines with appropriate stress and rhythm, individually and in a group.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'We sweep the compound every day, / We keep the gutters clean, / We plant young trees along the way, / To keep our village green.' What is the song about?
hints: Think about what all the actions in the song have in common.
The song mentions sweeping, keeping gutters clean, and planting trees.
questions.explanation: The song lists actions such as sweeping the compound, keeping gutters clean and planting trees. All of these actions are about keeping the village clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sweeping the classroom only' because one action matches, but the song is about the whole village.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'My mother wakes before the sun, / She cooks and sweeps and works till noon. / I watch her hands, I learn her care, / I want to be like her soon.' What is this song about?
options: A sister who plays all day
hints: Who does the song describe?
The person wakes before the sun and works till noon.
questions.explanation: The song describes someone who wakes early and works hard all morning. The singer calls her 'my mother' and wants to be like her. So the song is about a hard-working mother.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'market woman' because they think of work, but the song says the person is a mother who cooks and sweeps.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'The harmattan blows from the north, / It dries the ground and cracks the earth, / It brings the dust and cold at night, / And makes us wrap up warm and tight.' What is the song about?
hints: Which season is named?
The song mentions dry ground, dust and cold nights.
questions.explanation: The song names the harmattan and describes its effects: dry ground, cracked earth, dust and cold nights. So the song is about the harmattan season.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cold Christmas morning' because of the cold, but the song specifically names the harmattan.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Do not laugh at a friend who falls, / Do not mock the weak, / Help them up and hear their calls, / With kind words, softly speak.' What is the central message of the song?
options: Be kind and help those who need it
hints: What is the song telling you NOT to do?
Then it tells you what to do instead.
questions.explanation: The song warns against laughing at a friend who falls or mocking the weak. Instead it says to help them up and speak kindly. The central message is to be kind and help those who need it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'falling down is funny' because the song mentions falling, but the song is telling them NOT to laugh.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Work, work, every day, / Do not waste the morning away. / Small hands doing what they can, / Make a happy home and happy man.' What is the central message?
options: Work hard and do not waste time
Only work when you are told
hints: What does the song say about the morning?
It links small work with a happy home.
questions.explanation: The song says to work every day and not waste the morning. It says small hands doing what they can make a happy home. The central message is to work hard and not waste time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'only work when you are told' because they think work is forced, but the song encourages working willingly.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Our flag has red for the blood that flowed, / Gold for the wealth of our land, / Green for the forests along the road, / And the black star in our hand.' What is the central message?
options: Be proud of our country, Ghana
hints: What does the song describe?
The colours of the flag stand for things that make us proud of our country.
questions.explanation: The song explains what each colour of the flag stands for: red for the blood that flowed, gold for wealth, green for forests, and the black star. The central message is to be proud of Ghana.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'the flag has many colours' because that is a detail, but the central message is pride in the country.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'I did not see the water rise, / I did not hear the wind, / I only saw my mother's eyes, / And felt her pull me in. / Hold tight to those who care for you, / For love will see you through.' What is the central message?
options: Hold tight to those who care for you
hints: Look at the last two lines. What do they tell the listener to do?
The first four lines are an example; the message is in the last two.
questions.explanation: The first four lines tell a story about a storm and a mother pulling the singer to safety. The last two lines give the message: hold tight to those who care for you, because love will see you through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'storms are dangerous' because it is a detail, but the central message is about holding tight to people who care for us.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Sweep the compound, sweep it clean, / Wash the dishes, wash the plate, / Make your bed and fold your cloth, / Do not sit and wait. / When your home is neat and bright, / You will sleep in peace at night.' Which sentence gives the CENTRAL MESSAGE, not just a detail?
options: A clean home brings peace at night
hints: Which sentence is the big idea that covers all the actions?
The other three are examples of the cleaning work.
questions.explanation: The central message is in the last two lines: 'When your home is neat and bright, you will sleep in peace at night.' The sweeping, washing and folding are details that support this idea.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sweep the compound clean' because it is the first line, but it is a detail, not the central message.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Do not take what is not yours, / Even if no one sees. / The eye that watches from above / Sees the smallest breeze. / A truthful child will always find / Peace of mind and honest friends.' Which sentence gives the CENTRAL MESSAGE?
options: Be truthful and honest, even when no one is watching
hints: Which sentence summarises the whole idea?
The other sentences either describe part of the message or give a result of living by it.
questions.explanation: The central message is to be truthful and honest even when no one is watching. 'The eye that watches from above' is a detail that supports it, and 'honest people have friends' is a result of living by it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'never take anything' because it is stated in the first line, but the song is about honesty in general, not just taking things.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Our fathers built the roads we walk, / Our mothers taught us how to talk, / Our elders showed us what is right, / Our chiefs kept peace through day and night. / Respect the ones who came before, / For they have opened every door.' Which sentence gives the CENTRAL MESSAGE?
options: Respect those who came before us
Our mothers taught us to talk
hints: Which line gives the big idea that covers all four examples?
The first four lines are about what each group did.
questions.explanation: The first four lines give examples of what fathers, mothers, elders and chiefs did. The central message is in the last two lines: 'Respect the ones who came before, for they have opened every door.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'our fathers built the roads' because it is a strong line, but it is only one example, not the central message.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'Do not throw rubbish on the ground, / Do not block the drain, / For when the rains come falling down, / The water will complain. / A dirty town is a sad place, / A clean town is a joy.' The message is: 'Keep your town clean.' Which line BEST supports this message?
options: A clean town is a joy
Do not throw rubbish on the ground
A dirty town is a sad place
hints: Which line gives a reason to keep the town clean?
One line compares a clean town with a sad town.
questions.explanation: The message is 'Keep your town clean.' The line 'A clean town is a joy' directly gives a reason for keeping the town clean: it brings joy. The other lines describe what not to do or what happens when the town is dirty.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Do not throw rubbish on the ground' because it mentions dirt, but it is an instruction, not a support for the message.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'One finger cannot pick a nut, / One hand cannot sweep the room, / But many hands can lift a lot, / And chase away the gloom. / Together we are strong and bold, / Together we are gold.' The message is: 'We are stronger when we work together.' Which line BEST supports this message?
options: Many hands can lift a lot
One finger cannot pick a nut
One hand cannot sweep the room
hints: Which line gives a positive result of working together?
One line shows what many hands can do.
questions.explanation: The message is 'We are stronger when we work together.' The line 'Many hands can lift a lot' shows directly what people can do when they work together, which supports the message.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'One finger cannot pick a nut' because it mentions fingers and hands, but it shows what one cannot do, not what many can do.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song: 'A child who reads will always find / A world of wonder in the mind. / A child who reads will always know / The way to make the nation grow. / So open a book and read it well, / And watch your mind begin to swell.' The message is: 'Reading helps you and your nation grow.' Which line BEST supports this message?
options: A child who reads will always know the way to make the nation grow
A child who reads will always find a world of wonder in the mind
Open a book and read it well
Watch your mind begin to swell
hints: Which line mentions the nation?
One line links reading with making the nation grow.
questions.explanation: The message is 'Reading helps you and your nation grow.' The line that mentions the nation growing is 'A child who reads will always know the way to make the nation grow.' That supports the 'nation' part of the message.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A child who reads will always find a world of wonder in the mind' because it is about reading, but it supports only the 'you grow' part, not the 'nation' part. The message includes both.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song sung at a school assembly: 'Rise and shine, pupils all, / Answer when the teachers call, / Learn your books and play your part, / With a willing, cheerful heart.' Why is this song sung?
options: To encourage pupils to do their best at school
To sell books at the market
hints: Who is the song for?
What does it ask them to do?
questions.explanation: The song is sung at a school assembly to pupils. It tells them to rise, answer teachers, learn and play their part cheerfully. So it is sung to encourage pupils to do their best at school.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to warn pupils about danger' because songs are sometimes warnings, but this one encourages rather than warns.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a song sung by farmers: 'The rain has come, the soil is soft, / We thank the Lord who sends it oft. / Now plant the maize and plant the bean, / And sing to keep the spirit keen.' Why is this song sung?
options: To celebrate the rains and encourage planting
To sell maize at the market
hints: What season is it?
What does the song tell farmers to do now?
questions.explanation: The song says the rain has come and the soil is soft. It thanks the Lord and tells farmers to plant maize and beans. So it is sung to celebrate the rains and encourage planting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to warn farmers about drought' because farming is hard, but the song is about the rain arriving, not drought.

questions.stem: Listen carefully as your teacher sings or plays a short song about caring for the environment. In 2-3 sentences, explain the central message of the song aloud to your teacher or a small group.
hints: Listen for what the song tells people to do or feel.
Use the words of the song to support your answer.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric. The pupil should state the central message and give one reason from the song.

criteria.description: States the central message clearly and accurately
Gives one detail or line from the song as support

questions.stem: Listen carefully as your teacher sings or plays a short song about honesty. In 2-3 sentences, explain the central message of the song and give one reason why the message matters. Then say whether you agree with the message and why.
hints: First say what the song is telling people.
Then give a reason from the song or from life.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric. The pupil should state the message, give a reason, and give a personal opinion with a reason.

criteria.description: Gives one reason why the message matters
Gives a personal opinion with a reason
Speaks clearly and in complete sentences

questions.stem: Sing the first two lines of a familiar song with your teacher and the class. Use the right stress and rhythm so the song sounds natural.
hints: Listen to your teacher first.
Tap the beat with your hand.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Joins in the singing with the class
Keeps the rhythm (taps or claps on beat)
Puts stress on the right words

questions.stem: In a small group, choose a short song you know. Practise it once, then sing it to the class with the right stress and rhythm. Make sure every member of the group sings.
hints: Practise once before you sing to the class.
Listen to each other so you sing together.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Stress is placed on the right words

questions.stem: Sing a song of your choice on your own to the class. Use the right stress and rhythm, and show the meaning of the song with your face and actions.
hints: Choose a song you know well.
Think about what the song means as you sing.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Sings the whole song on their own
Stress is placed correctly to show meaning
Face and actions match the meaning of the song

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.1: Demonstrate knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the features of spoken language, e.g. use of discourse markers – well, also, finally

skills.description: Recognise a contraction in a short spoken-style text.
Expand a contraction to its full form or match contraction to full form.
Recognise ellipsis in a short dialogue.
Recognise a discourse marker in a short spoken text.
Match a discourse marker to its function.
Teacher-assessed oral: use contractions, ellipsis and at least one discourse marker in a short dialogue.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a spoken text and name the contractions, ellipsis and discourse markers heard.

questions.stem: Read this spoken sentence: 'I can't come to school today.' Which word is a contraction?
hints: A contraction is a shortened form of two words.
'Can't' is short for 'cannot'.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' is a contraction of 'cannot'. It is a feature of spoken language. The other words are not contractions.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not recognise 'can't' as a contraction because they see it as one word, but it stands for 'cannot'.

questions.stem: Read this spoken sentence: 'She shouldn't eat too much sugar.' Which word is a contraction?
hints: Look for the apostrophe.
It is short for 'should not'.
questions.explanation: 'Shouldn't' is a contraction of 'should not'. The apostrophe marks where letters are missing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'much' because it is a describing word, but contractions always involve an apostrophe and a shortened form.

questions.stem:
Read this spoken dialogue:
Ama: 'I'm going to the market.'
Kofi: 'Don't forget to buy tomatoes.'
Which words are contractions?
hints: Look for apostrophes.
'I'm' is short for 'I am', and 'don't' is short for 'do not'.
questions.explanation: The contractions are 'I'm' (I am) and 'Don't' (do not). The other words are not contractions.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'market and tomatoes' because they are spoken words, but contractions always have apostrophes and shortened forms.

questions.stem: What is the full form of the contraction 'can't'?
hints: 'Can't' stands for two words.
It is 'can' + 'not'.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' is the contraction of 'cannot' (can + not).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'can' because it is part of the contraction, but that leaves out 'not'.

questions.stem: What is the full form of the contraction 'shouldn't'?
hints: 'Shouldn't' stands for two words.
It is 'should' + 'not'.
questions.explanation: 'Shouldn't' is the contraction of 'should not'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'shall not' because it sounds similar, but the contraction is from 'should not'.

questions.stem:
Read this spoken dialogue:
Ama: 'How are you?'
Kofi: 'Fine.'
Which line shows ellipsis?
hints: Ellipsis means leaving out some words.
Kofi's answer is short — what is missing?
questions.explanation: Kofi says 'Fine.' instead of the full sentence 'I am fine.' Leaving out 'I am' is ellipsis — a feature of spoken language.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'Fine' is wrong because it is incomplete, but in speech, ellipsis is normal and correct.

questions.stem:
Read this spoken dialogue:
Ama: 'When will you come?'
Kofi: 'Tomorrow.'
Which line shows ellipsis?
hints: Ellipsis means leaving words out.
Kofi says just one word — what is missing?
questions.explanation: Kofi says 'Tomorrow.' instead of 'I will come tomorrow.' Leaving out 'I will come' is ellipsis.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'Tomorrow' is too short to be a reply, but ellipsis is normal in conversation.

questions.stem:
Read this spoken dialogue:
Ama: 'Did you finish your homework?'
Kofi: 'Not yet.'
Which is the full sentence that Kofi's reply is based on?
options: I have not finished my homework yet.
I did not finish my homework.
hints: Kofi says 'Not yet.'
What are the missing words?
questions.explanation: Kofi's reply 'Not yet.' stands for 'I have not finished my homework yet.' The missing words are an example of ellipsis.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I did not finish my homework' because it is negative, but 'not yet' means it is not finished but may still be finished — so 'have not finished yet' is the full form.

questions.stem: Read this spoken sentence: 'Well, I think we should go now.' Which word is a discourse marker?
hints: A discourse marker is a word that organises what we say.
'Well' often starts a spoken sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Well' is a discourse marker — it helps the speaker start or frame the sentence. The other words are content words.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'now' because it is about time, but 'now' is an adverb of time, not a discourse marker.

questions.stem: Read this spoken text: 'First, we wash the rice. Then we cook it. Finally, we serve it.' Which words are discourse markers?
hints: Discourse markers show the order of steps.
Look for words that sequence.
questions.explanation: 'First', 'Then' and 'Finally' are discourse markers — they signpost the order of steps.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'wash, cook, serve' because they are the actions, but those are verbs, not discourse markers.

questions.stem: Read this spoken text: 'I like mangoes. Also, I like oranges.' Which word is a discourse marker?
hints: Which word is used to add information?
'Also' adds a second idea.
questions.explanation: 'Also' is a discourse marker — it adds a second idea. The other words are content words.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'like' because it connects the ideas, but 'like' is the verb, not the marker.

questions.stem: What is the function of the discourse marker 'finally' in a spoken text?
options: To show the last item or step
To show the first item or step
hints: Think about the word 'final'.
It marks the end of a list or process.
questions.explanation: 'Finally' signals the last item or step in a sequence. It marks the end of a list or process.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to add extra information' because 'finally' can add a point, but its main function is to signal the end.

questions.stem: What is the function of the discourse marker 'also' in a spoken text?
hints: Think about what 'also' means.
It is used when you have one more thing to say.
questions.explanation: 'Also' adds extra information. It signals that the speaker has another point to add.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to show a contrast' because 'also' connects ideas, but it adds (not contrasts) — contrast would be 'but' or 'however'.

questions.stem: What is the function of the discourse marker 'well' at the start of a spoken sentence?
options: To show the speaker is thinking or starting
hints: Think about how people say 'well...' when they start to speak.
'Well' often signals thinking or hesitation.
questions.explanation: 'Well' at the start of a spoken sentence signals that the speaker is thinking, hesitating, or beginning. It is a common spoken discourse marker.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to show a contrast' because 'well' can introduce a disagreement, but its basic function is to signal the speaker is starting or thinking.

questions.stem: Have a short conversation with a partner. Use at least one contraction, one ellipsis and one discourse marker.
hints: Try 'can't' or 'don't' for a contraction.
Try 'Fine.' or 'Tomorrow.' for ellipsis.
Try 'well', 'also' or 'finally' as a discourse marker.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least one discourse marker

questions.stem: Have a conversation with a partner where you describe how to make tea. Use at least two discourse markers (first, then, finally) and at least one contraction.
hints: Start with 'First...'
Continue with 'Then...'
End with 'Finally...'
Use a contraction like 'I'll' or 'don't'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two discourse markers
Contractions and markers are used naturally

questions.stem: Tell a short story to a partner. Use at least two contractions, one ellipsis and one discourse marker.
hints: Try 'I'm', 'didn't' for contractions.
Try 'So?' or 'Fine.' for ellipsis.
Try 'well' or 'also' for a discourse marker.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least one discourse marker

questions.stem: Have a 2-minute conversation with a partner. Use contractions, ellipsis and at least three discourse markers naturally. Then explain why spoken language uses these features.
hints: Natural speech uses contractions and short answers.
Then say: 'We use these because...'
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three discourse markers
Explains why spoken language uses these features

questions.stem: Listen to a short spoken text your teacher reads. Then name the contractions you heard and one discourse marker.
hints: Listen for words with apostrophes.
Listen for words like 'well', 'also', 'finally'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names at least two contractions heard

questions.stem: Listen to a short spoken dialogue your teacher reads. Then name one contraction, one ellipsis and one discourse marker from it.
hints: Contraction: word with an apostrophe.
Ellipsis: short answer.
Discourse marker: word that organises speech.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.1: Demonstrate knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the differences between spoken and written forms of language, e.g. formal and informal register

skills.description: Identify whether a sentence is more typical of spoken or written English.
Identify whether a phrase is formal or informal.
Match a situation to the right register.
Choose the simpler, spoken-style version of a written sentence.
Teacher-assessed oral: give a short, simple speech on a familiar topic in informal register.
Teacher-assessed oral: give a short formal introduction using formal register.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more typical of SPOKEN English?
options: I have not eaten as of now.
hints: Which one uses a contraction?
Spoken English often uses contractions.
questions.explanation: 'I haven't eaten yet' is typical of spoken English because it uses the contraction 'haven't'. The other options are more formal and typical of written English.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I have not eaten yet' because it is grammatically correct, but both are correct — the spoken form uses a contraction.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more typical of WRITTEN English?
options: The committee has decided to postpone the meeting.
The committee's decided to postpone the meeting.
hints: Which sentence is the most formal and complete?
Written English uses full forms and formal vocabulary.
questions.explanation: 'The committee has decided to postpone the meeting' is the most formal and complete — typical of written English. The others are more spoken in style.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The committee's decided to postpone the meeting' because it is still about a meeting, but it uses a contraction and is more spoken.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more typical of SPOKEN English?
options: I am unable to attend today.
I regret that I am unable to attend today.
hints: Which one uses contractions and ellipsis?
Spoken English often shortens.
questions.explanation: 'Can't come today' is typical of spoken English — it uses a contraction and ellipsis (missing 'I'). The other options are more formal and written.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I cannot come today' because it is clear, but it is more written in style than 'Can't come today'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more typical of WRITTEN English?
options: The results of the survey indicate a significant increase in attendance.
The results show more people came.
hints: Which sentence uses formal vocabulary?
Written English often uses words like 'indicate' and 'significant'.
questions.explanation: 'The results of the survey indicate a significant increase in attendance' uses formal vocabulary and is typical of written English. The other options are spoken in style.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Attendance went up' because it is clear, but it is spoken, not written, in style.

questions.stem: Which phrase is FORMAL?
hints: Which one is polite and used in formal situations?
'Good morning, sir' is polite and complete.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, sir' is formal — it uses a polite greeting and a title. The other options are informal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Hi' because it is friendly, but 'hi' is informal, used with friends.

questions.stem: Which phrase is INFORMAL?
options: I would like to ask a question.
May I please speak to the head teacher?
hints: Which one would you use with close friends, not teachers?
'Hey, what's up?' is very casual.
questions.explanation: 'Hey, what's up?' is informal — used with friends. The other options are formal and polite.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'May I please speak to the head teacher?' because it is a question, but it is formal, not informal.

questions.stem: Which phrase is FORMAL?
options: I would like to respectfully request your assistance.
hints: Which one uses formal words like 'respectfully request'?
Formal English often uses longer, more polite phrases.
questions.explanation: 'I would like to respectfully request your assistance' uses formal vocabulary and phrasing. The other options are more informal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Can you help me?' because it is polite, but it is informal compared to 'respectfully request your assistance'.

questions.stem: Which phrase is INFORMAL?
options: Do you wish to accompany me?
hints: Which one uses 'wanna'?
'Wanna' is a very informal way of saying 'want to'.
questions.explanation: 'Wanna go?' is informal — 'wanna' is a casual contraction of 'want to'. The other options are more formal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Shall we go?' because it is short, but it is still formal in style.

questions.stem: You are speaking to the head teacher at assembly. Which register should you use?
hints: What kind of situation is a school assembly?
It is a formal setting.
questions.explanation: Speaking to the head teacher at assembly calls for formal register — polite, complete sentences and respectful language.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Informal' because they know the head teacher, but the setting is formal and the head teacher is in authority.

questions.stem: You are chatting with your best friend at break time. Which register should you use?
hints: What kind of situation is a chat with a close friend?
It is relaxed and personal.
questions.explanation: Chatting with a best friend at break time calls for informal register — relaxed language, contractions, casual words.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Formal' because they think all English should be formal, but formal English with a close friend sounds strange and distant.

questions.stem: You are speaking to a visitor at a school ceremony, introducing yourself. Which register should you use?
hints: What kind of situation is a school ceremony?
It is an official event with a visitor.
questions.explanation: Speaking to a visitor at a school ceremony is formal — you should use polite, complete language. Informal or slang register would be inappropriate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Informal' because it feels friendlier, but a ceremony is an official setting requiring formal language.

questions.stem: Which is the more spoken-style version of: 'I have not yet completed my assignment.'?
options: I haven't finished my homework yet.
I have not yet completed my assignment.
I am in the process of completing my assignment.
The assignment has not yet been completed by me.
hints: Which one uses a contraction and simpler words?
Spoken English uses simpler vocabulary.
questions.explanation: 'I haven't finished my homework yet' is simpler and more spoken in style — it uses a contraction, 'homework' instead of 'assignment', and shorter phrasing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick the original sentence because it is correct, but the question asks for the spoken version, which is shorter and simpler.

questions.stem: Which is the more spoken-style version of: 'She is unable to attend the meeting.'?
options: She can't come to the meeting.
She is unable to attend the meeting.
Her attendance at the meeting is not possible.
The meeting will not be attended by her.
hints: Which one uses a contraction and simpler words?
'Can't come' is simpler than 'unable to attend'.
questions.explanation: 'She can't come to the meeting' is the spoken version — it uses the contraction 'can't', the simpler verb 'come', and shorter phrasing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick the original because it sounds correct, but spoken style is simpler than written style.

questions.stem: Which is the more spoken-style version of: 'Please be advised that the examination will commence at nine o'clock.'?
options: Please be advised that the examination will commence at nine o'clock.
Kindly note the examination start time.
The examination is scheduled to begin at nine o'clock.
hints: Which one is the simplest and shortest?
'Exam starts at nine' is short and direct.
questions.explanation: 'The exam starts at nine' is the spoken version — 'exam' is simpler than 'examination', 'starts' is simpler than 'will commence', and the whole sentence is short and direct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kindly note the examination start time' because it is brief, but it is still formal written style, not spoken style.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 1 minute) to a small group about your favourite food, using informal register.
hints: Talk like you are speaking to friends.
Use 'I' and 'my'.
Use contractions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 1 minute) to a small group about a favourite place, using informal register.
hints: Speak naturally.
Use informal language you would use with friends.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 2 minutes) to a small group about a favourite hobby. Use informal register and include contractions and discourse markers.
hints: Use contractions.
Use 'also', 'well' or 'then'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 2 minutes) to the class about a favourite hobby. Use informal register. Then explain how you would say the same thing if you were speaking to the head teacher (in formal register).
hints: First give the informal version.
Then explain the formal version.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Introduce a visiting speaker to a school assembly. Use formal register — polite, complete sentences, no contractions.
hints: Start with 'Good morning...'
Use 'we are honoured' or 'please welcome'.
Avoid contractions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Welcome a visitor to your school during a ceremony. Use formal register — polite, complete sentences, no contractions.
hints: Use 'we welcome you...'
Be polite and complete.
Avoid contractions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Welcomes the visitor with formal language

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.1: Demonstrate knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of how meaning is conveyed through appropriate pace, stress, tone - through reciting poems.

skills.description: Identify how stressing a different word in a sentence changes the meaning.
Identify the effect of pace (slow/fast) on meaning in a short poem line.
Identify the feeling or tone conveyed by a given reading.
Recognise which of two readings better conveys the meaning of a poem line.
Teacher-assessed oral: recite a short poem with appropriate pace, stress and tone.
Teacher-assessed oral: perform the same poem a second time, improving pace, stress and tone after feedback.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a peer's recitation and comment on pace, stress or tone.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud with the stressed word in capital letters: 'I didn't say HE stole it.' Who is the speaker saying did NOT steal it?
hints: The stress is on 'HE'.
What does stressing 'HE' do to the meaning?
questions.explanation: When 'HE' is stressed, the speaker is pointing at the other person — saying it was not HE who stole it. The stress changes the meaning by identifying who is being talked about.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stress on 'HE' means the speaker did steal it, but the stress shifts attention away from the speaker and onto the other person.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud with the stressed word in capital letters: 'I didn't say he STOLE it.' What is the speaker denying?
hints: The stress is on 'STOLE'.
What action is being denied?
questions.explanation: Stressing 'STOLE' denies that the person stole the item. The speaker might mean the person borrowed or found it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'That the person said it' because 'say' is in the sentence, but the stress is on 'stole' — that is the action being denied.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud with the stressed word in capital letters: 'I DIDN'T say he stole it.' What is the speaker denying?
hints: The stress is on 'DIDN'T'.
What action is being denied?
questions.explanation: Stressing 'DIDN'T' denies that the speaker said it at all. It does not deny that the person stole — it denies the saying.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'That the person stole it' because it is in the sentence, but the stress is on 'didn't' — that is the denial.

questions.stem: Read: 'I didn't say he stole it.' Stressing 'I' versus stressing 'he' changes the meaning. Why?
options: Because the stressed word tells the listener which part is being emphasised or denied
Because the stressed word is always wrong
Because the stressed word is the verb
Because the stressed word changes the grammar
hints: What does stress do to a word?
It makes the listener pay attention to it.
questions.explanation: Stressing a different word tells the listener which part of the sentence is important or being denied. Stressing 'I' denies the speaker did it; stressing 'he' denies the other person did it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stress changes the grammar, but stress does not change grammar — it changes emphasis and meaning.

questions.stem: Which line should be read SLOWLY to show the meaning of a poem?
options: 'The tired old man walked slowly home.'
'The children ran and jumped and played.'
hints: Which line has a slow movement?
Read each line and decide which should sound slow.
questions.explanation: The line 'The tired old man walked slowly home' describes slow, tired movement. Reading it slowly matches its meaning. The other lines describe fast or energetic movement and should be read faster.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The children ran' because running can be slow, but the line describes running, which is usually read faster.

questions.stem: Which line should be read FAST to show the meaning?
options: 'The fire blazed and crackled and spread.'
'The moon rose slowly in the sky.'
'The old woman sat by the fire.'
'The river flowed gently to the sea.'
hints: Which line describes something that moves or spreads quickly?
Fire spreads fast.
questions.explanation: The line 'The fire blazed and crackled and spread' describes fire that is moving and spreading quickly. Reading it fast matches the meaning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The river flowed gently' because rivers move, but 'gently' suggests slow movement, not fast.

questions.stem: A poem line reads: 'The drum beats slow... slow... slow...' How should you read it?
options: Slowly, with pauses between the 'slow' words
hints: What does the word 'slow' tell you?
The dots (...) suggest pauses.
questions.explanation: The line uses 'slow... slow... slow...' — the dots suggest pauses. Reading slowly with pauses matches the sound of a slow drum.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a drum should always be read loudly, but here the drum is slow — so reading slowly is correct.

questions.stem: Which tone fits this line: 'We won the match! We won!'?
hints: What feeling do the words and exclamation marks suggest?
Winning is a happy event.
questions.explanation: The line uses exclamation marks and repeats 'We won!', which suggests excitement and joy. So the tone should be excited and happy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Angry and loud' because exclamation marks can show anger, but in this context, winning is happy — not angry.

questions.stem: Which tone fits this line: 'She left us on a cold, dark night.'?
hints: What do 'cold' and 'dark' suggest?
Leaving is a sad event in this line.
questions.explanation: The words 'cold, dark night' and the idea of leaving suggest sadness. So the tone should be sad and quiet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Angry' because leaving can cause anger, but the line's imagery is sad, not angry.

questions.stem: Which tone fits this line: 'Take care, my child, the road is long and dark.'?
hints: What is the speaker doing?
The speaker is warning someone they care about.
questions.explanation: The speaker says 'Take care, my child' and warns about a long, dark road. The tone is warning and caring — the speaker wants the child to be safe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Angry and loud' because the road is dark, but the words 'my child' show care, not anger.

questions.stem: Which reading of the line 'The storm is coming, hold on tight!' conveys the meaning better?
options: Loud, urgent, with a rising voice
Flat and quiet, as if bored
hints: What is happening in the line?
The line is a warning about a storm — what kind of voice fits?
questions.explanation: The line is a warning about a storm, so a loud, urgent voice with a rising tone fits the meaning. Flat, quiet or gentle readings do not convey the danger.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think reading gently is always better, but a warning line needs urgency, not softness.

questions.stem: Which reading of the line 'The little baby is fast asleep' conveys the meaning better?
options: Soft and slow, with gentle pauses
hints: What is happening in the line?
A sleeping baby needs a calm reading.
questions.explanation: The line describes a sleeping baby. Reading softly and slowly matches the quiet, gentle scene. Loud, angry or excited readings would break the mood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all recitations should be loud, but this line needs softness to convey the meaning.

questions.stem: Recite a short poem with appropriate pace (not too fast, not too slow).
hints: Read at a natural speed.
Do not rush.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Recite a short poem with appropriate stress on the important words.
hints: Stress the words that carry the meaning.
Do not stress every word equally.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Recite a short poem with appropriate pace, stress and tone that matches the poem's feeling.
hints: Think about the feeling.
Match your voice to the feeling.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses tone that matches the poem's feeling

questions.stem: Recite a poem that changes mood from happy to sad. Change your pace, stress and tone to match each part.
hints: Happy part: faster, brighter tone.
Sad part: slower, quieter tone.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Changes pace for the mood change
Changes stress for the mood change
Changes tone for the mood change

questions.stem: Recite a short poem. After feedback from your teacher, recite the same poem again, improving your pace, stress or tone.
hints: Listen to the feedback.
Focus on the one thing you need to improve.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Recites the poem a second time
Shows improvement in pace, stress or tone

questions.stem: Recite a poem. After feedback, recite the same poem again. Then explain what you changed and why it improved the meaning.
hints: What did you change?
How did the change help the meaning?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Recites the poem a second time
Explains why the change improved meaning

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate recite a short poem. After the recitation, give one comment about their pace, stress or tone.
hints: Was their pace too fast or too slow?
Did they stress the right words?
Did their tone match the poem?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one specific comment about pace, stress or tone

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate recite a short poem. Give one comment about what worked well in their pace, stress or tone, and one suggestion for improvement.
hints: What did they do well?
What could they improve?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Both comments focus on pace, stress or tone

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Gather and select facts and ideas from one or multiple print and non-print sources, appropriate to the purpose, audience, context and culture

skills.description: Choose the fact most relevant to a given speech topic.
Recognise an irrelevant fact for a given topic.
Match a fact to the audience or purpose it suits.
Identify whether a fact comes from a print or non-print source.
Teacher-assessed practical: research a topic from at least one print and one non-print source and list gathered facts.
Teacher-assessed oral: present a short speech using facts gathered from sources.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'The Importance of Trees'. Which fact is MOST relevant?
options: Trees give us shade and clean the air
hints: Which fact shows why trees are important?
'Importance' means how useful something is.
questions.explanation: Trees give us shade and clean the air — this fact directly shows why trees are important. The other facts are true but do not show importance.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Trees have green leaves' because it is a fact about trees, but it does not show why trees are important.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'Keeping Our Water Clean'. Which fact is MOST relevant?
options: Water is found in rivers and lakes
hints: Which fact shows why we should keep water clean?
It should link cleanliness with health.
questions.explanation: Dirty water can cause disease — this fact directly supports the topic of keeping water clean because it shows the danger of dirt.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Water is found in rivers and lakes' because it is true, but it does not show why we should keep it clean.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'Why Children Should Read Books'. Which fact is MOST relevant?
hints: Which fact shows why reading is good for children?
It should connect reading with a benefit.
questions.explanation: Reading improves vocabulary and imagination — this fact directly supports the topic because it shows why reading is good for children.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Books have pictures' because it is true, but it does not show why children should read.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'Why We Should Eat Fruits and Vegetables'. Which fact is MOST relevant?
options: Fruits and vegetables give us vitamins and keep us healthy
hints: Which fact shows why we should eat them?
It should connect them with health.
questions.explanation: Fruits and vegetables give us vitamins and keep us healthy — this fact directly supports the topic because it shows why we should eat them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Fruits are sweet' because it is true, but sweetness does not show why we SHOULD eat them.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'Keeping Our School Clean'. Which fact is IRRELEVANT?
options: Kofi is the fastest runner in the class
Dirty classrooms can make pupils sick
Sweeping every morning keeps the school clean
Rubbish should be thrown in the bin
hints: Which fact has nothing to do with keeping the school clean?
Running is not related to cleanliness.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi is the fastest runner' is unrelated to keeping the school clean. The other facts are all about cleanliness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Sweeping every morning' because it is a chore, but it is directly about keeping the school clean — so it is relevant.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'The Importance of Trees'. Which fact is IRRELEVANT?
options: Trees can be used to make furniture
hints: Which fact is not about what trees DO or GIVE us?
Furniture is one use, but the speech is on importance — does this fact show importance?
questions.explanation: Actually, all four facts are uses of trees. But if the speech is specifically about trees in the environment (shade, air, fruit), then 'using trees for furniture' is less about importance and more about consumption. For the test, the intended answer is 'Trees can be used to make furniture' because it is about cutting trees rather than the benefit of trees growing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Trees provide fruit' because fruit is a use of trees, but fruit is a direct benefit of trees, whereas cutting them for furniture is about using the tree up, not its importance as a growing tree.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'Why We Should Eat Fruits and Vegetables'. Which fact is IRRELEVANT?
options: Fruits and vegetables are sold in markets
Eating fruits and vegetables prevents illness
Fruits and vegetables help us grow strong
hints: Which fact does not show why we should eat them?
Selling is about shops, not about health.
questions.explanation: 'Fruits and vegetables are sold in markets' is about where they are bought, not about why we should eat them. The other facts all show health benefits.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Eating fruits and vegetables prevents illness' because it mentions illness, but that is a health benefit — not irrelevant.

questions.stem: You are speaking to young children about eating fruits. Which fact would be most suitable?
options: Fruits help you grow strong and play well
Fruits contain vitamin C and antioxidants
Fruits have a high water content
hints: Who is the audience?
Young children need simple, concrete facts.
questions.explanation: 'Fruits help you grow strong and play well' uses simple, concrete language suitable for young children. The other facts are too technical for this audience.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Fruits contain vitamin C' because it is factual, but it is too technical for young children.

questions.stem: You are speaking to farmers about improving their crops. Which fact would be most suitable?
options: Adding compost to the soil improves crop yield
hints: Who is the audience?
Farmers need practical facts about crops.
questions.explanation: 'Adding compost to the soil improves crop yield' is practical and directly useful to farmers. The other facts are general or not useful for crop improvement.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Crops need rain' because it is true, but farmers already know this — it does not help them improve crops.

questions.stem: You are speaking to teachers about pupils who do not read at home. Which fact would be most suitable?
options: Pupils who read at home do better in school
Some pupils do not like reading
hints: Who is the audience?
Teachers need facts about school performance.
questions.explanation: 'Pupils who read at home do better in school' is a fact that directly supports the topic and is relevant to teachers. It shows why the topic matters for school performance.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading is fun' because it is positive, but it is an opinion, not a fact, and not specific enough for teachers.

questions.stem: Which is a PRINT source?
hints: Print means something printed on paper.
Which source is a physical book?
questions.explanation: A textbook on health is a print source — it is printed on paper. The others are non-print sources.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A radio announcement' because it is a source of information, but 'print' specifically means written or printed on paper.

questions.stem: Which is a NON-PRINT source?
hints: Non-print means not on paper.
Which source is heard, not read?
questions.explanation: A radio interview is a non-print source — it is heard, not read. The other options are printed on paper.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A newspaper' because it delivers news, but newspapers are printed — they are print sources.

questions.stem: Choose a topic (e.g., malaria, keeping water clean). Gather facts from at least one PRINT source (a textbook, newspaper, or library book) and one NON-PRINT source (a radio/TV program, a teacher, or a parent). List at least four facts you found.
hints: Write down facts from each source.
You need at least four facts.
Say where each fact came from.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Facts come from at least one print source
Facts come from at least one non-print source
Sources are identified for each fact

questions.stem: Choose a topic and gather facts from at least two sources. Write down three facts and say which source each came from.
hints: Two sources — at least one print and one non-print.
Write down three facts.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Includes at least one of each source type

questions.stem: Gather facts on a topic from at least three sources (one print, one non-print, and one person). List five facts and note where each came from.
hints: Three sources: book, radio, and a person.
Five facts.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Research a topic of your choice. Gather at least four facts. For each fact, say whether it came from a print source or a non-print source.
hints: Write the fact.
Write 'print' or 'non-print' next to it.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each fact has a source type
At least one print and one non-print fact

questions.stem: Present a short speech (about 1-2 minutes) using at least three facts you gathered. State where each fact came from.
hints: Say the fact.
Say 'I learned this from...'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Present a short speech (about 2 minutes) using facts from at least one print and one non-print source.
hints: Use a fact from a book or newspaper.
Use a fact from a radio program or a person.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses facts from at least two sources
Includes at least one print and one non-print fact

questions.stem: Present a short speech (about 2 minutes) to a specific audience (e.g., young children). Choose facts that suit that audience and explain why you chose them.
hints: Who is your audience?
Choose simple, clear facts.
Explain your choices.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses appropriate facts for the audience
Explains why the facts were chosen

questions.stem: Present a short speech using at least four facts. After the speech, answer two questions from the audience about where you got your facts.
hints: Be ready to say where you found each fact.
Say 'I found this in...' or 'I heard this on...'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Support ideas and points of view by integrating selected visual and audio resources, verbal and non-verbal cues (e.g. gestures, facial expressions)

skills.description: Match a gesture to the point it supports.
Match a facial expression to the feeling of the point.
Choose a visual resource that supports a given point.
Choose an audio resource that suits a given point.
Teacher-assessed practical: deliver a short speech using at least two appropriate gestures.
Teacher-assessed practical: deliver a short speech with facial expression that matches the content.
Teacher-assessed practical: present with a visual resource that supports a point.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'everyone joining together to clean the school'. Which gesture best supports this point?
options: Open both palms and bring them together
hints: What gesture shows 'together'?
Open palms brought together symbolise unity.
questions.explanation: Open palms brought together suggests joining or unity — a good match for 'everyone joining together'. The other gestures mean different things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Point at one person' because it involves the hand, but pointing singles someone out — the opposite of 'everyone together'.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'a big problem facing the school'. Which gesture best supports this point?
options: Spread both hands wide to show size
hints: What gesture shows 'big'?
Spreading hands shows size.
questions.explanation: Spreading both hands wide shows size — a good match for 'a big problem'. Clapping, head-shaking and pointing at a shoe do not match the meaning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Clap your hands' because it is a clear gesture, but clapping shows approval or celebration, not size.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'three important reasons to read'. Which gesture best supports your point when you list them?
options: Count with your fingers — one, two, three
Wave your hand in the air
hints: How do you show 'three'?
Counting on fingers is a common gesture.
questions.explanation: Counting on fingers — one, two, three — supports the point of listing three reasons. The other gestures do not show counting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Wave your hand' because it is a gesture, but waving does not show 'three reasons' — counting does.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'stopping bad behaviour in the school'. Which gesture best supports this point?
options: Hold up one hand, palm facing out — a stop sign
hints: What gesture means 'stop'?
A raised palm is a universal stop sign.
questions.explanation: Holding up a hand, palm facing out, is the universal stop sign — a good match for 'stopping bad behaviour'. Pointing, nodding or smiling do not mean stop.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Smile widely' because a smile is friendly, but a smile does not signal stopping.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'the joy of helping others'. Which facial expression matches this point?
hints: What feeling does 'joy' suggest?
Joy is a happy feeling.
questions.explanation: A warm smile matches the joy of helping others. A frown, blank stare or angry look would contradict the feeling.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any expression is fine, but the expression should match the feeling of the point.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'the dangers of dirty water'. Which facial expression matches this point?
hints: What feeling does 'dangers' suggest?
Danger needs a serious expression.
questions.explanation: A serious, concerned look matches the topic of danger. Smiling, grinning or winking would not fit a serious topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think smiling is always good, but smiling while discussing danger sends the wrong message.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'how proud you are of your school'. Which facial expression matches?
options: A proud, bright look with a slight smile
hints: What does 'proud' look like?
Pride is positive but not overexcited.
questions.explanation: A proud, bright look with a slight smile matches pride in the school. Sadness, anger or fear would contradict the feeling.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A sad expression' because talking about school can be serious, but the topic is pride — which is positive.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'the sadness of losing a friend'. Which facial expression matches?
hints: What feeling does 'sadness' suggest?
Sad topics need soft, sombre expressions.
questions.explanation: A soft, sombre look matches sadness. A bright smile, angry glare or surprised expression would not fit this sad topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may smile to appear friendly, but a smile during a sad topic is inappropriate.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'keeping our water clean'. Which visual resource best supports your point?
options: A picture of a clean river and a dirty river side by side
A picture of a football match
hints: Which picture relates to water cleanliness?
A picture of rivers shows the topic directly.
questions.explanation: A picture of a clean river and a dirty river directly relates to keeping water clean. The other pictures have nothing to do with the topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick any picture because visuals are engaging, but the visual must support the specific point being made.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'the importance of trees in our community'. Which visual resource best supports your point?
options: A drawing of a village with many green trees
A drawing of a market woman
hints: Which drawing relates to trees?
The drawing should show trees in a community.
questions.explanation: A drawing of a village with many green trees directly supports the point about trees in the community. The other drawings have no connection.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A drawing of a market woman' because markets are part of the community, but that drawing does not show trees.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'eating a balanced diet'. Which visual resource best supports your point?
options: A chart showing different food groups
A picture of a single fruit
A picture of a person running
hints: What does 'balanced diet' mean?
A chart showing different groups is more complete than one food.
questions.explanation: A chart showing different food groups supports the point about a balanced diet because it shows the variety needed. A single fruit does not show balance; running and football are about exercise, not food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A picture of a single fruit' because it is about food, but one fruit cannot show a balanced diet — you need variety.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'the importance of reading'. Which audio resource best supports your point?
options: A short recording of a child reading a story aloud
A recording of a football match
A recording of a car engine
A recording of a loud drum
hints: Which recording relates to reading?
A child reading a story is about reading.
questions.explanation: A short recording of a child reading aloud supports the point about reading. The other recordings are unrelated to reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A loud drum' because drums are exciting, but excitement alone does not support the topic of reading.

questions.stem: You are speaking about 'the harmattan season'. Which audio resource best supports your point?
options: A short recording of a harmattan wind blowing
A recording of a bus engine
A recording of a baby laughing
hints: What is harmattan known for?
Harmattan brings dry wind — which recording matches?
questions.explanation: A short recording of harmattan wind directly supports a speech about the harmattan season. The other recordings are unrelated.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ocean waves' because both are sounds of nature, but ocean waves are not the harmattan.

questions.stem: Deliver a 1-minute speech on 'Why We Should Keep Our School Clean'. Use at least two appropriate gestures.
hints: Use a counting gesture if you list reasons.
Use a 'stop' gesture when talking about stopping littering.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gestures support the points being made
Gestures come at the right moment (not too late)

questions.stem: Deliver a 1-minute speech on 'The Importance of Reading'. Use at least two appropriate gestures.
hints: Open hands for 'many books'.
Point to your head for 'thinking'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute speech on a topic of your choice. Use at least three appropriate gestures and explain after the speech what each gesture was meant to show.
hints: Choose gestures that match your points.
After the speech, say 'I used this gesture because...'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains the purpose of each gesture
Gestures come at the right moment

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute speech on a topic of your choice. Use at least three gestures and coordinate them with visual resources (like a chart or picture).
hints: Use your hands to point to the visual when you mention it.
Use gestures to show size, counting, or emphasis.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gestures come at the right moment

questions.stem: Deliver a 1-minute speech on a happy topic (e.g., a festival you enjoy). Your facial expression should match the happy content.
hints: Smile when you talk about happy things.
Let your face show your feeling.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute speech on a serious topic (e.g., keeping safe on the road). Your facial expression should match the serious content.
hints: Use a serious, concerned face.
Do not smile while discussing danger.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute speech using at least one visual resource (chart, picture, or real object). Point to the visual when you mention the relevant point.
hints: Choose a visual that directly supports a point.
Point to it when you mention that point.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Points to visual at the right moment

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Use discourse markers to signpost stages in a presentation (e.g. 'For the next part', 'For example', 'In summary')

skills.description: Recognise a discourse marker in a short presentation transcript.
Match a discourse marker to its stage (opening, example, summary).
Choose the correct marker for a given stage of a presentation.
Choose the marker that suits formal vs informal contexts.
Teacher-assessed oral: deliver a short presentation using at least three discourse markers to signpost stages.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a peer's presentation and identify the discourse markers used.

questions.stem: Read this presentation: 'First, I will explain the problem. Next, I will give the solution. Finally, I will answer your questions.' Which words are discourse markers?
hints: Which words signpost the stages of the presentation?
They tell you the order of the parts.
questions.explanation: First, Next and Finally are discourse markers — they signpost the stages of the presentation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'explain, give, answer' because they are the actions, but those are verbs, not markers.

questions.stem: Read this presentation: 'For example, in our school we have a library. Also, we have a computer room. In summary, our school has many facilities.' Which are discourse markers?
hints: Which phrases signpost the stages of the presentation?
'For example', 'Also' and 'In summary' organise the presentation.
questions.explanation: For example, Also and In summary are discourse markers — they signpost the stages of the presentation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'have, have, has' because they are repeated, but repetition is not the same as discourse marking.

questions.stem: Read this presentation: 'Let us look at the first cause of the problem. Then, we will consider the second cause. In conclusion, we will suggest a solution.' Which are discourse markers?
options: Let us look at, Then, In conclusion
hints: Which phrases signpost stages?
'Let us look at', 'Then' and 'In conclusion' organise the parts.
questions.explanation: The phrases 'Let us look at', 'Then' and 'In conclusion' are discourse markers — they signpost the stages of the presentation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cause, problem, solution' because they are the topics, but they are content words, not markers.

questions.stem: What stage of a presentation does 'For example' signal?
hints: What does the phrase literally say?
It introduces an example.
questions.explanation: 'For example' signals that the speaker is giving an example to support a point.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'For example' is an opening, but it comes mid-presentation when an example is needed.

questions.stem: What stage of a presentation does 'In summary' signal?
hints: What does 'summary' mean?
It signals that the speaker is summing up.
questions.explanation: 'In summary' signals that the speaker is summing up the main points — it's a summary stage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Opening' because summary can be a new point, but it comes near the end to draw together what has been said.

questions.stem: What stage of a presentation does 'Let us now turn to' signal?
options: Moving to a new part of the presentation
hints: What does 'turn to' mean?
It signals moving to the next part.
questions.explanation: 'Let us now turn to' signals that the speaker is moving to a new part of the presentation. It is a transition marker.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it signals the end because it uses 'let us', but 'turn to' means move to a new topic, not end.

questions.stem: What stage of a presentation does 'Finally' signal?
hints: What does 'final' mean?
It marks the end.
questions.explanation: 'Finally' signals the end of the presentation or the last point. It is a closing marker.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Opening' because 'finally' comes after other markers, but it is used to mark the end, not the beginning.

questions.stem: You are opening your presentation. Which discourse marker is best?
hints: What marker opens a presentation?
'First' signals the beginning.
questions.explanation: 'First, I will talk about...' signals that the presentation is starting. It is the right marker for an opening.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'In summary' because it sounds important, but summary comes at the end, not the beginning.

questions.stem: You are giving an example in the middle of your presentation. Which marker is best?
options: For example, let us look at...
hints: What marker introduces an example?
'For example' is the most direct.
questions.explanation: 'For example' introduces an example. It is used in the middle of a presentation when you want to illustrate a point.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'First' because examples come first in their minds, but examples come in the middle, after the main point.

questions.stem: You are concluding your presentation. Which marker is best?
hints: What marker signals the end of a presentation?
'In summary' signals that you are summing up.
questions.explanation: 'In summary' signals that you are concluding the presentation and summing up the main points.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'First' because it is a common marker, but 'first' signals the beginning, not the end.

questions.stem: You want to move from the introduction to the first main point. Which marker is best?
options: Now, let us look at the first point.
hints: What marker signals a move to a new part?
'Now, let us look at' signals moving to a new point.
questions.explanation: 'Now, let us look at the first point' signals moving from the introduction to the first main point. It is a transition marker.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'For example' because examples follow the first point, but 'now let us look at' signals moving to the first point, not giving an example.

questions.stem: You are making a formal presentation to the head teacher. Which marker is most appropriate?
options: Let us now proceed to the next point.
hints: Which marker is formal?
Formal presentations use formal language.
questions.explanation: 'Let us now proceed to the next point' is formal and appropriate for a presentation to the head teacher. The other markers are informal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'So, yeah, moving on' because it is common, but it is too informal for a formal presentation.

questions.stem: You are speaking informally to your classmates. Which marker is most appropriate?
options: I shall now proceed to enumerate...
I move to the subsequent point...
hints: Which marker sounds relaxed and friendly?
'So, next up' is casual and natural.
questions.explanation: 'So, next up' is informal and works well with classmates. The other markers are too formal for a casual peer conversation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I shall now proceed to enumerate' because it sounds impressive, but it is far too formal for classmates.

questions.stem: Deliver a 1-minute presentation on a familiar topic. Use at least three discourse markers to signpost the stages.
hints: Use 'first', 'also', 'finally'.
Signal your stages clearly.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three discourse markers
Markers are appropriate to the stages
Markers come at the right moment

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute presentation on a social issue in your community. Use at least four discourse markers (e.g., first, for example, also, in summary).
hints: Open with 'First...'.
Give an example with 'For example...'.
Add a point with 'Also...'.
Close with 'In summary...'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Markers come at the right moment

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute presentation on a familiar topic. Use at least three discourse markers and make sure one is a transition marker (like 'Let us now turn to...').
hints: Include at least one marker that signals a move to a new part.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Markers come at the right moments

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute presentation. Use at least three discourse markers. After the presentation, name the markers you used and explain what stage each one signalled.
hints: First give the presentation.
Then say: 'I used "first" to open, "for example" to illustrate...'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Markers come at the right moments
Names the markers after the presentation
Explains the stage each marker signals

questions.stem: Deliver a 2-minute presentation using at least four discourse markers. Use both formal and informal markers appropriately. After the presentation, explain why each marker was appropriate for its stage.
hints: Use formal markers for formal stages.
Explain your choices after the presentation.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses both formal and informal markers appropriately
Explains why each marker fits its stage

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate's presentation. Afterwards, name three discourse markers they used and say what stage each one signalled.
hints: Listen for words like 'first', 'for example', 'in summary'.
What stage did each signal?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Identifies the stage for each marker

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate's presentation. Identify four discourse markers used, and comment on whether they were used at the correct stage.
hints: Were all the markers used at the right time?
Point out any that could be improved.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Comments on whether each marker was at the correct stage

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Elaborate on points using concrete examples

skills.description: Identify the concrete example in a short speech passage.
Choose the best concrete example to support a given point.
Recognise a vague statement vs a concrete example.
Choose the elaboration that adds detail to a point rather than repeating it.
Teacher-assessed oral: elaborate a point in a short speech using a concrete example.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a peer's speech and comment on whether the example used was concrete.

misconceptions: Example after the point has moved on

questions.stem: Read this speech passage: 'Our school needs a library. For example, last year only ten pupils in Basic 5 read more than five books. With a library, more pupils could read.' Which is the concrete example?
options: Last year only ten pupils in Basic 5 read more than five books
With a library, more pupils could read
hints: Which sentence gives a specific fact or event?
A concrete example has numbers or details.
questions.explanation: 'Last year only ten pupils in Basic 5 read more than five books' is the concrete example — it has specific numbers and details. The other sentences state or support the point.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Our school needs a library' because it is the main point, but that is the claim — the example supports it.

questions.stem: Read this speech passage: 'We must keep our environment clean. For instance, when we throw rubbish in the gutter, it blocks the drain and causes flooding.' Which is the concrete example?
options: Throwing rubbish in the gutter blocks drains and causes flooding
We must keep our environment clean
hints: Which sentence gives a specific situation?
A concrete example describes a real situation.
questions.explanation: The sentence about throwing rubbish in the gutter and causing flooding is the concrete example — it gives a specific situation that supports the main point.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'We must keep our environment clean' because it mentions the environment, but it is the main point, not the example.

questions.stem: Read this speech passage: 'Reading is important for success. For example, our head teacher said she read many books as a child, and that helped her become a teacher.' Which is the concrete example?
options: Our head teacher read many books as a child and became a teacher
hints: Which sentence gives a specific person and event?
A concrete example names a person or event.
questions.explanation: The sentence about the head teacher reading many books and becoming a teacher is the concrete example — it gives a specific person and event.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading is important for success' because it mentions importance, but that is the main point, not the example.

questions.stem: Point: 'Eating fruits is good for your health.' Which is the best concrete example to support this point?
options: Eating oranges gives you vitamin C, which helps fight colds
hints: Which example connects fruit to health?
It should give a specific health benefit.
questions.explanation: 'Eating oranges gives you vitamin C, which helps fight colds' is a concrete example that connects fruit to a specific health benefit. The other options are true but do not show health benefits.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Fruits are sweet' because it is true, but sweetness is not a health benefit — it does not support the point about health.

questions.stem: Point: 'Reading helps you do well in school.' Which is the best concrete example?
options: A pupil who reads every day learns new words and gets higher marks
