hints: Which example connects reading to school success?
It should show a specific outcome.
questions.explanation: 'A pupil who reads every day learns new words and gets higher marks' is a concrete example connecting reading to school success. The other options do not show a specific outcome.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading is fun' because it is positive, but it does not connect to school success.

questions.stem: Point: 'Playing football teaches teamwork.' Which is the best concrete example?
options: A player passes the ball to a teammate who scores, instead of trying to score alone
Football is played on a field
hints: Which example shows teamwork in action?
Look for a specific action involving two or more players.
questions.explanation: 'A player passes the ball to a teammate who scores, instead of trying to score alone' shows teamwork in action. The other options are general facts about football, not examples of teamwork.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Football is a popular sport' because it is about football, but it does not show teamwork.

questions.stem: Point: 'We should save water.' Which is the best concrete example?
options: Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth, saving several litres each time
hints: Which example shows a specific action we can take?
It should describe what to do, not just why water matters.
questions.explanation: 'Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth, saving several litres each time' is a concrete example of how to save water. The other options do not show a specific saving action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Water is important' because it is true, but it does not show how to save water.

questions.stem: Which is a CONCRETE example, not a vague statement?
options: Three pupils in my class were late because the trotro broke down on the way
Many pupils come late to school
hints: Which sentence gives specific details?
Look for numbers, names or specific events.
questions.explanation: 'Three pupils in my class were late because the trotro broke down' is concrete — it has numbers, names, and a specific event. The others are vague statements.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Many pupils come late to school' because it has a quantity word, but 'many' is vague — three is specific.

questions.stem: Which is a VAGUE statement, not a concrete example?
options: Some people say reading is good
My sister reads for thirty minutes every evening before bed
Our teacher read us a story last Friday
Two pupils borrowed five books from the library yesterday
hints: Which sentence does not give specific details?
Look for vague words like 'some' or 'good'.
questions.explanation: 'Some people say reading is good' is vague — 'some people' and 'good' are not specific. The other statements give specific details like times, names and numbers.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'My sister reads for thirty minutes' because it is simple, but thirty minutes is a specific detail — so it is concrete, not vague.

questions.stem: Which is more concrete?
options: Yesterday, twenty pupils brought their homework on time
hints: Which sentence gives a specific number and time?
Look for 'yesterday' and 'twenty'.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday, twenty pupils brought their homework on time' is the most concrete — it has a specific time (yesterday) and number (twenty). The others are vague.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Many pupils bring their homework' because it has a quantity word, but 'many' is vague — twenty is concrete.

questions.stem: Point: 'Our school needs a library.' Which sentence best elaborates this point?
options: A library would give pupils a quiet place to read and borrow books they cannot afford to buy
A library is a place with books
Every school should have a library
hints: Which sentence adds new detail about why the school needs a library?
It should explain, not just repeat or generalise.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'A library would give pupils a quiet place to read and borrow books they cannot afford' elaborates the point with details — it explains why the library is needed. The others are general statements.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Libraries are useful' because it says libraries are good, but it does not add detail — it just generalises.

questions.stem: Point: 'We should plant more trees.' Which sentence elaborates this point the best?
options: Trees provide shade, clean the air, and hold the soil in place with their roots
hints: Which sentence gives specific reasons?
It should list several concrete benefits.
questions.explanation: The sentence about trees providing shade, cleaning air and holding soil gives three specific benefits — this elaborates the point with detail. The others are general.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Trees are good' because it agrees with the point, but it does not add detail — it just repeats the idea in simpler words.

questions.stem: Point: 'Reading is important.' Which sentence elaborates this point best?
options: Reading builds vocabulary, improves concentration and opens doors to new ideas
hints: Which sentence lists specific benefits of reading?
It should add new information, not repeat.
questions.explanation: The sentence about vocabulary, concentration and new ideas gives three specific benefits — it elaborates the point with detail. The others only restate or generalise.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading is fun' because it adds a feeling, but it does not elaborate the point about importance.

questions.stem: Make a point about a familiar topic, then elaborate it using one concrete example.
hints: Say your point first.
Then say 'For example...' and give a specific example.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Make a point about a social issue, then elaborate it using two concrete examples.
hints: State the point.
Give two specific examples with details.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 1 minute) on a familiar topic. Include one point and elaborate it with a concrete example.
hints: State the point clearly.
Give a specific example with details.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 2 minutes) on a social issue. Include at least two points, and elaborate each with one concrete example. Explain why the examples support the points.
hints: Two points, two examples.
For each example, say why it supports the point.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how each example supports its point

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about 2 minutes) on a topic of your choice. Elaborate every point with a concrete example. After the speech, answer one question about one of your examples.
hints: Each point needs an example.
Be ready to explain your examples.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Elaborates every point with a concrete example
Answers a question about an example

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate's speech. Afterwards, say whether their example was concrete (specific) or vague, and explain why.
hints: Did the example have specific details?
Or was it vague?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Judges whether the example was concrete or vague

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate's speech. Identify one example they used. Say whether it was concrete or vague, and suggest how it could be made more concrete.
hints: What example did they use?
Could it use more specific details?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Judges whether it was concrete or vague
Suggests how to make it more concrete

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Respond to poems by discussing their central messages and expressing own opinion

skills.description: Say what a short poem is about from its lines.
Choose the best one-line statement of a poem's central message.
Pick the line that best supports a stated message.
Choose an opinion about the poem that is supported by the text.
Separate the central message from a supporting detail.
Name the feeling the poem creates and point to the word or line that creates it.
Teacher-assessed oral: recite a poem, then say in 2-3 sentences what it means and give a personal opinion with one reason.
Teacher-assessed performance: recite lines with correct stress, actions and rhythm.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The rain comes down upon the roof, / It taps and taps and will not stop. / It fills the gutters, fills the drain, / And waters every growing crop.' What is the poem about?
hints: What is the poem describing throughout?
Every line mentions something the rain does.
questions.explanation: Every line describes something the rain does — it comes down, taps, fills gutters and drains, and waters crops. So the poem is about the rain.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'a roof' because the rain lands on the roof, but the roof is only one thing the rain touches. The poem is about the rain itself.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The market wakes at break of day, / With yams and plantains on display. / The traders call, the buyers crowd, / The noise is happy, strong and loud.' What is the poem about?
hints: What happens in the poem?
Look at the first line: 'The market wakes at break of day.'
questions.explanation: The first line names the market and the poem describes its activity — traders calling, buyers crowding, and noise. So the poem is about a busy market.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'yams and plantains' because these are mentioned, but they are only items in the market. The poem is about the whole market.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'A little seed sleeps in the ground, / It waits for sun and rain. / It pushes up without a sound, / And grows to life again. / Be patient, little one, and wait, / For growth will come, though late.' What is the central message of this poem?
options: Be patient and keep waiting for good things
hints: Look at the last two lines — what do they tell the reader?
The seed waits, then grows. What does this teach us?
questions.explanation: The poem tells about a seed that waits for sun and rain, then grows. The last two lines give the message directly: 'Be patient, little one, and wait, for growth will come, though late.' So the central message is to be patient.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'seeds need sun and rain' because it is true of the poem, but that is the story used to teach the message. The message is patience.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The river runs from hill to sea, / It does not stop or wait for me. / It cuts through rocks and makes a way, / And flows to meet the sea each day. / When trouble blocks your path today, / Keep going — do not turn away.' What is the central message?
options: Keep going even when there are troubles
hints: What does the river do when rocks are in the way?
The last two lines give the message.
questions.explanation: The first four lines describe the river cutting through rocks to reach the sea. The last two lines give the message: 'When trouble blocks your path today, keep going — do not turn away.' So the message is to keep going even when there are troubles.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'rivers cut through rocks' because it is described, but that is the example. The message is about not giving up.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'A candle small is in my hand, / It gives a little light. / It cannot chase the dark from the land, / But it can chase my night. / One little light is not too small, / To light the way for all.' What is the central message?
options: Even one small act of good can help many
hints: What does the candle do for one person?
The last line says it can 'light the way for all.'
questions.explanation: The poem describes a small candle that gives a little light. The last two lines say that even one little light is not too small to light the way for all. So the message is that even one small act of good can help many.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'candles are useful at night' because the poem mentions night, but the poem uses the candle as a picture to teach a message about small good deeds.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'My father left before the sun, / He carried water, hoe and seed. / He worked alone till day was done, / To give us what we need. / A father's love is like the land, / It gives and gives without demand.' What is the central message?
options: A father's love is generous and unselfish
hints: What does the father do every day?
The last two lines compare a father's love with the land.
questions.explanation: The father works from before sunrise until day is done to give his family what they need. The last two lines compare his love with the land, which gives and gives without demand. The message is that a father's love is generous and unselfish.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'farmers wake early' because the poem mentions waking before the sun, but that is a detail. The message is about the father's love.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'I had a friend who told me lies, / He made me laugh and made me cry. / But when the wind began to blow, / He left me standing in the snow. / A friend who lies is not a friend, / So choose your friends with care, my friend.' What is the central message?
options: Choose friends who are truthful and stay with you
hints: What happened when trouble came?
The last two lines give the message.
questions.explanation: The poem describes a friend who lied and left when things got hard. The last two lines give the message: 'A friend who lies is not a friend, so choose your friends with care.' The message is to choose friends who are truthful and stay with you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'friends should be funny' because the friend made the poet laugh, but that is only one detail. The message is about truth and loyalty.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The bee works all the day, / From flower to flower she goes. / She gathers honey on her way, / And never stops to rest or doze. / Work hard, my little friend, and you / Will gather sweet rewards too.' The message is: 'Hard work brings good rewards.' Which line BEST supports this message?
options: The bee works all the day
From flower to flower she goes
She gathers honey on her way
hints: Which line talks about the reward of hard work?
Look at the last line.
questions.explanation: The message is 'Hard work brings good rewards.' The line 'Will gather sweet rewards too' directly connects the bee's hard work with a reward, which supports the message.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'The bee works all the day' because it mentions work, but it describes the work itself, not the reward.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The lonely tree stands on the hill, / It has no friend to share its shade. / The birds have gone, the winds are still, / Its leaves are brown and start to fade. / A friend is like a shady tree, / That gives you rest and lets you be.' The message is: 'A friend gives comfort.' Which line BEST supports this message?
options: That gives you rest and lets you be
The lonely tree stands on the hill
It has no friend to share its shade
Its leaves are brown and start to fade
hints: Which line describes what a friend does?
The last two lines compare a friend to a shady tree.
questions.explanation: The message is 'A friend gives comfort.' The line 'That gives you rest and lets you be' describes what a shady tree (and therefore a friend) does — it gives rest and lets you be yourself. This supports the message.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'The lonely tree stands on the hill' because it mentions the tree, but the lonely tree is the opposite of what the poem is praising.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The fire burns in the hearth at night, / It warms our hands and gives us light. / But fire that wanders on the grass, / Can burn our homes and burn them fast. / So watch the flame and keep it small, / For fire can bless or hurt us all.' The message is: 'Fire must be handled with care.' Which line BEST supports this message?
options: So watch the flame and keep it small
The fire burns in the hearth at night
It warms our hands and gives us light
For fire can bless or hurt us all
hints: Which line tells people what to do to stay safe?
Look for the line that gives an instruction about the flame.
questions.explanation: The message is 'Fire must be handled with care.' The line 'So watch the flame and keep it small' gives the instruction that supports this message. The other lines either describe fire or state its effects.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'For fire can bless or hurt us all' because it mentions hurt, but that line states the two sides of fire, not how to handle it. 'Watch the flame' is the care instruction.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'A child who reads a book each day, / Will find a friend along the way. / A book will teach and never mock, / And open doors that have no lock. / So read, my child, and read some more, / And see what wonders are in store.' Which opinion is supported by this poem?
options: Reading is a good habit for children
hints: What does the poem say about reading?
Which opinion fits the poem's encouragement to read?
questions.explanation: The poem encourages children to read because it will teach them, be a friend, and open doors. An opinion supported by the poem is that reading is a good habit for children.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Books are better than people' because the poem calls a book a friend, but the poem does not compare books to people. It only praises reading.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The harmattan has come again, / It dries the lips and cracks the skin. / It brings the dust that fills the air, / And cold that bites through cloth so thin. / So wear your coat and drink your water, / And take good care of one another.' Which opinion is supported by this poem?
options: It is wise to prepare for the harmattan
The harmattan is the best season
hints: What does the poem tell people to do?
Which opinion matches the advice in the last line?
questions.explanation: The poem describes the harmattan's discomforts and then tells people to wear a coat, drink water and care for one another. So the opinion supported by the poem is that it is wise to prepare for the harmattan.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'the harmattan is the best season' because seasons are mentioned, but the poem describes the harmattan as harsh, not best.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'They said the moon had silver wings, / But I have looked and seen no such things. / I only see a light that shines, / And changes shape by clear design. / So look, my friend, and think again, / Before you trust the words of men.' Which opinion is supported by this poem?
options: We should check things for ourselves before believing them
The moon has no light of its own
The moon changes shape every night
hints: What did the poet do instead of believing what 'they said'?
Look at the last two lines.
questions.explanation: The poet says others claimed the moon had silver wings, but the poet looked and saw no such thing. The last two lines give the opinion: 'look, my friend, and think again, before you trust the words of men.' So the opinion supported is that we should check things for ourselves before believing them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'the moon has no light of its own' because the poem says the poet only sees 'a light that shines', but the poem does not state the source of the light. The opinion is about checking for ourselves.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The ant is small but very wise, / She works before the rains arise. / She stores her food beneath the ground, / Where none of it can be found. / So plan ahead, my child, today, / Before the rains have gone away.' Which line gives the CENTRAL MESSAGE, not just a detail?
options: So plan ahead, my child, today
The ant is small but very wise
She stores her food beneath the ground
She works before the rains arise
hints: Which line tells the reader what to do?
The other lines are about the ant.
questions.explanation: The first four lines describe what the ant does — she works and stores food. The line 'So plan ahead, my child, today' tells the reader what to do. This is the central message. The others are details.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She stores her food beneath the ground' because it shows planning, but that is the ant's example, not the message to the reader.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The palm tree stands so tall and proud, / Its leaves spread out to greet the cloud. / It bends and sways in stormy weather, / But does not break, it holds together. / Be like the palm, my little one, / Stand firm till the storm is done.' Which line gives the CENTRAL MESSAGE, not just a detail?
options: Be like the palm, my little one
The palm tree stands so tall and proud
Its leaves spread out to greet the cloud
It bends and sways in stormy weather
hints: Which line speaks directly to the reader?
The other lines describe the palm tree.
questions.explanation: The first four lines describe what the palm tree does. The line 'Be like the palm, my little one' tells the reader what to do — the central message. The others are details about the tree.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It bends and sways in stormy weather' because it describes the tree's strength, but it is a detail. The message is 'Be like the palm'.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'My little sister laughed today, / She chased the chickens in the yard. / She tripped and tumbled in the hay, / And laughed so hard she hugged me hard.' What feeling does this poem create?
hints: What is happening in the poem?
The little sister laughs.
questions.explanation: The poem describes a happy scene — the little sister laughs, chases chickens, tumbles and hugs the poet. The feeling it creates is happiness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sister falling is sad, but the poem says she laughed, so the feeling is happy.

questions.stem: Read this poem: 'The day my mother went away, / The house was cold, the sky was grey. / I sat beside the empty chair, / And felt the silence everywhere.' What feeling does this poem create?
hints: What are the words used in the poem?
Words like 'cold', 'grey' and 'empty' are used.
questions.explanation: The poem uses words like 'cold', 'grey', 'empty chair' and 'silence' to create a feeling of loss. The feeling is sadness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mother coming back is happy, but the poem is about the mother going away.

questions.stem: Recite the poem your teacher has read to you. In 2-3 sentences, say what the poem means and give one opinion about it with a reason.
hints: Think about what the poem is teaching.
Your opinion can be 'I agree because…' or 'I disagree because…'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States the central meaning of the poem
Gives a personal opinion about the poem
Gives one reason to support the opinion

questions.stem: Recite a poem of your choice to a small group. Then say what the poem means and give one opinion with a reason. If you disagree with the poem, say why.
hints: Choose a poem you know well.
Say what the poem means before you give your opinion.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives an opinion with one reason

questions.stem: Recite the first two lines of a poem your teacher has taught, using good stress and rhythm.
hints: Listen to your teacher first.
Tap the beat gently with your hand.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses appropriate stress on the right words

questions.stem: Recite a short poem to the class with actions that fit the meaning. Use good stress and rhythm.
hints: Practise the poem first.
Let your actions match the words.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Recites the poem from start to finish
Uses stress and rhythm appropriate to the poem
Uses actions that fit the meaning
Faces the audience and speaks clearly

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Compose six-line poems

skills.description: Recognise a six-line poem or count lines correctly.
Choose the line that best fits the topic of a starter poem.
Arrange jumbled lines into a sensible short poem.
Recognise rhyming line-endings in a given set of lines.
Written: add one suitable line to a given three-line poem.
Teacher-assessed written: compose an original six-line poem on a given topic.
Teacher-assessed performance: read or recite own composed poem aloud with rhythm.

questions.stem: Read these lines: 'The sun is bright, / The sky is blue, / The birds take flight, / I think of you, / The day is warm, / I feel so new.' How many lines does this poem have?
hints: Count each line that starts on a new line.
There are six lines.
questions.explanation: Count the lines one by one: 'The sun is bright' (1), 'The sky is blue' (2), 'The birds take flight' (3), 'I think of you' (4), 'The day is warm' (5), 'I feel so new' (6). Six lines.
questions.misconception: Pupils may count sentences instead of lines, but each line in this poem is its own line. There are six.

questions.stem: A six-line poem has how many lines?
hints: The number is in the name.
Six-line poem.
questions.explanation: A six-line poem has six lines. That is what 'six-line' means.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the number of lines with the number of stanzas or sentences.

questions.stem: Read these first three lines of a poem about rain: 'The rain falls soft upon the roof, / It taps and taps and will not stop, / It fills the gutter to the top.' Which line best continues the poem?
options: My brother plays a game of ball
The market has a lot of fish
The sun is shining on the wall
hints: Which line is still about the rain?
The rain helps crops to grow.
questions.explanation: The poem is about rain. The line 'It waters every thirsty crop' is still about the rain and fits the poem. The other lines change the topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'The sun is shining on the wall' because it mentions weather, but the poem is about rain, not sunshine.

questions.stem: Read these first three lines of a poem about a mother: 'My mother wakes before the sun, / She sweeps the yard and cooks for one, / She hums a song and starts the day.' Which line best continues the poem?
options: She works so hard in every way
The bus is coming down the street
My friend is playing in the park
The sky is dark and full of stars
hints: Which line is still about the mother?
The poem describes her hard work.
questions.explanation: The poem is about the mother and her hard work. The line 'She works so hard in every way' is still about her and fits the poem. The other lines change the topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'The bus is coming down the street' because it happens in the morning, but the poem is about the mother, not the bus.

questions.stem: Read these first three lines of a poem about a river: 'The river runs from hill to sea, / It does not stop or wait for me, / It cuts through rocks and makes a way.' Which line best continues the poem?
options: And flows to meet the sea each day
My sister likes to sing and play
The stars are shining far away
The children eat their rice at noon
hints: Which line is still about the river and its journey?
The river flows to the sea.
questions.explanation: The poem is about the river's journey from the hills to the sea. The line 'And flows to meet the sea each day' continues this journey. The other lines change the topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose a line with water imagery, but only 'And flows to meet the sea each day' fits the journey described in the poem.

questions.stem:
These lines of a poem about a seed are jumbled. Which order makes the most sense?
A) A green shoot pushes through the soil
B) A little seed sleeps in the ground
C) The sun shines warm and the rain falls
D) And soon the plant stands tall and round
hints: What has to happen first? The seed sleeps.
Then what helps the seed? Sun and rain. Then the shoot grows. Then the plant stands tall.
questions.explanation: The natural order is: seed sleeps in the ground (B), sun and rain come (C), shoot pushes through (A), and the plant stands tall (D). This matches the growth process.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose A first because the shoot is visible, but the seed must sleep first before the shoot can grow.

questions.stem:
These lines of a poem about the harmattan are jumbled. Which order makes the most sense?
A) The dust blows all around the town
B) The harmattan has come to stay
C) So wrap up warm and drink your tea
D) It dries the lips and cracks the skin
hints: Which line introduces the harmattan? Start with 'The harmattan has come.'
Then describe its effects, then give advice.
questions.explanation: The natural order: 'The harmattan has come to stay' (B) introduces the topic. Then the dust (A) and the dry skin (D) describe its effects. Then 'So wrap up warm and drink your tea' (C) gives advice. B-A-D-C.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the advice line first because it is short, but the advice comes after the description.

questions.stem: Read these lines: 'The cat sat on the mat, / The dog chased the fat rat, / The bird sat on a hat.' Which words rhyme?
hints: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
Look at the last word of each line.
questions.explanation: The words 'cat', 'mat', 'rat' and 'hat' all end with the -at sound. They rhyme.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sat, chased, sat' because 'sat' repeats, but repetition is not rhyme — rhyme is when the ending sounds match.

questions.stem: Read these lines: 'The moon is bright, / It shines at night, / It gives us light.' Which line does NOT rhyme with the others?
hints: Which word does not end with the -ight sound?
Read each line aloud and listen to the ending.
questions.explanation: 'Bright', 'night' and 'light' all end with the -ight sound. 'Round' has a different ending, so it does not rhyme.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'round' rhymes because the moon is round, but rhyme is about sound, not meaning.

questions.stem: Read these three lines of a poem about a market: 'The market wakes at break of day, / With yams and plantains on display, / The traders call, the buyers crowd.' Write one more line that fits the poem. Keep it about the market.
answer: Accept any line that is about the market and fits the tone or rhyme of the poem. Award full marks if the line is about the market and adds to the description.
hints: What else happens at the market?
Try to keep the rhyme if you can.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Line fits the tone or rhyme of the poem
Line adds to the description of the market

questions.stem: Read these three lines of a poem about rain: 'The rain falls soft upon the roof, / It taps and taps and will not stop, / It fills the gutter to the top.' Write one more line that fits the poem. Keep it about the rain.
answer: Accept any line that is about the rain and fits the poem. Award full marks if the line is about the rain and adds to the description.
hints: What else does the rain do?
Try to keep the rhyme if you can — the last words are 'roof', 'stop', 'top'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Line fits the tone or rhyme of the poem
Line adds to the description of the rain

questions.stem: Read these three lines of a poem about a mother: 'My mother wakes before the sun, / She sweeps the yard and cooks for one, / She hums a song and starts the day.' Write one more line that fits the poem AND rhymes with 'day'.
answer: Accept any line about the mother that ends with a word rhyming with 'day' (e.g., 'way', 'play', 'say'). Award full marks if the line is about the mother and ends with a rhyme.
hints: What else does the mother do?
Your last word should rhyme with 'day' — try 'way', 'play' or 'say'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write an original six-line poem about the rain. Your poem must: have six lines, be about the rain throughout, and use at least one pair of rhyming words at the ends of lines.
hints: Start by listing words about rain: drops, cloud, wet, puddle, roof, sound.
Choose two words that rhyme to end two lines.
Count your lines to be sure there are six.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Poem stays on the topic of rain throughout
At least one pair of rhyming line-endings

questions.stem: Write an original six-line poem about a friend. Your poem must: have six lines, be about a friend throughout, and use at least one pair of rhyming words at the ends of lines.
hints: Think of what a friend does: plays, shares, helps, laughs.
Choose two words that rhyme to end two lines.
Count your lines — there must be six.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Poem stays on the topic of a friend throughout
At least one pair of rhyming line-endings

questions.stem: Write an original six-line poem about your school. Your poem must: have six lines, be about your school throughout, and use at least one pair of rhyming words at the ends of lines.
hints: Think about your school: teachers, books, pupils, compound, bell.
Choose two words that rhyme to end two lines.
Count your lines — there must be six.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Poem stays on the topic of school throughout
At least one pair of rhyming line-endings

questions.stem: Write an original six-line poem about a pet or an animal you know. Your poem must: have six lines, be about the animal throughout, and use at least one pair of rhyming words at the ends of lines.
hints: Think of what the animal does: runs, jumps, eats, sleeps.
Choose two words that rhyme to end two lines.
Count your lines — there must be six.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Poem stays on the topic of the animal throughout
At least one pair of rhyming line-endings

questions.stem: Write an original six-line poem about a value such as honesty, patience or kindness. Your poem must: have six lines, teach the value throughout, and use at least one pair of rhyming words at the ends of lines. The poem should also teach a message, not just describe.
hints: Think about what the value looks like in real life.
Choose two words that rhyme to end two lines.
Make sure the poem has a message, not just a description.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Poem stays on the chosen value throughout
At least one pair of rhyming line-endings
Poem teaches a clear message, not just a description

questions.stem: Write an original six-line poem about a place you love in your community. Your poem must: have six lines, be about the place throughout, and use at least one pair of rhyming words at the ends of lines. Your poem should make the reader feel something about the place.
hints: What do you love about the place? What do you see, hear, smell?
Choose two words that rhyme to end two lines.
Try to make the reader feel your love for the place.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Poem stays on the topic of the place throughout
At least one pair of rhyming line-endings
Poem uses language that creates feeling about the place

questions.stem: Read the six-line poem you wrote aloud to the class. Use a clear voice, good rhythm and expression that matches the feeling of the poem.
hints: Read once quietly to yourself first.
Let your voice rise and fall with the feeling of the poem.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Recite your six-line poem from memory to the class or a small group. Use actions that fit the meaning. Your voice should show the feeling of the poem.
hints: Practise the poem several times before you perform.
Let your actions match the words of the poem.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Recites the six lines from memory
Uses actions that fit the meaning
Faces the audience and speaks clearly

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding of lessons in stories by making relevant comments

skills.description: Identify the order of events in a short story, or pick the correct beginning-middle-ending arrangement.
Pick the key detail that matters to the lesson, as opposed to a minor detail.
State the moral lesson of a short story in one line.
Choose a relevant comment about a character's action that explains why the action mattered or what it teaches.
Judge whether a character's action was right or wrong and give the reason tied to the story.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a story, then retell it sequentially (beginning, middle, ending).
Teacher-assessed oral: give a relevant comment on the lesson of a story heard, and relate it briefly to real life.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kofi found a wallet on the road. He looked inside and saw some money. He took the wallet to the police station. The owner came and thanked him.' Which event happened FIRST?
options: Kofi found a wallet on the road
Kofi took the wallet to the police station
The owner came and thanked him
hints: What is the very first thing that happened?
Before Kofi could look inside, he had to find the wallet.
questions.explanation: The story begins with 'Kofi found a wallet on the road.' That is the first event. Everything else happens after.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi looked inside the wallet' because it is the next exciting action, but finding the wallet came first.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Ama was walking to school. She saw a small boy crying by the road. She stopped and asked him what was wrong. He had lost his way. Ama took him to his home, then continued to school.' Which event happened LAST?
options: Ama took the boy to his home
Ama saw a small boy crying
Ama asked the boy what was wrong
hints: What is the final thing Ama did in the story?
After she took him home, she continued to school.
questions.explanation: The story says Ama took the boy home, then continued to school. Taking the boy home is the last event in the story before the ending summary.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama asked the boy what was wrong' because it is a key moment, but she did that before taking him home.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A farmer had a goose that laid a golden egg every day. He wanted all the eggs at once. He cut the goose open. But there were no eggs inside. He lost the goose and the eggs too.' Which order matches the story?
options: Goose laid golden eggs → farmer wanted all at once → cut goose open → lost everything
Farmer cut goose open → goose laid eggs → farmer wanted all at once → lost everything
Lost everything → goose laid eggs → farmer wanted all at once → cut goose open
Goose laid golden eggs → farmer cut goose open → farmer wanted all at once → lost everything
hints: What did the goose do first?
Then what did the farmer want? Then what did he do?
questions.explanation: The correct order: (1) the goose laid a golden egg every day, (2) the farmer wanted all the eggs at once, (3) he cut the goose open, (4) he lost everything.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the cutting before the wanting because cutting is dramatic, but the farmer wanted all the eggs first, then acted.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Esi was hungry on her way home. She found a mango on the ground. She picked it up, wiped it on her dress, and ate it. Her friend Adjo came by and asked for a piece, but Esi said she had eaten it all.' Which detail matters MOST to the lesson of this story?
options: Esi ate the whole mango without sharing with Adjo
Esi wiped the mango on her dress
Esi was on her way home
hints: What is the story really teaching us about?
The story is about sharing (or not sharing).
questions.explanation: The story teaches a lesson about sharing. The key detail is that Esi ate the whole mango and refused to share with Adjo. The other details help set the scene but are not part of the lesson.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Esi was hungry' because it explains why she ate, but the lesson is about what she did when her friend asked for a piece.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kojo was playing football. His mother called him to come and fetch water. Kojo said he was busy and kept playing. When he finally went to fetch water, it was dark and the tap was closed.' Which detail matters MOST to the lesson of the story?
options: Kojo refused to fetch water when his mother called him
Kojo went to fetch water in the dark
hints: What did Kojo do that led to his problem?
The problem came from ignoring his mother.
questions.explanation: The lesson is about listening to parents and doing chores promptly. The key detail is that Kojo refused when his mother called. The dark and the closed tap are the results, not the cause.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the tap was closed' because it is the problem, but the tap closed because Kojo delayed.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two goats met on a narrow bridge. Neither would step aside. They pushed each other. Both fell into the river. Their keeper had to rescue them.' Which detail matters MOST to the lesson of the story?
hints: What caused the goats to fall?
What did each goat refuse to do?
questions.explanation: The lesson is about being stubborn and refusing to give way. The key detail is that neither goat would step aside. The narrow bridge, the falling and the rescue are results.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'both fell into the river' because it is the dramatic ending, but that is the result of the stubbornness, not the cause.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A farmer had a goose that laid a golden egg every day. He wanted all the eggs at once. He cut the goose open. But there were no eggs inside. He lost the goose and the eggs too.' What is the lesson of this story?
options: Be content with what you have and do not be greedy
Eggs are more valuable than geese
hints: Why did the farmer lose everything?
He wanted too much at once.
questions.explanation: The farmer had a good thing (golden eggs every day) but wanted more at once. His greed made him lose everything. The lesson is to be content and not greedy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Eggs are more valuable than geese' because the eggs are gold, but the lesson is about greed, not the value of eggs.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two goats met on a narrow bridge. Neither would step aside. They pushed each other. Both fell into the river.' What is the lesson of this story?
options: Being stubborn hurts everyone; it is wise to give way
It is good to be strong
hints: What did the goats refuse to do?
What happened as a result?
questions.explanation: Both goats were stubborn and refused to give way. They both fell. The lesson is that stubbornness hurts everyone and it is wise to give way sometimes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Bridges are dangerous' because the goats fell, but the bridge is not the problem — the goats' stubbornness is.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kofi found a wallet with money inside. He took it to the police station. The owner came and thanked him. He gave Kofi some money as a reward.' What is the lesson of this story?
options: Wallets should not be picked up
hints: What did Kofi do with the wallet?
What happened to him after?
questions.explanation: Kofi was honest — he took the wallet to the police. The owner rewarded him. The lesson is that honesty is rewarded.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Police stations are helpful' because they helped find the owner, but the lesson is about Kofi's honesty, not the police.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy was asked to mind a pot of soup. His friend called him to play. He went, thinking the fire would go out by itself. When he came back, the soup was burnt and the pot was black.' What is the lesson of this story?
options: Do not abandon your responsibilities for play
Pot blackening is a sign of fire
hints: What was the boy asked to do?
What did he do instead?
questions.explanation: The boy was trusted to mind the soup, but he abandoned his duty to play. The soup burnt. The lesson is that you should not abandon your responsibilities for play.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Friends are a distraction' because the friend called him, but the boy's choice to go is the real problem, not friendship.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Esi was hungry on her way home. She found a mango on the ground. Her friend Adjo came by and asked for a piece. Esi said she had eaten it all.' Which comment is MOST relevant to the story?
options: Esi was unkind to her friend when she could have shared
The mango was on the ground, so it was not safe to eat
Adjo should not ask people for food
Esi should have washed her hands before eating
hints: What is the story really about?
Think about how Esi treated her friend.
questions.explanation: The story teaches about sharing. The most relevant comment is that Esi was unkind when she could have shared with her friend. The other comments are about safety or manners, not the main lesson.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The mango was on the ground, so it was not safe' because it mentions safety, but that is not what the story is teaching.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kojo was playing football. His mother called him to fetch water. He kept playing. When he finally went, it was dark and the tap was closed.' Which comment is MOST relevant to the story?
options: Kojo's delay cost him and his family water that night
Kojo should have played a different game
The mother should have fetched the water herself
The tap should be open at night
hints: What happened because Kojo delayed?
The story is about the result of not doing chores on time.
questions.explanation: Kojo delayed, and the result was no water for the night. The most relevant comment is that his delay cost him and his family. The other comments avoid the lesson.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The mother should have fetched the water herself' because they blame the mother, but the story is about Kojo's responsibility.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two goats met on a narrow bridge. Neither would step aside. They pushed each other. Both fell into the river.' Which comment is MOST relevant to the story?
options: If one goat had stepped aside, both would have crossed safely
Goats should not be allowed on bridges
The keeper should have stopped them sooner
hints: What could have changed the ending?
Think about what one goat could have done differently.
questions.explanation: The most relevant comment is that if one goat had stepped aside, both would have crossed safely. This shows understanding of the lesson — giving way helps everyone. The other comments blame the bridge or keeper.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Bridges should be made wider' because it seems practical, but that avoids the lesson about stubbornness.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy was asked to mind a pot of soup. His friend called him to play. He went, thinking the fire would go out by itself. When he came back, the soup was burnt and the pot was black.' Which comment is MOST relevant to the story?
options: The boy should have told his friend he had work to do
The friend should not have called the boy to play
Soup should not be cooked on a fire
The pot was too small for the soup
hints: What could the boy have said to his friend?
The lesson is about responsibility, not about the friend.
questions.explanation: The most relevant comment is that the boy should have told his friend he had work to do. This shows understanding that the boy is responsible for his own choices. Blaming the friend ignores the lesson.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The friend should not have called him' because they blame the friend, but the boy chose to go.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Kofi found a wallet with money inside. He took it to the police station. The owner came and thanked him.' Was Kofi's action right or wrong?
options: Right, because he returned what did not belong to him
Wrong, because he should have kept the money
Right, because he got a reward
Wrong, because the wallet was not his
hints: What did Kofi do with the wallet?
Did he keep it or return it?
questions.explanation: Kofi's action was right because he returned what did not belong to him. He was honest. The reward is not the reason; the honesty is.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Right, because he got a reward' because they focus on the reward, but the reason his action was right is his honesty, not what he gained.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Esi was hungry on her way home. She found a mango. Her friend Adjo asked for a piece. Esi said she had eaten it all.' Was Esi's action right or wrong?
options: Wrong, because she did not share with her hungry friend
Right, because she found the mango first
Right, because Adjo had not asked politely
Wrong, because the mango was too small
hints: What did Esi do when Adjo asked for a piece?
Think about sharing.
questions.explanation: Esi's action was wrong because she did not share with her hungry friend. Finding the mango first does not make refusing to share right.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Right, because she found the mango first' — but the story teaches that sharing is right, even when you found it.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two goats met on a narrow bridge. Neither would step aside. They pushed each other. Both fell into the river.' Which judgment about the goats is right?
options: Both goats were wrong because neither would give way
Only the first goat was wrong
Only the second goat was wrong
Neither goat was wrong; the bridge was too narrow
hints: What did each goat refuse to do?
Did the story blame only one goat?
questions.explanation: Both goats were wrong because neither would give way. The story says 'neither would step aside' — so both are at fault, not just one.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Only the first goat was wrong' because they focus on one animal, but the story blames both goats equally.

questions.stem: Listen carefully as your teacher reads a short story. Then retell the story to your teacher or a small group, in order — the beginning, the middle and the ending.
hints: Listen for what happens first.
Then think about what happens next and how it ends.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Retells events in the correct order

questions.stem: Listen carefully as your teacher reads 'The Hawk and the Hen' (or a similar short story). Then retell the story to a small group, in the correct order, and add one comment about the lesson.
hints: Listen for the beginning, the middle and the end.
After retelling, say what lesson the story teaches.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Retells the story in the correct order
Gives a relevant comment on the lesson

questions.stem: Listen to a short story told by your teacher. Then give one relevant comment about the lesson of the story, and explain how the lesson applies to your own life.
hints: Think about what the story is teaching.
Then think of a real-life situation that connects to it.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States the lesson of the story clearly
Gives a relevant comment about the lesson
Explains how the lesson applies to real life
Speaks clearly and in complete sentences

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.5.1: Appreciate pieces of literary materials through dramatisation
indicator.objective: Use costume to dramatise or role-play parts/whole of stories

skills.description: Identify which character says or does a given line or action in a supplied scenario.
Choose a costume or prop that suits a named character in a given setting, and reject one that does not.
Give a reason why a chosen costume fits the character.
Choose an improvised line that fits the character's role at that point in the story.
Arrange the scenes of a short story for dramatisation in the correct order.
Teacher-assessed performance: perform a role using costume or prop, staying in character.
Teacher-assessed practical: plan and rehearse with group - share roles, select costume, rehearse.
Teacher-assessed oral: watch a group's performance and comment on costume and character portrayal.

questions.stem: Read this scene from a story: 'A greedy man sees a pot of gold. He says: "This gold belongs to me! I will take it all." ' Which character says this line?
hints: Who is the line about?
The line says 'This gold belongs to me!' — the speaker wants the gold.
questions.explanation: The line is spoken by the character who wants the gold for himself. The story calls him 'a greedy man', so he says the line.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A small child' because children like stories about gold, but the line is spoken by the greedy man in the story.

questions.stem: Read this scene from a story: 'A young girl is lost in the forest. She sees an old woman and says: "Please, can you help me find my way home?" ' Which character does the young girl speak to?
hints: Who does the girl see in the forest?
She speaks to the person she sees.
questions.explanation: The scene says the girl sees an old woman and speaks to her, asking for help to find her way home. So she speaks to the old woman.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A hunter' because hunters are in forests, but the story says she sees an old woman.

questions.stem: You are dramatising a story about a farmer going to his farm. Which costume fits the character best?
options: A simple cloth, a straw hat and a cutlass
A school uniform and a school bag
A white gown and a stethoscope
A dark suit and a tie
hints: What does a farmer do?
What does a farmer wear to the farm?
questions.explanation: A farmer works on a farm with tools like a cutlass and wears simple, comfortable clothes. A straw hat protects from the sun. So the simple cloth, straw hat and cutlass fit the farmer best.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A white gown and stethoscope' because they think of a doctor's costume, but the character is a farmer, not a doctor.

questions.stem: You are dramatising an Ananse story. Which costume fits Ananse the spider best?
options: Brown and black cloth with a spider-web pattern
hints: What is Ananse?
Ananse is a spider, so the costume should suggest a spider.
questions.explanation: Ananse is a spider. A brown and black cloth with a spider-web pattern suggests the spider's body and web. The other costumes belong to modern jobs, not to a spider.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A football jersey' because it is fun, but it does not fit the spider character.

questions.stem: You are dramatising a story about an old chief receiving visitors. Which prop fits the chief best?
options: A decorated stool and a beaded necklace
hints: What does a chief sit on in stories?
Chiefs sit on stools and wear beads.
questions.explanation: In Ghanaian stories, a chief sits on a decorated stool and wears a beaded necklace. These props fit the chief. The other items belong to school or modern life, not to the chief's role in a story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A mobile phone' because chiefs today have phones, but in a story about a chief receiving visitors, the stool and beads suggest his role most clearly.

questions.stem: You are playing a fisherman in a story. You choose to wear a torn singlet, rolled-up trousers and a hat. Explain in one sentence why this costume fits the fisherman.
answer: Accept any answer that links the costume to the fisherman's work - for example, 'Fishermen work in water and need simple clothes that can get wet' or 'He wears a hat to protect from the sun while fishing.' Award full marks if the reason names an aspect of fishing (water, sun, work).
hints: What does a fisherman do all day?
What clothes would be comfortable for that work?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Names an aspect of fishing (water, sun, work)
Links it to the costume chosen

questions.stem: You are playing a poor farmer in a story. You wear a patched cloth and carry a hoe. Explain in two sentences why this costume fits the character and the story.
answer: Accept any answer that links the costume to the farmer's poverty and work - for example, 'The patched cloth shows that the farmer is poor and cannot buy new clothes. The hoe shows he works on a farm.' Award full marks if the answer mentions both poverty (patched cloth) and work (hoe).
hints: What does the patched cloth tell us about the farmer?
What does the hoe tell us?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Links both to the character and story

questions.stem: In a story, a young girl is lost in the forest. She meets an old woman. Which improvised line fits the girl's role at this point?
options: "Please, can you help me find my way home?"
"I am the queen of this forest."
hints: How would a lost child speak to a stranger?
She needs help to find her way home.
questions.explanation: A lost young girl would politely ask for help. The line 'Please, can you help me find my way home?' fits her role. The other lines are rude or boastful and do not fit a lost child.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Go away, I don't need you' because they think lost children are scared, but the girl needs help, so she would ask for it.

questions.stem: In a story, a chief is receiving visitors to his palace. Which improvised line fits the chief's role?
options: "Welcome, my people. Sit and share your news."
hints: What does a chief do with visitors?
How does a chief speak to his people?
questions.explanation: A chief welcomes visitors politely and invites them to speak. The line 'Welcome, my people. Sit and share your news' fits the chief's role. The other lines are rude or out of place.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Get out of my palace!' because they think chiefs are fierce, but a chief receives visitors with welcome, not with rudeness.

questions.stem: In a story, a greedy man sees a pot of gold. Which improvised line fits the greedy man's role at this point?
options: "This gold belongs to me! I will take it all!"
"Let us share this gold fairly with everyone."
"I will give this gold to the poor."
hints: What does a greedy man want?
Greedy means wanting everything for yourself.
questions.explanation: A greedy man wants the gold for himself. The line 'This gold belongs to me! I will take it all!' fits the greedy character. The other lines are generous, the opposite of greedy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick the generous line because it sounds nice, but the character is greedy, so he would not share.

questions.stem: You are dramatising the story of Kofi who finds a wallet. Arrange these scenes in the correct order: A) The owner comes and thanks Kofi. B) Kofi finds a wallet on the road. C) Kofi takes the wallet to the police station.
hints: What happens first?
What happens after Kofi takes the wallet to the police?
questions.explanation: The correct order: Kofi finds the wallet (B), takes it to the police (C), and the owner comes and thanks him (A). So B, C, A.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the owner's thanks first because it is the ending, but the story begins with finding the wallet.

questions.stem: You are dramatising the story of the two stubborn goats. Arrange these scenes in the correct order: A) Both goats fall into the river. B) Two goats meet on a narrow bridge. C) Neither goat will step aside. D) The keeper rescues them.
hints: What is the first event?
The goats meet, they argue, they fall, they are rescued.
questions.explanation: The correct order: the goats meet on the bridge (B), neither will step aside (C), they push and fall (A), and the keeper rescues them (D). So B, C, A, D.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the falling before the arguing because falling is dramatic, but the stubbornness comes first and causes the fall.

questions.stem: Perform the role of Kofi in the wallet story, using a small bag as a prop (the wallet). Show Kofi finding the wallet, looking surprised, and deciding to take it to the police. Stay in character.
hints: Show your face when you find the wallet.
Show your decision by your actions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the prop as a wallet
Shows the discovery with face and body

questions.stem: Perform the role of the greedy man in the pot-of-gold story, using a bowl as a prop (the pot). Show greed in your face, words and actions. Then show his disappointment at the end.
hints: Show greed with your eyes and hands.
Show disappointment when the gold is gone.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the prop as the pot of gold
Shows greed in face and body

questions.stem: Perform the role of a chief receiving visitors, using a small stool and a cloth as props. Show welcome with your words and body. Invite the visitors to sit and speak.
hints: How does a chief sit?
How does a chief welcome people?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the props as a stool and cloth
Shows welcome in words and body
Invites visitors to sit and speak

questions.stem: In a pair, perform the scene where the young girl meets the old woman in the forest. Use a stick as the old woman's walking stick. Show the girl's fear and the old woman's kindness. Stay in character.
hints: How would a lost child look and speak?
How would a kind old woman respond?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the stick as a walking stick
Shows the girl's fear in face and voice

questions.stem: In a group of four, prepare a short dramatisation of a familiar story. Share roles, choose simple costumes from what you are wearing, and rehearse once. Then perform to the class.
hints: Who will play each character?
What simple item can be a costume or prop?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Every group member has a role
Group chose simple costumes or props

questions.stem: In a group of five, prepare a short dramatisation of an Ananse story. One person is Ananse, others are the animals or villagers. Choose costumes from classroom materials, rehearse twice, and perform to the class.
hints: How will you show that one person is Ananse?
What will the villagers wear?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: All members participate in the performance

questions.stem: Watch a group perform a short story. Afterwards, give one comment about how well their costumes fit the characters, and one comment about how well they stayed in character.
hints: Look at the costumes - do they fit the story?
Watch how each actor speaks and moves.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Watch a group perform the goat-bridge story. Afterwards, give one comment about what worked well and one suggestion for improvement, focusing on costume and character portrayal.
hints: What did the performers do well?
What could they do better next time?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one clear positive comment about costume or character
Gives one specific suggestion for improvement
Comments are focused on costume or character, not other things

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.5.2: Appreciate key issues in stories/sketches
indicator.objective: Interpret moral values in plays/stories

skills.description: Name the moral value a short play or story teaches.
Pick the event or line that best shows the value.
Separate the moral value from a mere event in the play.
Explain in own words what a character's action means about the value.
Apply the value to a real-life situation.
Judge whether a character upheld or broke the value, with a reason drawn from the play.
Teacher-assessed oral: interpret the moral value of a scene watched or heard and explain it to the class.
Teacher-assessed practical: discuss in groups and share interpretation with the class.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A boy sees a classmate being bullied. He steps in and says: "Leave him alone. We are all friends here." ' What moral value does this scene teach?
hints: What did the boy do?
He stood up for his classmate.
questions.explanation: The boy stood up to protect a classmate from bullying. This shows courage (standing up) and kindness (protecting someone). The scene teaches these values.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Patience' because standing up can take time, but the scene is about standing up for others, which is courage and kindness.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A servant finds a gold ring in the palace. She takes it to the queen and says: "I found this, Your Majesty. It is not mine." ' What moral value does this scene teach?
hints: What did the servant do with the ring?
She returned it instead of keeping it.
questions.explanation: The servant found a gold ring and returned it to the queen instead of keeping it. This shows honesty — doing the right thing with what is not yours.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Respect' because she addressed the queen respectfully, but the key action is returning the ring, which is honesty.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'Two pupils want the same book. One says: "You can have it first. I will wait." ' What moral value does this scene teach?
hints: What did the pupil do when they wanted the book?
They offered to wait.
questions.explanation: The pupil gave up the book first and said they would wait. This shows patience (waiting) and sharing (letting the other have it). So the values are patience and sharing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Courage' because giving up something is hard, but the value here is patience and sharing, not courage.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A servant finds a gold ring. She takes it to the queen. The queen says: "You are the most honest servant in this palace." ' The value is honesty. Which line BEST shows this value?
options: She takes it to the queen
A servant finds a gold ring
The queen says you are honest
She found it in the palace
hints: What did the servant DO that showed honesty?
Finding a ring is not honesty. What she did with it is.
questions.explanation: Honesty is shown by the action of taking the ring to the queen. Finding the ring is not honesty; the action that follows is. So 'She takes it to the queen' best shows the value.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The queen says you are honest' because it mentions honesty, but a character saying it is not the same as showing it. The action of returning the ring is what shows honesty.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A boy sees a classmate being bullied. He steps in and says: "Leave him alone." The bullies walk away. The classmate thanks him.' The value is courage. Which line BEST shows this value?
options: He steps in and says: "Leave him alone."
A boy sees a classmate being bullied
hints: What did the boy DO that showed courage?
Watching is not courage. Stepping in is.
questions.explanation: The boy's courage is shown when he steps in and tells the bullies to leave the classmate alone. Seeing the bullying is not courage; acting on it is. The other lines are results.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A boy sees a classmate being bullied' because it is the first thing, but seeing is not courage; stepping in is.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'Two pupils want the same book. One says: "You can have it first. I will wait." The other pupil takes the book and smiles.' The value is patience. Which line BEST shows this value?
options: You can have it first. I will wait
Two pupils want the same book
The other pupil takes the book
hints: What words show patience?
Waiting is the key action.
questions.explanation: Patience is shown when the pupil says 'You can have it first. I will wait.' The willingness to wait is the evidence of patience. The other lines are details about the situation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Two pupils want the same book' because it explains the problem, but the problem is not the value. The value is shown when one pupil offers to wait.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A servant finds a gold ring. She takes it to the queen. The queen praises her.' Which of the following is the VALUE, not just the event?
hints: Which word names a quality?
A quality is something inside a person, not an action.
questions.explanation: Honesty is a value — a quality shown by the actions in the play. Finding the ring, taking it to the queen and being praised are events. The value is honesty.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Taking it to the queen' because it is the honest action, but the action is the evidence of the value, not the value itself.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'Two goats meet on a bridge. Neither will step aside. They push. Both fall in the river.' Which of the following is the VALUE, not just the event?
hints: Which word names a quality (even a bad one)?
Meeting, pushing and falling are events.
questions.explanation: Stubbornness is a (negative) value shown by the goats. Meeting, pushing and falling are events. The value is the quality the story illustrates.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Falling into the river' because it is the dramatic result, but that is the consequence of the value, not the value itself.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A servant finds a gold ring. She takes it to the queen.' What does this action tell us about the servant's character? Answer in one sentence.
answer: Accept any answer that interprets the action as honesty or trustworthiness (e.g., 'She is honest because she returned something that was not hers.'). Award full marks if the answer names the value and links it to the action.
hints: What value does returning the ring show?
What kind of person would do that?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Links the value to the servant's action (returning the ring)

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A boy sees a classmate being bullied. He steps in and says: "Leave him alone." ' What does this action tell us about the boy's character? Answer in two sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that interprets the action as courage and kindness (e.g., 'He is brave because he stood up to the bullies. He is also kind because he wanted to protect his classmate.'). Award full marks if the answer names a value and links it to the action.
hints: What two values does stepping in show?
Bravery and kindness.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Names at least one value (courage or kindness)
Links the value to the action of stepping in

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'Two pupils want the same book. One says: "You can have it first. I will wait." ' What does this action tell us about the pupil's character? Answer in two sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that interprets the action as patience or sharing (e.g., 'The pupil is patient because they are willing to wait. They are also generous because they let the other pupil have the book first.'). Award full marks if the answer names a value and links it to the action.
hints: What value does offering to wait show?
Patience or sharing.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Links the value to the action of offering to wait

questions.stem: The play teaches honesty. Which real-life situation shows honesty in action?
options: Telling the teacher that you broke the ruler
Blaming a friend for breaking the ruler
Hiding the broken ruler in your bag
Pretending the ruler was already broken
hints: What does honesty mean in real life?
Telling the truth is honesty.
questions.explanation: Honesty means telling the truth, even when it is hard. Telling the teacher that you broke the ruler shows honesty. The other options are lies or blaming others.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Pretending the ruler was already broken' because it avoids trouble, but it is a lie, not honesty.

questions.stem: The play teaches patience. Which real-life situation shows patience in action?
options: Waiting quietly in the queue for lunch
Pushing to the front of the queue
Shouting at the person in front
Leaving the queue and going to play
hints: What does patience look like in a queue?
Waiting your turn is patience.
questions.explanation: Patience means waiting your turn without pushing or complaining. Waiting quietly in the queue for lunch shows patience. The other options are impatient actions.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Leaving the queue and going to play' because it feels free, but it does not show patience.

questions.stem: The play teaches courage. Which real-life situation shows courage in action?
options: Standing up to someone who is bullying a classmate
Watching someone being bullied and saying nothing
Running away when someone needs help
hints: What does courage look like in real life?
Doing the right thing even when it is hard.
questions.explanation: Courage means doing the right thing even when it is hard or frightening. Standing up to a bully shows courage. The other options are fear or cruelty, not courage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'Running away' because it keeps them safe, but running away is the opposite of courage.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A pupil finds money on the classroom floor. He puts it in his pocket and says nothing.' Was this pupil's action right or wrong, and why?
options: Wrong, because the money was not his and he should have reported it
Right, because he found it first
Right, because the money was on the floor
Wrong, because the money was too little
hints: Whose money was it?
What should you do with money you find?
questions.explanation: The pupil's action was wrong because the money was not his. The right action would be to report it so the owner could be found. Finding it first does not make it his.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Right, because he found it first' because they think finding something makes it yours, but the play teaches honesty, so that is wrong.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'Two boys are playing. One boy falls and hurts his knee. The other boy laughs and walks away.' Was the second boy's action right or wrong, and why?
options: Wrong, because he should have helped his friend instead of laughing
Right, because the boy fell by himself
Wrong, because the boy should not have been playing
hints: What did the second boy do when his friend fell?
How should a friend act when someone is hurt?
questions.explanation: The second boy's action was wrong. He should have helped his hurt friend instead of laughing and walking away. Kindness is the right response.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Right, because laughter is healthy' because laughing is normal, but laughing at someone's pain is unkind, not healthy.

questions.stem: Read this short play scene: 'A pupil is asked to sweep the classroom. She asks her friend to do it so she can play. The friend agrees. The teacher finds out.' Was this pupil's action right or wrong, and why?
options: Wrong, because she tried to avoid her responsibility and use her friend
Right, because she needed to play
Wrong, because the teacher found out
hints: Was it the pupil's job to sweep?
What does it mean to avoid your work?
questions.explanation: The pupil's action was wrong because she tried to avoid her responsibility and use her friend to do her work. Even though the friend agreed, that does not make it right.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Right, because the friend agreed' because both people agreed, but the value of responsibility is broken when one pupil avoids her own work.

questions.stem: Watch a short scene from a play your teacher has chosen. Then tell the class what moral value the scene teaches and explain how the scene shows it.
hints: What is the main lesson of the scene?
Which actions or words show that lesson?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how the scene shows the value

questions.stem: Watch a short scene from a play. Then tell the class what moral value the scene teaches, how the scene shows it, and give one real-life example of living by that value.
hints: Value first. Then evidence. Then real-life example.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how the scene shows it
Gives a real-life example of living by the value

questions.stem: In a small group, discuss the value taught by a scene your teacher has shown. Each member shares one example of how the value applies to their own life. Present the group's ideas to the class.
hints: Each member should speak.
The group should agree on one value and give one example each.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Group agrees on one moral value
Each member gives a real-life example
Group presents ideas to the class

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.5.2: Appreciate key issues in stories/sketches
indicator.objective: Develop sketches from stories read or heard

skills.description: Identify the parts of a supplied story that could become scenes.
Choose a line of dialogue that fits a named character at a named point in the story.
Recognise what a sketch needs (characters, setting, dialogue, action) and what it does not need.
Arrange sketch scenes in the order of the story.
Short answer: retell one part of a story as if it were a scene (who, where, what is said).
Teacher-assessed written: develop a short sketch (5-8 lines) from a given story.
Teacher-assessed practical: perform the developed sketch before the class.
Teacher-assessed oral: comment on another group's sketch - what worked, what could improve.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy finds a lost dog. He feeds it and takes it to the vet. The owner comes and thanks him.' Which part of this story could become a scene?
options: The boy feeding the lost dog
The story has a happy ending
hints: Which part is a real action that could be acted out?
