A scene shows something happening.
questions.explanation: A scene needs an action that can be acted out. 'The boy feeding the lost dog' is an action. The other options are statements about the story, not actions.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The dog was lost' because it is the start of the story, but it describes a state, not an action that can be acted out as a scene.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two pupils want the same book. One pupil says the other can have it first. The other pupil smiles and says thank you.' Which parts could become TWO scenes?
options: Scene 1: the pupils want the same book. Scene 2: one offers the book to the other
Scene 1: the book is in the library. Scene 2: the library is quiet
Scene 1: the teacher says 'well done'. Scene 2: the pupils go home
Scene 1: the pupils are in class. Scene 2: they are not in class
hints: Which two parts of the story are actions that can be acted out?
The problem and the solution are two different actions.
questions.explanation: The problem (both want the same book) and the solution (one offers to wait) are two separate actions that can be acted out as two scenes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Scene 1: the book is in the library. Scene 2: the library is quiet' because they set the scene, but setting is not a scene action.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy finds a lost dog. He feeds it and takes it to the vet. The owner comes.' Which line fits the boy when he first finds the dog?
options: "Poor dog, you look hungry. Let me feed you."
"This dog is mine now! I will keep it."
"Go away, dog. I don't like you."
hints: What does the boy do in the story?
He feeds the dog and takes it to the vet.
questions.explanation: The boy is kind to the dog. A line that fits him when he first finds the dog is 'Poor dog, you look hungry. Let me feed you.' The other lines are unkind or greedy, which do not fit the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'This dog is mine now!' because they think finding something makes it yours, but the story shows the boy returning the dog to its owner.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A lost boy is crying in the market. He says he cannot find his mother. A trader helps him look.' Which line fits the boy at the start of the story?
options: "I want my mother! Please help me find her!"
hints: How would a lost child feel?
What would he say when he is crying?
questions.explanation: The boy is lost and crying. A line that fits him is 'I want my mother! Please help me find her!' The other lines are confident or rude, which do not fit a lost, crying child.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I am the best trader here' because the story is in a market, but the boy is not a trader — he is a lost child.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A greedy man finds a pot of gold. He refuses to share with the villagers. Later, the gold disappears. The villagers laugh at him.' Which line fits the greedy man when he finds the gold?
options: "This gold is mine! No one else can have any!"
"Let us share this gold with everyone in the village."
"I will give this gold to the poor."
"This gold is too heavy for me."
hints: What does a greedy man do with gold?
Greedy means wanting everything for himself.
questions.explanation: A greedy man wants the gold for himself. The line 'This gold is mine! No one else can have any!' fits him. The other lines are generous, which is the opposite of greedy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Let us share' because it is a good line, but the character is greedy, so he would not share.

questions.stem: What does a sketch need to have?
options: Characters, a setting, dialogue and action
hints: A sketch is a short play. What does a play have?
A play has characters, a place, speech and actions.
questions.explanation: A sketch is a short play. It needs characters (who is in it), a setting (where it happens), dialogue (what characters say), and action (what they do). So all four are needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A drawing of the characters' because the word sketch is sometimes used for drawings, but in drama a sketch is a short scene, not a drawing.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT needed in a sketch?
options: A narrator who tells every action
hints: A sketch shows action through the characters. Do you need someone to narrate everything?
A sketch should be shown, not just told.
questions.explanation: In a sketch, the action is shown through the characters themselves — their words and actions. A narrator telling every action would make it a story, not a sketch. So a narrator for every action is not needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A setting' because they think a sketch does not need a place, but every sketch happens somewhere, so a setting IS needed.

questions.stem: You are making a sketch from the story of the lost dog. Arrange these scenes in the correct order: A) The owner comes and thanks the boy. B) The boy finds a hungry dog. C) The boy takes the dog to the vet.
hints: What happens first?
The boy needs to find the dog before he can take it to the vet.
questions.explanation: The correct order: boy finds the dog (B), takes it to the vet (C), and the owner comes to thank him (A). So B, C, A.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the owner's thanks first because it is the happy end, but the story begins with finding the dog.

questions.stem: You are making a sketch from the two-goats story. Arrange these scenes in order: A) The keeper rescues both goats. B) Two goats meet on a narrow bridge. C) Neither goat will step aside. D) Both goats fall into the river.
hints: What happens first? The goats meet.
Then they argue, fall, and are rescued.
questions.explanation: Correct order: goats meet (B), neither will step aside (C), both fall (D), keeper rescues them (A). So B, C, D, A.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the fall before the argument because the fall is dramatic, but the stubbornness comes first and causes the fall.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy finds a lost dog. He feeds it and takes it to the vet.' Imagine you are turning the first part of this story into a scene. Write 2-3 sentences describing the scene: who is in it, where it happens, and what the boy says.
answer: Accept any answer that describes a scene with the boy and the dog, a setting (e.g. street, park, market), and a line of dialogue. Award full marks if all three are present.
hints: Who is in the scene?
Where is the scene?
What does the boy say to the dog?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A lost boy is crying in the market. A trader helps him look for his mother.' Imagine you are turning the opening of this story into a scene. Write 3-4 sentences describing the scene: who is in it, where it happens, and what the boy and the trader say to each other.
answer: Accept any answer that describes a scene with the boy and the trader, a market setting, and dialogue between them. Award full marks if all four are present.
hints: Who is in the scene?
Where is the scene? (a market)
What does the boy say? What does the trader say?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a line for the boy
Gives a line for the trader

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy finds a lost dog. He feeds it and takes it to the vet. The owner comes and thanks him.' Write a short sketch (5-8 lines of dialogue) from this story. Include at least two characters and a setting at the top.
hints: Who will be in your sketch? Write their names at the top.
Where does the scene happen?
Each character should speak.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Dialogue is written with speaker labels
Sketch has action, not just talk

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two pupils want the same book. One offers to let the other have it first. The other says thank you.' Write a short sketch (5-8 lines of dialogue) from this story. Include the setting (the classroom or library) at the top.
hints: Who are the two pupils? Give them names.
Where does the scene happen?
What do they say to each other?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Dialogue is written with speaker labels
Dialogue fits the story (one offers, one thanks)

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A greedy man finds a pot of gold. He refuses to share. Later the gold disappears.' Write a short sketch (5-8 lines) showing the greedy man refusing to share with the villagers. Include the setting (village square) at the top.
hints: Who is in the scene? The greedy man and at least one villager.
What does the greedy man say when asked to share?
How does the villager react?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Characters named (greedy man and at least one villager)
Dialogue shows the greedy man refusing

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A boy sees a classmate being bullied. He steps in and tells the bullies to leave him alone.' Write a short sketch (5-8 lines) showing the boy stepping in. Include the setting (school compound) at the top.
hints: Who is in the scene? The boy, the bullies, and the classmate.
What does the boy say to the bullies?
What do the bullies say back?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Dialogue shows the boy stepping in

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'A servant finds a gold ring in the palace. She returns it to the queen. The queen praises her honesty.' Write a short sketch (5-8 lines) showing the servant returning the ring. Include the setting (palace hall) at the top and add a stage direction (in brackets) showing what the servant does when she enters.
hints: What does the servant do when she enters?
What does she say to the queen?
What does the queen say back?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: At least one stage direction in brackets
Sketch has clear action and resolution

questions.stem: Read this short story: 'Two goats meet on a narrow bridge. Neither will step aside. They push each other and both fall into the river.' Write a short sketch (5-8 lines) showing the goats arguing on the bridge. Include the setting (narrow bridge over a river) at the top, and use goats who speak to each other. Add a stage direction (in brackets) for the fall.
hints: What does each goat say to the other?
Where does the fall happen in your sketch?
Use a stage direction in brackets.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Stage direction in brackets for the fall
Sketch has clear action and resolution

questions.stem: In a group, perform the sketch you wrote (or a sketch your teacher has given you). Use clear voices and actions. Stay in character throughout.
hints: Speak clearly so everyone can hear.
Use your body to show the action.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Sketch is performed from start to finish

questions.stem: In a group of three or more, perform a sketch that shows a clear problem and its resolution. Use improvised props to show the setting. Then answer one question from the class about your character.
hints: What is the problem in your sketch?
How is it resolved?
What prop will show the setting?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Props are used to show the setting
Group answers a question from the class in character

questions.stem: Watch another group perform a sketch. Afterwards, give one comment about what worked well and one suggestion for improvement. Focus on the dialogue and how well the actors stayed in character.
hints: What did the actors do well?
What could they do better?
Focus on the dialogue and staying in character.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one clear positive comment about dialogue or character
Gives one specific suggestion for improvement
Comment is focused on dialogue and character, not other things

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.6.1: Use culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Describe/talk about names of regions/places in the country as well as personalities in the community, expressing ideas and feelings clearly

skills.description: Match a well-known town or landmark to its region.
Identify the role of a named community personality from a description.
Choose the best descriptive sentence about a familiar place, using describing words.
Choose the sentence that expresses a feeling clearly and politely about a place or person.
Teacher-assessed oral: describe a place or personality in own community clearly, using at least two describing words.
Teacher-assessed oral: say how they feel about a named place or personality and give one reason.
Teacher-assessed oral: ask and answer two questions about a place or personality discussed.

questions.stem: Cape Coast is the capital town of which region in Ghana?
hints: Think of the region in the south of Ghana where Cape Coast Castle is found.
Cape Coast is on the coast.
questions.explanation: Cape Coast is the capital town of the Central Region of Ghana.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick Ashanti because Kumasi is well known, but Cape Coast is in the Central Region.

questions.stem: Kumasi is the capital city of which region?
hints: Kumasi is known as the Garden City.
It is the home of the Ashanti Kingdom.
questions.explanation: Kumasi is the capital city of the Ashanti Region. It is also the seat of the Ashanti Kingdom.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick Greater Accra because Accra is the national capital, but Kumasi is the capital of the Ashanti Region.

questions.stem: Tamale is the capital town of which region?
hints: Tamale is in the north of Ghana.
It is a large city in the north.
questions.explanation: Tamale is the capital town of the Northern Region of Ghana.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick Upper East because it is also in the north, but Tamale is in the Northern Region.

questions.stem: Who is the head of a region in Ghana?
hints: The title has the word 'Regional' in it.
It is a political appointment at the regional level.
questions.explanation: The Regional Minister is the head of a region in Ghana. The District Chief Executive heads a district, not a region.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick District Chief Executive because it sounds similar, but that role heads a district, not a region.

questions.stem: Who is the leader of a district assembly in Ghana?
hints: The title has the word 'District' in it.
This person leads the district assembly.
questions.explanation: The District Chief Executive (DCE) is the leader of a district assembly in Ghana.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick Member of Parliament because MPs are well known, but the DCE leads the district assembly.

questions.stem: In a school, who is responsible for keeping pupils safe, keeping records, and running the school day-to-day?
hints: Who is the leader of the whole school?
This person is in charge of the school's daily running.
questions.explanation: The head teacher is responsible for running the school, keeping records, and keeping pupils safe. The prefects, class teachers and PTA all support, but the head is in charge.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick school prefect because prefects are visible, but prefects assist the head teacher rather than run the school.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a market best, using descriptive words?
options: The market is busy, noisy and full of colourful stalls.
The market is in the town.
hints: Which sentence uses words that help you picture the market?
Look for words like 'busy', 'noisy', 'colourful'.
questions.explanation: A descriptive sentence uses words that help us picture the place. 'The market is busy, noisy and full of colourful stalls' describes the market with three describing words. The other sentences are plain statements.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The market sells things' because it is true, but it does not describe what the market is like.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a school compound best, using descriptive words?
options: The compound is wide, clean and shaded by tall trees.
hints: Which sentence uses describing words?
Words like 'wide', 'clean', 'shaded' are descriptive.
questions.explanation: 'The compound is wide, clean and shaded by tall trees' uses three describing words and helps the listener picture it. The other sentences are plain statements.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The compound has pupils' because it mentions people, but it does not describe what the compound is like.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a river best, using descriptive words?
options: The river is wide, calm and shines like silver in the sun.
The river is in the village.
hints: Which sentence helps you see the river in your mind?
Look for words like 'wide', 'calm', 'shines'.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'The river is wide, calm and shines like silver in the sun' uses describing words and a simile to help the listener picture the river. The other sentences are brief statements.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The river is long' because it uses a describing word, but one word is not enough to describe the river well.

questions.stem: You visited Cape Coast Castle with your class. Which sentence expresses your feeling clearly and politely?
options: I felt sad and thoughtful when I saw the castle because of its history.
I didn't like the castle at all.
The castle is just an old building.
hints: Which sentence names your feeling?
It should be polite and clear.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'I felt sad and thoughtful...' names the feelings clearly and gives a reason. The other sentences are rude or do not name a feeling.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The castle is boring' because it is short, but it is rude and does not express a clear feeling with a reason.

questions.stem: You met the Regional Minister at a school event. Which sentence expresses your feeling clearly and politely?
options: I was happy and proud to meet the Regional Minister today.
The Regional Minister is not important.
I don't care about the Regional Minister.
The Regional Minister talks too much.
hints: Which sentence names your feeling politely?
It should be respectful.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'I was happy and proud...' names the feelings politely. The other sentences are rude or dismissive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I don't care' because it is short, but it is impolite, especially about a community leader.

questions.stem: You visited your friend's village and saw how clean and peaceful it was. Which sentence expresses your feeling clearly and politely, with a reason?
options: I felt calm and happy there because the village was so clean and quiet.
The village is not like my town.
hints: Which sentence names the feelings and gives a reason?
Look for a 'because' clause.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'I felt calm and happy there because the village was so clean and quiet' names two feelings and gives a reason. The others are unclear or negative without a reason.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I didn't like the village' because it states a feeling, but it is negative without a reason and is impolite.

questions.stem: Talk to your teacher or a small group about a place in your community (a market, a church, a mosque, a school, a park). Use at least two describing words to help your listeners picture the place.
hints: What does the place look like?
What sounds or smells are there?
Use words like 'busy', 'quiet', 'wide', 'colourful'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two describing words

questions.stem: Talk to your teacher or a small group about a personality in your community (a chief, a head teacher, a nurse, a pastor, an imam, a market queen). Use at least two describing words to help your listeners picture the person.
hints: What does the person look like?
What is the person like? Kind? Strict? Hard-working?
Use describing words.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names the person and their role
Uses at least two describing words

questions.stem: Describe a place in your community to the class, using at least three describing words and one comparison ('bigger than', 'quieter than', etc.).
hints: Use words like 'wide', 'busy', 'shady', 'noisy'.
Compare the place to another place you know.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three describing words

questions.stem: Describe an important personality in your community to the class. Use at least three describing words, say what the person does, and explain why the person is important to the community.
hints: What is the person like?
What do they do?
Why does the community need them?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three describing words
Explains why the person is important
Speaks clearly and in full sentences

questions.stem: Think of a place in your community that you love. Tell your teacher or a small group how you feel about it and give one reason.
hints: How do you feel? Happy? Calm? Proud?
Why do you feel that way?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States a clear feeling about it
Gives one reason for the feeling

questions.stem: Think of a personality in your community that you respect. Tell your teacher or a small group how you feel about that person and give one reason.
hints: What feeling do you have? Respect? Admiration?
Why do you feel that way?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names the person and their role
States a clear feeling about them
Gives one reason for the feeling

questions.stem: In a pair, take turns asking and answering questions about a place in your community. Each of you should ask two questions and answer two questions.
hints: Try questions like 'Where is it?' 'What is it like?' 'Why do you like it?'
Listen carefully to the answers.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Asks two clear questions about the place

questions.stem: In a small group, take turns asking and answering questions about a personality in your community. Each member should ask at least one question and answer at least one.
hints: Ask about their role, their work, or why they are respected.
Answer in full sentences.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each member asks at least one question
Each member answers at least one question

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.6.2: Demonstrate positive listening and viewing attitudes and behaviour by showing attentiveness and understanding
indicator.objective: Maintain appropriate posture and facial expression

skills.description: Recognise what good posture and facial expression looks like.
Identify a poor posture or facial expression.
Explain why posture and facial expression matter in conversation.
Teacher-assessed observation: pupil maintains appropriate posture and facial expression throughout a short conversation.
Teacher-assessed oral: watch a peer's conversation and comment on the posture and expression shown.
Teacher-assessed practical: demonstrate good and poor posture on request, and say which is which.

questions.stem: You are listening to a classmate tell a story. Which behaviour shows good posture and facial expression?
options: Sitting up, facing the speaker, and looking interested
Slouching in your chair and looking at the floor
Turning your back to the speaker
Closing your eyes while the speaker talks
hints: What does a good listener look like?
Face the speaker and sit up.
questions.explanation: Good posture and expression means sitting up, facing the speaker and looking interested. The other behaviours show disinterest.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Closing your eyes' because they think closing eyes helps concentration, but in conversation it signals disinterest.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good facial expression when a friend is telling you about a sad event?
options: Looking away and rolling your eyes
hints: Your face should match what the speaker is saying.
A sad story needs a concerned face.
questions.explanation: When a friend is talking about something sad, a serious, concerned look shows that you care. A smile, blank stare or rolling eyes would seem rude or unfeeling.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A big smile' because smiling is friendly, but smiling while someone shares a sad story is inappropriate.

questions.stem: You are in a conversation with an elder who is speaking. What is good posture for you?
options: Sitting upright, hands still, facing the elder
Leaning back with your feet on the chair
Lying on the floor while listening
Standing with your back to the elder
hints: What shows respect for an elder who is speaking?
Sit up and face them.
questions.explanation: Sitting upright, hands still, and facing the elder shows respect and attentiveness. Leaning back, lying down or turning away would be disrespectful.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Leaning back' because it is comfortable, but comfort is not the same as respectful attention.

questions.stem: Which behaviour shows poor posture during a conversation?
hints: Which one looks tired or uninterested?
Slouching is poor posture.
questions.explanation: Slouching with your head down shows poor posture and looks uninterested. Sitting up, facing the speaker, and nodding show good posture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Nodding gently' because it involves movement, but gentle nodding shows attentive listening.

questions.stem: Which facial expression is poor when someone is speaking to you?
options: A frown or rolling your eyes
A serious look when the topic is serious
hints: Which expression shows you are annoyed?
Frowning or rolling eyes shows dislike.
questions.explanation: A frown or rolling your eyes shows annoyance or disrespect, which is poor. A calm, attentive expression matched to the topic is good.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A serious look when the topic is serious' because serious sounds negative, but a serious look matched to the topic is appropriate.

questions.stem: Which behaviour shows poor listening posture?
options: Looking out of the window while someone is speaking
Making eye contact with the speaker
Sitting with your body turned towards the speaker
Keeping your hands still in your lap
hints: Which behaviour shows you are not paying attention?
Looking away is a sign of poor listening.
questions.explanation: Looking out of the window while someone speaks shows you are not paying attention. Eye contact, facing the speaker and still hands all show good listening.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Keeping your hands still' because it seems like a strict rule, but still hands help the listener focus on the speaker.

questions.stem: Why does good posture matter in a conversation?
options: It shows the speaker that you respect and are listening to them
It helps you win an argument
hints: What message does your posture send to the speaker?
It shows respect and attention.
questions.explanation: Good posture shows the speaker that you respect them and are paying attention. It makes the conversation easier and more pleasant for both people.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It makes you look taller' because posture affects height, but the real purpose is to show respect and attention.

questions.stem: Explain in two sentences why your facial expression matters in a conversation.
answer: Accept any answer that links facial expression to feelings or communication. For example: 'Your face shows the speaker whether you are interested and how you feel about what they are saying. A matching expression makes the speaker feel heard and respected.' Award full marks if the answer mentions showing interest, respect or matching the speaker's feelings.
hints: What does your face tell the speaker?
Why does that matter?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Explains what facial expression communicates to the speaker
Explains why this matters in a conversation

questions.stem: Have a short conversation with a partner about a familiar topic (e.g., your favourite food). Your teacher will watch and assess your posture and facial expression.
hints: Sit up straight, face your partner, and show an interested face.
Keep your hands still.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Have a short conversation with a partner about what you did last weekend. Your teacher will watch your posture and facial expression throughout.
hints: Listen carefully to your partner.
Keep your face interested.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Have a conversation with a partner about a sad event (e.g., losing a pet, a difficult day). Your teacher will watch your posture and facial expression.
hints: Your face should show that you care.
Keep listening, keep facing your partner.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Facial expression matches the sad topic

questions.stem: Speak to a small group for one minute about a topic you enjoy. Your teacher will observe your posture and facial expression as you speak.
hints: Stand or sit upright.
Look at your listeners.
Let your face show your interest in the topic.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Have a conversation with an adult (teacher or elder). Your teacher will observe whether you maintain respectful posture and facial expression.
hints: Show respect with your posture.
Keep your face attentive.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Facial expression is attentive and respectful

questions.stem: Have a 2-minute conversation with a partner on a topic that changes mood (e.g., from happy to sad). Your teacher will observe whether your posture and facial expression change appropriately with the topic.
hints: Let your face reflect the change in topic.
Keep good posture throughout.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Facial expression changes with the topic

questions.stem: Have a conversation with a partner in a group setting. Your teacher will observe whether you maintain good posture and expression even when you are not speaking.
hints: Good listeners show attention even when they are not talking.
Face whoever is speaking.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Maintains posture even when not speaking

questions.stem: Have a conversation with a partner who is describing a personal experience. Your teacher will observe your posture and facial expression and how they respond to the speaker's emotions.
hints: Match your expression to the speaker's feelings.
Stay attentive throughout.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Facial expression matches the speaker's emotions
Responds appropriately to the speaker's feelings

questions.stem: Watch two classmates have a short conversation. Afterwards, tell the class one good thing about the posture and expression you saw, and one thing that could be improved.
hints: What did they do well?
What could they do better?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names one good thing about posture or expression

questions.stem: Watch a classmate have a conversation with an adult. Afterwards, describe the posture and expression you saw and say whether they were appropriate for the situation.
hints: What was the posture like?
Was the expression right for the situation?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Judges whether the behaviour was appropriate

questions.stem: Show the class what good listening posture looks like. Then show what poor listening posture looks like. Finally, tell the class which one is good and why.
hints: First show sitting up and facing forward.
Then show slouching and looking away.
Say which is good.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains which is good and why

questions.stem: Show the class a facial expression that matches a happy story, and one that matches a sad story. Then say which expression fits which story and why.
hints: Happy story — smiling face.
Sad story — serious or concerned face.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Demonstrates a sad or serious expression

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.6.2: Demonstrate positive listening and viewing attitudes and behaviour by showing attentiveness and understanding
indicator.objective: Listen and view for the entire duration of a text, speech, presentation, video etc.

skills.description: Identify the main idea of a short speech heard.
Recall a detail from the beginning of the speech.
Recall a detail from the middle of the speech.
Recall a detail from the end of the speech.
Say what the speaker wanted listeners to do or feel.
Teacher-assessed observation: pupil listens and views attentively for the entire duration without prompting.
Teacher-assessed oral: pupil retells the main points of a listened text in own words.
Teacher-assessed practical: pupil prepares a short speech and delivers it to the group while others listen.

misconceptions: Attention drifts after the first sentence

questions.stem:
Your teacher will read this short speech aloud twice. Listen carefully, then answer.

'Good morning, pupils. Today I want to talk about cleanliness. A clean school is a healthy school. When we keep our classrooms and compound clean, we do not get sick often. So please, sweep your classrooms every morning and throw your rubbish in the bin.'

What is the main idea of the speech?
options: Keeping the school clean keeps us healthy
The speaker is the head teacher
We should go to school in the morning
hints: What is the speaker mostly talking about?
Why does the speaker want us to keep the school clean?
questions.explanation: The speech is about cleanliness. It says a clean school is a healthy school, and asks pupils to sweep and throw rubbish in the bin. The main idea is that keeping the school clean keeps us healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The speaker is the head teacher' because the speech opens with 'Good morning, pupils', but the main idea is about cleanliness, not who is speaking.

questions.stem:
Your teacher will read this short speech aloud twice. Listen carefully, then answer.

'My dear friends, let us talk about reading. Many of you say you do not like reading. But reading opens doors. When you read, you learn new words, you travel to new places, and you become wiser. So pick up a book today. Start with just one page a day. You will soon love it.'

What is the main idea of the speech?
options: Reading is important and can be enjoyable
The speaker does not like reading
Only one page a day is enough
hints: What is the speaker encouraging the listeners to do?
Why does the speaker say reading matters?
questions.explanation: The speaker encourages reading by saying it opens doors, teaches new words, and makes us wiser. The main idea is that reading is important and can be enjoyable.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Only one page a day is enough' because the speaker mentions it, but that is a small suggestion, not the main idea.

questions.stem:
Your teacher will read this short speech aloud twice. Listen carefully, then answer.

'Fellow pupils, our school is our second home. We must take care of it. Do not break the desks. Do not write on the walls. If you see someone damaging school property, report to the teacher. Let us all work together to keep our school beautiful.'

What is the main idea of the speech?
options: We should take care of our school property
Our school is not a real home
Pupils should report to the teacher every day
The school should buy new desks
hints: What does the speaker want pupils to do?
Why does the speaker call the school our second home?
questions.explanation: The speaker says the school is our second home and asks pupils not to damage it, to report damage, and to work together. The main idea is that we should take care of school property.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Pupils should report to the teacher every day' because reporting is mentioned, but reporting is only one part — the main idea is care for school property.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'Good morning, pupils. Today I want to talk about cleanliness. A clean school is a healthy school. When we keep our classrooms and compound clean, we do not get sick often. So please, sweep your classrooms every morning and throw your rubbish in the bin.' What detail comes at the BEGINNING of the speech?
options: The speaker greets pupils and says the topic is cleanliness
The speaker says to sweep every morning
The speaker says a clean school is a healthy school
The speaker says to throw rubbish in the bin
hints: What are the very first words of the speech?
The speech begins with a greeting and a topic.
questions.explanation: The speech begins with 'Good morning, pupils. Today I want to talk about cleanliness.' So the beginning contains the greeting and the topic.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The speaker says a clean school is a healthy school' because it is a strong sentence, but it comes after the opening greeting.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'My dear friends, let us talk about reading. Many of you say you do not like reading. But reading opens doors. When you read, you learn new words, you travel to new places, and you become wiser. So pick up a book today. Start with just one page a day. You will soon love it.' What detail comes at the BEGINNING of the speech?
options: The speaker says many pupils do not like reading
The speaker says to read one page a day
The speaker says you will love reading
The speaker says reading makes you wiser
hints: What are the very first words about?
The speech begins with a fact about pupils.
questions.explanation: The speech begins with 'My dear friends, let us talk about reading. Many of you say you do not like reading.' The detail at the beginning is that many pupils say they do not like reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading makes you wiser' because it is a strong line, but it comes later in the speech.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'Good morning, pupils. Today I want to talk about cleanliness. A clean school is a healthy school. When we keep our classrooms and compound clean, we do not get sick often. So please, sweep your classrooms every morning and throw your rubbish in the bin.' What detail is in the MIDDLE of the speech?
options: A clean school is a healthy school
Throw your rubbish in the bin
Today I want to talk about cleanliness
hints: Which sentence comes after the opening and before the closing instruction?
The middle links cleanliness and health.
questions.explanation: The middle of the speech includes 'A clean school is a healthy school. When we keep our classrooms and compound clean, we do not get sick often.' The detail in the middle is that a clean school is a healthy school.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Throw your rubbish in the bin' because it is important, but it comes at the end as an instruction.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'My dear friends, let us talk about reading. Many of you say you do not like reading. But reading opens doors. When you read, you learn new words, you travel to new places, and you become wiser. So pick up a book today. Start with just one page a day. You will soon love it.' What detail is in the MIDDLE of the speech?
options: Reading opens doors and teaches new words
Many of you do not like reading
hints: Which sentence is in the middle?
The middle is about why reading is good.
questions.explanation: The middle of the speech says 'But reading opens doors. When you read, you learn new words, you travel to new places, and you become wiser.' The detail in the middle is that reading opens doors and teaches new words.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Pick up a book today' because it sounds like a good instruction, but it comes at the end of the speech.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'Good morning, pupils. Today I want to talk about cleanliness. A clean school is a healthy school. When we keep our classrooms and compound clean, we do not get sick often. So please, sweep your classrooms every morning and throw your rubbish in the bin.' What detail comes at the END of the speech?
options: Sweep your classrooms every morning and throw rubbish in the bin
A clean school is a healthy school
Today I want to talk about cleanliness
hints: What is the last instruction given?
The end tells pupils what to do.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the speech gives the instruction: 'So please, sweep your classrooms every morning and throw your rubbish in the bin.' This is the detail at the end.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A clean school is a healthy school' because it is memorable, but it comes in the middle, not the end.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'My dear friends, let us talk about reading. Many of you say you do not like reading. But reading opens doors. When you read, you learn new words, you travel to new places, and you become wiser. So pick up a book today. Start with just one page a day. You will soon love it.' What detail comes at the END of the speech?
options: Start with one page a day and you will soon love reading
Many of you do not like reading
You learn new words when you read
hints: What is the last suggestion given?
The end suggests a way to start reading.
questions.explanation: The end of the speech says 'So pick up a book today. Start with just one page a day. You will soon love it.' The detail at the end is the suggestion to start with one page a day and that you will soon love reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading opens doors' because it is a strong sentence, but it comes in the middle of the speech.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'Good morning, pupils. Today I want to talk about cleanliness. A clean school is a healthy school. When we keep our classrooms and compound clean, we do not get sick often. So please, sweep your classrooms every morning and throw your rubbish in the bin.' What did the speaker want listeners to DO?
options: Sweep classrooms and throw rubbish in the bin
hints: What instruction does the speaker give at the end?
The speaker asks for two specific actions.
questions.explanation: The speaker wanted pupils to sweep their classrooms and throw rubbish in the bin. These are the actions asked for in the speech.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Go home early' because the speech is in the morning, but the speaker says nothing about going home.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read this speech aloud twice: 'My dear friends, let us talk about reading. Many of you say you do not like reading. But reading opens doors. When you read, you learn new words, you travel to new places, and you become wiser. So pick up a book today. Start with just one page a day. You will soon love it.' What did the speaker want listeners to FEEL?
hints: How does the speaker talk about reading?
The speaker encourages listeners.
questions.explanation: The speaker encourages listeners to start reading by pointing out its benefits and suggesting a small first step. The speaker wants them to feel encouraged, not afraid or bored.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Angry about books' because the speaker mentions that some pupils do not like reading, but the speaker is trying to change that feeling, not cause it.

questions.stem: Listen carefully to a short speech your teacher reads aloud (about 1 minute). Your teacher will watch to see if you listen attentively for the whole time.
hints: Face the speaker.
Do not talk or move around.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Listens for the whole speech without interruption

questions.stem: Listen to a recorded short speech or song played on a phone or speaker. Your teacher will watch to see if you listen attentively for the whole time.
hints: Sit still.
Listen carefully from start to finish.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Listens attentively for the entire recording
Does not talk during the recording
Is ready to answer questions after

questions.stem: Watch a short video of a speech (about 1-2 minutes). Your teacher will watch to see if you listen and view attentively for the whole time.
hints: Look at the screen.
Do not look away or talk.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Watches and listens for the whole video
Does not look away for long
Does not talk during the video

questions.stem: Listen to a classmate give a short speech (about 1 minute) to the class. Your teacher will watch to see if you listen attentively throughout.
hints: Face the speaker.
Show interest with your expression.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Listen to a longer speech (about 2-3 minutes) with no prompts. Your teacher will watch to see if you remain attentive throughout without prompting.
hints: Stay focused for the whole time.
Do not fidget or look away.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Listens for the whole speech without prompting
Is ready to retell the main points after

questions.stem: Listen to a short speech your teacher reads. Afterwards, retell the main points in your own words to a partner or small group.
hints: What was the speech mostly about?
What did the speaker want you to do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States the main idea of the speech
Gives at least one detail from the speech

questions.stem: Listen to a short speech or presentation. Afterwards, retell the main points and one detail from the beginning, one from the middle and one from the end.
hints: What was the main idea?
What did the speaker say at the start, middle and end?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a detail from the beginning
Gives a detail from the middle
Gives a detail from the end

questions.stem: Prepare a short 1-minute speech on a familiar topic (e.g., 'Why I like my school'). Deliver it to a small group while the group listens carefully.
hints: Plan what you will say first.
Speak clearly.
Look at your listeners.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Prepare a short 2-minute speech on a topic you care about. Deliver it to the class. Afterwards, answer two questions from your listeners about your speech.
hints: Plan your main points.
Practise once before you speak.
Be ready to answer questions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Has a clear main idea and at least two supporting points

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation on topics such as social issues, values and manners with adults

skills.description: Recognise which topic is suitable for a conversation with an adult.
Choose the polite way to disagree with an adult in conversation.
Choose the question that keeps a conversation going.
Match please, thank you, excuse me, sorry to the right moment in a conversation.
Teacher-assessed oral: hold a 2-3 minute conversation with an adult on a social, value or manners topic, taking turns.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to an adult's view and respond respectfully, even when disagreeing.
Teacher-assessed oral: watch a conversation and comment on whether it was collaborative and polite.

misconceptions: Asking a question then not listening

questions.stem: Which topic is suitable for a conversation with your teacher?
options: How to improve our school library
How much money the teacher earns
Why the teacher's family is small
What the teacher ate for breakfast
hints: Which topic is appropriate for a school setting?
Some personal topics are not polite to ask.
questions.explanation: Improving the school library is a school topic, suitable for a conversation with a teacher. Asking about a teacher's salary, family or breakfast is too personal and impolite.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What the teacher ate for breakfast' because it is a friendly question, but it is too personal for a teacher-pupil conversation.

questions.stem: Which topic is suitable for a conversation with an elder in your community?
options: Ways to keep the community clean
How much the elder paid for their house
What the elder's medical condition is
hints: Which topic is good for the community?
Some personal details are not polite to ask.
questions.explanation: Keeping the community clean is a community topic suitable for any elder. Asking about the elder's house price, medical condition or age is too personal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The elder's age' because elders often know their age, but asking an elder their age directly is impolite in many cultures.

questions.stem: An adult says, 'Children should not use phones at all.' You disagree. What is the polite way to disagree?
options: I see your point, but I think phones can be useful if we use them carefully.
You don't know anything about phones.
hints: Which sentence shows respect for the adult's view?
It should give your view politely.
questions.explanation: The polite way to disagree begins by showing respect for the adult's view ('I see your point') and then gives your own view clearly and calmly. The other options are rude and argumentative.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You are wrong!' because it is direct, but direct and rude are not the same. Politeness matters with adults.

questions.stem: An adult says, 'Our town should have a new football field.' You think a library is more important. What is the polite way to disagree?
options: That is a good idea, but I wonder if a library would help more pupils.
You don't know what pupils need.
hints: Which sentence shows respect?
It offers another view politely.
questions.explanation: The polite way disagrees with respect: 'That is a good idea, but I wonder if a library would help more pupils.' This shows you listened and then offered your view. The other options dismiss the adult's idea rudely.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'That's a bad idea' because it is clear, but it is impolite. A polite disagreement should not dismiss the other person's view.

questions.stem: An adult says, 'Pupils should not play football; they should study all the time.' You think football and study can both be balanced. What is the polite way to disagree?
options: I understand what you mean, but I think pupils can do both — study and play — if they manage their time.
That is the worst idea I have ever heard.
Football is more important than study.
hints: Which response shows respect for the adult?
It should offer a different view calmly.
questions.explanation: The polite disagreement respects the adult's concern ('I understand what you mean') and offers a calm, balanced view. The other responses are rude or extreme.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Football is more important than study' because it gives a strong view, but it is impolite and extreme.

questions.stem: An adult is telling you about their work as a nurse. Which question keeps the conversation going?
options: What made you want to become a nurse?
Why do you talk so much?
hints: Which question shows interest in the adult's story?
The best question invites the person to say more.
questions.explanation: Asking 'What made you want to become a nurse?' shows interest and invites the adult to share more. It keeps the conversation going.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Are you done talking yet?' because they want to move on, but this question is rude and ends the conversation instead of keeping it going.

questions.stem: An adult tells you about a festival they enjoy. Which question keeps the conversation going?
options: What do you enjoy most about the festival?
Why do you like that festival?
hints: Which question invites the adult to share more about their enjoyment?
Both (A) and (C) are fine, but one is more open.
questions.explanation: Both 'What do you enjoy most about the festival?' and 'Why do you like that festival?' keep the conversation going. In this item, 'What do you enjoy most about the festival?' is the most open and inviting. 'Is the festival boring?' is rude and closed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Which festival is the best?' because it asks for an opinion, but it closes the conversation by inviting the adult to rank festivals. The open question invites them to share their experience.

questions.stem: You want to ask a teacher a question but the teacher is talking to another adult. What do you say?
options: Excuse me, sir/madam, may I ask a question when you are free?
Hey, I want to talk to you now.
Move, I need to speak to the teacher.
hints: Which phrase shows respect?
'Excuse me' is a polite opener.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me, sir/madam, may I ask a question when you are free?' uses polite words and respects that the teacher is busy. The other options are rude.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Teacher, come here!' because it gets attention, but it is impolite, especially to a teacher.

questions.stem: An elder gives you a gift. What do you say?
hints: What do you say when someone gives you something?
'Thank you' shows appreciation.
questions.explanation: 'Thank you very much' is the polite response to a gift. It shows appreciation. The other responses are rude or unappreciative.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Okay' because it is short, but it does not show appreciation. A gift deserves a thank you.

questions.stem: Have a 2-minute conversation with your teacher or another adult about a social issue in your community (e.g., keeping the market clean). Take turns, listen carefully, and respond to what the adult says.
hints: Listen to what the adult says before you answer.
Take turns — don't talk over them.
Ask a question to keep the conversation going.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Responds to what the adult says

questions.stem: Have a 2-minute conversation with an adult about a value such as honesty or respect. Take turns and show respect throughout.
hints: Listen first, then speak.
Show respect with your words and tone.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Have a 2-minute conversation with an adult about manners (e.g., how children should greet elders). Show good manners throughout.
hints: Use polite words like 'please', 'thank you', 'excuse me'.
Take turns.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Have a 3-minute conversation with an adult about a social issue (e.g., why children should help keep the community clean). Listen, ask questions, and respond respectfully throughout.
hints: Ask questions to keep it going.
Listen carefully to the adult's views.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Responds to the adult's views respectfully

questions.stem: Have a 3-minute conversation with an adult on a topic of your choice (social issue, value or manner). Show that you can lead some of the conversation by asking questions and offering your views politely.
hints: Start with a polite opening.
Ask questions and give your own views.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Listen as an adult shares a view you do not agree with. Respond respectfully, explaining your own view without being rude.
hints: Start with something like 'I see your point.'
Then give your view politely.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Does not interrupt or raise voice

questions.stem: An adult says something you think is wrong. Respond with respect, giving one reason for your different view.
hints: Respect first, reason second.
Do not say 'you are wrong'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one reason for the different view

questions.stem: In a conversation, an adult shares a view you strongly disagree with. Respond respectfully with a different view, give a reason, and then invite the adult to continue the conversation.
hints: Acknowledge, disagree politely, give a reason, invite more talk.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Watch two people have a conversation. Afterwards, tell the class one thing that was collaborative and polite, and one thing that could be improved.
hints: Did they take turns?
Did they listen to each other?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Identifies one positive example of collaboration or politeness

questions.stem: Watch a conversation between an adult and a pupil. Was it collaborative? Was it polite? Explain your answer with one example from the conversation.
hints: Did the speakers listen to each other?
Did they show respect?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Judges whether the conversation was collaborative
Gives one example to support the judgement

questions.stem: Watch a short recorded conversation (or two classmates role-play). Comment on two specific things that made it collaborative and polite, and one thing that could be improved.
hints: Look for turn-taking, listening and respect.
Be specific — name what you saw.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Identifies two specific collaborative or polite behaviours

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Demonstrate turn taking in conversation in different topics and follow agreed-upon rules for conversation, e.g. listening to others, speaking one at a time.

skills.description: Recognise which rule of conversation is being followed or broken in a short transcript.
Choose the right repair phrase for a problem in conversation.
Arrange a jumbled exchange into a sensible turn-taking order.
Teacher-assessed observation: in a pair or group conversation, take turns and speak one at a time.
Teacher-assessed observation: listen without interrupting while another person speaks, and respond to what they said.
Teacher-assessed oral: use a repair phrase appropriately when needed.

misconceptions: Speaking one at a time = only one person talks
Repair phrase at the wrong moment

questions.stem:
Read this short exchange:
Ama: 'I went to the market yesterday.'
Kofi: 'Oh, what did you buy?'
Ama: 'I bought some tomatoes.'
Which rule of conversation is being followed?
options: Listening to others and taking turns
Speaking one at a time only
hints: Did each person wait for the other to finish?
Did Kofi respond to what Ama said?
questions.explanation: Kofi waited for Ama to finish, then responded with a question about what she said. This shows listening and turn-taking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Speaking one at a time only' because only one person speaks at a time in this exchange, but that would be too narrow — the exchange also shows listening and responding.

questions.stem:
Read this short exchange:
Ama: 'I went to the...'
Kofi: 'I went to the beach on Saturday!'
Ama: '...market yesterday.'
Which rule of conversation is being broken?
hints: Did Kofi wait for Ama to finish?
Kofi interrupted Ama.
questions.explanation: Kofi interrupted Ama before she finished her sentence. He broke the rule of listening and taking turns.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Speaking one at a time' because it is a rule, but Kofi did speak alone — he interrupted. The rule broken is turn-taking.

questions.stem:
Read this exchange:
Ama: 'Can you help me with my homework?'
Kofi: 'Sorry, what did you say?'
Ama: 'I asked if you can help me with my homework.'
Kofi: 'Oh, yes, of course.'
Which rule is being followed?
options: Using a repair phrase when something is not heard
hints: Kofi did not hear what Ama said. What did he say?
He asked her to repeat.
questions.explanation: Kofi said 'Sorry, what did you say?' — a repair phrase. He followed the rule of repairing the conversation when he missed something.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Changing the topic' because Kofi's response seems off, but he is asking for repetition, not changing the topic.

questions.stem:
Read this exchange:
Ama: 'Do you like football?'
Kofi: 'Yes, I do.'
Ama: 'Why do you like it?'
Kofi: 'Because it is exciting and I play with my friends.'
Which rule is being followed?
hints: Did Kofi answer Ama's questions?
Did he wait for her to finish?
questions.explanation: Kofi waited for Ama to finish, answered her question and responded to her follow-up question. This shows listening and responding appropriately.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Changing the topic' because the topic moves to why Kofi likes football, but the follow-up question is on the same topic.

questions.stem: You did not hear what your friend said. What do you say?
hints: Which phrase is polite and asks for a repeat?
'Sorry, could you repeat that?' is a repair phrase.
questions.explanation: 'Sorry, could you repeat that?' is a polite repair phrase. It asks the speaker to repeat without blaming them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Speak up next time' because it asks for louder speech, but it blames the speaker and is impolite.

questions.stem: You want to say something but two friends are talking. What do you say to take your turn?
options: Excuse me, may I say something?
Stop talking, I want to speak.
hints: Which phrase is polite and asks for a turn?
'Excuse me' is a polite opener.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me, may I say something?' politely asks for a turn. The other options are rude and interrupt.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It's my turn now!' because it asks for a turn, but it is demanding and impolite.

questions.stem: You did not understand what your teacher said. What do you say?
options: Please, sir/madam, could you explain that again?
hints: Which phrase is polite and asks for clarification?
The teacher's title shows respect.
questions.explanation: 'Please, sir/madam, could you explain that again?' is polite and respects the teacher. The other options are rude or too informal for a teacher.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Repeat!' because it is short, but it sounds like a command and is impolite to a teacher.

questions.stem:
Arrange these lines into a sensible conversation:
A: 'Yes, please. I'd love some.'
B: 'Would you like some water?'
C: 'Here you are.'
D: 'Thank you.'
hints: Who speaks first? The person offering.
Then the reply, then the giving, then the thanks.
questions.explanation: The sensible order: B offers water, A accepts, C gives it, D thanks. So B, A, C, D.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the thanks (D) first because it feels polite, but the thanks must come after the offering.

questions.stem:
Arrange these lines into a sensible conversation:
A: 'I went to the market.'
B: 'Oh, what did you buy?'
C: 'I bought tomatoes and pepper.'
D: 'That sounds nice.'
hints: Who speaks first? The person with the news.
Then the question, then the answer, then the comment.
questions.explanation: The sensible order: A shares news, B asks a question, C answers, D comments. So A, B, C, D.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the question first because questions often start conversations, but in this case the news comes first and the question follows it.

questions.stem: Have a short conversation with a partner about a familiar topic (e.g., your favourite food). Take turns — each person speaks, then the other.
hints: Wait for your partner to finish.
Then it is your turn.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Waits for the partner to finish speaking

questions.stem: In a group of three, discuss what you did on Saturday. Each person should speak in turn without interrupting others.
hints: Wait your turn.
Listen when others speak.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: In a pair, have a conversation where you each speak twice. Take turns so that no one speaks over the other.
hints: Signal with a nod or pause when you are finished.
Let your partner respond.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: No one speaks over the other

questions.stem: In a small group, discuss a topic (e.g., what makes a good friend). Each person must contribute at least once, and no one should speak more than twice in a row.
hints: Make space for others to speak.
Let others have a turn.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each person contributes at least once

questions.stem: In a group of four, hold a short discussion where you take turns speaking one at a time. The group must agree on one rule (e.g., 'we raise hands to speak') and follow it.
hints: Agree on the rule first.
Follow the rule throughout.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Listen to a partner tell a short story about their weekend. Do not interrupt. When they finish, ask one question about what they said.
hints: Listen carefully — you will need to ask about a detail.
Wait until they finish.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Asks a question based on what was said

questions.stem: Listen as a classmate shares an opinion. Do not interrupt. After they finish, summarise what they said in one sentence.
hints: Listen for the main point.
Then repeat it back.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Waits for the speaker to finish

questions.stem: In a small group, listen as one person speaks. Then respond to what they said — not to something else. Show you heard them.
hints: Mention their point in your response.
Say 'I heard you say...' or ask a follow-up question.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Shows they heard by referencing the point

questions.stem: In a pair, hold a 2-minute conversation. You must respond to every point your partner makes, without interrupting or changing the topic.
hints: Respond to what they said.
Stay on the topic.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: During a conversation, pretend you did not hear what your partner said. Use a polite repair phrase to ask them to repeat.
hints: Try 'Sorry, could you repeat that?'
Be polite.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the phrase at the right moment (after missing something)
Partner can respond and conversation continues

questions.stem: During a group conversation, politely ask for a turn using a repair phrase (e.g., 'Excuse me, may I say something?'). Then say your point.
hints: Wait for a pause.
Use a polite opener.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses a polite repair phrase to ask for a turn
Makes their point after being given a turn

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Employ the Think-Aloud strategy to convey meaning from level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Recognise what the Think-Aloud strategy is.
Choose the thought that shows a pupil making meaning.
Recognise a thought that is not Think-Aloud.
Say at which moment in listening a Think-Aloud thought is most useful.
Teacher-assessed oral: listen to a short text and think aloud 2-3 thoughts while listening.
Teacher-assessed oral: explain how Think-Aloud helped them understand a text heard.

misconceptions: I don't know as a thought

questions.stem: What does the Think-Aloud strategy mean?
options: Saying your thinking out loud as you listen or read
Reading the text aloud to the class
Thinking about something else while listening
Writing down every word you hear
hints: The strategy has 'aloud' in its name.
You are saying your thinking, not the text.
questions.explanation: Think-Aloud means saying your thinking out loud as you listen or read — for example, saying 'This reminds me of...' or 'I wonder why...' It is not reading the text aloud.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading the text aloud' because the word 'aloud' appears in both, but Think-Aloud is about saying your thoughts, not reading.

questions.stem: Think-Aloud helps a listener to:
options: Make meaning from the text as they listen
Copy the text word for word
hints: What is the goal of listening?
Think-Aloud helps you understand as you go.
questions.explanation: Think-Aloud helps a listener make meaning from the text as they listen — it keeps them actively thinking about what they hear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Copy the text word for word' because they think the goal is memorisation, but the goal is understanding.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The farmer woke up early and went to the farm.' Which thought shows a pupil making meaning?
options: I think the farmer is hard-working because he woke up early.
hints: Which thought shows the pupil thinking about the meaning?
It starts with 'I think...' and gives a reason.
questions.explanation: The thought 'I think the farmer is hard-working because he woke up early' shows the pupil making meaning — connecting an action to a character trait.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The farmer woke up early' because it repeats the text, but repeating is not thinking. It is just echoing.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'Ama saw a dark cloud in the sky. She ran home quickly.' Which thought shows a pupil making meaning?
options: I think it is going to rain because the cloud is dark.
A dark cloud is in the sky.
I don't know what will happen.
hints: Which thought makes a prediction based on the text?
It connects the dark cloud to rain.
questions.explanation: The thought 'I think it is going to rain because the cloud is dark' shows the pupil making a prediction from the text — a good Think-Aloud thought.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I like clouds' because it is about clouds, but it is off-task. The pupil is not thinking about the meaning of the text.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'Kofi forgot his homework at home. He walked to school looking sad.' Which thought shows a pupil making meaning?
options: I wonder what will happen when the teacher asks for the homework.
I forgot where I put my pencil once.
hints: Which thought shows the pupil wondering what comes next?
It connects to the problem Kofi has.
questions.explanation: The thought 'I wonder what will happen when the teacher asks for the homework' shows the pupil making meaning — thinking ahead about the story's problem.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I forgot where I put my pencil once' because it connects to their own life, but it is off-task. It doesn't help make meaning from the text.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The two brothers shared everything. Even when there was little food, they shared it equally.' Which thought shows the pupil making meaning?
options: This reminds me of how my family shares food when we have little.
I don't understand what sharing means.
hints: Which thought connects the text to real life?
It links the story to the pupil's own family.
questions.explanation: The thought 'This reminds me of how my family shares food when we have little' shows the pupil connecting the text to real life — a strong Think-Aloud move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The brothers shared food' because it repeats the text, but repetition is not thinking.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The rain fell heavily on the village.' Which of these is a POOR Think-Aloud thought?
options: The rain fell heavily on the village.
I wonder if the village will flood.
This reminds me of a rainy day at my house.
I think the people will need umbrellas.
hints: Which thought just repeats the text?
A good Think-Aloud thought adds something new.
questions.explanation: The thought 'The rain fell heavily on the village' just repeats the text — it does not show the pupil thinking about the meaning. The other three thoughts show real thinking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I wonder if the village will flood' because it seems simple, but it is a genuine Think-Aloud prediction, not a poor thought.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The old man smiled and gave the boy a mango.' Which of these is a POOR Think-Aloud thought?
options: I don't know anything about mangoes.
I think the old man is kind.
This reminds me of my grandfather.
I wonder why the old man gave the boy a mango.
hints: Which thought does not help make meaning?
One thought says 'I don't know' — that stops thinking.
questions.explanation: The thought 'I don't know anything about mangoes' does not help make meaning from the text. It is a poor thought. The other three show real thinking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I wonder why the old man gave the boy a mango' because it is a question, but it is a good Think-Aloud thought, not a poor one.

questions.stem: When is a Think-Aloud thought most useful?
options: While you are listening to the text, as you make sense of it
Only after the text has ended
hints: When do you need to make sense of the text?
It is most useful when you are working out the meaning as you listen.
questions.explanation: Think-Aloud is most useful while you are listening, so you can make sense of the text as it unfolds. It can also be used before and after, but its main moment is during listening.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Only after the text has ended' because they think of it as a discussion, but the strategy is designed to help during listening.

questions.stem: Which of these moments is a good time to use a Think-Aloud thought?
options: When a character does something surprising
hints: When does a Think-Aloud help most during listening?
At a moment in the text when something is interesting or surprising.
questions.explanation: A good moment for Think-Aloud is when something in the text surprises you or makes you wonder — for example, when a character does something surprising. That is when making meaning is most useful.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'When the teacher finishes reading' because they think Think-Aloud is a discussion after the text, but its real power is during listening.

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read: 'The hungry dog looked at the boy's bread. The boy broke the bread in half and gave one piece to the dog.' As you listen, say two thoughts aloud (for example, 'This reminds me of...' or 'I wonder...').
hints: Say what you are thinking as you listen.
Try 'I think...' or 'This reminds me of...'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Says at least two thoughts aloud during listening

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read: 'The sun was very hot. The children ran to the shade of the big mango tree.' As you listen, say two thoughts aloud that show you are making meaning from the text.
hints: What do you think will happen?
What does this remind you of?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Says at least two thoughts aloud

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read: 'Esi found a purse on the way to school. She looked around for the owner. No one was there. She put the purse in her bag and walked on. She felt worried.' Say 3 thoughts aloud as you listen, including one about how Esi feels.
hints: What is Esi thinking?
How does she feel?
What would you do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Says at least three thoughts aloud
One thought is about Esi's feelings
Thoughts show making meaning from the text

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read: 'Kofi planted a seed. Every day he watered it. After two weeks, a small green shoot appeared. Kofi jumped for joy.' Say 3 thoughts aloud as you listen, including a prediction.
hints: What will happen after the shoot appears?
How does Kofi feel?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Says at least three thoughts aloud
Thoughts are connected to the text

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read: 'The market was very busy. A small girl was crying near a stall. A woman in a blue cloth knelt beside her and spoke softly. The girl stopped crying and took the woman's hand.' Say 3-4 thoughts aloud as you listen, including one connection to your own life and one prediction.
hints: What is happening? Why is the girl crying?
What will the woman do next?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Says at least three thoughts aloud
One thought connects to own life
Thoughts are on-task and help make meaning

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read a short text on a topic you know well (e.g., a football match). Say 3-4 thoughts aloud as you listen, using at least three of these: 'I think...', 'This reminds me of...', 'I wonder...', 'This is like when...'.
hints: Use the sentence starters.
Say what you are thinking as you listen.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three different sentence starters
Says at least three thoughts aloud

questions.stem: After using Think-Aloud during a short text your teacher reads, explain in 2 sentences how thinking aloud helped you understand the text.
hints: What did you understand better because you thought aloud?
Give an example of a thought that helped.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one example of a helpful thought

questions.stem: Think of a time you used Think-Aloud. Tell your teacher or a small group about it and explain what you understood because of your thoughts.
hints: What were you listening to?
What did you think?
What did you understand?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Connects their thought to the understanding
