questions.stem: Listen to a short text your teacher reads. Then explain in 3 sentences: (a) what the text was about, (b) what you thought while listening, and (c) how your thoughts helped you understand.
hints: First say what the text was about.
Then say what you thought.
Then say how the thinking helped.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States what the text was about
Explains how the thought helped understanding

questions.stem: Compare two ways of listening: (1) just listening without thinking aloud, and (2) listening with Think-Aloud. Which one helps you understand better, and why?
hints: Which one keeps you active as a listener?
Why does that help?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a reason (keeps active, helps make meaning, etc.)
Explains with an example or detail

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Make connections with events in drama

skills.description: Identify the order of events in a short drama.
Place a given event in the beginning, middle or ending of the drama.
Choose a real-life situation that matches an event in the drama.
Explain why an event in the drama reminds them of something in their own life.
Link an event to the character who caused it.
Teacher-assessed oral: retell the events of a drama heard, in order.
Teacher-assessed oral: say which event in the drama is like something in their own life and why.

questions.stem:
Your teacher will read this short drama aloud twice:

(Narrator) Ama and Kofi are in the market.
Ama: Oh no, I have lost my money!
Kofi: Don't worry. Let us look for it together.
Ama: I found it! It was under my cloth.
Kofi: Thank God.

Which event happens FIRST?
options: Ama and Kofi are in the market
hints: What is the very first thing that happens in the drama?
The narrator sets the scene first.
questions.explanation: The drama begins with the narrator setting the scene: Ama and Kofi are in the market. Then Ama loses her money, Kofi says not to worry, and Ama finds it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama loses her money' because it is the first line of dialogue, but the narrator's setting line comes first.

questions.stem:
Your teacher will read this short drama aloud twice:

(Narrator) Two boys are playing football.
Kojo: Pass the ball!
Yaw: I am passing it!
(The ball goes over the wall.)
Kojo: Oh no! Now we have lost the ball.
Yaw: Let us go and find it.

Which event happens LAST?
options: They go to find the ball
The ball goes over the wall
hints: What is the last thing said or done in the drama?
The last line is 'Let us go and find it.'
questions.explanation: The last line of the drama is Yaw saying 'Let us go and find it.' So going to find the ball is the last event.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The ball goes over the wall' because it is the big moment, but the story continues after that.

questions.stem:
Your teacher will read this short drama aloud twice:

(Narrator) A girl is walking home.
Girl: I am so tired and hungry.
(An old woman appears at the roadside.)
Old Woman: My child, would you like a piece of bread?
Girl: Oh, thank you, Grandma!
Old Woman: God bless you, my child.

Which order matches the events?
options: Girl walks home → girl is tired → old woman appears → old woman offers bread
Old woman offers bread → girl walks home → girl is tired → old woman appears
Girl is tired → old woman offers bread → girl walks home → old woman appears
Old woman appears → girl walks home → girl is tired → old woman offers bread
hints: What happens first?
The narrator sets the scene first, then the girl speaks.
questions.explanation: Correct order: girl walks home (narrator), girl is tired, old woman appears, old woman offers bread.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the old woman appearing first because she seems like the main character, but the girl is introduced first.

questions.stem: In the drama about Ama losing her money in the market, in which part does the event 'Ama finds her money under her cloth' happen?
hints: What part of the drama brings it to a close?
The finding solves the problem.
questions.explanation: 'Ama finds her money under her cloth' happens at the end — after she has lost it and Kofi has helped her look. This resolves the problem.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Middle' because the finding is exciting, but it is the resolution, which comes at the end.

questions.stem: In the drama about the boys playing football and losing the ball, in which part does the event 'Kojo says pass the ball' happen?
hints: What part sets up the action?
The game is just starting.
questions.explanation: 'Pass the ball' happens at the beginning, when the boys are starting to play. It sets up the action of the drama.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Middle' because Kojo is being active, but 'pass the ball' is an early line before the ball goes over the wall.

questions.stem: In the drama about the girl and the old woman, in which part does the event 'old woman offers bread' happen?
hints: The girl is walking and tired first. Then the old woman appears and offers bread.
It is not the very first event, nor the resolution.
questions.explanation: The old woman offering bread happens in the middle. First the girl walks home and is tired, then the old woman appears and offers bread, and at the end the girl thanks her.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Beginning' because the old woman appears early, but the girl walking home comes first, and the thanks come last.

questions.stem: In the drama about Ama losing her money, which real-life situation is most like Ama's?
options: You lost your pencil in class and your friend helped you find it
You ate too much at break time
You did not do your homework
hints: What happened to Ama?
What did she need? Who helped her?
questions.explanation: Ama lost something, was worried, and a friend helped her look. This is most like losing a pencil and being helped by a friend.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You ate too much at break time' because it is about food or the market, but the event in the drama is about losing something.

questions.stem: In the drama about the boys losing the football, which real-life situation is most like their problem?
options: You were playing and your ball went over a fence
You watched a match on TV
hints: What happened to the ball?
Where did it go?
questions.explanation: The boys were playing and the ball went over the wall. This is most like your ball going over a fence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You scored a goal' because both are about football, but the drama is about losing the ball, not scoring.

questions.stem: In the drama about the girl and the old woman, which real-life situation is most like the drama?
options: A neighbour offers you food when you are hungry
You buy food from a market
You refuse food from a stranger
hints: What did the old woman do?
How did the girl feel?
questions.explanation: The girl was tired and hungry, and the old woman offered her bread. This is most like a neighbour offering you food when you are hungry.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You buy food from a market' because it is about food, but the drama is about a gift, not a purchase.

questions.stem: In a drama, a boy is afraid to speak in front of the class. He finally speaks, and the class claps. Which real-life situation is most like the boy's?
options: You were shy about reading aloud and finally did it, and your friends clapped
You were the best reader in class
hints: What did the boy overcome?
How did the class respond?
questions.explanation: The boy was afraid, finally spoke, and the class clapped. This is most like being shy about reading aloud, finally doing it, and being clapped.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You were the best reader in class' because both involve reading, but the drama is about overcoming fear, not being the best.

questions.stem: In a drama, a boy is afraid to speak in front of the class. He finally speaks, and the class claps. Explain why this reminds you of a real-life experience (yours or someone you know). Write 2-3 sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that gives a real-life experience of overcoming fear or shyness, and explains the connection. Award full marks if the answer describes the situation and links it to the drama.
hints: What did you or someone you know do that was hard?
How is that like the boy in the drama?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Describes a real-life situation of overcoming fear or shyness
Explains the connection to the drama

questions.stem: In a drama, two brothers share the last piece of bread. Explain why this reminds you of a real-life experience (yours or someone you know). Write 2-3 sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that describes sharing with someone in real life. Award full marks if the answer describes the sharing and explains the connection to the drama.
hints: When have you shared something with someone?
How is that like the brothers in the drama?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Describes a real-life situation of sharing
Explains the connection to the drama

questions.stem: In a drama, a girl is lost in a new town. Explain why this reminds you of a real-life experience (yours or someone you know). Write 2-3 sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that describes a real-life situation of being lost or unfamiliar. Award full marks if the answer describes it and explains the connection.
hints: Have you ever been lost or in a new place?
How did you feel? How did it end?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Describes a real-life situation of being lost or unfamiliar
Explains the connection to the drama

questions.stem: In the drama about Ama losing her money, who says 'I found it! It was under my cloth'?
hints: Who lost the money?
Who looked for it?
questions.explanation: Ama says 'I found it! It was under my cloth' — she is the one who lost the money and found it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi' because he helped look, but Ama found the money and said the line.

questions.stem: In the drama about the boys losing the football, who says 'Let us go and find it'?
hints: Who is the second boy in the drama?
Look at the last line of the drama.
questions.explanation: Yaw says 'Let us go and find it.' He is the one who suggests looking for the ball.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kojo' because Kojo has more lines, but the last line belongs to Yaw.

questions.stem: In the drama about the girl and the old woman, who offers the bread?
hints: Who is the kind character in the drama?
Who appears at the roadside?
questions.explanation: The old woman offers the bread. The narrator introduces her, and she speaks the line 'My child, would you like a piece of bread?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The girl' because she is the one who is hungry, but she receives the bread — she does not offer it.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read a short drama aloud. Retell the events of the drama in the correct order — what happened at the beginning, what happened next, and how it ended.
hints: Begin with what happened first.
Then say what happened next.
Then how it ended.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Speaks clearly and in complete sentences

questions.stem: Your teacher will read a short drama aloud. Retell the events in order, name the characters, and say what problem the characters had.
hints: Who was in the drama?
What was the problem?
How did it end?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: After listening to a short drama, tell your teacher or a small group about one event in the drama that is like something in your own life. Say what the event was and why it is like your experience.
hints: What event in the drama felt familiar?
Why did it feel familiar?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names one event in the drama

questions.stem: After listening to a short drama, tell your teacher or a small group about TWO events in the drama that connect to your life, and explain why each one connects.
hints: Name the event.
Say what real-life experience it reminds you of.
Explain the connection.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names two events from the drama

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Use background knowledge to understand and build new knowledge while listening to drama

skills.description: Identify what you already know about a topic before listening.
Match the drama to a familiar story or real-life situation with a similar plot.
Say one new thing learnt from the drama.
Choose how background knowledge helps understand a character's action in the drama.
Say whether the drama confirmed or changed what they already thought.
Teacher-assessed oral: discuss in a group what was known, added, and now believed.
Teacher-assessed oral: share one thing learnt and how it connects to prior knowledge.

questions.stem: Before you listen to a drama about a farmer, what would you want to think about first?
options: What I already know about farming and farmers
hints: What is the drama about?
What do you already know about it?
questions.explanation: Before listening to a drama about a farmer, you should activate your background knowledge — what you already know about farming and farmers. This helps you understand the drama better.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What I ate for breakfast' because it is something they know, but it has nothing to do with the drama.

questions.stem: You are about to listen to a drama set in a market. Which of these is background knowledge you can use?
options: What markets look like and what happens there
The names of planets in the solar system
How to solve a maths problem
What happened in a football match
hints: Which of these is about markets?
Background knowledge should connect to the drama's setting.
questions.explanation: Background knowledge about markets — what they look like, what happens there — helps you understand a drama set in a market.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What happened in a football match' because both are lively, but football knowledge does not help with a market drama.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads a drama about a boy who disobeys his mother and gets lost. Which familiar story is most like this?
options: A story about a child who disobeyed and lost his way
A story about a boy who wins a race
A story about a rich king
A story about a farmer and his crops
hints: What is the main plot of the drama?
Which familiar story has a similar problem?
questions.explanation: The drama is about disobedience and getting lost. A familiar story with the same plot is one about a child who disobeyed and lost his way. They share a similar lesson and events.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A story about a boy who wins a race' because it is about a boy, but the plot is different — winning a race is not like getting lost.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads a drama about a kind stranger who helps a lost child. Which familiar story or real-life situation is most like this?
options: A stranger helped you find your way home when you were lost
You won a prize at school
You ate lunch with your friends
You watched a film about animals
hints: What is the drama about?
Which situation has the same action — a stranger helping a lost child?
questions.explanation: The drama is about a kind stranger helping a lost child. The real-life situation most like this is when a stranger helped you find your way when you were lost.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You won a prize at school' because it is a happy situation, but it does not share the same plot.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads a drama about two friends who quarrel over a toy and later make up. Which familiar story is most like this?
options: A story about two brothers who quarrel and then forgive each other
A story about a lion and a mouse
A story about a farmer and a golden egg
A story about a girl who becomes a queen
hints: What happens between the friends?
Which story has the same quarrel-then-forgive pattern?
questions.explanation: The drama shows quarrelling and forgiving. A story about two brothers who quarrel and forgive each other has the same pattern.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A story about a lion and a mouse' because it is a well-known story about friends, but the plot is about a lion sparing a mouse, not about quarrelling and forgiving.

questions.stem: Listen to a short drama your teacher reads about a boy who lives on a cocoa farm. Write one thing you learned about cocoa farming from the drama that you did not know before.
answer: Accept any answer that names a specific fact about cocoa farming from the drama. Award full marks if the fact is clearly from the drama.
hints: What did the boy do on the farm?
What did you learn that you did not know before?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Names one new fact from the drama
The fact is about cocoa farming

questions.stem: Listen to a short drama your teacher reads about a nurse at a clinic. Write one thing you learned about a nurse's work from the drama that you did not know before.
answer: Accept any answer that names a specific fact about a nurse's work from the drama. Award full marks if the fact is clearly from the drama.
hints: What did the nurse do in the drama?
What was new to you?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Names one new fact from the drama

questions.stem: Listen to a short drama your teacher reads about a fisherman. Write two things you learned about fishing from the drama that you did not know before.
answer: Accept any answer that names two specific facts about fishing from the drama. Award full marks if both facts are clearly from the drama.
hints: What did the fisherman do?
What tools did he use?
What did you learn?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Names two new facts from the drama

questions.stem: In a drama, a trader in a market is shouting 'Buy my tomatoes! Fresh tomatoes!' Why does the trader shout?
options: Because shouting is how traders attract buyers in the market
Because the trader has no customers
hints: What do you know about markets?
Why do traders call out to buyers?
questions.explanation: Background knowledge about markets tells us that traders shout to attract buyers. The trader is not angry or impolite — shouting is part of market life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because the trader is angry' because shouting can mean anger, but in a market, shouting is a normal way to call buyers.

questions.stem: In a drama, a girl bows her head when she greets an elder. Why does she bow her head?
options: Because bowing shows respect for elders in many Ghanaian communities
hints: What do you know about greeting elders?
In many communities, bowing shows respect.
questions.explanation: Background knowledge tells us that bowing the head when greeting an elder shows respect in many Ghanaian communities. It is not about tiredness or shyness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because she is shy' because bowing can look shy, but in this context it shows respect.

questions.stem: In a drama, a boy refuses to eat food offered by a stranger. Why might he do this?
options: Because he has been taught not to accept food from strangers
Because he does not like the food
hints: What safety lesson have you been taught about strangers?
Why might a child refuse food from a stranger?
questions.explanation: Background knowledge about safety tells us that children are often taught not to accept food from strangers. The boy's refusal is safety, not rudeness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because he is rude' because refusing food can seem rude, but when it is a stranger, refusing is a safety lesson.

questions.stem: Before listening, you thought that all fishermen are poor. After listening to a drama about a successful fisherman who owns three boats, what should you do with your first thought?
options: Change it — not all fishermen are poor
Keep it — one drama cannot change my mind
Ignore the drama and stick with my thought
Forget both the thought and the drama
hints: What did the drama show you?
Should you stick with your first thought or change it?
questions.explanation: The drama showed a successful fisherman who owns three boats, which contradicts the idea that all fishermen are poor. We should change our first thought based on this new evidence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Keep it' because they are stubborn, but a good listener adjusts their thinking when new evidence arrives.

questions.stem: Before listening, you thought that all market women are old. After listening to a drama about a young market woman, what should you do?
options: Change it — not all market women are old
Keep it — the drama was wrong
Believe both — market women are old and young at once
hints: What did the drama show?
Should your first thought change?
questions.explanation: The drama showed a young market woman, which contradicts the idea that all market women are old. We should change our thought based on this evidence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Believe both' because it sounds open-minded, but the two ideas contradict — if not all are old, the 'all are old' thought is wrong.

questions.stem: Before listening, you thought that farming is hard work. After listening to a drama about a farmer who works from dawn to dusk, what should you do?
options: Keep it — the drama confirmed that farming is hard work
Change it — the drama showed farming is easy
Believe that farming is only for lazy people
hints: Did the drama agree with your first thought?
If yes, what should you do?
questions.explanation: The drama showed a farmer working from dawn to dusk, which confirms that farming is hard work. We should keep our thought when the drama supports it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Change it' because change sounds open-minded, but the drama confirmed the thought, so keeping it is correct.

questions.stem: In a small group, discuss a short drama your teacher has read. Each person should say: (a) one thing they already knew about the topic, (b) one new thing they learned, and (c) whether the drama changed or confirmed their thinking.
hints: What did you already know?
What did you learn?
Did your thinking change?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each member shares something they already knew
Each member shares something new they learned
Each member says whether thinking changed or was confirmed

questions.stem: In a small group, discuss a short drama about a community issue (e.g., cleaning the market). Each person should share prior knowledge, new knowledge, and one action they could take.
hints: What do you know about the issue?
What did the drama teach you?
What could you do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Shares new knowledge from the drama

questions.stem: In a small group, discuss a drama that challenged what you thought about a topic. Each person should say what they used to think, what the drama showed, and what they now think.
hints: What did you use to think?
What did the drama show?
What do you think now?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each member says what they used to think
Each member says what the drama showed
Each member says what they think now

questions.stem: In a small group, discuss how background knowledge helped you understand a drama your teacher read. Each person should give one example of background knowledge they used and explain how it helped.
hints: What did you already know?
How did that knowledge help you understand the drama?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each member gives one example of background knowledge

questions.stem: After listening to a short drama, share with the class one new thing you learned and explain how it connects to what you already knew.
hints: What did you learn?
How does it connect to what you already knew?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains the connection to prior knowledge

questions.stem: After listening to a short drama, share with the class one thing you learned, how it connects to what you already knew, and how your thinking changed or was confirmed.
hints: New knowledge, then connection, then change/confirmation.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains change or confirmation of thinking

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Distinguish between causes and effects of events in a story

skills.description: Identify the cause of a named event in the story.
Identify the effect of a named action or event.
Tell which of two statements is the cause and which is the effect.
Follow a cause-effect-further-effect chain in a short story.
Teacher-assessed oral: explain the cause and effect of a key event in a story heard.
Teacher-assessed oral: retell a story linking events by cause and effect.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Ama forgot her umbrella at home. On her way home, it started to rain. She got wet.' What was the cause of Ama getting wet?
options: She forgot her umbrella at home
hints: Why did Ama get wet?
What was missing that would have kept her dry?
questions.explanation: Ama got wet because she had no umbrella when it rained. The cause is that she forgot her umbrella at home.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It started to rain' because rain makes people wet, but the rain would not have wet Ama if she had her umbrella. The forgetting is the cause of her being wet.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Kojo did not do his homework. The teacher was angry with him. He was asked to stay after school.' What was the cause of the teacher being angry?
options: Kojo did not do his homework
hints: Why was the teacher angry?
What had Kojo failed to do?
questions.explanation: The teacher was angry because Kojo did not do his homework. That is the cause.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kojo stayed after school' because it is a punishment, but that is the effect of the teacher's anger, not the cause.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'The children planted trees around the school. The compound became cool and shady. The pupils enjoyed playing outside.' What was the cause of the compound becoming cool and shady?
hints: Why did the compound become cool?
What did the children do?
questions.explanation: The children planted trees, and the trees made the compound cool and shady. Planting is the cause.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The pupils enjoyed playing outside' because it mentions the compound, but that is the effect of the cool compound, not the cause.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Esi did not sweep her room for three days. Dust collected on every surface. She began to sneeze whenever she entered the room. Her mother told her to sweep.' What was the cause of Esi's sneezing?
options: Dust collected on every surface because she had not swept
Her mother told her to sweep
hints: Why was Esi sneezing?
What was in the room that made her sneeze?
questions.explanation: The dust that collected on every surface made Esi sneeze. The dust was there because she had not swept. So the cause of her sneezing was the dust, not her mother's instruction.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She entered the room' because it is in the same sentence, but entering just put her near the dust — the dust is the cause.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'It rained heavily all night. The road was flooded in the morning. Vehicles could not pass.' What was the effect of the heavy rain?
options: The road was flooded in the morning
hints: What happened because of the rain?
Which event follows the rain and is caused by it?
questions.explanation: The road being flooded in the morning is a direct effect of the heavy rain. Vehicles not passing is a further effect of the flooding.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Vehicles could not pass' because it is a later event, but the flooding is the more direct effect of the rain, and vehicles not passing is caused by the flooding.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'The pupils cleaned the school compound and planted flowers. Visitors to the school were impressed by the beauty.' What was the effect of the pupils' work?
options: Visitors were impressed by the beauty
The visitors came to the school
hints: What happened because of the pupils' work?
What did the visitors think?
questions.explanation: The visitors being impressed is the effect of the pupils' work. The work itself is the cause.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The pupils cleaned the compound' because it is mentioned, but that is the action (the cause), not the effect.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Kofi ate too much at the party. He had a stomach ache all evening.' What was the effect of Kofi eating too much?
options: He had a stomach ache all evening
hints: What happened after Kofi ate too much?
What was the result?
questions.explanation: The stomach ache is the effect of Kofi eating too much. Eating too much is the cause.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'He ate too much' because it is in the story, but that is the cause, not the effect.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Adjoa studied every day for the exam. When the results came out, she had the highest score in the class.' What was the effect of her studying every day?
options: She had the highest score in the class
hints: What was the result of her hard work?
What does the text say she achieved?
questions.explanation: The highest score is the effect of studying every day. Studying is the cause.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The results came out' because it is mentioned, but the results coming out is just the time — the effect of studying is the score.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Esi did not sweep her room. Dust collected on every surface.' Which is the CAUSE and which is the EFFECT?
options: Cause: Esi did not sweep. Effect: Dust collected.
Cause: Dust collected. Effect: Esi did not sweep.
Cause: The room was dirty. Effect: Esi did not sweep.
Cause: Esi sneezed. Effect: Dust collected.
hints: Which action happened first?
Which is the result of the other?
questions.explanation: Esi not sweeping came first and caused the dust to collect. So not sweeping is the cause, dust collecting is the effect.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the cause and effect because dust is 'the thing that happened'. But the dust collected BECAUSE she did not sweep.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'The children cleaned the compound. Visitors were impressed.' Which is the CAUSE and which is the EFFECT?
options: Cause: The children cleaned. Effect: Visitors were impressed.
Cause: Visitors were impressed. Effect: The children cleaned.
Cause: The compound was clean. Effect: The visitors came.
Cause: The visitors came. Effect: The children cleaned.
hints: Which happened because of the other?
The visitors came, saw the clean compound, and were impressed.
questions.explanation: The cleaning caused the visitors to be impressed. So cleaning is the cause and being impressed is the effect.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the order because they think visitors cause cleaning, but the visitors were impressed BECAUSE of the cleaning.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Kofi ate too much at the party. He had a stomach ache.' Which is the CAUSE and which is the EFFECT?
options: Cause: Kofi ate too much. Effect: Kofi had a stomach ache.
Cause: Kofi had a stomach ache. Effect: Kofi ate too much.
Cause: The party was fun. Effect: Kofi had a stomach ache.
Cause: Kofi's mother cooked. Effect: Kofi had a stomach ache.
hints: Which action came first?
Which is the result of the other?
questions.explanation: Kofi ate too much, and the result was a stomach ache. Eating too much is the cause; the stomach ache is the effect.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse because they see 'stomach ache' as an event, but the stomach ache came BECAUSE of eating too much.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Esi did not sweep her room. Dust collected on every surface. She began to sneeze. Her mother told her to sweep every day from now on.' Follow the chain. What leads to Esi sneezing?
options: Dust collecting on every surface, which happened because she did not sweep
Her mother telling her to sweep
Esi's decision to sweep every day
hints: What is the chain?
Esi did not sweep → dust collected → sneezing
questions.explanation: The chain is: Esi did not sweep → dust collected → Esi sneezed. So the immediate cause of sneezing is the dust, which collected because she did not sweep.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Her mother told her to sweep' because it is mentioned, but the mother's instruction comes AFTER the sneezing, as a result.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'The pupils cleaned the compound and planted flowers. Visitors were impressed. The school won a prize for the cleanest campus.' Follow the chain. What leads to the school winning a prize?
options: The pupils cleaning the compound, which impressed visitors
hints: What is the chain?
Cleaning → visitors impressed → school won prize
questions.explanation: The chain is: pupils cleaned → visitors impressed → school won a prize. The cleaning is the root cause of the prize.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The visitors coming' because visitors are involved, but the visitors came and were impressed because of the cleaning.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Kofi forgot his umbrella at home. It rained while he walked home. He got wet. He became sick the next day.' Follow the chain. What leads to Kofi becoming sick?
options: Forgetting his umbrella, which led to getting wet in the rain
Going to school the next day
hints: What is the chain?
Forgot umbrella → got wet → sick
questions.explanation: The chain is: Kofi forgot his umbrella → walked in rain → got wet → became sick. The root cause of becoming sick is forgetting the umbrella.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Walking home slowly' because walking in the rain is relevant, but the chain starts with forgetting the umbrella, not the speed of walking.

questions.stem: Listen to a short story. Explain the cause and effect of one key event in the story.
hints: What happened?
Why did it happen?
What was the result?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains the cause of the event
Explains the effect of the event

questions.stem: Listen to a short story. Explain the cause and effect of the main character's action.
hints: What did the character do?
Why?
What happened as a result?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Listen to a short story. Explain two cause-effect pairs in the story and how they are linked.
hints: Pair 1: What caused what?
Pair 2: What caused what?
How are the two pairs connected?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how the pairs are linked

questions.stem: Listen to a short story. Explain the chain of causes and effects that leads from the beginning to the end of the story.
hints: Start with the first event.
Then say how each event caused the next.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains the first event and its effect
Explains how one event led to another

questions.stem: Listen to a short story. Retell it, using 'because', 'so', 'then' to show the cause-and-effect chain.
hints: Use linking words: 'because', 'so', 'then'.
Show how each event led to the next.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Listen to a short story. Retell it in your own words, making the cause-and-effect chain clear. Use at least three cause-and-effect words.
hints: Use words like 'because', 'so', 'as a result', 'then', 'after that'.
Show what caused what.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three cause-and-effect words

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Draw conclusions from main ideas, key details and specific examples from texts

skills.description: Identify the main idea of a short text heard.
Pick the key detail that supports the main idea.
Choose the best conclusion from the main idea and details.
Tell a detail apart from a conclusion.
Draw a conclusion from two or three specific examples given in a text.
Teacher-assessed oral: state a conclusion from a text heard and give one detail that supports it.
Teacher-assessed oral: justify a conclusion by pointing to main idea and key details.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'The children of Boti built their own school. They made bricks from mud. They used grass for the roof. Every year they work hard to improve their school.' What is the main idea of this text?
options: The children of Boti work hard to build and improve their school
The children make bricks from mud
The children use grass for the roof
hints: What is the text mostly about?
Every detail supports this idea.
questions.explanation: The text tells how the children of Boti build and improve their school. Making bricks and using grass for the roof are details that support this main idea.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The children make bricks from mud' because it is one of the first things mentioned, but it is a detail, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Your teacher will read aloud twice: 'Every morning before school, Ama fetches water for her grandmother. She sweeps the compound and waters the plants. She never complains. Her grandmother says she is a blessing.' What is the main idea?
options: Ama is a helpful and hard-working child
hints: What kind of person is Ama?
What do all the details show about her?
questions.explanation: The text shows Ama doing many helpful chores every morning without complaining. The main idea is that Ama is a helpful and hard-working child.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama fetches water every morning' because it is mentioned, but that is one detail. The main idea covers all her helpful actions.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'The children of Boti built their own school. They made bricks from mud. They used grass for the roof.' Which detail supports the main idea that the children work hard?
options: They go to school every day
hints: Which detail shows hard work?
Making bricks from mud is hard work.
questions.explanation: Making bricks from mud is a detail that shows hard work — it supports the main idea. The other options are not in the text or do not show hard work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'They go to school every day' because it is about school, but the text does not say this, and it does not show hard work in the same way.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'Every morning before school, Ama fetches water for her grandmother. She sweeps the compound and waters the plants.' Which detail supports the main idea that Ama is helpful?
options: She fetches water for her grandmother
hints: Which detail shows Ama helping someone?
Fetching water is helping.
questions.explanation: Fetching water for her grandmother is a detail that supports the main idea — it shows Ama being helpful.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Her grandmother is old' because it is in the text, but age does not show Ama being helpful.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'The children of Boti built their own school. They made bricks from mud. They used grass for the roof. Every year they work hard to improve their school.' What conclusion can you draw about the children of Boti?
options: They have a lot of money
hints: What do their actions show about them?
Building a school from mud is hard work.
questions.explanation: The children built their school, made bricks and improved it every year. From these actions, we can conclude they are determined and hard-working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'They have a lot of money' because building a school costs money, but they built it from mud and grass, which suggests they had little money and worked hard instead.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'Every morning before school, Ama fetches water for her grandmother. She sweeps the compound and waters the plants. She never complains.' What conclusion can you draw about Ama?
options: She does not like her grandmother
hints: What do Ama's actions show?
She does many helpful chores without complaining.
questions.explanation: Ama does many chores for her grandmother without complaining. From these details, we can conclude she is responsible and caring.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She is unkind' because she never complains — but never complaining actually shows she is kind and responsible, not unkind.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'Every day after school, Kofi helps his father at the shop. He counts the money carefully. He arranges the goods neatly. He greets every customer with a smile. His father says he is a great help.' What conclusion can you draw about Kofi?
hints: What do Kofi's daily actions show?
He helps, counts carefully, arranges neatly, and greets with a smile.
questions.explanation: Kofi's careful work and friendly manner show he is reliable and helpful. His father also says he is a great help — this confirms the conclusion.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'He dislikes his father' because he works with him, but working with someone and helping them shows the opposite.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'Adjoa studies every day. She asks questions in class. She does all her homework. When the results came out, she had the highest score.' What conclusion can you draw?
hints: What did Adjoa do that led to her result?
Her hard work caused her success.
questions.explanation: Adjoa studied every day, asked questions and did her homework, and she got the highest score. The conclusion is that hard work leads to success.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Adjoa cheated in the exam' because her result was high, but the text shows she worked hard — cheating is not mentioned and contradicts the story.

questions.stem: Text: 'The children of Boti built their own school. They made bricks from mud. They used grass for the roof.' Which of these is a CONCLUSION, not a detail?
options: The children of Boti are hard-working
They used grass for the roof
hints: Which one is an inference you make from the details?
The others are stated in the text.
questions.explanation: 'The children of Boti are hard-working' is a conclusion you draw from the details. The other three are stated details.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'They built their own school' because it is about their effort, but it is a stated fact, not an inference.

questions.stem: Text: 'Adjoa studies every day. She asks questions in class. She does her homework. She got the highest score.' Which of these is a CONCLUSION, not a detail?
hints: Which one is the lesson or inference you draw?
The others are stated in the text.
questions.explanation: 'Hard work leads to success' is the conclusion — a general lesson drawn from Adjoa's story. The other three are specific details from the text.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She got the highest score' because it is the result, but it is a stated fact, not a conclusion you draw.

questions.stem: Text: 'Kofi helps his father at the shop. He counts money carefully. He greets customers with a smile.' Which of these is a CONCLUSION, not a detail?
options: He greets customers with a smile
hints: Which one is an inference?
The others are stated actions.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi is reliable and helpful' is a conclusion from his actions. The other three are stated details.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi helps at the shop' because it sounds like a conclusion, but it is a stated fact.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'Ama swept the classroom. She arranged the desks. She wiped the board. She opened the windows for fresh air.' What conclusion can you draw from these examples?
options: Ama takes care of her classroom
hints: What did Ama do for the classroom?
She took care of it.
questions.explanation: All four actions — sweeping, arranging, wiping and opening windows — show that Ama takes care of her classroom. That is the conclusion from these examples.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama is the class prefect' because she does prefect-like tasks, but the text does not say she is the prefect — only that she takes care.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'The farmer woke before dawn. He cleared the weeds. He planted the seeds. He watered them. He worked until sunset.' What conclusion can you draw from these examples?
hints: What do all of the farmer's actions show?
He worked from before dawn until sunset.
questions.explanation: The farmer worked from before dawn until sunset doing difficult tasks. The conclusion is that he is hard-working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The farmer is old' because working hard can seem related to age, but the text says nothing about the farmer's age.

questions.stem: Text (read aloud twice): 'Esi arrived at school early. She swept the classroom. She arranged the chairs. She helped a new pupil find his class. She shared her lunch with a friend who had none.' What conclusion can you draw from these examples?
options: Esi is new to the school
hints: What do all of Esi's actions have in common?
Each action helps someone or takes care of the school.
questions.explanation: Every action Esi takes shows care — for her classroom, for a new pupil and for a hungry friend. The conclusion is that Esi is kind and helpful.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Esi is new to the school' because the text mentions a new pupil, but the new pupil is not Esi — she is the one helping.

questions.stem: Listen to a short text. State a conclusion you can draw and give one detail from the text that supports it.
hints: What do the details add up to?
Which detail supports your conclusion?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one supporting detail from the text

questions.stem: Listen to a short text about a character. State a conclusion about the character's personality and give one detail that supports it.
hints: What kind of person is this character?
Which action shows that?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States a clear conclusion about personality

questions.stem: Listen to a short text. Draw a conclusion from two details in the text and explain how both details support your conclusion.
hints: What conclusion does the evidence lead to?
Which two details support it?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how each detail supports the conclusion

questions.stem: Listen to a short text. Draw a conclusion about what might happen next, and explain why you reached it.
hints: What will probably happen?
What in the text makes you think so?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States a reasonable conclusion or prediction
Gives a reason from the text

questions.stem: After listening to a short text, justify a conclusion by pointing to the main idea and one key detail.
hints: State your conclusion.
Say what the main idea is.
Point to one detail that supports it.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: After listening to a short text, justify a conclusion with the main idea and two key details. Explain how the details support the conclusion.
hints: Conclusion first, then main idea, then two details, then the link.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how the details support the conclusion

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Asking and Answering Questions / Question Tags
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.8.1: Demonstrate understanding in asking and answering questions correctly
indicator.objective: Use the various forms of 'do', 'be', 'have', appropriately in questions and responses

skills.description: Choose the correct form of do/does/did for a given subject and tense in a Yes/No question.
Choose the correct form of be (am/is/are/was/were) for a given subject and tense in a Yes/No question.
Choose the correct form of have (have/has/had) for a given subject and tense in a Yes/No question.
Choose the correct short response to a given question.
Choose the correct Wh-word and correct form of do/be/have to complete a Wh-question.
Teacher-assessed oral: ask Yes/No and Wh-questions using do/be/have correctly in a pair or group activity.
Teacher-assessed oral: answer questions using do/be/have correctly in speech.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ you like mangoes?'
hints: The subject is 'you'.
With 'you', use 'do'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'you', which takes 'do' in the present tense. So we say 'Do you like mangoes?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Does' because it is a form of do, but 'does' is for he/she/it — not for 'you'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ Kofi like pepper?'
hints: The subject is 'Kofi' — one person.
For he/she/it, use 'does'.
questions.explanation: Kofi is one person, so the subject is third-person singular. In the present tense, use 'does'. 'Does Kofi like pepper?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Do' because it is the most common form, but 'Kofi' is singular — it needs 'does'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ they go to the market yesterday?'
hints: Look at the time word: 'yesterday'.
Yesterday is past tense.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' tells us the question is in the past. The past form of 'do' is 'did'. 'Did they go to the market yesterday?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Do' because the sentence looks like a present-tense question, but 'yesterday' signals the past.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ you ready for school?'
hints: The subject is 'you'.
For 'you', use 'are'.
questions.explanation: For 'you', the form of 'be' is 'are'. So 'Are you ready for school?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Am' because they hear it in 'I am', but 'am' is only for 'I', not for 'you'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ the girls in the classroom?'
hints: The subject is 'the girls' — plural.
For plural subjects, use 'are'.
questions.explanation: The girls is a plural subject, so the present form of 'be' is 'are'. 'Are the girls in the classroom?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Is' because it is shorter, but 'is' is for singular, not plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ the boy at school yesterday?'
hints: The subject is 'the boy' — one person.
Yesterday is past tense.
questions.explanation: The subject is singular (the boy) and the time is past (yesterday). The past form of 'be' for singular subjects is 'was'. 'Was the boy at school yesterday?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Were' because it is a past form, but 'were' is for plural subjects, not singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ you eaten your breakfast?'
hints: The subject is 'you'.
For 'you', use 'have'.
questions.explanation: For 'you', the form of 'have' is 'have'. 'Have you eaten your breakfast?' is the correct present perfect question.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Has' because it is also a form of 'have', but 'has' is for third-person singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ Amina finished her work?'
hints: The subject is 'Amina' — one person.
For she, use 'has'.
questions.explanation: Amina is third-person singular, so use 'has'. 'Has Amina finished her work?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Have' because it is more common, but 'Amina' is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: '___ they finished their homework before the bell rang?'
hints: Two actions: finishing homework and the bell ringing. Which came first?
The past form of 'have' is 'had'.
questions.explanation: The sentence uses 'before the bell rang' — one past action happened before another. That calls for the past perfect, which uses 'had'. 'Had they finished their homework before the bell rang?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Have' because it is present perfect, but the sentence refers to a past time before another past time, so 'had' is needed.

questions.stem: Question: 'Do you like pepper?' Which is the correct short answer?
hints: The question uses 'Do'.
The short answer should also use 'do'.
questions.explanation: The question is 'Do you like pepper?' — it uses 'do'. The short answer should match: 'Yes, I do.' Using a different auxiliary (am, have) would not fit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Yes, I am' because it sounds natural in some contexts, but the correct auxiliary here is 'do'.

questions.stem: Question: 'Are you ready?' Which is the correct short answer?
hints: The question uses 'Are'.
The short answer should use 'am'.
questions.explanation: The question is 'Are you ready?' — it uses 'be'. The correct short answer for 'I' is 'Yes, I am.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Yes, I do' because it is a common short answer, but the question uses 'be', so the response must too.

questions.stem: Question: 'Has she left?' Which is the correct short answer?
hints: The question uses 'Has'.
The short answer should use 'has'.
questions.explanation: The question is 'Has she left?' — it uses 'has'. The correct short answer is 'Yes, she has.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Yes, she had' because it is also a form of have, but the question is present perfect, so the answer must use 'has'.

questions.stem: Question: 'Did they win the match?' Which is the correct short answer?
hints: The question uses 'Did' — past tense.
The short answer should use 'did'.
questions.explanation: The question is 'Did they win the match?' — it uses 'did', the past tense of do. The correct short answer is 'Yes, they did.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Yes, they do' because it is common, but the question is past tense, so the answer must be past tense too.

questions.stem: Choose the correct words: '___ ___ you want for lunch?'
hints: The subject is 'you'.
For 'you' in present tense, use 'do'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'you' and the question is about what you want in the present. So 'What do you want for lunch?' The correct pair is 'What do'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What does' because 'does' is also a form of do, but 'does' is for he/she/it, not 'you'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct words: '___ ___ Kofi live?'
hints: The question is about place — 'Where'.
The subject is 'Kofi' — one person.
questions.explanation: The question asks about place, so we use 'Where'. The subject is 'Kofi' (third-person singular), so we use 'does'. 'Where does Kofi live?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Where do' because it is more common, but 'Kofi' is singular, so 'does' is needed.

questions.stem: Choose the correct words: '___ ___ they go yesterday?'
hints: The question is about place — 'Where'.
'Yesterday' tells us it is past tense.
questions.explanation: The question asks about place (Where) and the time is past (yesterday). So the auxiliary should be 'did'. 'Where did they go yesterday?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Where do' because it is common, but the question is in the past.

questions.stem: In a pair, ask each other three questions using 'do', 'does' or 'did'. Then ask two more using 'is', 'are' or 'was'.
hints: For 'you' use 'do'. For he/she/it use 'does'. For past use 'did'.
For 'be' questions use 'is/are/was/were'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Listens to and answers partner's questions

questions.stem: In a small group, take turns asking Wh-questions using do, be or have. Each person must ask at least two questions.
hints: Ask 'What do you...?', 'Where did you...?', 'Have you ever...?'
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Each member asks at least two Wh-questions

questions.stem: In a pair, answer your partner's questions using short responses (Yes, I do / No, she doesn't / Yes, they are / No, he hasn't).
hints: Match the auxiliary in the question.
Use short answers, not just 'yes' or 'no'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Matches the auxiliary in the question

questions.stem: In a small group, take turns answering questions. When you answer, give the short response and then add one more sentence with information.
hints: Start with 'Yes, I do' or 'No, I don't'.
Then add a sentence: 'I like mangoes because they are sweet.'
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Asking and Answering Questions / Question Tags
indicator.content_standard: Not printed on page 108 (see Phase 1 inventory)
indicator.objective: Use positive tags, negative tags and auxiliaries in speech

skills.description: Choose the correct negative tag for a positive statement.
Choose the correct positive tag for a negative statement.
Choose the correct auxiliary in the tag when the statement has no auxiliary.
Choose the tag whose pronoun matches the subject of the statement.
Choose the correct answer to a question containing a tag.
Identify the question tag in a given sentence.
Teacher-assessed oral: use positive and negative tags in a short spoken dialogue in pairs.
Teacher-assessed oral: take part in a Question-and-Answer Drill round the class using tags.

misconceptions: Answering the statement not the tag

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'You are coming to the party, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive.
The tag should be negative.
questions.explanation: The statement 'You are coming' is positive, so the tag must be negative: 'aren't you?' The auxiliary 'are' matches the statement.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are you' because the words are the same, but a positive statement takes a negative tag.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'She likes mangoes, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive.
The verb is 'likes' (present) — use 'does' in the tag.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag is negative. The verb 'likes' takes the auxiliary 'does' → 'doesn't she?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'isn't she' because it uses 'she' and looks right, but the verb 'likes' needs 'does', not 'is'.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'The children have finished their homework, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive.
The auxiliary is 'have'. The subject is 'the children' → 'they'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive ('have finished'), so the tag is negative ('haven't'). The subject 'the children' becomes 'they'. 'Haven't they?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'don't they' because it uses 'they', but the verb is present perfect ('have finished'), so the tag must use 'have'.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'The boys aren't in school today, ___?'
hints: The statement is negative.
The tag should be positive.
questions.explanation: The statement is negative ('aren't'), so the tag is positive: 'are they?' The subject 'the boys' becomes 'they'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'aren't they' because it repeats the statement's form, but the tag should be the opposite polarity.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'Kofi doesn't like pepper, ___?'
hints: The statement is negative.
The tag should be positive.
questions.explanation: The statement is negative ('doesn't'), so the tag is positive: 'does he?' The subject 'Kofi' becomes 'he'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'doesn't he' because it repeats the same form, but the tag needs opposite polarity.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'She hasn't eaten yet, ___?'
hints: The statement is negative.
The auxiliary is 'has'.
questions.explanation: The statement is negative ('hasn't eaten'), so the tag is positive: 'has she?' The auxiliary stays the same.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'does she' because it sounds natural, but the statement uses 'has', so the tag must also use 'has'.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'You like rice, ___?'
hints: The statement has no auxiliary.
The verb is 'like' — use 'do' in the tag.
questions.explanation: The statement 'You like rice' has no auxiliary verb — 'like' is a main verb. To make the tag, we add 'do'. 'Don't you?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'aren't you' because they confuse the auxiliary, but the verb 'like' needs 'do', not 'be'.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'Ama went to the market, ___?'
hints: The statement has no auxiliary.
The verb 'went' is past — use 'did' in the tag.
questions.explanation: The statement is in the past tense ('went'), and has no auxiliary. To make the tag, use 'did'. 'Didn't she?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'doesn't she' because the present tense is common, but the statement is past, so 'didn't' is needed.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'The pupils play football, ___?'
hints: The statement is positive.
The subject is 'the pupils' → 'they'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive and has no auxiliary. The verb 'play' takes 'do'. The subject 'the pupils' becomes 'they'. 'Don't they?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'aren't they' because it uses 'they', but the verb is 'play', not 'be'.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'Ama is a good singer, ___?'
hints: The subject is 'Ama' — a girl.
Use the pronoun 'she'.
questions.explanation: Ama is a girl, so the pronoun in the tag should be 'she'. 'Isn't she?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'isn't he' because 'he' is common, but Ama is a female name — use 'she'.

questions.stem: Complete the tag: 'The children are happy, ___?'
hints: The subject is 'the children' — plural people.
Use the pronoun 'they'.
questions.explanation: 'The children' is plural people, so the pronoun is 'they'. 'Aren't they?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'aren't we' because both refer to people, but 'we' would mean the speaker is included — the children does not include the speaker here.

questions.stem: Someone asks: 'You are coming to the party, aren't you?' You are NOT coming. What do you say?
hints: The statement is 'You are coming'.
You are NOT coming — so the answer is negative.
questions.explanation: The statement is 'You are coming', and you are NOT coming. So you answer negatively: 'No, I'm not.' This matches the auxiliary 'are'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Yes, I am' because the question sounds positive, but the question is a tag — you answer according to the FACTS, not the tag.

questions.stem: Someone asks: 'Kofi isn't in school today, is he?' Kofi IS in school. What do you say?
hints: The statement is 'Kofi isn't in school'.
Kofi IS in school — so the answer is positive.
questions.explanation: The statement says 'Kofi isn't in school', but the fact is he IS. So the answer is positive: 'Yes, he is.' The auxiliary matches the statement ('is').
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'No, he isn't' because the question says 'isn't', but the question asks about the FACT, not the tag — the fact is that Kofi IS in school.

questions.stem: Someone asks: 'You don't eat meat, do you?' You DO eat meat. What do you say?
hints: The statement is 'You don't eat meat'.
You DO eat meat — so the answer is positive.
questions.explanation: The statement says 'you don't eat meat', but the fact is you DO. So the answer is positive: 'Yes, I do.' This matches the auxiliary 'do'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'No, I don't' because the question uses 'don't', but the answer is about the FACTS, not the tag.

questions.stem: Identify the question tag in this sentence: 'You are coming to the party, aren't you?'
hints: The tag comes at the end.
It is a short question at the end of a statement.
questions.explanation: The question tag is 'aren't you' — it is a short question added to the end of the statement 'You are coming to the party'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You are coming' because it is the main statement, but the tag is the short question at the end.

questions.stem: Identify the question tag in this sentence: 'Kofi doesn't like pepper, does he?'
hints: The tag is a short question at the end.
It reverses the polarity of the statement.
questions.explanation: The question tag is 'does he' — a short positive question added to the negative statement 'Kofi doesn't like pepper'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi doesn't like pepper' because it is the main sentence, but that is the statement, not the tag.

questions.stem: In a pair, use question tags in a short dialogue. Each of you should use at least one positive tag and one negative tag.
hints: Positive statement → negative tag.
Negative statement → positive tag.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least one positive tag
Uses at least one negative tag

questions.stem: In a pair, have a short conversation where you use at least three question tags (at least one positive and one negative). Respond to your partner's tags correctly.
hints: Use tags that match your statement's auxiliary.
Answer tags based on the facts.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Includes at least one positive and one negative tag

questions.stem: Take part in a Question-and-Answer Drill: your teacher (or a classmate) makes a statement with a tag, and you answer it correctly based on the facts.
hints: Listen carefully to the tag.
Answer based on the facts, not the tag.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Take part in a round-the-class Question-and-Answer Drill using tags. When it is your turn, first make a statement with a tag, then answer a tag question from a classmate.
hints: Make a statement, then add the correct tag.
Listen to the classmate's tag question and answer based on facts.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Makes a statement with a correct tag

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.9.1: Use verbs in commands, instructions, requests and directions appropriately in speech
indicator.objective: Give and respond to commands, instructions; give and follow directions with clear landmarks

skills.description: Choose the correct imperative verb to give a command or instruction.
Arrange jumbled direction steps into a sensible order.
Choose the direction that uses a clear landmark, not a vague one.
From a direction given in the stem, identify the destination or the next step.
Choose the correct spoken response to a command.
Teacher-assessed oral: give directions from a given point to a named place, using at least two clear landmarks.
Teacher-assessed practical: follow a series of three spoken commands or instructions accurately.
Teacher-assessed oral: respond appropriately to a command or direction.

questions.stem: Your teacher says: '___ the door when you leave.' Which word completes the command?
hints: A command uses the base form of the verb.
Which form gives an order?
questions.explanation: A command uses the imperative, which is the base form of the verb. So 'Close the door when you leave.' The other forms are not imperatives.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Closing' because it is a verb form, but 'closing' is not a command — it is a present participle.

questions.stem: Which of these is a correct command?
options: Bring your exercise book to me.
You are bringing your exercise book to me.
Brought your exercise book to me.
To bring your exercise book to me.
hints: A command starts with the base form of the verb.
It does not have a subject like 'you'.
questions.explanation: 'Bring your exercise book to me' is a correct imperative command. It starts with the base verb 'bring' and has no explicit subject.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You are bringing your exercise book to me' because it mentions the book, but it is a statement, not a command.

questions.stem: Your teacher says: '___ right at the junction, then walk twenty steps.' Which word completes the direction?
hints: A direction uses the base form of the verb.
Which form gives an instruction?
questions.explanation: Directions use the imperative — the base form of the verb. So 'Turn right at the junction, then walk twenty steps.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Turning' because it sounds like an action, but 'turning' is not a command form.

questions.stem:
These direction steps are jumbled. Which order makes the most sense?
A) Stop at the water tank.
B) Walk past the head teacher's office.
C) Turn left at the school gate.
hints: What is the first thing you do after leaving the gate?
You start at the gate, walk past the office, then stop.
questions.explanation: The sensible order: turn left at the school gate (C), walk past the head teacher's office (B), and stop at the water tank (A). So C, B, A.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the stop first because it is the destination, but the destination comes last in a set of directions.

questions.stem:
These steps for a classroom instruction are jumbled. Which order makes the most sense?
A) Sit down quietly.
B) Stand up.
C) Open your books to page 10.
hints: What comes first — standing up or sitting down?
After sitting down, you open the book.
questions.explanation: The sensible order: stand up (B), sit down quietly (A), then open your books to page 10 (C). So B, A, C.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put 'Open your books' first because it is the task, but the instructions begin with standing up.

questions.stem:
These steps to reach the chief's palace are jumbled. Which order makes the most sense?
A) Ask for the chief at the gate.
B) Turn right at the big mango tree.
C) Walk down the main road for five minutes.
D) You will see the palace on your left.
hints: What is the first step in a journey?
You start by walking down the road.
questions.explanation: The sensible order: walk down the main road for five minutes (C), turn right at the big mango tree (B), see the palace on your left (D), and ask for the chief at the gate (A). So C, B, D, A.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put 'Ask for the chief' first because it is the goal, but asking comes after arriving at the palace.

questions.stem: Which direction uses a clear landmark?
options: Walk until you reach the big mango tree, then turn left.
Walk somewhere over there and then turn.
Walk a bit, then turn that way.
hints: Which direction helps you know exactly where to turn?
A landmark is a clear, visible thing.
questions.explanation: 'Walk until you reach the big mango tree' uses a clear landmark — the big mango tree. The other options are vague and do not tell you where to turn.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Walk somewhere over there' because it tells you to walk, but 'over there' is not a landmark — it is vague.

questions.stem: Which direction is clearest?
options: Turn right at the water tank, then walk to the blue gate.
Turn at the thing and walk to the place.
Turn this way and walk a little.
Turn and walk until you stop.
hints: Which direction names specific things you can see?
Look for specific nouns like 'water tank' and 'blue gate'.
questions.explanation: 'Turn right at the water tank, then walk to the blue gate' is clearest because it names specific landmarks: the water tank and the blue gate. The other options use vague words like 'the thing' and 'this way'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Turn this way' because it is short, but it is unclear — the listener does not know which way 'this way' is.

questions.stem: A stranger asks you how to get to the chief's palace. Which direction is clearest?
options: Walk straight down this road until you see the big mosque, then turn left. The palace is the big house with red pillars.
Walk down the road and turn. You will see it.
Go straight, then turn somewhere near the shops.
Walk a bit and ask someone else.
hints: Which direction gives specific landmarks?
It should tell the stranger what to look for.
questions.explanation: The clearest direction names the mosque as a landmark, gives a clear turn ('turn left'), and describes the palace ('big house with red pillars'). The other options are too vague.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Walk a bit and ask someone else' because it admits uncertainty, but it does not help the stranger reach the palace.

questions.stem: Direction: 'From the classroom door, turn right and walk ten steps. Stop at the water tank.' Where will you end up?
hints: Where does the direction tell you to stop?
Look at the last sentence.
questions.explanation: The direction says 'Stop at the water tank.' So if you follow it, you will end up at the water tank.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'At the classroom' because the direction starts there, but the destination is the water tank.

questions.stem: Direction: 'Walk to the end of this corridor. Turn left. The library is the third door on your right.' Where is the library?
options: The third door on your right after you turn left
The first door on your left
The third door on your left
At the end of the corridor
hints: What does the direction say after 'turn left'?
It tells you exactly which door.
questions.explanation: After you turn left, the library is 'the third door on your right'. That is where the library is.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'At the end of the corridor' because the direction mentions the end, but the library is beyond that — it is on the right after turning left.

questions.stem: Direction: 'Go out of the classroom and turn left. Walk past the school canteen. The first building after the canteen is the computer room.' What comes just BEFORE the computer room?
hints: What building do you pass before reaching the computer room?
The direction says the computer room is the FIRST building AFTER something.
questions.explanation: The direction says you walk past the school canteen, and the computer room is the first building after the canteen. So the canteen comes just before the computer room.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The classroom' because it is where you start, but the question asks what comes just BEFORE the computer room, which is the canteen.

questions.stem: Your teacher says: 'Bring your exercise book to my desk.' What is the best response?
options: Yes, sir/madam. I will bring it now.
hints: How should you respond to a teacher's command?
Be polite and clear.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, sir/madam. I will bring it now' is a polite, clear response. It shows you understood and will obey. The other responses are rude or unclear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What book?' because they might actually be confused, but the polite response is to say you will bring it and ask if you are unsure — not to refuse.

questions.stem: A stranger says: 'Turn left at the next junction.' You did not hear clearly. What is the best response?
hints: You didn't hear. How do you ask politely?
Use 'please' and 'could you'.
questions.explanation: 'Please, could you repeat that?' is the polite way to ask someone to repeat. The other options are too abrupt or rude, especially to a stranger.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What?' because it is short, but it is impolite, especially to a stranger.

questions.stem: Your teacher will set up a simple map of the school on the board (or describe it). Give directions from the school gate to the head teacher's office, using at least two clear landmarks.
hints: Start from the gate.
Name at least two landmarks (e.g., the water tank, the library).
Say 'turn left/right' and 'walk'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two clear landmarks

questions.stem: A stranger stops you on the road. Give directions from your school to the nearest market or chief's palace, using at least two clear landmarks and at least three steps.
hints: Start with the first step.
Name at least two landmarks.
Say 'turn left/right' and 'walk'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names at least two clear landmarks

questions.stem: Give directions to a stranger from the main road to your house, using at least three clear landmarks and at least four steps. Include one instruction to ask someone for confirmation.
hints: Start from the main road.
Use three or more landmarks.
Include a step like 'ask for Mr. Kofi's house at the junction'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names at least three clear landmarks
Directions are in correct order and clearly spoken

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you three spoken commands in a row. Listen carefully and follow them in order.
hints: Listen to all three commands first if you can.
Then do them in order.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Follows all three commands in order

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you a set of four spoken directions on the school compound (or in the classroom). Follow them in order and end at the correct place.
hints: Follow each step in order.
End where the last direction tells you.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Follows all four directions in order

questions.stem: A stranger gives you a direction you cannot follow (e.g., 'Turn left at the blue house' but there is no blue house). Respond politely by asking for clarification.
hints: Use polite words.
Say what you do not understand.
Ask a question.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.9.1: Use verbs in commands, instructions, requests and directions appropriately in speech
indicator.objective: Make and respond to polite requests for help from familiar adults

skills.description: Choose the polite request form over the impolite one.
Choose the polite way to grant a request.
Choose the polite way to decline a request.
Explain why a given request is polite or impolite.
