questions.stem: Listen to this sentence: 'The children and their teacher went to the market.' Name two content words and two function words.
hints: Find the nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs.
Find the determiners, conjunctions, prepositions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.6.4: Use words appropriately for purpose, audience, context and culture
indicator.objective: Use words suitable for purpose, audience, context and culture in relation to: type of texts, medium, register etc.

skills.description: Choose the word or phrase that suits a named text type.
Choose the word that suits formal vs informal register.
Choose the word or phrase that suits spoken vs written medium.
Choose the word or phrase that suits a named audience.
Choose the word or phrase that suits a named context.
Explain why a word choice is or is not suitable for a given purpose or audience.
Teacher-assessed oral: role-play a simple character or situation using words suited to the audience and context.
Teacher-assessed oral: justify one word choice for purpose or audience in a short sentence.

questions.stem: You are writing an explanatory text about how to make tea. Which word fits best?
hints: An explanatory text tells how something is done.
It uses steps and sequence words like 'first', 'then'.
questions.explanation: 'First, boil the water' fits an explanatory text because it gives a clear step with a sequence word. The other options are informal comments or commands, not explanatory.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Tea is nice' because it is about tea, but it is not explanatory — it does not explain how to make tea.

questions.stem: You are writing a persuasive text about reading. Which sentence fits best?
options: You should read every day because it helps you learn.
hints: Persuasive text tries to convince the reader.
It uses words like 'should' or 'must'.
questions.explanation: 'You should read every day because it helps you learn' fits a persuasive text — it uses 'should' and gives a reason. The other options are descriptive or narrative.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I read yesterday' because it is about reading, but it is narrative, not persuasive — it does not try to convince.

questions.stem: You are writing an argumentative text about homework. Which sentence fits best?
options: Homework should be banned because it takes up time for family and rest.
Homework is a thing pupils do.
hints: Argumentative text makes a claim and gives reasons.
It takes a clear position.
questions.explanation: 'Homework should be banned because it takes up time for family and rest' fits argumentative writing — it states a position and gives a reason. The others are descriptive or narrative.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Homework is a thing pupils do' because it states a fact about homework, but it does not argue a position.

questions.stem: You are speaking to the head teacher. Which word is most suitable?
hints: Use formal register for the head teacher.
'Good morning, sir' is polite.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, sir' is formal and polite — suitable for a head teacher. The other options are informal greetings.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Hey' because it is friendly, but it is too informal for a head teacher.

questions.stem: You are writing a formal letter to the District Chief Executive. Which word is most suitable?
options: I am writing to respectfully request your assistance.
I wanna ask you for help.
hints: Formal letters use formal vocabulary.
'Respectfully request your assistance' is formal.
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to respectfully request your assistance' uses formal vocabulary suitable for a letter to a DCE. The other options are informal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Can you help me out?' because it is polite, but it is too casual for a formal letter to a government official.

questions.stem: You are chatting with a friend at break time. Which word is most suitable?
options: I would like to purchase a snack.
I shall now proceed to consume food.
hints: Informal language with a friend is natural.
'Let's grab' is informal.
questions.explanation: 'Let's grab some kelewele' uses informal language suitable for a friend. The other options are too formal for a chat with a peer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I would like to purchase a snack' because it sounds polite, but it is far too formal for chatting with a friend.

questions.stem: You are speaking on the radio. Which sentence is better for the SPOKEN medium?
options: Listeners, join us after the break.
Readers, please turn to page three.
As indicated in paragraph two, the following...
hints: Spoken medium should be short and clear for listeners.
Listeners cannot go back and re-read.
questions.explanation: 'Listeners, join us after the break' fits the spoken medium — it uses direct address and is simple. The other options use written-medium language (paragraphs, 'aforementioned') that does not work on radio.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Readers, please turn to page three' because it is direct, but it is written language — radio listeners cannot turn pages.

questions.stem: You are writing a textbook. Which sentence is better for the WRITTEN medium?
options: As shown in Figure 1, the plant needs sunlight.
hints: Written textbooks use formal, clear language.
They can refer to figures and diagrams.
questions.explanation: 'As shown in Figure 1, the plant needs sunlight' fits the written medium — it refers to a figure and uses formal language. The other options are casual spoken language.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Look at the plant now' because it is clear, but it is spoken-style and lacks the formal reference appropriate for a textbook.

questions.stem: You are speaking to young children about washing hands. Which words fit this audience?
options: Wash your hands to keep the germs away!
Ensure you sanitise your hands regularly.
Handwashing is a critical public health intervention.
hints: Young children need simple, lively words.
'Germs' is simpler than 'pathogens'.
questions.explanation: 'Wash your hands to keep the germs away!' uses simple words suitable for young children. The other options use adult or technical vocabulary that children may not understand.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ensure you sanitise your hands' because it sounds important, but 'sanitise' and 'ensure' are too formal for young children.

questions.stem: You are writing a letter to the elders of your community. Which words fit this audience?
options: We respectfully invite you to our school ceremony.
hints: Elders deserve formal, respectful language.
'Respectfully invite' is appropriate.
questions.explanation: 'We respectfully invite you to our school ceremony' uses respectful, formal language suitable for elders. The other options are too casual and even rude.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Drop by if you can' because it is friendly, but it is far too informal for elders — respect is required.

questions.stem: You are explaining a difficult maths idea to your younger brother. Which words fit this audience?
options: Think of it like sharing sweets equally among friends.
The numerator represents the dividend of the fraction.
This is a complex mathematical concept.
Refer to the equation on page five.
hints: Younger children understand everyday examples.
Sharing sweets is a simple, concrete idea.
questions.explanation: 'Think of it like sharing sweets equally among friends' uses a familiar, concrete example suitable for a younger brother. The other options use technical or abstract language.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The numerator represents the dividend' because it is precise, but it is too technical for a younger child.

questions.stem: You are speaking at a school assembly. Which words fit the context?
options: Fellow pupils, let us keep our school clean.
hints: School assembly is a formal setting.
Use respectful language for the whole school.
questions.explanation: 'Fellow pupils, let us keep our school clean' fits the school assembly context — it is respectful and uses the right vocabulary. The other options are too casual.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Hey guys, clean up' because it is clear, but it is too informal for an assembly.

questions.stem: You are speaking at a funeral. Which words fit this context?
options: We are deeply saddened by the loss of our beloved elder.
hints: A funeral is a solemn, respectful context.
Use formal and gentle words.
questions.explanation: 'We are deeply saddened by the loss of our beloved elder' uses respectful, solemn language suitable for a funeral. The other options are too casual or insensitive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It's sad, isn't it?' because it acknowledges sadness, but it is too casual for a funeral — respect and formality are required.

questions.stem: Why is 'Give me the book' NOT suitable when speaking to a teacher? Explain in one or two sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that explains: the phrase is a command, not a polite request — it lacks 'please' and respectful language. Award full marks if the answer explains both the command form and the lack of politeness.
hints: Is it a command or a request?
What polite words are missing?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Explains that the phrase is a command
Explains that it lacks politeness (no 'please', no 'may I')

questions.stem: Why is 'Hand hygiene prevents pathogen transmission' NOT suitable when speaking to young children? Explain in one or two sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that explains: the vocabulary is too technical (pathogen, transmission) for young children, who need simpler words. Award full marks if the answer names the technical words and the audience.
hints: Who is the audience?
Are 'pathogen' and 'transmission' easy words for young children?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Names young children as the audience who would not understand

questions.stem: Why is 'Hey, what's up?' NOT suitable when greeting the Regional Minister? Explain in one or two sentences.
answer: Accept any answer that explains: 'Hey, what's up?' is informal and casual, not respectful enough for a government official. Award full marks if the answer names the informality and the respectful alternative.
hints: Is this greeting formal or informal?
What kind of greeting would a Regional Minister expect?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Explains that a Regional Minister needs respectful/formal language

questions.stem: Role-play: you are a shopkeeper serving a customer. Use words suited to the context (polite, clear, helpful).
hints: Use 'Good morning', 'How can I help you?'.
Use polite language.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Role-play: you are a pupil speaking to the head teacher about a school issue. Use words suited to the audience and context.
hints: Use respectful language.
Address the head teacher as 'sir' or 'madam'.
Be clear and polite.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Words suit the context of a pupil speaking to a head teacher

questions.stem: You used the phrase 'Please, may I borrow your pen?' to a teacher. Justify this word choice in one sentence.
hints: Why is 'please' important?
Why 'may I' rather than 'give me'?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains why the choice suits the audience

questions.stem: You used the phrase 'First, boil the water' in an explanatory text. Justify this word choice in one sentence, mentioning the text type.
hints: What text type are you writing?
Why 'first'?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains why 'first' suits the text type

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Construct meaning from text read

skills.description: Use what you already know to make sense of a line or event.
Predict what the passage will be about from the title or first line.
Work out the meaning of a word from the surrounding words in the passage.
State what the whole passage is about in one line.
Pick the detail that supports the stated meaning.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a short passage aloud and say in own words what it means, using prior knowledge or prediction.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. When a mosquito bites a sick person, it picks up the germ. Then it bites a healthy person and gives the germ to them.' What do you already know that helps you understand this passage?
hints: What do you know about mosquitoes and sickness?
This is common knowledge in Ghana.
questions.explanation: The passage says mosquitoes spread malaria germs. What we already know — that mosquitoes can make people sick — helps us understand this passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Mosquitoes only bite at night' because it is a common belief, but the passage does not say that — it says mosquitoes spread the malaria germ.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'A balanced meal has foods from all the food groups. It gives us energy and keeps us healthy. It should include fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins.' Which of these is something you ALREADY know that helps you understand the passage?
options: Fruits and vegetables are good for the body
hints: What do you know about fruits and vegetables?
The passage includes them in a balanced meal.
questions.explanation: We already know that fruits and vegetables are good for the body — this prior knowledge helps us understand why they are part of a balanced meal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'All meals must include meat' because proteins are mentioned, but the passage lists proteins without saying meat is required.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'It is dangerous to play near the road. Cars move fast, and drivers may not see you in time. Always play in a safe place, like a park or a compound.' Which prior knowledge helps you understand this passage?
options: Cars are heavy and move fast, so they can hurt people
Cars are always blue or red
Drivers never look at the road
hints: Why is the road dangerous?
What do you know about cars?
questions.explanation: We know that cars are heavy and move fast, so they can hurt people. This prior knowledge helps us understand why playing near the road is dangerous.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Drivers never look at the road' because the passage mentions drivers, but the passage says drivers may not see you — not that they never look.

questions.stem: Read this title: 'How to Save Energy at Home'. What do you predict the passage will be about?
options: Ways to use less electricity at home
Why we should use more electricity
hints: What does 'save energy' mean?
At home — what kind of energy?
questions.explanation: The title says 'How to Save Energy at Home' — so we predict the passage will give ways to use less electricity at home.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Why we should use more electricity' because it mentions electricity, but 'save' means to use less, not more.

questions.stem: Read this first line: 'The harmattan wind blew across the village, carrying dust and dry leaves.' What do you predict the next part of the passage will describe?
options: The effects of the harmattan on the village
hints: What is the harmattan?
What does the first line focus on?
questions.explanation: The first line sets the scene — the harmattan blowing dust and dry leaves. So we predict the next part will describe the effects of the harmattan on the village.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A rainy afternoon' because weather is mentioned, but the passage is about the harmattan (dry wind), not rain.

questions.stem: Read this first line: 'Esi opened the letter and began to smile.' What do you predict the letter said?
hints: What does a smile suggest?
The letter made her smile.
questions.explanation: Esi began to smile after opening the letter — so we predict the letter said something good or happy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Something sad' because letters can carry bad news, but the smile tells us the news was good.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The doctor said the medicine would cure the sickness. After taking it for a week, Ama felt much better.' What does 'cure' mean here?
options: To make the sickness go away
To buy medicine from a shop
To ask the doctor a question
hints: What happened to Ama after taking the medicine?
She felt better.
questions.explanation: The passage says the medicine would 'cure' the sickness, and Ama felt better after taking it. So 'cure' means to make the sickness go away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'To buy medicine' because medicine is mentioned, but 'cure' means to heal — not to buy.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The farmer ploughed the land and planted the seeds. He watered them every day. Soon small green shoots appeared.' What does 'shoots' mean here?
options: Small new plants growing from the seeds
hints: What appeared after the farmer watered the seeds?
They were small and green.
questions.explanation: 'Shoots' here means small new plants growing from the seeds. The context — planting, watering, green — tells us this.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think of 'shoots' as guns because the word has another meaning, but in a passage about planting, shoots are young plants.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The villagers were overjoyed when the rains finally came. They danced and sang in the streets, grateful for the water that would save their crops.' What does 'overjoyed' mean?
hints: What did the villagers do? They danced and sang.
How do people act when they are extremely happy?
questions.explanation: 'Overjoyed' means extremely happy. The passage shows the villagers dancing and singing with gratitude — the context tells us they were very happy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A little bit happy' because 'joy' can be mild, but 'overjoyed' means very happy — the 'over-' makes it stronger.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The old man was very frail. He walked slowly with a stick and needed help to sit down.' What does 'frail' mean?
hints: What does the old man use to walk?
He needs help to sit down — what does that suggest?
questions.explanation: 'Frail' means weak and easily tired. The old man walks slowly with a stick and needs help to sit — these clues tell us he is frail.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Tall and thin' because being thin can look frail, but the passage focuses on weakness, not thinness.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. When a mosquito bites a sick person, it picks up the germ. Then it bites a healthy person and gives the germ to them. Malaria is dangerous, so we must sleep under treated nets.' What is the main meaning of this passage?
options: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes and we should protect ourselves
Malaria is caused by dirty water
hints: What is the passage mostly about?
It explains how malaria is spread and what to do.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how mosquitoes spread malaria and asks us to sleep under treated nets. The main meaning is that malaria is spread by mosquitoes and we should protect ourselves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Malaria is caused by dirty water' because it is a common belief, but the passage says mosquitoes spread it.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Fruits and vegetables give our bodies vitamins. They help us grow strong and fight sickness. We should eat them every day.' What is the main meaning?
options: Eating fruits and vegetables keeps us healthy
hints: What do fruits and vegetables do for us?
The passage tells us to eat them every day.
questions.explanation: The passage says fruits and vegetables give vitamins, help us grow and fight sickness, and should be eaten every day. The main meaning is that eating them keeps us healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Fruits are sweet' because it is true, but sweetness is not the main point — health is.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Forests are being cut down for firewood and building. When forests disappear, the soil washes away, animals lose their homes, and the land becomes dry. We must protect our forests.' What is the main meaning?
options: Forests are important and must be protected
hints: What is happening to the forests?
What does the passage ask us to do?
questions.explanation: The passage explains the harmful effects of cutting forests and asks us to protect them. The main meaning is that forests are important and must be protected.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Forests are made of trees' because it is true, but the main meaning is about protecting forests, not defining them.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. The passage says we should sleep under treated nets.' Which detail supports the meaning 'we should protect ourselves from malaria'?
hints: Which detail tells us what to do?
It is a way of protecting ourselves.
questions.explanation: The detail 'Sleep under treated nets' supports the meaning that we should protect ourselves from malaria — it tells us a protective action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Mosquitoes are insects' because it is a fact, but it does not support protection.

questions.stem: Passage: 'A balanced meal gives us energy and keeps us healthy.' Which detail supports this meaning?
options: It includes fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins
hints: Which detail explains what a balanced meal contains?
It lists the food groups.
questions.explanation: The detail 'It includes fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins' supports the meaning that a balanced meal gives energy and keeps us healthy — it shows what makes the meal balanced.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Fruits are colourful' because it is true, but it does not support the meaning about health.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Forests are important and must be protected.' Which detail supports this meaning?
options: When forests disappear, the soil washes away and animals lose their homes
hints: Which detail explains WHY forests are important?
It describes what happens when forests disappear.
questions.explanation: The detail 'When forests disappear, the soil washes away and animals lose their homes' explains the negative consequences of losing forests — this supports why we must protect them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Forests have many trees' because it is true, but it does not show why forests are important.

questions.stem: Read this short passage aloud: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. We should sleep under treated nets.' Then say in your own words what the passage means.
hints: What is the passage about?
What should we do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States the main meaning in own words

questions.stem: Read this short passage: 'The harmattan brings cold, dry winds. It cracks the lips and makes the skin dry.' Then say what the passage means and use something you already know about the harmattan to explain it.
hints: What is the harmattan like?
What do you already know about it?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Look at the title 'How to Save Energy at Home'. Predict what the passage will be about, then read it aloud and say whether your prediction was right.
hints: What does the title suggest?
Read the passage and check.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Makes a sensible prediction from the title
Says whether the prediction was correct

questions.stem: Read this short passage: 'The old man was frail. He walked slowly with a stick.' Say what the passage means, what prior knowledge helped you, and how you worked out the meaning of 'frail'.
hints: What does 'frail' mean?
What clues told you?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains the meaning of 'frail' from context

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Note and recall main ideas in a sequence

skills.description: Recognise/name the five SQ3R steps.
Arrange the SQ3R steps in the correct order.
Identify the main idea of each paragraph in the order they appear.
Arrange the main ideas in the order they occur in the passage.
Pick the main idea that is missing from a partial list.
Teacher-assessed oral: use SQ3R on a short passage and report the main ideas in sequence.

misconceptions: Sequence = story order not main ideas

questions.stem: What does SQ3R stand for?
hints: S = Survey
Q = Question
3R = Read, Recite, Review
questions.explanation: SQ3R stands for Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review. These are the five steps of the strategy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'SQ3R' is one word or one step, but it is an acronym for five steps.

questions.stem: In SQ3R, what does 'Survey' mean?
options: Look over the text quickly to see its headings and structure
hints: Survey means 'look over' quickly.
Do not read every word — just get an overview.
questions.explanation: In SQ3R, 'Survey' means to look over the text quickly — checking headings, sub-headings and structure before detailed reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Read every word carefully' because reading is the goal, but Survey is the quick overview, not the detailed reading.

questions.stem: In SQ3R, what does the 'Recite' step mean?
options: Say or write what you remember from the text without looking at it
hints: Recite means to say aloud.
After reading, try to recall without looking.
questions.explanation: In SQ3R, 'Recite' means to say or write what you remember from the text without looking at it — this checks your understanding.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Read the text aloud' because 'recite' sounds like reading aloud, but in SQ3R, Recite means recalling from memory.

questions.stem: Arrange the SQ3R steps in the correct order:
hints: Start with Survey.
Then Question, then Read, Recite, Review.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: Survey (look over), Question (ask questions), Read (read for answers), Recite (recall), Review (go over again). So Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put 'Read' before 'Question' because reading feels like the natural first step, but in SQ3R, you ask questions first — then read to answer them.

questions.stem: In SQ3R, which step comes right AFTER 'Read'?
hints: The letters are S-Q-R-R-R.
After the first R (Read), the next R is Recite.
questions.explanation: After 'Read', the next step is 'Recite' — you say or write what you remember from the text. The order is Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Review' because it is also an R-word, but Review comes last, after Recite.

questions.stem:
Read this passage:
'Paragraph 1: The harmattan comes with dry winds and dust.
Paragraph 2: It dries the skin and cracks the lips.
Paragraph 3: We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter.'
What is the main idea of Paragraph 1?
options: The harmattan brings dry winds and dust
hints: What is the first paragraph about?
It describes what comes with the harmattan.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'The harmattan comes with dry winds and dust' — that is the main idea of the first paragraph.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It dries the skin' because it comes next, but that is the main idea of Paragraph 2, not Paragraph 1.

questions.stem:
Read this passage:
'Paragraph 1: The harmattan comes with dry winds and dust.
Paragraph 2: It dries the skin and cracks the lips.
Paragraph 3: We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter.'
What is the main idea of Paragraph 2?
options: It dries the skin and cracks the lips
hints: What does Paragraph 2 describe?
It is about what happens to the skin and lips.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says 'It dries the skin and cracks the lips' — that is its main idea.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The harmattan brings dust' because it is about the harmattan, but that is Paragraph 1's idea, not Paragraph 2's.

questions.stem:
Read this passage:
'Paragraph 1: The harmattan comes with dry winds and dust.
Paragraph 2: It dries the skin and cracks the lips.
Paragraph 3: We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter.'
What is the main idea of Paragraph 3?
options: We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter
hints: What does Paragraph 3 tell us to do?
It is about protection.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter' — that is its main idea.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Shea butter comes from trees' because shea butter is mentioned, but Paragraph 3 is about using it for protection, not where it comes from.

questions.stem:
Read this passage:
'Paragraph 1: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes.
Paragraph 2: Pregnant women and young children are most at risk.
Paragraph 3: Use treated nets and clear standing water.'
Which statement best summarises all three paragraphs in order?
options: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes; some people are at high risk; we can prevent it
hints: What does each paragraph say?
Put the three main ideas together.
questions.explanation: The three main ideas in order: (1) mosquitoes spread malaria, (2) some groups are at high risk, (3) we can prevent it. So the best summary is 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes; some people are at high risk; we can prevent it'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Malaria is a sickness' because it is true, but it does not summarise the three main ideas in order.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'First, the farmer clears the land. Then, he plants the seeds. Next, he waters them. Finally, he harvests the crops.' Which is the correct order of events?
options: Clears land, plants seeds, waters, harvests
Plants seeds, clears land, waters, harvests
Harvests, plants seeds, waters, clears land
Waters, plants seeds, clears land, harvests
hints: The passage uses words like 'first', 'then', 'next', 'finally'.
Follow the sequence words.
questions.explanation: The passage gives the sequence directly: First → clear land, then → plant seeds, next → water, finally → harvest. So the order is clears land, plants seeds, waters, harvests.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put planting before clearing because planting is the 'main' action, but you must clear the land before planting.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Esi woke up late. She missed the bus. She ran all the way to school. She arrived just as the bell rang.' Which is the correct order?
options: Woke late, missed bus, ran to school, arrived as bell rang
Woke late, ran to school, missed bus, arrived as bell rang
Missed bus, woke late, ran to school, arrived as bell rang
Ran to school, woke late, missed bus, arrived as bell rang
hints: What is the first event?
What happened because she woke late?
questions.explanation: The passage gives the order: woke late → missed bus → ran to school → arrived just as the bell rang. So the first is 'woke late', then 'missed bus', then 'ran to school', then 'arrived as the bell rang'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put 'missed bus' before 'woke late' because the bus is more interesting, but waking late caused her to miss the bus.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Kofi found a wallet on the road. He took it to the police station. The owner came and thanked him. The owner gave him some money as a reward.' Which is the correct order?
options: Found wallet, took to police, owner thanked, gave reward
Found wallet, owner thanked, took to police, gave reward
Owner thanked, found wallet, took to police, gave reward
Found wallet, gave reward, took to police, owner thanked
hints: What happened first?
The police came before the owner.
questions.explanation: The order: found wallet → took to police station → owner came and thanked → owner gave reward.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the reward before the thanks because rewards are exciting, but the thanks comes before the reward in the passage.

questions.stem: Here are three main ideas from a passage: (1) mosquitoes spread malaria, (2) some people are at high risk, (3) ???. Which idea is missing?
hints: What is the third part of a health passage?
The first two ideas are cause and risk; what comes next?
questions.explanation: The third idea should be about prevention — 'We can prevent malaria' completes the sequence: cause → risk → prevention.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Mosquitoes are insects' because it is about mosquitoes, but it does not complete the cause-risk-prevention pattern.

questions.stem: Here are three main ideas from a passage: (1) the harmattan brings dry winds, (2) it dries the skin and lips, (3) ???. Which idea is missing?
hints: What comes after the problem is described?
It is a solution or action.
questions.explanation: After describing the harmattan and its effects, the missing idea is what we can do — 'We can protect ourselves'. This completes the sequence: problem → effects → solution.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Shea butter is sold' because it relates to protection, but the missing idea is the general action of protection, not a specific product.

questions.stem: Here are three main ideas from a passage: (1) forests are being cut down, (2) this causes soil to wash away and animals to lose homes, (3) ???. Which idea is missing?
hints: What does the passage call us to do?
After the problem and its effects, what is needed?
questions.explanation: The passage describes a problem (cutting forests) and its effects. The missing idea is the solution — 'We must protect our forests'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Animals are wild' because animals are mentioned, but that does not complete the problem-effects-solution pattern.

questions.stem: Use SQ3R on this short passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. Pregnant women and children are most at risk. Use treated nets and clear standing water.' Go through all five steps, then report the main ideas in sequence.
hints: Survey: look at the passage.
Question: what is it about?
Read: read carefully.
Recite: say what you remember.
Review: check.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Use SQ3R on this short passage: 'The harmattan comes with dry winds. It dries the skin. We can protect ourselves by drinking water.' Go through all five steps, then report the main ideas in order.
hints: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
Say the three main ideas in order.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Use SQ3R on a short passage your teacher provides. After the five steps, report the main ideas in the order they appear and explain how Recite and Review helped you remember.
hints: Go through each SQ3R step.
Then explain how Recite and Review helped.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read a passage using SQ3R. Then name the main idea of each paragraph in order. Finally, say which step (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review) helped you most and why.
hints: Report each paragraph's main idea in order.
Which step was most helpful?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names each paragraph's main idea in order

questions.stem: Use SQ3R on a passage about a familiar topic. Report the main ideas in sequence and compare your Recite with the actual passage. Did you miss any main idea?
hints: After Recite, check against the passage.
What did you miss?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Scan texts for details

skills.description: Recognise what scanning means.
Distinguish skimming (for the gist) from scanning (for a detail).
Find a named detail in a short passage.
Match a question to the detail that answers it.
Say where in the passage a given detail appears.
Teacher-assessed oral: given a short passage and three questions, find the three details within a set time and read them out.

questions.stem: What does 'scanning' mean when you read?
options: Looking quickly for a specific detail
hints: Scanning is fast.
You are looking for one specific thing.
questions.explanation: Scanning means looking quickly for a specific detail — like a number, a name or a date — without reading every word.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Reading every word slowly' because reading usually means that, but scanning is a fast, focused search.

questions.stem: You want to find the date of Ghana's Independence Day in a passage. What should you do?
options: Scan the passage for a date
Skim the passage for the main idea
hints: You need one specific detail — a date.
Scanning is best for specific details.
questions.explanation: To find a specific date, scan the passage quickly with your eyes looking for numbers and the word 'Independence'. You do not need to read every word.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Read every word carefully' because it feels thorough, but for a specific detail, scanning is faster and works well.

questions.stem: What is the difference between skimming and scanning?
options: Skimming is for the main idea; scanning is for a specific detail
Skimming is slow; scanning is fast
Skimming is for details; scanning is for the main idea
hints: Skim = gist.
Scan = specific detail.
questions.explanation: Skimming is reading quickly for the main idea (the gist). Scanning is looking quickly for a specific detail. Both are fast, but they have different goals.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'They are the same thing' because both are fast reading, but they have different purposes: gist vs detail.

questions.stem: You need to know the main idea of a passage. Which strategy should you use?
hints: Main idea = gist.
Skim for the main idea.
questions.explanation: Skimming is the right strategy for finding the main idea — you read quickly through the headings, first and last sentences of paragraphs to get the gist.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Scan' because it is fast, but scanning is for specific details, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The harmattan season begins in December and lasts until February. It brings cold, dry winds.' When does the harmattan season begin?
hints: Look for the month the season begins.
Scan for a month name.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'The harmattan season begins in December and lasts until February.' So it begins in December.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'February' because it is also mentioned, but February is when the season ends, not when it begins.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. The female anopheles mosquito carries the germ. It bites mostly at night.' Which mosquito carries the malaria germ?
hints: Which specific mosquito does the passage name?
It mentions the female of a specific type.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'The female anopheles mosquito carries the germ.' So that is the specific mosquito that carries the malaria germ.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Any mosquito' because the passage is about mosquitoes, but the passage names the female anopheles mosquito specifically.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The school was built in 1995 by the community. It has twelve classrooms and a library. Mr. Mensah is the current head teacher.' In what year was the school built?
hints: Look for a year.
Scan for numbers.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'The school was built in 1995.' So the school was built in 1995.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick another year because they confuse the years, but the passage clearly gives 1995.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Esi was born in Tamale on 15th March 2012. She moved to Accra with her family in 2018.' Where was Esi born?
hints: Look for the birthplace, not where she moved to.
The passage gives two place names.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Esi was born in Tamale.' So she was born in Tamale, not in Accra (where she moved to).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Accra' because it is also mentioned, but Accra is where she moved to, not where she was born.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The harmattan brings dry winds. It causes cracked lips and dry skin. People use shea butter to protect their skin.' Which question is answered by 'shea butter'?
options: What do people use to protect their skin?
hints: What does 'shea butter' refer to in the passage?
It is used for protection.
questions.explanation: 'Shea butter' in the passage is what people use to protect their skin. So the question 'What do people use to protect their skin?' is answered by 'shea butter'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'When does the harmattan come?' because it is about the harmattan, but the passage does not give a time — 'shea butter' answers the protection question.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The head teacher, Mr. Mensah, announced the new rules on Monday. He said pupils must wear school uniforms every day.' Which question is answered by 'Monday'?
options: When did the head teacher announce the rules?
Why did the head teacher announce the rules?
hints: What does 'Monday' refer to in the passage?
It tells you when something happened.
questions.explanation: 'Monday' in the passage answers the question 'When did the head teacher announce the rules?'. The other questions are answered by other parts of the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Who announced the rules?' because Mr. Mensah is named, but 'Monday' answers 'when', not 'who'.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The school library has over five hundred books. Pupils can borrow two books at a time for two weeks. The library is open from 8am to 4pm on school days.' Which question is NOT answered in the passage?
options: Who donated the books to the library?
How many books does the library have?
How long can pupils keep a borrowed book?
hints: Which question asks for information that is not given?
The passage mentions books, loans and hours, but not donors.
questions.explanation: The passage does not say who donated the books. It does say how many books (over five hundred), how long pupils can keep them (two weeks) and when the library is open (8am–4pm). So 'Who donated the books?' is not answered.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the passage answers every question, but not every detail is given.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. Pregnant women are most at risk. Use treated nets.' Where does the detail 'pregnant women are most at risk' appear?
options: It is not in the passage
hints: Where does the sentence about pregnant women appear?
It comes after the first sentence and before the last.
questions.explanation: The sentence about pregnant women is in the middle of the passage — after the opening about mosquitoes and before the closing about treated nets.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'At the beginning' because 'at risk' sounds like important information, but it appears in the middle.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The harmattan comes in December. It brings cold, dry winds. It causes cracked lips. People use shea butter for protection.' Where does the detail 'people use shea butter for protection' appear?
options: It is not in the passage
hints: Where does 'shea butter' appear in the passage?
It is the last sentence.
questions.explanation: 'People use shea butter for protection' is the last sentence in the passage — it appears at the end.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'In the middle' because it is important, but the shea butter sentence is the final one.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The library opens at 8am. It has many books. Pupils can borrow two books at a time. It closes at 4pm.' Where does the detail 'pupils can borrow two books at a time' appear?
options: It is not in the passage
hints: Where does the borrowing sentence appear?
It is after the opening time and before the closing time.
questions.explanation: 'Pupils can borrow two books at a time' is the third sentence, appearing in the middle of the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'At the end' because it is important information, but the closing time (4pm) is the last sentence.

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you a short passage and three questions. Scan the passage to find the three details as quickly as you can, then read them out.
hints: Look for the specific detail in each question.
Do not read every word — scan.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Finds them within the time given

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you a passage with a date, a name and a number. Scan the passage to find each of these details, then read them out.
hints: Scan for a number — that is the date.
Scan for a capital letter — that may be the name.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you a passage and four questions. Scan to find the answers to two of the questions as quickly as possible, then read them out.
hints: Choose two questions to start.
Scan for each answer one at a time.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you a passage and ask you to scan for three specific details. After finding them, explain what strategy you used (scan, not read every word).
hints: Scan by looking for the target word.
Do not read every word.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you a longer passage and four questions. Scan for the answers and read them out. Then say which question was easiest to find and why.
hints: Scan for one detail at a time.
Which question had the most obvious clue?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains which was easiest and why

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you two short passages and three questions. Decide which passage to scan for each question, find the answers, and read them out.
hints: Match each question to the right passage.
Then scan that passage.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Matches each question to the correct passage
Scans rather than reading every word

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.1: Process and comprehend level appropriate texts
indicator.objective: Read level-appropriate texts silently and closely for comprehension.

skills.description: Recognise the three reading stages (Before, During, After).
Match an activity to its stage.
Answer factual comprehension questions on a passage read silently.
Answer a question that requires reading the whole passage, not one line.
Set a pre-reading question that would guide silent reading.
Teacher-assessed observation: pupil reads silently and closely for a set time, then answers questions without re-reading aloud.

questions.stem: What are the three stages of reading?
options: Before Reading, During Reading, After Reading
hints: Before, during and after what?
The stages match the timeline of reading.
questions.explanation: The three stages of reading are Before Reading (preparation), During Reading (reading itself) and After Reading (follow-up).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Skimming, Scanning, Summarising' because these are reading skills, but the three stages are Before, During and After.

questions.stem: At which stage of reading should you ask yourself 'What will this passage be about?'
hints: When do you make predictions?
Before you read the passage.
questions.explanation: Asking 'What will this passage be about?' is a prediction — a Before Reading activity. You predict before reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'After Reading' because they think questions come after, but prediction questions come before.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the BEFORE reading stage?
options: Making a prediction from the title
hints: Before reading — what can you do with the title?
You have not read the passage yet.
questions.explanation: Making a prediction from the title is a Before Reading activity — you do it before reading the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Answering questions' because questions are common in reading lessons, but those come after reading.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the DURING reading stage?
options: Noting important details as you read
hints: During reading — what do you do while reading?
You pay attention to details.
questions.explanation: Noting important details as you read is a During Reading activity — you do it while reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Writing a summary' because it is important, but summaries come after reading.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the AFTER reading stage?
hints: After reading — what do you do once you finish?
You check what you understood.
questions.explanation: Answering comprehension questions is an After Reading activity — you do it after reading to check your understanding.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Skimming' because it is a reading strategy, but skimming happens during reading, not after.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The school library has over five hundred books. Pupils can borrow two books at a time for two weeks. The library is open from 8am to 4pm on school days.' How many books can a pupil borrow at a time?
hints: Look for the number next to 'books at a time'.
Scan the second sentence.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Pupils can borrow two books at a time.' So the answer is two.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Five' because 'five hundred' is in the passage, but that is the total number of books, not the number a pupil can borrow.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. Pregnant women and children are most at risk. Use treated nets and clear standing water.' Who is most at risk of malaria?
hints: Which group does the passage name?
Look at the second sentence.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Pregnant women and children are most at risk.' So they are the group most at risk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Everyone equally' because malaria affects everyone, but the passage says some groups are MORE at risk.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The harmattan begins in December. It brings dry winds and dust. People use shea butter to protect their skin.' When does the harmattan begin?
hints: Look for the month.
It is the first sentence.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'The harmattan begins in December.' So it begins in December.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick a different month because they confuse the harmattan with other seasons, but the passage gives December.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The farmer cleared the land and planted maize. He watered the crops daily. After three months, the maize was ready for harvest.' What crop did the farmer plant?
hints: Which crop does the passage name?
Look for the crop name.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'planted maize'. So the crop is maize.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Rice' because it is a common crop, but the passage specifically says maize.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Esi woke up late. She missed the bus. She ran all the way to school. She arrived just as the bell rang. She was out of breath but happy.' What does this passage tell us about Esi?
options: She was late and had to hurry but still arrived on time
She was lazy and did not care
hints: What happened to Esi?
What did she do to get to school?
questions.explanation: The passage says Esi woke late, missed the bus, ran to school and arrived just as the bell rang. So she was late and had to hurry but still arrived on time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She was lazy' because she woke late, but the passage shows her running to school — not lazy.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The head teacher asked the pupils to keep the school clean. Some pupils swept the classrooms. Others picked up litter. By the end of the day, the school looked beautiful.' Why did the school look beautiful?
options: Because the pupils worked together to clean it
Because the head teacher cleaned it herself
Because it was a new school
hints: What did the pupils do?
Cleaning is the key action.
questions.explanation: The pupils swept, picked up litter and worked together. The school looked beautiful because of their work — the passage does not mention rain, the head teacher cleaning or a new school.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because it rained' because clean places can look fresh after rain, but the passage attributes the change to the pupils' work.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi found a wallet with money in it. He took it to the police station. The owner came and thanked him. Kofi felt proud of what he had done.' Why did Kofi feel proud?
options: Because he did the right thing by returning the wallet
hints: What did Kofi do with the wallet?
Was it the right thing to do?
questions.explanation: Kofi took the wallet to the police and the owner came to thank him. He felt proud because he did the right thing — not because he kept the money or got a reward.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because he got a reward' because rewards are common in such stories, but the passage does not mention a reward — only that the owner thanked him.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The harmattan season can be hard for farmers. The dry winds dry up the soil. Crops fail to grow well. Farmers must water their crops more often.' What does this passage suggest about farming during the harmattan?
options: It is difficult and requires extra watering
It is the best season for farming
It is the same as other seasons
hints: What happens to the soil and crops?
What must farmers do?
questions.explanation: The passage says the harmattan is hard for farmers, crops fail to grow and farmers must water more often. So farming during the harmattan is difficult and requires extra watering.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'It is the best season for farming' because they think dry weather is good for crops, but the passage says the opposite.

questions.stem: You are about to read a passage titled 'How to Prevent Malaria'. Which pre-reading question would best guide your silent reading?
options: What are the ways to prevent malaria?
hints: The title tells you the topic.
Which question matches the title?
questions.explanation: The title is 'How to Prevent Malaria', so the best pre-reading question is 'What are the ways to prevent malaria?' — it guides you to look for prevention methods as you read.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'How long is the passage?' because it is practical, but it does not help you understand the topic.

questions.stem: You are about to read a passage titled 'Keeping Our Water Clean'. Which pre-reading question would best guide your silent reading?
options: Why is it important to keep our water clean?
How many words are in the passage?
hints: What does the title tell you?
Ask a question about the topic.
questions.explanation: 'Why is it important to keep our water clean?' matches the title and guides you to look for reasons as you read.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'What is the title?' because it is easy, but it does not help you understand the passage's content.

questions.stem: You are about to read a passage about a boy who finds a lost dog. Which pre-reading question would best guide your reading?
options: What will the boy do with the dog?
What is the boy's favourite colour?
How many pages are in the book?
hints: What is the story about?
What prediction can you make about the dog?
questions.explanation: 'What will the boy do with the dog?' is a prediction question based on the title — it guides you to look for the boy's actions as you read.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'How old is the boy?' because it is about the character, but the passage may not answer it — the prediction question is more useful.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently for two minutes: 'The school library has over five hundred books. Pupils can borrow two books at a time for two weeks.' Then answer: How many books does the library have?
hints: Read silently — no whispering.
Look for the number in the passage.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Reads silently for the set time

questions.stem: Read this passage silently for three minutes: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. Pregnant women and children are most at risk. Use treated nets.' Then answer two questions: (1) What spreads malaria? (2) Who is most at risk?
hints: Read silently and carefully.
Answer both questions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Reads silently for the set time

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Esi woke late. She missed the bus. She ran to school. She arrived as the bell rang.' After reading, answer three questions without re-reading aloud: (1) Why did Esi miss the bus? (2) How did she get to school? (3) When did she arrive?
hints: Read carefully — you will answer three questions.
Do not re-read aloud.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Reads silently for the set time

questions.stem: Read a longer passage silently for five minutes. Then answer: (1) What is the main idea? (2) What is one detail from the beginning? (3) What is one detail from the end?
hints: Read the whole passage — beginning to end.
Answer all three questions.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a detail from the beginning
Gives a detail from the end

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.2: Apply critical reading, implied meaning, higher order thinking, judgment and evaluation
indicator.objective: Respond to a text with simple judgment

skills.description: Choose a judgment about a character or event that is supported by the text.
Recognise a judgment that is not supported by the text.
Identify what a passage allows you to picture.
Give one reason from the text for a stated judgment.
Distinguish a feeling from a judgment.
Teacher-assessed oral: state a judgment about a passage and give a reason from the text.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Kofi found a wallet with money in it. He took it straight to the police station. The owner came and thanked him.' Which judgment about Kofi is SUPPORTED by the passage?
hints: What did Kofi do with the wallet?
Honesty is about returning what is not yours.
questions.explanation: Kofi found a wallet and took it to the police instead of keeping it — this supports the judgment that he is honest. The other judgments are contradicted by the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi is greedy' because money is involved, but he did not keep the money — the passage shows honesty, not greed.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Esi saw a small boy crying in the market. He had lost his mother. Esi held his hand and helped him find her. The mother thanked Esi warmly.' Which judgment about Esi is SUPPORTED by the passage?
hints: What did Esi do for the crying boy?
Holding his hand and helping him find his mother is kind.
questions.explanation: Esi helped a lost boy find his mother — this supports the judgment that she is kind and helpful. The other judgments are contradicted or not supported.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Esi is tired' because she is in a market, but the passage says nothing about her being tired.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The farmer woke before dawn every day. He worked in the field until sunset. His crops were the best in the village.' Which judgment about the farmer is SUPPORTED?
hints: What does the farmer do every day?
Waking before dawn and working until sunset shows hard work.
questions.explanation: The farmer wakes before dawn and works until sunset — this supports the judgment that he is hard-working. The passage says nothing about his wealth or kindness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The farmer is rich' because his crops are the best, but the passage does not say he is rich — only that he works hard.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Adjoa studied every evening. She asked questions in class. She read extra books from the library. When the exam results came out, she was top of the class.' Which judgment about Adjoa is SUPPORTED?
hints: What does Adjoa do every evening?
Her study habits show determination.
questions.explanation: Adjoa studies every evening, asks questions and reads extra books — this supports the judgment that she is determined and hard-working. The other judgments are not supported by the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Adjoa is lucky' because she came top, but the passage shows her hard work — luck is not mentioned.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children cleaned the compound and planted flowers. The school looked beautiful. The head teacher praised them.' Which judgment is NOT supported by the passage?
hints: Which judgment contradicts what the passage says?
The children cleaned and planted — did they work or not?
questions.explanation: 'The children are lazy' is contradicted by the passage — they cleaned and planted. The other judgments (helpful, worked together, head teacher pleased) are all supported.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The children worked together' because it is a judgment, but the passage supports it — cleaning and planting together shows teamwork.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Ama was walking home from school. She saw a small boy crying by the road. She stopped and helped him find his way home.' Which judgment is NOT supported by the passage?
hints: Which judgment contradicts the story?
Ama helped — is that unkind?
questions.explanation: 'Ama is unkind' is contradicted by the passage — she helped the boy. The other judgments (helpful, caring, responsible) are all supported.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama is responsible' because it is a strong judgment, but the passage supports it — she took responsibility for the boy's safety.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Kofi studied hard for the exam. He read every day. He asked the teacher questions. He passed with the highest marks.' Which judgment is NOT supported by the passage?
options: Kofi passed because he was lucky
hints: Which judgment adds an idea not in the passage?
The passage shows hard work — not luck.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi passed because he was lucky' adds an idea (luck) not in the passage. The passage shows his hard work — the other judgments (hard-working, determined, worked for success) are supported.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi worked for his success' because it sounds like a general statement, but it is supported — the passage shows him studying, reading and asking questions.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The market was crowded. Traders called out their prices. The air smelled of ripe mangoes and fresh fish. Women in bright cloths carried baskets on their heads.' Which of these can you PICTURE from the passage?
options: Women in bright cloths with baskets on their heads
hints: What does the passage describe?
Which option matches the details in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage describes a busy market with women in bright cloths carrying baskets — you can picture this. The other options are not in the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A snowy mountain' because they are imagining an interesting scene, but the passage does not mention snow or mountains.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The harmattan wind blew through the village. Dry leaves swirled in the air. The sky was pale and dusty. People wrapped themselves in warm cloths.' Which of these can you PICTURE from the passage?
options: People wrapped in warm cloths in dusty air
hints: What season does the passage describe?
Match the details in the passage to the options.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the harmattan with dry leaves, dusty sky and people in warm cloths — you can picture this. The other options are not in the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'People swimming in a river' because rivers are common, but the passage does not mention swimming — it is about dry harmattan weather.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The old fisherman pulled his net onto the shore. Silver fish jumped and flopped in the sun. Seagulls cried above his head. He smiled as he counted his catch.' Which of these can you PICTURE from the passage?
options: Silver fish flopping on the sand while seagulls fly overhead
A boy running on a road
hints: What is the fisherman doing?
Which option matches the details in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage describes a fisherman with silver fish and seagulls crying above — you can picture this. The other options are not in the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A farmer ploughing' because farming and fishing are similar work, but the passage is about a fisherman, not a farmer.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Kofi found a wallet and took it to the police station. The owner came and thanked him.' Judgment: 'Kofi is honest.' Give one reason from the passage for this judgment.
answer: Accept any answer that uses a detail from the passage — e.g., 'Kofi took the wallet to the police station instead of keeping it' or 'He returned the wallet to its owner.' Award full marks if the reason clearly supports the judgment of honesty.
hints: What did Kofi do with the wallet?
Why does that show honesty?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one reason from the passage

questions.stem: Passage: 'Esi saw a lost boy crying. She held his hand and helped him find his mother.' Judgment: 'Esi is kind.' Give one reason from the passage.
answer: Accept any answer that uses a detail from the passage — e.g., 'She held the boy's hand and helped him find his mother.' Award full marks if the reason supports the judgment of kindness.
hints: What did Esi do for the boy?
How does that show kindness?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one reason from the passage

questions.stem: Passage: 'The farmer worked from dawn to dusk. His crops were the best in the village.' Judgment: 'The farmer is hard-working.' Give one reason from the passage.
answer: Accept any answer that uses a detail from the passage — e.g., 'He worked from dawn to dusk' or 'His crops were the best in the village because he worked hard.' Award full marks if the reason supports the judgment.
hints: When did the farmer work?
What was the result of his work?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Gives one reason from the passage

questions.stem: Which of these is a JUDGMENT, not a feeling?
hints: A judgment is about the character's qualities.
A feeling is about how the reader feels.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi is honest' is a judgment — it describes Kofi's character. 'I like Kofi', 'Kofi makes me happy' and 'I admire Kofi' are feelings — they describe how the reader feels about Kofi.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'I admire Kofi' because admiration is a strong response, but it is a feeling, not a judgment about Kofi's character.

questions.stem: Which of these is a FEELING, not a judgment?
options: I feel sad when I read about the lost boy
hints: Which sentence is about how the reader feels?
'I feel sad' is the reader's feeling.
questions.explanation: 'I feel sad when I read about the lost boy' is a feeling — it describes the reader's emotion. The other sentences are statements or judgments about the boy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The boy is sad' because it mentions sadness, but that is a judgment about the boy's state, not the reader's feeling.

questions.stem: Read this short passage: 'Ama helped a lost boy find his mother.' State a judgment about Ama and give one reason from the passage.
hints: What kind of person is Ama?
What did she do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a reason from the passage

questions.stem: Read this short passage: 'Kofi found a wallet and took it to the police. The owner thanked him.' State a judgment about Kofi and give two reasons from the passage.
hints: What kind of person is Kofi?
What two things did he do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives two reasons from the passage

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children cleaned the compound. The school looked beautiful.' State a judgment about the children and give one reason from the passage.
hints: What kind of children are they?
What did they do?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a reason from the passage

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The farmer worked from dawn to dusk every day. His crops were the best in the village.' State a judgment about the farmer, give one reason from the passage, and give one reason why you think so.
hints: What kind of farmer is he?
What does the passage say?
Why does that support your judgment?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a reason from the passage
Explains why the reason supports the judgment

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Adjoa studied every day and passed with the highest marks.' State a judgment, give a reason from the passage, and tell how this judgment could apply to your own life.
hints: What kind of pupil is Adjoa?
What does the passage say?
How does this apply to you?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a reason from the passage
Connects the judgment to own life

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.2: Apply critical reading, implied meaning, higher order thinking, judgment and evaluation
indicator.objective: Relate two or more ideas in a text

skills.description: Link two ideas within one passage (cause/effect, problem/solution).
Link an idea in one short passage to an idea in a second short passage.
Link a passage idea to a real-life experience.
Say how two ideas are similar or different.
Explain the link between two ideas in one sentence.
Teacher-assessed oral: relate two ideas from a passage to each other and to a real-life experience.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Kofi did not do his homework. The teacher was angry with him.' How are the two ideas related?
options: Kofi not doing his homework caused the teacher to be angry
Kofi's homework and the teacher are unrelated
The teacher's anger caused Kofi not to do homework
The two ideas have no connection
hints: Why was the teacher angry?
What did Kofi do (or not do)?
questions.explanation: The two ideas are linked by cause and effect: Kofi did not do his homework (cause) → the teacher was angry (effect).
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the order — saying the teacher's anger caused Kofi not to do his homework — but the passage shows the opposite: his homework came first, then the anger.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The village had no clean water. The people became sick. The chief called a meeting to find a solution.' How are the first two ideas related?
options: The lack of clean water caused the people to become sick
The people became sick because they were lazy
The two ideas are not related
hints: What caused the sickness?
What was missing in the village?
questions.explanation: The lack of clean water (cause) led to the people becoming sick (effect). The chief's meeting is a response to this problem.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The people became sick because they were lazy' because they think sickness is caused by behaviour, but the passage says the lack of clean water is the cause.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Ama studied hard for the exam. She passed with the highest marks. Her parents were very proud of her.' How are the first and third ideas related?
options: Ama studying hard led to her success, which made her parents proud
Ama's parents being proud caused her to study
Ama passed because her parents were proud
hints: What was the result of studying hard?
How did her parents feel about the result?
questions.explanation: Ama studied hard → she passed with the highest marks → her parents were proud. So studying caused success, which caused pride.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the chain — saying the parents' pride caused Ama to study — but the passage shows studying came first.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The forest was cut down. The soil washed away. The crops could not grow.' How are these three ideas related?
options: Cutting the forest caused soil to wash away, which led to poor crops
The three ideas are separate events
Poor crops caused the forest to be cut down
The soil washing away caused the forest to be cut down
hints: What happened first?
What caused what next?
questions.explanation: The chain is: forest cut down (cause) → soil washed away (effect 1, which becomes cause 2) → crops could not grow (effect 2). Each event leads to the next.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put poor crops first because they think farming causes deforestation, but the passage shows the opposite order: cutting trees first, then poor crops.

questions.stem:
Read these two short passages:
Passage A: 'Kofi studied hard and passed his exam.'
Passage B: 'Ama practised football every day and became the best player in her school.'
What idea connects both passages?
options: Exams are more important than sports
hints: What is the same in both passages?
Both characters worked hard and succeeded.
questions.explanation: Both passages show a character working hard (studying / practising) and succeeding (passing / becoming the best). The shared idea is that hard work leads to success.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama is better than Kofi' because both are mentioned, but the passages are about two different people — no comparison is made.

questions.stem:
Read these two short passages:
Passage A: 'The village had no clean water, so the people became sick.'
Passage B: 'The school had no clean toilets, so the pupils became sick.'
What idea connects both passages?
options: Lack of cleanliness leads to sickness
Schools are less healthy than villages
Both village and school are in Ghana
hints: What is missing in both places?
What is the result of that lack?
questions.explanation: Both passages show a lack of cleanliness (no clean water / no clean toilets) leading to sickness. The shared idea is that lack of cleanliness leads to sickness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Both village and school are in Ghana' because it is a true fact, but it is not the IDEA that connects the two passages.

questions.stem:
Read these two short passages:
Passage A: 'Kofi found a wallet and took it to the police.'
Passage B: 'Ama found a purse and returned it to its owner.'
What idea connects both passages?
hints: What did both Kofi and Ama do?
They both returned what they found.
questions.explanation: Both Kofi and Ama returned what they found. The shared idea is honesty in returning lost things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Police stations are helpful' because Kofi went to the police, but that is a detail from one passage — the shared idea is honesty, which both passages illustrate.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Esi saw a lost boy crying. She helped him find his mother.' Which personal experience connects to this passage?
options: You once helped a younger child who was crying
You once cried because you lost your pencil
You once visited a big market
You once saw a famous person
hints: What did Esi do?
Which personal experience shows the same kind of action?
questions.explanation: Esi helped a lost boy. The personal experience that connects is 'You once helped a younger child who was crying' — it shows the same kind of helpful action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You once cried because you lost your pencil' because it mentions crying, but the passage is about HELPING someone who is crying, not being the one crying.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Adjoa studied every day and passed her exam with the highest marks.' Which personal experience connects?
options: You studied every day for a test and did well
hints: What did Adjoa do?
Which personal experience shows the same effort?
questions.explanation: Adjoa studied every day and succeeded. The personal experience that connects is studying every day and doing well — it shows the same pattern.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You went to the market' because it is a common activity, but it does not connect to studying and success.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The village had no clean water, so the people became sick.' Which personal experience connects to this passage?
options: You once drank dirty water and became sick
You once went to the market with your mother
You once played football with your friends
You once watched a film about animals
hints: What caused the sickness?
Which personal experience shows the same cause?
questions.explanation: The passage says dirty water caused sickness. The personal experience that connects is drinking dirty water and becoming sick — it shows the same cause-and-effect.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You once played football' because it is an activity, but it does not connect to dirty water and sickness.

questions.stem: Kofi studied hard and passed. Ama studied hard and passed. How are the two ideas SIMILAR?
options: Both people studied hard and passed
Kofi is a boy and Ama is a girl
Kofi passed but Ama did not
hints: What is the same in both cases?
Both studied and passed.
questions.explanation: Both Kofi and Ama studied hard and passed. That is what makes the two ideas similar.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi is a boy and Ama is a girl' because it is a difference, but the question asks how they are SIMILAR — not different.

questions.stem: Kofi studied hard and passed. Ama did not study and failed. How are the two ideas DIFFERENT?
options: Kofi studied and passed, while Ama did not study and failed
hints: What did each person do?
What happened to each person?
questions.explanation: Kofi studied and passed; Ama did not study and failed. The difference is in both their actions (studying vs not studying) and their results (passing vs failing).
