questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Both studied hard and passed' because studying is mentioned, but Ama did NOT study — that is the difference.

questions.stem: Passage A: 'The village had no clean water, so the people became sick.' Passage B: 'The village had clean water, so the people stayed healthy.' How are the two passages DIFFERENT?
options: Passage A describes sickness from dirty water; Passage B describes health from clean water
hints: What is the same? What is different?
Look at the cause (clean vs dirty water) and the effect (health vs sickness).
questions.explanation: Passage A is about dirty water causing sickness; Passage B is about clean water keeping people healthy. The difference is in the cause (dirty vs clean) and the effect (sick vs healthy).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Both describe sickness' because both mention health-related ideas, but Passage B describes health, not sickness.

questions.stem: Explain the link between these two ideas in one sentence: 'Kofi did not do his homework' and 'The teacher was angry.'
answer: Accept any answer that links the two ideas by cause and effect — e.g., 'The teacher was angry because Kofi did not do his homework.' Award full marks if the sentence clearly links the two ideas using because, so, or similar.
hints: Why was the teacher angry?
Use 'because' or 'so'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Links the two ideas in one sentence

questions.stem: Explain the link between these two ideas in one sentence: 'The village had no clean water' and 'The people became sick.'
answer: Accept any answer that links the two ideas by cause and effect — e.g., 'The people became sick because the village had no clean water.' Award full marks if the sentence clearly links the two ideas.
hints: What caused the sickness?
Use 'because' or 'so'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Links the two ideas in one sentence

questions.stem: Explain the link between these three ideas in two sentences: 'Ama studied hard', 'She passed her exam', 'Her parents were proud of her.'
answer: Accept any answer that links all three ideas by cause and effect — e.g., 'Ama studied hard, so she passed her exam. Her parents were proud of her because she passed.' Award full marks if both sentences clearly link the ideas.
hints: What did studying lead to?
What did passing lead to?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Links the second and third ideas

questions.stem: Read a short passage. Relate two ideas from the passage to each other, and then relate one of them to a real-life experience.
hints: How are the two ideas connected?
Have you seen something similar in real life?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Relates two ideas within the passage
Relates one idea to real life

questions.stem: Read two short passages about the same topic. Relate one idea from each passage, and explain how they connect.
hints: What is the same idea in both passages?
Explain the connection.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Names one idea from each passage

questions.stem: Read a passage. Relate two ideas from the passage to each other and to a real-life experience. Explain the link clearly.
hints: How are the two ideas connected?
What real-life experience is similar?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Relates two ideas within the passage
Relates them to a real-life experience

questions.stem: Read a passage. Relate two ideas from the passage to each other and to a real-life experience. Then explain whether the passage's idea is similar to or different from your experience.
hints: How are the two ideas connected?
Is your experience similar or different?
Why?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Relates two ideas within the passage

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.2: Apply critical reading, implied meaning, higher order thinking, judgment and evaluation
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the structure of texts (e.g. introduction, body, conclusion)

skills.description: Identify whether a given sentence or paragraph is the introduction, body or conclusion.
Say what the introduction, body or conclusion does.
Arrange jumbled parts into the correct order.
Summarise one of the three parts in one line.
Combine three part-summaries into a full summary.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a passage and name its introduction, body and conclusion, summarising each part in a sentence.

misconceptions: Body = everything except first and last

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease in Ghana. This passage will explain how malaria is spread and how we can prevent it.' Which part of a text is this?
hints: It tells you what the passage will be about.
It introduces the topic.
questions.explanation: This paragraph introduces the topic (malaria) and says what the passage will cover. That is the introduction.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Body' because it contains information about malaria, but it introduces the topic rather than developing it — the body would give the details.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'In conclusion, malaria can be prevented if we all sleep under treated nets and clear standing water around our homes.' Which part of a text is this?
hints: It uses the phrase 'In conclusion'.
It sums up the passage.
questions.explanation: This paragraph uses 'In conclusion' and sums up the main points — that is the conclusion.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Body' because it mentions prevention methods, but the phrase 'in conclusion' tells us it is the conclusion.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. The female anopheles mosquito carries the germ. It bites mostly at night. Pregnant women and children are most at risk.' Which part of a text is this?
hints: It gives the main information about how malaria is spread.
It does not introduce or conclude.
questions.explanation: This paragraph gives detailed information about how malaria is spread and who is at risk — that is the body of the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Introduction' because it is the first paragraph of information, but the introduction would state the topic, while this paragraph develops it.

questions.stem:
Read this short passage:
P1: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease in Ghana.'
P2: 'It is spread by mosquitoes and affects pregnant women and children most.'
P3: 'So we must all sleep under treated nets to prevent it.'
Which paragraph is the body?
hints: Which paragraph gives the main information?
P2 develops the topic introduced in P1.
questions.explanation: P1 introduces the topic (malaria is dangerous). P2 gives the main information (how it is spread and who is affected). P3 concludes (what we should do). So P2 is the body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick P1 because it is first, but P1 only introduces — it does not develop the topic.

questions.stem: What does the INTRODUCTION of a passage do?
options: Introduces the topic and tells the reader what to expect
hints: Introduction = the beginning.
What does 'introduce' mean?
questions.explanation: The introduction introduces the topic and tells the reader what the passage will be about.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Gives the main details' because details are important, but the introduction sets up the topic — the body gives the details.

questions.stem: What does the BODY of a passage do?
options: Develops the topic with details and explanations
hints: Body = the main part.
What happens in the main part?
questions.explanation: The body develops the topic with details, explanations and examples.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Introduces the topic' because the body comes early, but the introduction does that — the body develops.

questions.stem: What does the CONCLUSION of a passage do?
options: Wraps up the passage and restates the main point
hints: Conclusion = the ending.
What does 'conclude' mean?
questions.explanation: The conclusion wraps up the passage — it restates the main point or gives a final thought.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Introduces new ideas' because the conclusion can add a final thought, but a good conclusion does not introduce completely new ideas — it wraps up what has been said.

questions.stem:
Arrange these parts into the correct passage structure:
A) 'Mosquitoes spread malaria and pregnant women are most at risk.'
B) 'Malaria is a dangerous disease in Ghana.'
C) 'So we must all sleep under treated nets.'
hints: Which part introduces the topic?
Which part concludes?
questions.explanation: The correct order: introduction (B), body (A), conclusion (C). So B, A, C.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the body first because it has the most information, but the introduction always comes first.

questions.stem:
Arrange these parts into the correct order:
A) 'The harmattan brings dry winds and dust.'
B) 'In conclusion, we must protect our skin during harmattan.'
C) 'The harmattan is a season that affects many people in Ghana.'
hints: Which part introduces?
Which part concludes?
questions.explanation: The correct order: introduction (C), body (A), conclusion (B). So C, A, B.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the conclusion first because it is short, but the conclusion always comes last.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. It affects pregnant women and children most. We can prevent it by using treated nets.' Summarise the INTRODUCTION of this passage in one line.
answer: Accept any answer that identifies the topic — e.g., 'The passage is about malaria.' or 'Malaria is the topic of this passage.' Award full marks if the answer states the topic in one line.
hints: What is the passage about?
Keep it to one line.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: States the topic in one line

questions.stem: Passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. It affects pregnant women and children most. We can prevent it by using treated nets.' Summarise the BODY of this passage in one line.
answer: Accept any answer that captures the main information — e.g., 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes and affects pregnant women and children most.' Award full marks if the answer captures the key details.
hints: What are the main details in the body?
Keep it to one line.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. It affects pregnant women and children most. We can prevent it by using treated nets.' Summarise the CONCLUSION of this passage in one line.
answer: Accept any answer that states the conclusion — e.g., 'We can prevent malaria by using treated nets.' Award full marks if the answer states the final point.
hints: What is the last point in the passage?
Keep it to one line.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Malaria is a dangerous disease. It is spread by mosquitoes. Pregnant women and children are most at risk. We can prevent it by using treated nets.' Write a full summary in three sentences: one for the introduction, one for the body, one for the conclusion.
answer: Accept any summary that has three sentences matching introduction, body and conclusion — e.g., (1) Malaria is a dangerous disease. (2) It is spread by mosquitoes and affects pregnant women and children most. (3) We can prevent it by using treated nets. Award full marks if all three parts are covered.
hints: Sentence 1: topic. Sentence 2: main details. Sentence 3: conclusion.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Passage: 'The harmattan is a season in Ghana. It brings dry winds and dust. It dries the skin and cracks the lips. We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter.' Write a full summary in three sentences.
answer: Accept any summary with three sentences covering introduction, body and conclusion — e.g., (1) The harmattan is a season in Ghana. (2) It brings dry winds, dust and cracked skin. (3) We can protect ourselves by drinking water and using shea butter. Award full marks if all three parts are covered.
hints: Sentence 1: topic. Sentence 2: main details. Sentence 3: conclusion.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Passage: 'Forests are important. They give us shade and clean the air. They also provide homes for animals. But forests are being cut down. We must protect our forests.' Write a full summary in three sentences.
answer: Accept any summary with three sentences covering introduction, body and conclusion — e.g., (1) Forests are important. (2) They give shade, clean air and homes for animals, but they are being cut down. (3) We must protect our forests. Award full marks if all three parts are covered.
hints: Sentence 1: topic. Sentence 2: main details. Sentence 3: conclusion.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Read a short passage aloud. Then name its introduction, body and conclusion, and summarise each part in one sentence.
hints: Which part introduces the topic?
Which part gives details?
Which part wraps up?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Summarises each part in one sentence

questions.stem: Read a short passage. Identify the introduction, body and conclusion. Then explain the function of each part.
hints: What does each part do?
Introduction sets up, body develops, conclusion wraps up.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains the function of the introduction
Explains the function of the body
Explains the function of the conclusion

questions.stem: Read a short passage. Name its introduction, body and conclusion. Summarise each part in one sentence, then say which part was easiest to summarise and why.
hints: Which part had the most details?
Which part was clear?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Summarises each part in one sentence
Says which was easiest and why

questions.stem: Read a short passage. Name its introduction, body and conclusion. Then make a full summary of the passage in three sentences, one for each part.
hints: Use the three parts to build a full summary.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read a short passage. Identify the introduction, body and conclusion. Then explain how the conclusion links back to the introduction.
hints: How does the conclusion tie back to the topic?
What idea is repeated?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Explains how conclusion links to introduction
Gives one example from the passage

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.7.3: Demonstrate an understanding of the use of words and phrases as used in a text
indicator.objective: Use knowledge of prefixes and suffixes to read and interpret unfamiliar words.

skills.description: Identify the prefix in a given word.
Identify the suffix in a given word.
Work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word from its prefix or suffix.
Distinguish the meaning an affix adds from the meaning of the root.
Use an unfamiliar word containing a known affix in a meaningful sentence.
Teacher-assessed oral: given an unfamiliar word with a known affix, read it aloud and say what it means.

questions.stem: What is the prefix in the word 'misunderstanding'?
hints: A prefix is added to the BEGINNING of a word.
'Mis-' is at the start.
questions.explanation: The prefix in 'misunderstanding' is 'mis-' — it is added to the beginning of the root word.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick '-ing' because it is part of the word, but '-ing' is a suffix (added to the end), not a prefix (added to the beginning).

questions.stem: What is the prefix in the word 'unkind'?
hints: A prefix is added to the beginning.
'Un-' is at the start of 'unkind'.
questions.explanation: The prefix in 'unkind' is 'un-'. It means 'not' — so 'unkind' means 'not kind'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'kind' because it is the main part of the word, but 'kind' is the root — the prefix is 'un-'.

questions.stem: What is the prefix in the word 'disagree'?
hints: Which part comes before 'agree'?
The prefix is at the start.
questions.explanation: The prefix in 'disagree' is 'dis-'. It means 'not' or 'opposite of' — so 'disagree' means 'not agree'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'agree' because it is the main word, but 'agree' is the root — the prefix is 'dis-'.

questions.stem: What is the suffix in the word 'careful'?
hints: A suffix is added to the END of a word.
'-ful' is at the end of 'careful'.
questions.explanation: The suffix in 'careful' is '-ful'. It means 'full of' — so 'careful' means 'full of care'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'care-' because it is at the start, but 'care' is the root — the suffix is '-ful'.

questions.stem: What is the suffix in the word 'kindness'?
hints: Which part comes after 'kind'?
The suffix is at the end.
questions.explanation: The suffix in 'kindness' is '-ness'. It turns the adjective 'kind' into a noun meaning 'the quality of being kind'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick '-ss' because it is at the end, but '-ss' is only part of the suffix. The full suffix is '-ness'.

questions.stem: What is the suffix in the word 'helpful'?
hints: Which part comes after 'help'?
The suffix is '-ful'.
questions.explanation: The suffix in 'helpful' is '-ful' — it means 'full of' or 'giving' help.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'help-' because it comes first, but 'help' is the root word — the suffix is '-ful'.

questions.stem: What does the word 'unhappy' mean?
hints: What does the prefix 'un-' mean?
It means 'not'.
questions.explanation: 'Un-' means 'not'. So 'unhappy' means 'not happy'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Very happy' because 'un-' looks like it strengthens the word, but 'un-' negates — it makes the word mean the opposite.

questions.stem: What does the word 'careless' mean?
hints: What does the suffix '-less' mean?
It means 'without'.
questions.explanation: '-less' means 'without'. So 'careless' means 'without care'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Full of care' because 'care' is in the word, but '-less' negates it — it means WITHOUT care.

questions.stem: What does the word 'misunderstand' mean?
hints: What does the prefix 'mis-' mean?
It means 'wrongly'.
questions.explanation: 'Mis-' means 'wrongly'. So 'misunderstand' means 'to understand wrongly'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'To not understand at all' because 'mis-' sounds negative, but 'mis-' means 'wrongly', not 'not at all'.

questions.stem: What does the word 'unbelievable' mean?
hints: Break the word: 'un-' + 'believe' + '-able'.
'Un-' = not, '-able' = able to.
questions.explanation: 'Un-' means 'not', 'believe' is the root, and '-able' means 'able to'. So 'unbelievable' means 'not able to be believed' — it is so surprising that it seems impossible.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Easy to believe' because 'believe' is in the word, but 'un-' makes it the opposite — not believable.

questions.stem: What does the word 'disrespectful' mean?
hints: Break the word: 'dis-' + 'respect' + '-ful'.
'Dis-' = not, '-ful' = full of.
questions.explanation: 'Dis-' means 'not' or 'opposite of', 'respect' is the root, and '-ful' means 'full of'. So 'disrespectful' means 'full of the opposite of respect' — i.e., not showing respect.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Full of respect' because '-ful' is in the word, but 'dis-' makes it the opposite — not full of respect, but full of disrespect.

questions.stem: In the word 'unkind', what does the prefix 'un-' add to the meaning of the root 'kind'?
options: It changes the word to a noun
hints: What does 'un-' mean?
'Un-' is a negative prefix.
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' adds the meaning 'not'. So 'unkind' = 'not' + 'kind' = 'not kind'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'un-' makes the word stronger, but 'un-' negates — it makes the word mean the opposite.

questions.stem: In the word 'hopeless', what does the suffix '-less' add to the meaning of the root 'hope'?
options: It means 'full of' — so 'hopeless' means 'full of hope'
It means 'a person who' — so 'hopeless' means 'a person who hopes'
hints: What does '-less' mean?
'-less' means 'without'.
questions.explanation: The suffix '-less' adds the meaning 'without'. So 'hopeless' means 'without hope'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'full of' because suffixes can add many meanings, but '-less' specifically means 'without' — the opposite of '-ful'.

questions.stem: Use the word 'misunderstanding' in a meaningful sentence.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'misunderstanding' correctly — e.g., 'There was a misunderstanding between the two friends, but they made up.' or 'The misunderstanding caused a big problem.' Award full marks if the word is used correctly and the sentence makes sense.
hints: What does 'misunderstanding' mean?
It means understanding something wrongly.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Use the word 'careless' in a meaningful sentence.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'careless' correctly — e.g., 'The careless driver caused an accident.' or 'She was careless with her books and lost one.' Award full marks if the word is used correctly and the sentence makes sense.
hints: What does 'careless' mean?
It means 'without care'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Use the word 'disagree' in a meaningful sentence.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'disagree' correctly — e.g., 'I disagree with you on this point.' or 'They disagreed about the plan.' Award full marks if the word is used correctly and the sentence makes sense.
hints: What does 'disagree' mean?
It means 'not agree'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Read this word aloud: 'unkind'. Then say what it means, using the prefix 'un-' to explain.
hints: 'Un-' means 'not'.
So 'unkind' means 'not kind'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this word aloud: 'careless'. Then say what it means, using the suffix '-less' to explain.
hints: '-less' means 'without'.
So 'careless' means 'without care'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this word aloud: 'misunderstanding'. Then explain its meaning by breaking it into prefix, root and suffix.
hints: 'Mis-' = wrongly, 'understand' = the root, '-ing' = suffix.
What does it mean as a whole?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this word aloud: 'unbelievable'. Then explain its meaning by breaking it into prefix, root and suffix.
hints: 'Un-' = not, 'believe' = root, '-able' = able to.
Put it together.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this word aloud: 'disrespectful'. Then explain its meaning by breaking it into prefix, root and suffix, and use it in a sentence.
hints: 'Dis-' = not, 'respect' = root, '-ful' = full of.
Use it in a sentence.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the word in a meaningful sentence

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.8.1: Construct meaning from texts read
indicator.objective: Infer meaning from level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Infer a character's feeling from what is said or done in the passage.
Infer an unstated cause from the events in the passage.
Infer what will probably happen next from clues in the passage.
Tell a stated fact from an inferred idea.
Choose what a good reader does when a line does not make sense.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a short passage silently, then state one inference and the clue that led to it.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama opened her gift. She jumped up and down, clapping her hands.' How does Ama feel?
hints: What did Ama do? She jumped and clapped.
Jumping and clapping show a feeling.
questions.explanation: Ama jumped up and down and clapped her hands. These actions show she is happy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think she is tired because she jumped, but jumping and clapping are signs of joy, not tiredness.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi's dog was lost. He walked slowly home with his head down.' How does Kofi feel?
hints: What happened to his dog?
How does walking slowly with head down look?
questions.explanation: Kofi's dog is lost, and he walks slowly with his head down. This shows he is sad.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Angry' because losing something can make you angry, but the passage shows sadness (slow walk, head down), not anger.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Esi waited for her turn. When her name was called, she stood up slowly and her hands were shaking.' How does Esi feel?
hints: What do shaking hands suggest?
She is about to do something in front of others.
questions.explanation: Esi's hands are shaking as she stands up to speak. This suggests she is nervous.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Excited' because hands shaking can show excitement, but the slow standing up and waiting suggest nervousness, not excitement.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The ground was wet. The leaves were shiny. The children carried umbrellas.' Why was the ground wet?
hints: What makes leaves shiny and ground wet?
Why carry umbrellas?
questions.explanation: Wet ground, shiny leaves and umbrellas all suggest it had rained.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think someone spilled water because that also makes things wet, but the umbrellas and shiny leaves point to rain.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The pupils were very quiet. They sat still and listened carefully. The teacher smiled.' Why were the pupils quiet?
options: They were listening to something important
hints: What were they doing? Sitting still and listening.
Why would the teacher smile?
questions.explanation: The pupils are quiet, sitting still and listening. This suggests they are paying attention to something important.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they were sleeping because they were quiet, but they were sitting still and listening, not sleeping.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The farmer looked at the sky and frowned. He quickly gathered his tools and hurried home.' Why did the farmer hurry home?
options: He thought it was going to rain
hints: Why look at the sky and frown?
What does a farmer do if rain is coming?
questions.explanation: The farmer looked at the sky, frowned, and hurried home with his tools. This suggests he thought rain was coming and wanted to get home before it started.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think he was hungry because he hurried, but looking at the sky and frowning points to weather, not hunger.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi was running to school. He looked at his watch and saw it was 8:05. The bell rings at 8:00.' What will probably happen next?
options: Kofi will be late for school
hints: What time does the bell ring?
What time is it now?
questions.explanation: The bell rings at 8:00, and it is already 8:05. Kofi is still running, so he will probably be late.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think he will arrive early because he is running, but the time shows he is already late.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama looked at the dark clouds. She picked up her umbrella and put on her raincoat.' What will probably happen next?
hints: Why take an umbrella and raincoat?
What do dark clouds mean?
questions.explanation: Dark clouds, an umbrella and a raincoat suggest it will rain soon.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think she will stay home because of the clouds, but the passage says she picks up her umbrella and raincoat, suggesting she is going out into the rain.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The pot was on the fire. The water began to bubble. The girl reached for the lid.' What will probably happen next?
options: She will take the lid off
She will turn off the fire
hints: What is she reaching for?
Why would she reach for the lid?
questions.explanation: The girl reaches for the lid as the water bubbles. She will probably take the lid off — perhaps to stir the food or check it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think she will turn off the fire, but she is reaching for the lid, not the fire.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Kofi's dog was lost. He walked slowly home with his head down.' Which statement is a STATED FACT, not an inference?
options: Kofi will look for the dog
hints: Which statement is directly in the passage?
The others are inferences.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi's dog was lost' is stated directly in the passage. 'Kofi was sad' is inferred from his behaviour; the others are predictions or guesses.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi was sad' because the passage shows sadness, but it is inferred from his slow walk and bowed head — the fact stated is that the dog was lost.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Esi waited for her turn. When her name was called, she stood up slowly and her hands were shaking.' Which statement is an INFERENCE, not a stated fact?
hints: Which statement is not directly in the passage?
The passage does not say 'nervous'.
questions.explanation: 'Esi was nervous' is an inference — we infer it from her shaking hands and slow standing. The other three statements are directly stated.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Her name was called' because it seems less important, but it is directly stated in the passage — the inference is 'nervous'.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The ground was wet. The leaves were shiny. The children carried umbrellas.' Which statement is an INFERENCE?
hints: Which statement is not directly in the passage?
The passage does not say 'rained'.
questions.explanation: 'It had rained' is inferred from the wet ground, shiny leaves and umbrellas. The other three statements are directly stated.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The children carried umbrellas' because it mentions children, but that is directly stated. 'Rained' is the inference.

questions.stem: You are reading silently and you come to a sentence you do not understand. What should you do?
options: Re-read the sentence and look for clues
Stop reading and close the book
Ask a friend to read it aloud
hints: What is a good reader's first step?
Try to work it out.
questions.explanation: A good reader re-reads the sentence and looks for clues — sometimes reading on helps too. Stopping, skipping or asking a friend interrupts your silent reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stopping is best when stuck, but a good reader tries to work it out first.

questions.stem: You are reading silently and you realise you have not understood the last paragraph. What is the best strategy?
options: Re-read the paragraph slowly and think about the main idea
Read the paragraph aloud to yourself
hints: How can you fix understanding?
Which strategy helps you understand?
questions.explanation: Re-reading the paragraph slowly and thinking about the main idea is the best strategy — it helps you understand without disturbing others. Reading aloud may disturb silent reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Read aloud' because hearing it can help, but silent reading time is for quiet reading — re-reading silently is better.

questions.stem: When a sentence does not make sense during silent reading, a good reader might:
options: Read on a little and see if the meaning becomes clear
hints: Sometimes the next sentence explains the confusing one.
What does a good reader do before giving up?
questions.explanation: A good reader might read on a little — sometimes the next sentence explains the previous one. Giving up, asking every time or closing the book are not independent strategies.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ask the teacher every time' because it seems helpful, but good readers try to solve it themselves first.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama opened her gift. She jumped up and down, clapping her hands.' State one inference about Ama's feeling and the clue that led to it.
hints: How does she feel?
What clues show this?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a clue from the passage (jumping, clapping)

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi's dog was lost. He walked slowly home with his head down.' State one inference about Kofi and give two clues from the passage.
hints: How does Kofi feel?
What two things show this?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives two clues (slow walk, head down)

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The ground was wet. The leaves were shiny. The children carried umbrellas.' State one inference and the clues that led to it.
hints: What caused the wet ground?
What three clues point to this?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The farmer looked at the sky and frowned. He quickly gathered his tools and hurried home.' State one inference about why he hurried, and explain the clue that led to it.
hints: What was he looking at?
What does frowning suggest?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a clue (looking at sky, frowning)
Explains how the clue supports the inference

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Esi waited for her turn. When her name was called, she stood up slowly and her hands were shaking.' State one inference about Esi's feeling, the clues that show it, and what she might do next.
hints: How does she feel?
What is she about to do?
What might happen next?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.8.1: Construct meaning from texts read
indicator.objective: Find the meaning of words as used in context

skills.description: Recognise that a word can have more than one meaning.
Choose the meaning of a word as it is used in the passage.
Identify the words in the passage that help reveal the target word's meaning.
Choose a synonym that could replace the target word without changing the meaning.
Recognise a meaning that does not fit the passage.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a short passage silently, pick a target word, and explain its meaning using context.

questions.stem: The word 'bank' can have more than one meaning. Which of these is a meaning of 'bank'?
hints: Think of a river.
Where does the water flow?
questions.explanation: 'Bank' can mean the side of a river or a place where money is kept. So 'the side of a river' is one meaning of 'bank'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A type of food' because 'bank' is a common word, but that is not a meaning of 'bank'.

questions.stem: The word 'bat' can have more than one meaning. Which of these is a meaning of 'bat'?
options: A small animal that flies at night
hints: Think of an animal.
It flies at night.
questions.explanation: 'Bat' can mean a small flying animal or a piece of wood used in cricket. So 'a small animal that flies at night' is one meaning of 'bat'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A type of food' because 'bat' is a word, but it does not mean food.

questions.stem: The word 'watch' can have more than one meaning. Which of these is a meaning of 'watch'?
hints: Think of what you do with your eyes.
You 'watch' a game.
questions.explanation: 'Watch' can mean a timepiece (noun) or to look at something carefully (verb). So 'to look at something carefully' is one meaning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A type of shoe' because 'watch' is a common word, but that is not a meaning of 'watch'.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children played near the bank of the river. They caught small fish.' What does 'bank' mean here?
hints: Where were the children playing?
They were near the river.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the bank of the river' — so 'bank' means the side of the river, not a money bank.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think of a money bank because that is a common meaning, but the context 'of the river' tells us it is the riverbank.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'My mother asked me to watch the soup while she went to the market.' What does 'watch' mean here?
options: To look after and take care of
hints: Why is mother asking this?
She is going out — what should the child do?
questions.explanation: In this context, 'watch the soup' means to look after it and make sure it does not burn. It is not a timepiece or a request to look at the time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'watch' means a clock because that is a common meaning, but the context 'watch the soup' means to take care of it.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The baby was crying. The mother rocked him gently in her arms.' What does 'rocked' mean here?
hints: What do mothers do with crying babies?
They hold and move them gently.
questions.explanation: In this context, 'rocked' means moved gently back and forth to soothe the baby. It does not mean threw stones.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'rocked' means threw stones because 'rock' is a stone, but the context 'the baby' shows it is the gentle movement.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The old man was very frail. He walked slowly with a stick.' What does 'frail' mean here?
hints: What does he use to walk?
He needs a stick.
questions.explanation: 'Frail' means weak and easily tired. The old man uses a stick to walk, which supports this meaning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'frail' means tall because tall people use sticks too, but 'frail' specifically means weak, which fits the slow walk with a stick.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children played near the bank of the river. They caught small fish.' Which words help you understand the meaning of 'bank'?
hints: What tells you which 'bank' is meant?
It relates to a river.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'of the river' tells us 'bank' means the side of the river. Without that clue, 'bank' could mean a money bank.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'caught small fish' because it is about the river, but it does not directly tell us the meaning of 'bank'. The clue 'of the river' does.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The old man was very frail. He walked slowly with a stick.' Which words help you understand the meaning of 'frail'?
hints: What action shows frailty?
He uses a stick to walk.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'walked slowly with a stick' tells us what 'frail' means — weak and easily tired. The old man needs help to walk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'old man' because frail is often used for older people, but the actual clue to the meaning is the walking slowly with a stick — the description of his weakness.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The soup was very tasty. Everyone asked for more.' Which words help you understand the meaning of 'tasty'?
hints: What happened after people ate the soup?
They wanted more.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone asked for more' tells us the soup was tasty — people enjoyed it so much they wanted more. This is the clue to the meaning of 'tasty'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The soup was' because it mentions soup, but it does not reveal the meaning. Asking for more is the clue.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The old man was very frail.' Which word could replace 'frail' without changing the meaning?
hints: What does frail mean?
Which option has the same meaning?
questions.explanation: 'Weak' has the same meaning as 'frail' — both describe someone who lacks strength or is easily tired.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Strong' because it is a common word, but 'strong' is the opposite of 'frail'.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children played near the bank of the river.' Which word could replace 'bank' without changing the meaning?
hints: What does 'bank' mean here?
Which option has the same meaning?
questions.explanation: In this context, 'bank' means the side of the river. 'Side' can replace it without changing the meaning. 'Money' would be a different meaning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Money' because that is a common meaning of bank, but in this passage, it is the side of the river, so 'side' is the correct substitute.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The soup was very tasty.' Which word could replace 'tasty' without changing the meaning?
hints: What does tasty mean?
Which option has the same meaning?
questions.explanation: 'Delicious' means very tasty — it is a synonym. 'Cold', 'hot' and 'thick' do not mean tasty.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Hot' because hot food is often tasty, but 'hot' is about temperature, not taste.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children played near the bank of the river.' Which meaning of 'bank' does NOT fit the passage?
options: A place where money is kept
hints: Which meaning does not fit 'river'?
A money bank is not by a river.
questions.explanation: 'A place where money is kept' does not fit the passage — the passage is about a river, so 'bank' means the riverside, not a money bank.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The side of a river' because it is a meaning of bank, but it DOES fit the passage — the question asks which meaning does NOT fit.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The mother rocked the baby in her arms.' Which meaning of 'rocked' does NOT fit the passage?
hints: Which action does not fit 'the baby in her arms'?
You cannot throw stones at a baby.
questions.explanation: 'Threw stones' does not fit — the passage says the mother rocked the baby in her arms, which means moved gently. Throwing stones would hurt the baby.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Moved gently' because it is a meaning of rocked, but it DOES fit the passage — the question asks which meaning does NOT fit.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The children played near the bank of the river.' Explain what 'bank' means in this passage and give the clue that helped you.
hints: What does bank mean here?
Which words tell you?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: States the meaning (side of the river)

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The old man was very frail. He walked slowly with a stick.' Explain what 'frail' means and give two clues from the passage.
hints: What does frail mean?
What two things show this?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The soup was very tasty. Everyone asked for more.' Explain what 'tasty' means and give the clue that helped you.
hints: What does tasty mean?
What happened after people ate?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The baby was crying. The mother rocked him gently in her arms.' Explain what 'rocked' means, give the clue that helped, and use the word 'rocked' in a sentence of your own.
hints: What does rocked mean here?
What clue tells you?
Use it in a sentence.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read a passage with two words that have more than one meaning (e.g., 'bank', 'watch'). Explain the meaning of each word as used in the passage, and explain how the context helped you decide.
hints: Pick two words.
Explain each meaning.
How did context help?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.8.1: Construct meaning from texts read
indicator.objective: Answer questions based on the passage read

skills.description: Answer a who/what/where/when question drawn directly from the passage.
Answer a why/how question that requires reading between the lines.
Answer a 'how did it make them feel?' or 'was this right?' question with a reason from the passage.
Generate a relevant question about a passage.
Teacher-assessed oral: after silent reading, ask a peer one relevant question and respond to one from a peer.
Teacher-assessed oral: answer two questions about a silently-read passage accurately.

misconceptions: Answer from memory of the title only

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama went to the market on Saturday. She bought tomatoes, onions and pepper.' Where did Ama go?
hints: What place is mentioned in the first sentence?
It starts with 'm'.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Ama went to the market.' So the answer is 'to the market'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'To school' because it is a common place, but the passage clearly says market.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi woke up at 6 o'clock. He brushed his teeth and had his breakfast.' What time did Kofi wake up?
hints: Look for the time in the passage.
It is the first sentence.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Kofi woke up at 6 o'clock.' So he woke up at 6 o'clock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick another hour because they confuse the time, but the passage clearly says 6 o'clock.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The teacher gave the pupils a test. Esi scored 90 out of 100. Kofi scored 85.' Who scored higher?
hints: Compare the two scores.
90 is higher than 85.
questions.explanation: Esi scored 90 and Kofi scored 85. So Esi scored higher.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick Kofi because his name is mentioned last, but the numbers show Esi scored higher.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama opened her gift. She jumped up and down, clapping her hands.' Why did Ama jump and clap?
options: She was happy with the gift
hints: What does jumping and clapping show?
What kind of gift makes someone do this?
questions.explanation: Ama jumped and clapped because she was happy with the gift. The passage does not say she was angry, tired or hungry.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think she was excited because she jumped, but the question asks why — she was happy with the gift.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi's dog was lost. He walked slowly home with his head down.' Why did Kofi walk slowly with his head down?
options: He was sad about losing his dog
He was looking for something on the ground
He was angry with his dog
hints: What happened to his dog?
How does a sad person walk?
questions.explanation: Kofi walked slowly with his head down because he was sad about losing his dog. The passage does not mention running, looking for something or anger.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think he was looking for something because his head was down, but the passage says his dog was lost — he is sad, not searching.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The ground was wet. The leaves were shiny. The children carried umbrellas.' Why did the children carry umbrellas?
options: It was raining or about to rain
They were going to the beach
They wanted to be like adults
hints: What does wet ground and shiny leaves suggest?
What are umbrellas used for?
questions.explanation: The wet ground, shiny leaves and umbrellas all suggest it was raining or about to rain. That is why the children carried umbrellas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they were going to the beach because umbrellas are also used for sun, but wet ground and shiny leaves point to rain, not sun.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The farmer looked at the sky and frowned. He quickly gathered his tools and hurried home.' Why did the farmer hurry home?
options: He thought a storm was coming
hints: Why look at the sky?
What does frowning suggest?
questions.explanation: Looking at the sky and frowning suggests he saw bad weather coming. He hurried home to avoid the storm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think he was hungry because he hurried, but looking at the sky and frowning is about weather, not hunger.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Esi found a purse on the ground. She gave it to the teacher, who found the owner.' Was Esi's action right or wrong, and why?
options: Right, because she returned what was not hers
Wrong, because she should have kept it
Right, because she got a reward
Wrong, because she did not look for the owner herself
hints: What did Esi do with the purse?
Was it hers?
questions.explanation: Esi's action was right because she returned what was not hers by giving it to the teacher. This is honest behaviour.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think she was wrong for not looking for the owner herself, but giving it to the teacher is a responsible action.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The children cleaned the compound and planted flowers. The school looked beautiful.' How did the children probably feel?
hints: What did they do?
How do people feel when their work makes something beautiful?
questions.explanation: The children cleaned and planted flowers, and the school looked beautiful. They probably felt proud of their work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Tired' because cleaning is hard work, but the passage does not mention tiredness; it focuses on the beautiful result.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi found a wallet with money. He took it to the police station. The owner came and thanked him.' Was Kofi's action right or wrong, and why?
options: Right, because he returned the wallet to its owner
Wrong, because he should have kept the money
Right, because he got a reward
Wrong, because he opened the wallet
hints: What did Kofi do with the wallet?
Did he keep it?
questions.explanation: Kofi's action was right because he returned the wallet to its owner by taking it to the police. This is honest behaviour.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think he was right because of a reward, but the passage does not mention a reward — the rightness is about honesty.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama went to the market on Saturday. She bought tomatoes, onions and pepper.' Write one relevant question you could ask about this passage.
answer: Accept any question that is relevant to the passage and can be answered from it or by inference — e.g., 'When did Ama go to the market?' or 'What did Ama buy?' Award full marks if the question is relevant and well-formed.
hints: Ask about the time, place or items.
Your question should be answerable from the passage.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Question is relevant to the passage

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi's dog was lost. He walked slowly home with his head down.' Write one relevant question you could ask about this passage.
answer: Accept any question that is relevant to the passage and can be answered from it or by inference — e.g., 'Why was Kofi sad?' or 'What happened to Kofi's dog?' Award full marks if the question is relevant.
hints: Ask about the dog or Kofi's feelings.
Your question should be answerable.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Question is relevant to the passage

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'The children cleaned the compound and planted flowers. The school looked beautiful.' Write one relevant question that requires thinking about the passage, not just recalling a fact.
answer: Accept any question that requires inference or evaluation — e.g., 'Why did the children clean the compound?' or 'How did the children feel about their work?' Award full marks if the question is relevant and requires thinking.
hints: Ask 'why' or 'how' rather than 'what'.
The answer should require thinking, not just copying.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Question is relevant to the passage

questions.stem: Read a short passage silently. Then ask a partner one relevant question about the passage. After your partner answers, respond to a question they ask you about the same passage.
hints: Think of a question about the passage.
Listen carefully to your partner's answer.
Then answer their question.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read a short passage silently. Then ask a partner two questions: one factual and one inferential. Answer two questions your partner asks you.
hints: Ask one 'who/what/where' question and one 'why/how' question.
Listen carefully to answer.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Answers two of partner's questions accurately

questions.stem: Read a short passage silently. In a small group, ask one question and answer one question. Then say which question in the group was the most interesting and why.
hints: Ask a thoughtful question.
Listen to others' questions.
Which was the most interesting?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Says which was most interesting and why

questions.stem: Read a passage silently. Prepare one factual, one inferential and one evaluative question. Ask all three to a partner and answer three from your partner.
hints: Factual: who/what/where.
Inferential: why/how.
Evaluative: was it right? how did they feel?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Asks one of each type of question

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Ama went to the market on Saturday. She bought tomatoes, onions and pepper.' Answer two questions: (1) Where did Ama go? (2) What did she buy?
hints: Look for the place.
Look for the items.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Kofi's dog was lost. He walked slowly home with his head down.' Answer two questions: (1) Why was Kofi sad? (2) How do you know he was sad?
hints: What happened to his dog?
What clues show his sadness?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage silently: 'Esi found a purse and gave it to the teacher.' Answer: (1) Was Esi's action right or wrong? (2) Why?
hints: What did she do?
Was it honest?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Gives a reason from the passage

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.9.1: Read fluently to enhance comprehension
indicator.objective: Read grade-level texts with good speed and accuracy

skills.description: Recognise what 'good speed' means (not too fast, not too slow, natural pace).
Recognise what 'accuracy' means (reading words correctly, not skipping or substituting).
Match an activity to its stage (Before/During/After reading).
Recognise what a Herringbone diagram is used for.
Recognise what KWL stands for and what each column does.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a short grade-level passage aloud with accuracy.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a short grade-level passage aloud at a natural pace.

questions.stem: What does 'good speed' mean when reading aloud?
options: A natural pace — not too fast, not too slow
Reading word by word very slowly
Reading only the first word of each line
hints: Good speed should sound natural.
Like a conversation.
questions.explanation: Good speed means a natural pace — not too fast so listeners can follow, and not too slow so the reading flows.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fast reading is best because it sounds fluent, but good speed is natural — too fast makes it hard to understand.

questions.stem: Which reading shows good speed?
options: Reading at a steady pace, pausing at full stops
Reading every word as fast as possible
Reading one word at a time with long pauses
hints: Good speed is steady and natural.
Pauses at full stops help the listener.
questions.explanation: Reading at a steady pace and pausing at full stops is good speed — it flows naturally and helps the listener understand.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick fast reading because it sounds impressive, but too fast means the listener cannot follow.

questions.stem: What does 'accuracy' mean when reading?
options: Reading the words correctly without skipping or changing them
hints: Accurate = correct.
Which option describes reading correctly?
questions.explanation: Accuracy means reading the words correctly — not skipping words, not substituting one word for another.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think speed is more important than accuracy, but reading words incorrectly changes the meaning.

questions.stem: A pupil is reading and says 'The boy ran to the shop' when the text says 'The boy ran to the ship.' What has the pupil done?
options: Read with low accuracy — changed a word
hints: What did the pupil say?
What does the text say? Are they the same?
questions.explanation: The pupil said 'shop' instead of 'ship'. This is a substitution — the pupil has read with low accuracy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'shop' sounds close enough, but 'shop' and 'ship' are different words — this is an accuracy error.

questions.stem: Which reading shows GOOD accuracy?
options: Reading every word as it appears in the text
Reading only the first and last words of a sentence
Changing words to ones that are easier
hints: Good accuracy = correct reading.
The reader should read every word as it is written.
questions.explanation: Good accuracy means reading every word as it appears in the text. Skipping or changing words lowers accuracy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skipping difficult words is smart, but it hurts accuracy and comprehension.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the BEFORE reading stage?
options: Predicting what the passage will be about
hints: Before reading — what can you predict?
You haven't read it yet.
questions.explanation: Predicting what the passage will be about is a Before Reading activity — you do it before reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Answering comprehension questions' because questions are common in reading lessons, but those come after reading.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the DURING reading stage?
options: Thinking about what is happening as you read
Discussing the passage with a friend
hints: During reading — what do you do while reading?
You think about the passage as you go.
questions.explanation: Thinking about what is happening as you read is a During Reading activity — you do it while reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Writing a summary' because it is important, but summaries come after reading.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the AFTER reading stage?
options: Retelling the passage in your own words
hints: After reading — what do you do once you finish?
You retell or summarise.
questions.explanation: Retelling the passage in your own words is an After Reading activity — you do it after reading to check your understanding.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Skimming for the main idea' because it is a reading skill, but skimming happens during reading, not after.

questions.stem: What is a Herringbone diagram used for?
options: Organising who, what, when, where, why and how from a text
hints: A Herringbone has a skeleton pattern.
It organises information about events or ideas.
questions.explanation: A Herringbone diagram organises the who, what, when, where, why and how of a text — it is a comprehension strategy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a Herringbone is a drawing of a fish because of the name, but it is an information organiser — not a picture.

questions.stem: In a Herringbone diagram, what question does the 'main spine' usually answer?
hints: The spine is the central line.
It holds the main event or topic.
questions.explanation: In a Herringbone diagram, the main spine holds the main event or topic, and the ribs hold the who, what, when, where, why and how.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the spine answers only the setting, but it holds the main topic.

questions.stem: What does KWL stand for?
hints: K = Know.
W = Want to know.
L = Learned.
questions.explanation: KWL stands for Know, Want to know, Learned. Each column helps you track your learning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may guess other K-words, but the standard KWL chart uses Know, Want, Learned.

questions.stem: In a KWL chart, what goes in the 'K' column?
options: What you already know about the topic
hints: K = Know.
What does 'know' mean here?
questions.explanation: The 'K' column holds what you ALREADY know about the topic before reading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put what they want to know in the K column, but that goes in the W (Want to know) column.

questions.stem: In a KWL chart, what goes in the 'L' column?
options: What you already knew before reading
hints: L = Learned.
What does 'learned' mean here?
questions.explanation: The 'L' column holds what you learned AFTER reading the passage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put what they already knew in the L column, but that goes in the K column — L is for new learning.

questions.stem: Read this short passage aloud with accuracy: 'The children went to the market with their mother. They bought tomatoes and onions. Then they went home.'
hints: Read each word correctly.
Do not skip or change words.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this short passage aloud with accuracy: 'Ama woke up early. She swept the compound. She then helped her mother cook breakfast.'
hints: Read every word.
Do not skip or change.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud with accuracy: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. The female anopheles mosquito carries the germ. We should sleep under treated nets to avoid malaria.'
hints: Read carefully.
Watch for longer words like 'mosquitoes' and 'anopheles'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Does not skip or substitute words

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud with accuracy: 'The harmattan wind blew across the village. Dry leaves swirled in the air. The sky was pale and dusty. People wrapped themselves in warm cloths and drank plenty of water.'
hints: Read every word.
Keep accuracy high throughout.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Does not skip or substitute words

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud at a natural pace: 'The children went to the market. They bought tomatoes and onions. Then they went home.'
hints: Read at a steady pace — not too fast, not too slow.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Paces evenly (not too fast or too slow)

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud at a natural pace: 'The farmers work hard in the fields. They plant maize and cassava. They water their crops every day. In three months, they will harvest their crops.'
hints: Steady pace throughout.
Do not rush.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this longer passage aloud at a natural pace: 'The school library has over five hundred books. Pupils can borrow two books at a time. The library is open from 8am to 4pm on school days. Pupils should return their books on time so others can borrow them.'
hints: Steady pace throughout.
Pause at full stops.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Maintains a steady pace throughout the passage

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.9.1: Read fluently to enhance comprehension
indicator.objective: Use context to confirm or self-correction strategies to confirm understanding of level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Recognise what self-correction means.
Choose the right self-correction strategy when meaning breaks down.
Use context to confirm or correct a word.
Use punctuation to guide phrasing and meaning.
Recognise when a word has been misread and pick the correction.
Teacher-assessed oral: read a short passage aloud and self-correct at least one error using context or re-reading.

questions.stem: What does 'self-correction' mean when reading aloud?
options: Stopping to fix a word you have read wrong
Skipping words you do not know
hints: Self-correction = fixing yourself.
You notice a mistake and fix it.
questions.explanation: Self-correction means noticing when you have read a word wrong and correcting yourself.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think self-correction is reading the whole passage again, but it is fixing the specific error, not restarting.

questions.stem: Why is self-correction important for comprehension?
options: Because it fixes mistakes so the meaning stays clear
Because it is required by the teacher
hints: Why do you correct a mistake?
What happens to the meaning if the word is wrong?
questions.explanation: Self-correction is important because it fixes mistakes so the meaning stays clear — otherwise a wrong word can confuse the meaning of the sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think self-correction is about impressing the teacher, but it is about understanding what you read.

questions.stem: You read a sentence aloud but it doesn't make sense. What is the best first strategy?
options: Re-read the sentence and think about the meaning
hints: What can you do on your own?
Try re-reading first.
questions.explanation: The best first strategy is to re-read the sentence and think about the meaning — this often solves the problem before asking the teacher.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think asking the teacher is always best, but trying on your own first builds independence.

questions.stem: You have read the same word wrong twice. Which strategy should you try?
options: Use the surrounding words (context) to work out the correct word
hints: What helps you work out the word?
Look at the words around it.
questions.explanation: Using the surrounding words (context) helps you work out the correct word when you have read it wrong.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think reading louder or faster will help, but louder and faster do not solve the misreading — context does.

questions.stem: You are reading and you skip a difficult word. The sentence no longer makes sense. What should you do?
options: Go back, try to read the word using context, then re-read the sentence
Continue reading and hope it gets better
Close the book and start over
Ask your neighbour for the answer
hints: Which strategy builds self-correction?
Go back and try again.
questions.explanation: Go back, try to read the word using context, then re-read the sentence. This is self-correction — you fix the mistake using context, not by skipping or relying on others.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think asking a neighbour is fine, but self-correction means trying to fix it yourself first.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The farmer used a cutlass to ___ the grass.' Which word best fits the blank based on context?
hints: What do farmers do with a cutlass?
It involves grass.
questions.explanation: The context 'cutlass' and 'grass' tells us the word should be 'cut' — a farmer uses a cutlass to cut grass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cat' because it is a similar spelling, but a cutlass is not used to cat grass — context tells us the meaning.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The pupils sat on the ___ in the classroom.' Which word best fits the blank based on context?
hints: What do pupils sit on in a classroom?
It is furniture.
questions.explanation: The context 'sat on' and 'in the classroom' tells us the word should be 'chairs' — chairs are what pupils sit on in a classroom.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'chess' because it is a similar spelling, but chess is a game, not something to sit on.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The pot of soup was ___ on the fire.' Which word best fits the blank based on context?
hints: What happens to soup on a fire?
It bubbles and cooks.
questions.explanation: The context 'pot of soup' and 'on the fire' tells us the word should be 'boiling' — soup on a fire boils.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'bouncing' because it starts with 'b', but soup does not bounce — context tells us the meaning.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The children ___ the compound every morning before school.' Which word best fits based on context?
hints: What do children do to the compound to keep it clean?
It involves a broom.
questions.explanation: The context 'compound' and 'every morning' tells us the word should be 'sweep' — children sweep the compound to keep it clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sleep' because it starts with 's', but you do not sleep the compound — you sweep it.

questions.stem: What does a full stop (.) tell you when you are reading aloud?
hints: A full stop marks the end of a sentence.
What should you do at the end of a sentence?
questions.explanation: A full stop tells you to pause briefly — it marks the end of a sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a full stop means to read faster, but a full stop is a signal to pause and let the meaning settle.

questions.stem: What does a comma (,) tell you when reading aloud?
options: Pause briefly for a short breath
hints: A comma is a short pause.
It separates parts of a sentence.
questions.explanation: A comma tells you to pause briefly — a shorter pause than a full stop — to let the sentence flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a comma is a full stop, but a comma is a short pause, not the end of a sentence.

questions.stem: How should you read this sentence aloud? 'I bought rice, beans, and oil at the market.'
options: Read straight through with no pauses
Pause only at the full stop
hints: What does the comma in a list mean?
It separates items in a list.
questions.explanation: The commas in the list tell you to pause briefly after 'rice' and after 'beans' — this makes the list clear to listeners.
questions.misconception: Pupils may read straight through because the list is short, but the commas signal pauses that make the meaning clearer.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The dog chased the cat up the tree.' But the text says: 'The dog chased the rat up the tree.' What is the correction?
options: The pupil should read 'rat' instead of 'cat'
The pupil should read 'tree' instead of 'up'
The pupil should read 'chased' instead of 'the'
The pupil read the sentence correctly
hints: What is the difference between what was read and the text?
One word is different.
questions.explanation: The pupil said 'cat' but the text says 'rat'. So the pupil should correct 'cat' to 'rat'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'cat' is fine because a dog can chase a cat, but the text specifically says 'rat' — the correction is needed.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The farmer planted maze in his field.' But the text says: 'The farmer planted maize in his field.' What is the correction?
hints: 'Maze' and 'maize' sound the same but have different meanings.
Which word is the actual crop?
questions.explanation: The pupil said 'maze' (a puzzle) but the text says 'maize' (a crop). The correction is to read 'maize'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'maze' is correct because it sounds the same, but 'maize' is the crop — the spelling and meaning differ.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The children had a lot of fun at the beach.' But the text says: 'The children had a lot of fun at the fair.' What is the correction?
hints: What word is different in the text?
Beach vs fair — which one is in the text?
questions.explanation: The text says 'fair', not 'beach'. The pupil should correct 'beach' to 'fair'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'beach' is fine because fun happens there too, but the text specifically says 'fair' — accuracy matters.

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud: 'The children went to the market. They bought tomatoes and onions.' If you make a mistake, stop, fix it, and continue.
hints: Read carefully.
If you say the wrong word, correct it.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Self-corrects at least one error (if any)

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud. If you make a mistake, use context to work out the correct word, fix it, and continue: 'The farmer used a cutlass to cut the grass. He worked hard all morning.'
hints: If you read a wrong word, use the context to find the right one.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud. If you make a mistake, use re-reading or context to correct it: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. The female anopheles mosquito carries the germ.'
hints: Re-read if a word does not make sense.
Use the surrounding words as clues.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses re-reading or context to fix errors

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud. If you make a mistake, self-correct using re-reading, context, or punctuation clues: 'The children cleaned the compound and planted flowers. The school looked beautiful. The head teacher praised them.'
hints: Use punctuation to guide your pace.
Self-correct any errors.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud. If you make a mistake, self-correct using context or re-reading. After reading, explain which strategy you used and why.
hints: Use context or re-reading.
Explain what you did.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.1.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use nouns or noun phrases to refer to quantities or units.

skills.description: Identify the noun phrase that refers to a quantity or unit in a short sentence.
Choose the correct unit noun for a given noun.
Tell a unit noun apart from the whole noun.
Complete a sentence with the correct quantity/unit phrase.
Write a short sentence containing a given quantity/unit noun phrase.
Recognise a wrong unit for a noun.
Choose the correct verb form when a unit noun phrase is the subject.

misconceptions: A piece of applied to everything

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Please give me a piece of paper.' Which phrase refers to a quantity or unit?
hints: Which phrase tells us how MUCH paper?
It is a unit that measures paper.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of paper' refers to a quantity or unit — it tells us one unit of paper, not the whole stock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'of paper' because it contains 'paper', but the full unit phrase is 'a piece of paper' — the 'a piece' tells us the quantity.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She bought a bunch of bananas from the market.' Which phrase refers to a quantity or unit?
hints: Which phrase tells us how MANY bananas?
It is a group unit.
questions.explanation: 'A bunch of bananas' refers to a quantity — it tells us a group of bananas held together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the market' because it is a noun, but the market is not a unit — the bunch is.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'He drank a bottle of water.' Which phrase refers to a quantity or unit?
hints: Which phrase tells us how MUCH water?
It is a container unit.
questions.explanation: 'A bottle of water' refers to a quantity — the bottle is the unit that holds the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'of water' because it names water, but the full unit phrase is 'a bottle of water'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of trousers.'
hints: What word do we use for clothes that have two legs?
Trousers always come with two legs.
questions.explanation: We say 'a pair of trousers' because trousers have two legs. 'Pair' is the correct unit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'piece' because it is common, but we do not say 'a piece of trousers' — we say 'a pair'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of bread.'
hints: What is a whole baked bread called?
It is often cut into slices.
questions.explanation: A whole baked bread is called 'a loaf'. So 'a loaf of bread' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'piece' because we also say 'a piece of bread', but 'a loaf' is a whole bread — the most common unit for bread.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of water.'
hints: What do we keep water in?
It has a lid and holds liquid.
questions.explanation: Water is often kept in a bottle, so 'a bottle of water' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'loaf' because it is a unit, but we do not say 'a loaf of water' — water goes in a bottle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of keys.'
hints: What do we call a group of keys held together?
It is like a bunch of bananas.
questions.explanation: A group of keys held together is called 'a bunch of keys'. 'Bunch' is the correct unit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pair' because keys can come in pairs, but a group of keys is called a bunch.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'a slice of cake', which word is the UNIT?
hints: Which word tells us how MUCH cake?
It is not the whole cake.
questions.explanation: 'Slice' is the unit — it tells us how much of the cake we have. 'Cake' is the whole thing, 'of' is a linking word, and 'a' is a determiner.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cake' because it is a noun, but 'cake' is the whole thing — 'slice' is the unit that measures it.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'a bottle of water', which is the WHOLE thing and which is the UNIT?
hints: What is being measured?
What is measuring it?
questions.explanation: Water is the whole thing being measured. The bottle is the unit that holds it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the two because bottle is a physical object, but it is the measuring unit — water is what is being measured.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Mother bought a ___ of bread from the shop.'
hints: What unit is used for bread?
It is a whole baked bread.
questions.explanation: 'A loaf of bread' is the correct unit for bread. 'Pair' is for trousers, 'bunch' is for bananas or keys, and 'bottle' is for liquids.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pair' because it is a common unit, but we do not say 'a pair of bread'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She gave me a ___ of paper to write on.'
hints: What do we call one sheet of paper?
It is a small part of a larger whole.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of paper' is the correct unit — one sheet is one piece.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pair' because it is a common unit, but we do not say 'a pair of paper'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Father drank a ___ of tea this morning.'
hints: What do we drink tea from?
It is a small container.
questions.explanation: 'A cup of tea' is the correct unit — tea is drunk from a cup.
