questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Of all the pupils, Adjoa sang the ___ .'
hints: Comparing many pupils — use superlative.
Good → best (irregular).
questions.explanation: 'Of all the pupils' means we are comparing many — so we use the superlative 'best'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'better' because it is a form of 'good', but 'better' is comparative (two) — for many, use 'best'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG comparative form?
options: She is more taller than me.
She is the tallest in the class.
She is taller than her sister.
hints: 'More' + '-er' is a double comparative.
Which sentence uses both 'more' and '-er'?
questions.explanation: 'More taller' is wrong — it uses both 'more' and '-er'. The correct form is just 'taller'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add 'more' to strengthen a comparative, but adding 'more' to an -er form is a double comparative — just use 'taller'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG superlative form?
options: He is the most tallest boy.
hints: 'Most' + '-est' is a double superlative.
Which sentence uses both 'most' and '-est'?
questions.explanation: 'Most tallest' is wrong — it uses both 'most' and '-est'. The correct form is just 'the tallest'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add 'most' to strengthen a superlative, but adding 'most' to an -est form is a double superlative — just use 'the tallest'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG comparative form?
options: This mango is gooder than that one.
This mango is better than that one.
This mango is the best of all.
This mango is worse than that one.
hints: 'Good' is irregular — no -er form.
Which sentence adds -er to 'good'?
questions.explanation: 'Gooder' is wrong — 'good' is irregular, and its comparative is 'better'. So 'gooder than' should be 'better than'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -er to 'good' to make 'gooder', but 'good' is irregular — the comparative is 'better'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use different types of verbs in sentences: Main verb; Helping verb (primary auxiliary and modal auxiliary)

skills.description: Identify the main verb in a short sentence.
Identify the helping/auxiliary verb in a short sentence.
Tell a primary auxiliary apart from a modal auxiliary.
Choose the correct auxiliary to complete a sentence.
Identify both the main verb and the helping verb in one sentence.
Recognise a sentence where the auxiliary is missing.
Write a sentence using a given main verb with a helping verb.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The boy runs to school.' Which word is the MAIN verb?
hints: The main verb shows the action.
What is the boy doing?
questions.explanation: 'Runs' is the main verb — it shows the action. 'Boy' and 'school' are nouns, and 'to' is a preposition.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'boy' because it is the subject, but the main verb is the action word — 'runs'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She sings beautifully.' Which word is the MAIN verb?
hints: Which word shows the action?
'Sings' is the action.
questions.explanation: 'Sings' is the main verb — the action. 'Beautifully' is an adverb, 'she' is a pronoun.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'beautifully' because it describes the action, but it is an adverb — the verb is 'sings'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The children were playing outside.' Which word is the MAIN verb?
hints: The main verb shows the action.
'Were' is a helping verb.
questions.explanation: 'Playing' is the main verb — it shows the action. 'Were' is a helping verb (auxiliary). 'Children' is a noun, 'outside' is an adverb.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'were' because it is a verb form, but 'were' is the helping verb — 'playing' is the main verb (the action).

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The girl is reading a book.' Which word is the HELPING verb?
hints: The helping verb helps the main verb.
'Is' comes before 'reading'.
questions.explanation: 'Is' is the helping verb — it helps the main verb 'reading'. 'Reading' is the main verb.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'reading' because it is an action, but 'reading' is the main verb — 'is' is the helping verb.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'They have finished their work.' Which word is the HELPING verb?
hints: The helping verb comes before the main verb.
'Have' is the helping verb.
questions.explanation: 'Have' is the helping verb — it works with the main verb 'finished' to form the present perfect tense.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'finished' because it is an action, but 'finished' is the main verb — 'have' is the helping verb.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She can swim very well.' Which word is the HELPING verb?
hints: The helping verb comes before the main verb.
'Can' is a modal helping verb.
questions.explanation: 'Can' is the helping verb (modal auxiliary) — it helps the main verb 'swim' show ability.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'swim' because it is the action, but 'swim' is the main verb — 'can' is the helping verb.

questions.stem: Which of these is a PRIMARY auxiliary verb?
hints: Primary auxiliaries are forms of 'be', 'have' and 'do'.
'Is' is a form of 'be'.
questions.explanation: 'Is' is a primary auxiliary (a form of 'be'). 'Can', 'must' and 'should' are modal auxiliaries.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'can' because it is a common helping verb, but 'can' is a modal auxiliary — primary auxiliaries are forms of be, have and do.

questions.stem: Which of these is a MODAL auxiliary verb?
hints: Modals show possibility, ability or obligation.
'Must' shows obligation.
questions.explanation: 'Must' is a modal auxiliary — it shows obligation. 'Is', 'are' and 'have' are primary auxiliaries.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because it is a common helping verb, but 'is' is a primary auxiliary — 'must' is modal.

questions.stem: Which pair shows a PRIMARY auxiliary and a MODAL auxiliary?
hints: Primary auxiliaries: be, have, do.
Modals: can, may, must, should, will, would, could, might.
questions.explanation: 'Is' (a form of 'be') is a primary auxiliary, and 'can' is a modal auxiliary. The other pairs reverse or mislabel the categories.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the categories, but primary auxiliaries are forms of be/have/do, and modals are can/may/must/should/will/would/could/might.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The boy ___ going to school.'
hints: The subject is 'the boy' — singular.
For singular subjects, use 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'The boy' is singular, so the helping verb is 'is': 'The boy is going to school.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because it is a common form of 'be', but 'the boy' is singular — 'is' is correct.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The girls ___ reading their books.'
hints: The subject is 'the girls' — plural.
For plural subjects, use 'are'.
questions.explanation: 'The girls' is plural, so the helping verb is 'are': 'The girls are reading their books.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because it is short, but 'the girls' is plural — 'are' is correct.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ finished her homework.'
hints: The subject is 'she' — singular.
For singular subjects in present perfect, use 'has'.
questions.explanation: 'She' is singular, so the helping verb is 'has': 'She has finished her homework.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'have' because it is a common auxiliary, but 'she' is singular — 'has' is correct.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The children are singing a song.' What are the helping verb and the main verb?
hints: The helping verb comes before the main verb.
'Are' is the helping verb, 'singing' is the main verb.
questions.explanation: The helping verb is 'are' and the main verb is 'singing'. Together they form the present continuous tense.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse them because 'singing' shows the action, but 'singing' is the main verb — 'are' is the helper.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'He can drive a car.' What are the helping verb and the main verb?
hints: The helping verb comes before the main verb.
'Can' is a modal helping verb.
questions.explanation: The helping verb is 'can' (modal) and the main verb is 'drive'. Together they show ability.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'drive' as the helping verb because it is an action, but 'drive' is the main verb — 'can' is the helper.

questions.stem: Which sentence is MISSING a helping verb?
options: The girls are reading their books.
The girl is reading a book.
hints: Which sentence sounds incomplete?
The subject needs a helping verb before '-ing'.
questions.explanation: 'The girls reading their books' is missing the helping verb 'are' — it should be 'The girls are reading their books.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think '-ing' verbs stand alone, but in present continuous, they need a helping verb (is/are/am).

questions.stem: Which sentence is MISSING a helping verb?
options: He has gone to the market.
She is going to the market.
They are going to the market.
hints: Which sentence has a past participle without 'have/has/had'?
Past participles need 'have', 'has' or 'had'.
questions.explanation: 'He gone to the market' is missing the helping verb 'has' — it should be 'He has gone to the market.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'gone' can stand alone as past tense, but 'gone' is a past participle — it needs 'has/have/had'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is MISSING a helping verb?
options: She has finished her work already.
hints: Which sentence lacks 'have/has' before a past participle?
Present perfect needs 'has/have'.
questions.explanation: 'She finished her work already' is not wrong, but in the present perfect sense it should be 'She has finished her work already.' The first version uses simple past — the second uses present perfect with 'has'. Both can be correct in different contexts, but in this set, the first is missing 'has' for the present perfect meaning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'finished' alone is always correct, but when the meaning is present perfect (completed with relevance now), the helping verb 'has' is needed.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the main verb 'run' with a helping verb.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'run' with a helping verb — e.g., 'They are running to school.' or 'She can run very fast.' or 'He has run a race.' Award full marks if the sentence uses 'run' as the main verb with a helping verb.
hints: Use 'is/are' + running, or 'can' + run, or 'has/have' + run.
The helping verb comes before the main verb.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the main verb 'go' with a modal helping verb.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'go' with a modal — e.g., 'She can go to the market.' or 'You must go now.' or 'They will go tomorrow.' Award full marks if the sentence uses 'go' with a modal.
hints: Modals: can, may, must, should, will, would, could, might.
Use one modal + 'go'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the main verb 'eat' with a primary auxiliary helping verb.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'eat' with a primary auxiliary (is/are/was/were/has/have/had) — e.g., 'She is eating rice.' or 'They have eaten already.' or 'He was eating when I arrived.' Award full marks if the primary auxiliary is correct.
hints: Primary auxiliaries: is/are/was/were/has/have/had.
Use one of these with 'eat'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use appropriate subject-verb agreement

skills.description: Choose the singular verb form to agree with a singular subject.
Choose the plural verb form to agree with a plural subject.
Choose the singular verb form after a collective noun.
Choose the plural verb form after two subjects joined by 'and'.
Choose the singular verb form after an indefinite pronoun.
Identify the subject and verb and state whether they agree.
Write a sentence with correct subject-verb agreement for a given subject.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boy ___ in the room.'
hints: 'The boy' is singular.
Singular subject → singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'The boy' is singular, so the verb is 'is': 'The boy is in the room.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because it is a common form of 'be', but 'the boy' is singular — 'is' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'She ___ to school every day.'
hints: 'She' is third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb for third-person singular.
questions.explanation: 'She' is third-person singular, so the verb takes -s: 'She walks to school every day.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'walk' because it is the base form, but 'she' is third-person singular — add -s.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The cat ___ on the mat.'
hints: 'The cat' is singular.
Add -s to the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'The cat' is singular, so the verb is 'sleeps': 'The cat sleeps on the mat.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sleep' because it is the base verb, but with a singular subject in simple present, add -s.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The girls ___ happy.'
hints: 'The girls' is plural.
Plural subject → plural verb.
questions.explanation: 'The girls' is plural, so the verb is 'are': 'The girls are happy.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because it is common, but 'the girls' is plural — 'are' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boys ___ football every Saturday.'
hints: 'The boys' is plural.
Plural subject → base verb (no -s).
questions.explanation: 'The boys' is plural, so the verb is 'play' (no -s): 'The boys play football every Saturday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'plays' because it looks correct for the present tense, but 'plays' is for third-person singular — 'the boys' is plural, so 'play'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The pupils ___ in the classroom.'
hints: 'The pupils' is plural.
Plural subject → plural verb.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils' is plural, so the verb is 'are': 'The pupils are in the classroom.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because it is short, but 'the pupils' is plural — 'are' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The team ___ playing tomorrow.'
hints: A collective noun takes a singular verb.
'Team' is one unit.
questions.explanation: 'The team' is treated as one unit — singular — so the verb is 'is': 'The team is playing tomorrow.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because a team has many players, but grammatically, the team is treated as one unit — singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The family ___ going on a trip.'
hints: A collective noun takes a singular verb.
'Family' is one unit.
questions.explanation: 'The family' is treated as one unit — singular — so the verb is 'is': 'The family is going on a trip.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because a family has many members, but the collective noun is treated as singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'A flock of sheep ___ grazing in the field.'
hints: The head noun is 'flock' — singular.
Sheep describes the flock.
questions.explanation: 'A flock of sheep' — the head noun 'flock' is singular, so the verb is 'is': 'A flock of sheep is grazing in the field.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because sheep is plural, but the subject is 'a flock' — the phrase 'of sheep' just describes the flock.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boy and the girl ___ here.'
hints: Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural verb.
The boy + the girl = plural.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: 'The boy and the girl are here.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because each subject is singular, but when joined by 'and', the compound subject is plural — 'are'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Ama and Kofi ___ friends.'
hints: Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural verb.
Ama + Kofi = two people.
questions.explanation: 'Ama and Kofi' is a compound subject — plural — so the verb is 'are': 'Ama and Kofi are friends.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because each name is singular, but joined by 'and', the compound subject is plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The teacher and the pupils ___ in the classroom.'
hints: Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural verb.
The teacher + the pupils = plural.
questions.explanation: 'The teacher and the pupils' is a compound subject — plural — so the verb is 'are': 'The teacher and the pupils are in the classroom.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because 'the teacher' is singular, but the 'and' makes the subject plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Everyone ___ happy today.'
hints: 'Everyone' is treated as singular.
Singular subject → singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is treated as singular, so the verb is 'is': 'Everyone is happy today.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because 'everyone' means many people, but grammatically 'everyone' is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Nobody ___ the answer.'
hints: 'Nobody' is singular.
Singular subject → singular verb with -s.
questions.explanation: 'Nobody' is singular, so the verb is 'knows': 'Nobody knows the answer.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'know' because 'nobody' feels plural, but grammatically 'nobody' is singular.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The girl with the bags is here.' What is the subject and the verb? Do they agree?
options: Subject: the girl; Verb: is — they agree
Subject: the bags; Verb: is — they disagree
Subject: the girl; Verb: is — they disagree
Subject: the bags; Verb: is — they agree
hints: The subject is 'the girl' — 'with the bags' just describes her.
'Is' is singular — matches 'the girl'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the girl' (singular). The verb is 'is' (singular). They agree. The phrase 'with the bags' does not change the subject.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the subject is 'the bags' because it is closest to the verb, but the subject is 'the girl' — 'with the bags' is a describing phrase.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The box of books is heavy.' What is the subject and the verb? Do they agree?
options: Subject: the box; Verb: is — they agree
Subject: the books; Verb: is — they disagree
Subject: the box; Verb: is — they disagree
Subject: the books; Verb: is — they agree
hints: The subject is 'the box' — 'of books' describes it.
'Is' is singular — matches 'the box'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the box' (singular). The verb is 'is' (singular). They agree. The phrase 'of books' does not change the subject.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the subject is 'the books' because it is plural, but 'the box' is the subject — 'of books' is a describing phrase.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The children in the field are playing.' What is the subject and the verb? Do they agree?
options: Subject: the children; Verb: are — they agree
Subject: the field; Verb: are — they disagree
Subject: the children; Verb: are — they disagree
Subject: the field; Verb: are — they agree
hints: The subject is 'the children' — 'in the field' describes them.
'Are' is plural — matches 'the children'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the children' (plural). The verb is 'are' (plural). They agree. The phrase 'in the field' does not change the subject.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the subject is 'the field' because it is closest to the verb, but the subject is 'the children' — 'in the field' is a describing phrase.

questions.stem: Write a sentence with the subject 'The boys' and a verb that agrees with it.
answer: Accept any sentence with 'The boys' followed by a plural verb — e.g., 'The boys are playing football.' or 'The boys run fast.' Award full marks if the subject is plural and the verb agrees.
hints: 'The boys' is plural.
Use a plural verb (no -s).
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses a plural verb that agrees

questions.stem: Write a sentence with the subject 'She' and a verb that agrees with it.
answer: Accept any sentence with 'She' followed by a singular verb — e.g., 'She walks to school.' or 'She is happy.' Award full marks if the subject is singular and the verb agrees.
hints: 'She' is third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb or use 'is'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses a singular verb that agrees

questions.stem: Write a sentence with the subject 'The team' and a verb that agrees with it.
answer: Accept any sentence with 'The team' followed by a singular verb — e.g., 'The team is playing well.' or 'The team wins every match.' Award full marks if the collective noun takes a singular verb.
hints: A collective noun takes a singular verb.
Use 'is' or add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses a singular verb that agrees

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the simple present form of verbs to express: Needs/preferences; Thoughts and ideas

skills.description: Identify a simple present verb in a sentence.
Choose the correct simple present verb to express a need or preference.
Choose the correct simple present verb to express a thought or idea.
Add -s to a simple present verb for a third-person singular subject.
Choose the correct negative form in the simple present.
Recognise a sentence where a past tense is wrongly used instead of simple present.
Write a sentence in the simple present expressing a need or thought.

misconceptions: Past tense used for present need

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She likes mangoes.' Which word is in the simple present tense?
hints: The simple present describes habits or facts.
'Likes' shows a present fact.
questions.explanation: 'Likes' is the simple present verb — it shows a fact about what she enjoys.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'mangoes' because it is a noun, but the verb is 'likes'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'I think you are right.' Which word is in the simple present tense?
hints: 'Think' is the verb in the main clause.
It shows a thought.
questions.explanation: 'Think' is the simple present verb — it shows the speaker's thought. 'Are' is also present, but 'think' is the main verb in this sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because it is also present, but the question asks for the simple present verb that expresses a thought — 'think'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ new clothes for school.'
hints: The subject is 'I'.
For 'I', use the base verb.
questions.explanation: With the subject 'I', the simple present verb is the base form: 'I need new clothes for school.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -s to make 'needs', but -s is only for he/she/it — with 'I', use 'need'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ playing football more than volleyball.'
hints: The subject is 'she' — third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: 'She' is third-person singular, so the verb takes -s: 'She likes playing football more than volleyball.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'like' because it is the base form, but 'she' needs 'likes' with -s.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ to play outside every evening.'
hints: The subject is 'they' — plural.
For plural subjects, use the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'They' is plural, so the verb is 'want' (no -s): 'They want to play outside every evening.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'wants' because it is a form of the verb, but 'they' is plural — use 'want'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'My brother ___ to eat rice every day.'
hints: The subject is 'my brother' — third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: 'My brother' is third-person singular, so the verb is 'prefers': 'My brother prefers to eat rice every day.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'prefer' because it is the base form, but 'my brother' needs 'prefers' with -s.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ you are right.'
hints: The subject is 'I'.
For 'I', use the base verb.
questions.explanation: With 'I', we use the base form 'think': 'I think you are right.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'thinks' because it is a form of the verb, but 'thinks' is for he/she/it — with 'I', use 'think'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ that reading is important.'
hints: The subject is 'she' — third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: 'She' is third-person singular, so the verb is 'believes': 'She believes that reading is important.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'believe' because it is the base form, but 'she' needs 'believes' with -s.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'We ___ that education is the key to success.'
hints: The subject is 'we' — plural.
For plural subjects, use the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'We' is plural, so the verb is 'believe' (no -s): 'We believe that education is the key to success.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'believes' because it is a form of the verb, but 'we' is plural — use 'believe'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'He ___ to school every day.'
hints: 'He' is third-person singular.
Add -es to 'go'.
questions.explanation: 'He' is third-person singular, so the verb is 'goes': 'He goes to school every day.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'go' because it is the base verb, but with 'he', add -es (goes).

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Ama ___ rice every day.'
hints: 'Ama' is one person — third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: 'Ama' is third-person singular, so the verb is 'cooks': 'Ama cooks rice every day.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cook' because it is the base form, but 'Ama' needs 'cooks' with -s.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'It ___ a lot in June.'
hints: 'It' is third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: 'It' is third-person singular, so the verb is 'rains': 'It rains a lot in June.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'rain' because it is the base form, but 'it' needs 'rains' with -s.

questions.stem: Choose the correct negative: 'She ___ like pepper.'
hints: 'She' is third-person singular.
For third-person singular, use 'doesn't'.
questions.explanation: 'She' is third-person singular, so the negative is 'doesn't': 'She doesn't like pepper.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'don't' because it is common, but 'don't' is for I/you/we/they — 'she' needs 'doesn't'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct negative: 'They ___ like to wake up early.'
hints: 'They' is plural.
For plural subjects, use 'don't'.
questions.explanation: 'They' is plural, so the negative is 'don't': 'They don't like to wake up early.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'doesn't' because it is a form of 'do', but 'doesn't' is for he/she/it — 'they' uses 'don't'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct negative: 'He ___ want anything.'
hints: 'He' is third-person singular.
For third-person singular, use 'doesn't'.
questions.explanation: 'He' is third-person singular, so the negative is 'doesn't': 'He doesn't want anything.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'don't' because it is common, but 'he' needs 'doesn't'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
hints: Which sentence uses a past tense with a present time word?
'Now' signals present tense.
questions.explanation: 'I needed clothes now' is wrong — 'needed' is past, but 'now' signals present. It should be 'I need clothes now.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'needed' is fine because it sounds past, but 'now' means the need is present — 'need' is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
hints: Which sentence has a past time word but a present verb?
'Yesterday' signals past tense.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday I need money' is wrong — 'yesterday' signals past, but 'need' is present. It should be 'Yesterday I needed money.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use present tense with past time words, but 'yesterday' requires the past tense 'needed'.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple present expressing a NEED.
answer: Accept any sentence using simple present to express a need — e.g., 'I need water.' or 'She needs new shoes.' Award full marks if the verb is in simple present and expresses a need.
hints: Use 'need' or 'wants'.
Keep it in the present.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple present expressing a PREFERENCE.
answer: Accept any sentence in simple present expressing a preference — e.g., 'I like mangoes more than oranges.' or 'She prefers tea to coffee.' Award full marks if the verb is simple present and expresses a preference.
hints: Use 'like' or 'prefer'.
Keep it in the present.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple present expressing a THOUGHT or IDEA.
answer: Accept any sentence in simple present expressing a thought or idea — e.g., 'I think we should go home.' or 'She believes that reading is important.' Award full marks if the verb is simple present and expresses a thought.
hints: Use 'think', 'believe' or 'know'.
Keep it in the present.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the simple past form of verbs to express past needs, interest and feeling

skills.description: Form the simple past of a regular verb by adding -ed.
Choose the correct simple past verb to express a past need.
Choose the correct simple past verb to express past interest.
Choose the correct simple past verb to express a past feeling.
Recognise a sentence where a present tense is wrongly used in a past context.
Identify the time marker that signals past tense.
Write a sentence in the simple past expressing a need, interest or feeling.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'need'?
hints: Add -ed to the base verb.
Need → needed.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'need' is 'needed' — add -ed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'need' because it is the base form, but simple past needs -ed: 'needed'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'like'?
hints: Add -ed to the base verb.
Like → liked.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'like' is 'liked' — add -ed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'like' because it is the base form, but simple past needs -ed: 'liked'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'walk'?
hints: Add -ed to the base verb.
Walk → walked.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'walk' is 'walked' — add -ed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'walk' because it is the base form, but simple past needs -ed: 'walked'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Yesterday, I ___ some money.'
hints: 'Yesterday' signals past tense.
Use the past form of 'need'.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' tells us the sentence is about the past, so we use 'needed': 'Yesterday, I needed some money.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'need' because the sentence structure looks present, but 'yesterday' signals past — use 'needed'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Last week, she ___ a new book.'
hints: 'Last week' signals past tense.
Use the past form of 'want'.
questions.explanation: 'Last week' signals past tense, so we use 'wanted': 'Last week, she wanted a new book.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'wants' because it is present tense, but 'last week' signals past — use 'wanted'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'When I was young, I ___ a lot of toys.'
hints: 'When I was young' signals past tense.
Use the past form of 'need'.
questions.explanation: 'When I was young' signals past tense, so we use 'needed': 'When I was young, I needed a lot of toys.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use present tense because the sentence describes a habit, but the habit is in the past — use 'needed'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Last year, she ___ in winning the competition.'
hints: 'Last year' signals past tense.
Use 'was' (past of 'be') with 'interested'.
questions.explanation: 'Last year' signals past tense, so we use 'was interested': 'Last year, she was interested in winning the competition.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is interested' because 'interested' looks present, but 'last year' signals past — use 'was interested'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'As a child, Kofi ___ in playing football.'
hints: 'As a child' signals past tense.
Use 'was' with 'interested'.
questions.explanation: 'As a child' signals past tense, so we use 'was interested': 'As a child, Kofi was interested in playing football.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is interested' because 'interested' looks like a description, but the time is past — use 'was interested'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'When she was in Basic 3, she ___ in reading storybooks.'
hints: 'When she was in Basic 3' signals past tense.
Use 'was' with 'interested'.
questions.explanation: 'When she was in Basic 3' signals past tense, so we use 'was interested': 'When she was in Basic 3, she was interested in reading storybooks.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is interested' because 'interested' describes a feeling, but the time is past — use 'was interested'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'He ___ sad when he heard the news.'
hints: 'When he heard the news' signals past tense.
Use the past form of 'feel'.
questions.explanation: 'When he heard the news' signals past tense, so we use 'felt' (irregular past of 'feel'): 'He felt sad when he heard the news.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'feels' because it is present, but 'when he heard' signals past — use 'felt'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ tired after the long journey.'
hints: 'After the long journey' signals past tense.
Use the past form of 'be' for 'I'.
questions.explanation: 'After the long journey' signals past tense, so we use 'was': 'I was tired after the long journey.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'am' because they are used to 'I am', but the past context needs 'was'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ happy when their team won the match.'
hints: 'When their team won' signals past tense.
For 'they', use 'were' in the past.
questions.explanation: 'When their team won' signals past tense, so we use 'were': 'They were happy when their team won the match.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because they are used to 'they are', but the context is past — use 'were'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
hints: Which sentence has a past time word but a present verb?
'Yesterday' signals past tense.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday I need money' is wrong — 'yesterday' signals past, but 'need' is present. It should be 'Yesterday I needed money.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use present tense with past time words, but 'yesterday' requires the past form 'needed'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
options: Last year she is interested in winning.
Last year she was interested in winning.
This year she is interested in winning.
She is interested in winning this year.
hints: Which sentence has a past time word but a present verb?
'Last year' signals past tense.
questions.explanation: 'Last year she is interested' is wrong — 'last year' signals past, but 'is' is present. It should be 'was interested'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'is' because the adjective 'interested' looks present, but the time word 'last year' signals past — use 'was'.

questions.stem: Which of these is a TIME MARKER for the simple past?
hints: Which word refers to a past time?
'Yesterday' is a past time word.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' is a past time marker — it tells us the sentence is about the past, so the verb should be in the past tense.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'now' because it signals a specific time, but 'now' signals present, not past.

questions.stem: Which of these is a TIME MARKER for the simple past?
hints: Which one refers to a past year?
'Last year' is the past.
questions.explanation: 'Last year' is a past time marker — it signals that the sentence is about the past.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'every year' because it signals a time frame, but 'every year' signals a habit (present), not past.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple past expressing a NEED.
answer: Accept any sentence using simple past to express a past need — e.g., 'Yesterday I needed water.' or 'She needed a new pen.' Award full marks if the verb is in simple past and expresses a need.
hints: Use 'needed' or 'wanted'.
Include a past time marker.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple past expressing past INTEREST.
answer: Accept any sentence using simple past to express past interest — e.g., 'She was interested in reading as a child.' or 'He was interested in football last year.' Award full marks if the verb is in simple past and expresses interest.
hints: Use 'was interested' or 'liked'.
Include a past time marker.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple past expressing a past FEELING.
answer: Accept any sentence using simple past to express a past feeling — e.g., 'I felt happy yesterday.' or 'She was sad when she heard the news.' Award full marks if the verb is in simple past and expresses a feeling.
hints: Use 'felt' or 'was'.
Include a past time marker.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence in the simple past expressing a past need, interest or feeling, AND include an appropriate time marker.
answer: Accept any sentence with simple past and a past time marker — e.g., 'Last year I was interested in football.' or 'Yesterday I felt happy.' Award full marks if the sentence uses simple past and includes a past time marker.
hints: Use a past time marker like 'yesterday', 'last week', 'as a child'.
Use a past verb form.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use irregular form of the simple past tense of verbs

skills.description: Identify the simple past of a given irregular verb.
Choose the correct irregular past form to complete a sentence.
Tell a regular past form apart from an irregular past form.
Recognise an over-regularised form.
Choose the correct irregular past form for a given context.
Recognise a sentence with an incorrect irregular past form and pick the correction.
Write a sentence using a given irregular past form.

questions.stem: What is the simple past of 'build'?
hints: 'Build' is irregular — do not add -ed.
The vowel changes to 'ui'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'build' is 'built' — it is irregular, not 'builded'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'builded', but 'build' is irregular — the correct form is 'built'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past of 'go'?
hints: 'Go' has a very irregular past.
It is not 'goed'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'go' is 'went' — it is highly irregular, not 'goed'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'goed', but 'go' is irregular — the correct form is 'went'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past of 'eat'?
hints: 'Eat' is irregular.
The vowel changes to 'a'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'eat' is 'ate' — it is irregular, not 'eated'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'eated', but 'eat' is irregular — the correct form is 'ate'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ the book yesterday.'
hints: 'Take' is irregular.
'Yesterday' signals past tense.
questions.explanation: 'Take' is irregular, so the simple past is 'took': 'She took the book yesterday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'taked', but 'take' is irregular — the correct form is 'took'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'He ___ his friend at the market.'
hints: 'See' is irregular.
The past form is 'saw', not 'seen'.
questions.explanation: 'See' is irregular — the simple past is 'saw': 'He saw his friend at the market.' 'Seen' is the past participle, not the simple past.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'seen' because it is a form of 'see', but 'seen' is the past participle (used with 'have') — the simple past is 'saw'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ to the party last night.'
hints: 'Go' is irregular.
The past form is 'went', not 'gone'.
questions.explanation: 'Go' is irregular — the simple past is 'went': 'They went to the party last night.' 'Gone' is the past participle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'gone' because it is a form of 'go', but 'gone' is the past participle (used with 'have') — the simple past is 'went'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The children ___ a sandcastle on the beach.'
hints: 'Build' is irregular.
The past form is 'built'.
questions.explanation: 'Build' is irregular — the simple past is 'built': 'The children built a sandcastle on the beach.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'builded', but 'build' is irregular — the correct form is 'built'.

questions.stem: Which past form is IRREGULAR?
hints: Regular pasts end in -ed.
Irregular pasts do not end in -ed.
questions.explanation: 'Went' is irregular — it does not end in -ed. 'Walked', 'played' and 'looked' are regular.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any past form is regular, but irregular pasts do not follow the -ed rule.

questions.stem: Which past form is REGULAR?
hints: Regular past forms end in -ed.
Which one ends in -ed?
questions.explanation: 'Needed' is regular — it ends in -ed. 'Ate', 'saw' and 'took' are irregular.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'ate' because it is common, but 'ate' is irregular — regular pasts end in -ed.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG irregular past form?
hints: Which sentence adds -ed to an irregular verb?
'Go' is irregular.
questions.explanation: 'Goed' is wrong — 'go' is irregular, and its past form is 'went'. The other sentences use correct irregular pasts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to 'go' to make 'goed', but 'go' is irregular — use 'went'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG irregular past form?
hints: Which sentence adds -ed to an irregular verb?
'Eat' is irregular.
questions.explanation: 'Eated' is wrong — 'eat' is irregular, and its past form is 'ate'. The other sentences use correct irregular pasts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to 'eat' to make 'eated', but 'eat' is irregular — use 'ate'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG irregular past form?
hints: Which sentence adds -ed to an irregular verb?
'Know' is irregular.
questions.explanation: 'Knowed' is wrong — 'know' is irregular, and its past form is 'knew'. The other sentences use correct irregular pasts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to 'know' to make 'knowed', but 'know' is irregular — use 'knew'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ a strange noise last night.'
hints: 'Hear' is irregular.
The past form is 'heard'.
questions.explanation: 'Hear' is irregular — the simple past is 'heard': 'I heard a strange noise last night.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'heared', but 'hear' is irregular — the correct form is 'heard'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ the answer to the question.'
hints: 'Know' is irregular.
The past form is 'knew'.
questions.explanation: 'Know' is irregular — the simple past is 'knew': 'She knew the answer to the question.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'knowed', but 'know' is irregular — the correct form is 'knew'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ the ball over the wall.'
hints: 'Throw' is irregular.
The past form is 'threw', not 'thrown'.
questions.explanation: 'Throw' is irregular — the simple past is 'threw': 'They threw the ball over the wall.' 'Thrown' is the past participle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'thrown' because it is a form of 'throw', but 'thrown' is the past participle (used with 'have') — the simple past is 'threw'.

questions.stem: A pupil wrote: 'She goed to school yesterday.' What is the correct sentence?
hints: 'Go' is irregular.
The past form is 'went'.
questions.explanation: 'Goed' is wrong — 'go' is irregular, and its past form is 'went'. The correct sentence is 'She went to school yesterday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'goed' is correct because it follows the -ed rule, but 'go' is irregular.

questions.stem: A pupil wrote: 'He eated the mango quickly.' What is the correct sentence?
hints: 'Eat' is irregular.
The past form is 'ate'.
questions.explanation: 'Eated' is wrong — 'eat' is irregular, and its past form is 'ate'. The correct sentence is 'He ate the mango quickly.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'eated' is correct because it follows the -ed rule, but 'eat' is irregular.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the irregular past form 'went'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'went' correctly — e.g., 'She went to the market.' or 'They went home early.' Award full marks if 'went' is used as the simple past of 'go'.
hints: 'Went' is the past of 'go'.
Use it to describe a completed action.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the irregular past form 'ate'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'ate' correctly — e.g., 'She ate rice for lunch.' or 'We ate together yesterday.' Award full marks if 'ate' is used as the simple past of 'eat'.
hints: 'Ate' is the past of 'eat'.
Use it to describe a completed meal.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using TWO irregular past forms.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses two irregular past verbs correctly — e.g., 'He went to the market and bought rice.' or 'She saw the bird and heard it sing.' Award full marks if both verbs are irregular past forms.
hints: Choose two irregular verbs from: went, ate, saw, took, gave, ran, drank, wrote, read, bought, brought, thought, caught, taught, found, sat, stood, broke, spoke, began, swam, sang, rang, knew, grew, threw, flew, fell, forgot, got, lost, won, told, sold, held, made, said, paid, slept, kept, felt, left, met, sent, spent, heard.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses two irregular past forms correctly
Both verbs are irregular past forms

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the past continuous form of verbs to talk about actions/events that were going on when a second action/event took place

skills.description: Form the past continuous (was/were + -ing).
Identify which action in a sentence was ongoing (past continuous).
Identify which action interrupted the ongoing action (simple past).
Choose the correct past continuous form to complete a sentence.
Choose the sentence that correctly pairs past continuous (ongoing) with simple past (interrupting).
Recognise a wrong past continuous form.
Write a sentence using past continuous for an ongoing action interrupted by a second action.

questions.stem: What is the past continuous form of 'play' for 'we'?
hints: Past continuous = was/were + -ing.
For 'we', use 'were'.
questions.explanation: For 'we', the past continuous is 'were playing' — 'were' + 'playing'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'was playing' because it is a form of past continuous, but 'was' is for I/he/she/it — for 'we', use 'were'.

questions.stem: What is the past continuous form of 'sing' for 'she'?
hints: Past continuous = was/were + -ing.
For 'she', use 'was'.
questions.explanation: For 'she', the past continuous is 'was singing' — 'was' + 'singing'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'were singing' because it is a form of past continuous, but 'were' is for you/we/they — for 'she', use 'was'.

questions.stem: What is the past continuous form of 'run' for 'they'?
hints: Past continuous = was/were + -ing.
For 'they', use 'were'.
questions.explanation: For 'they', the past continuous is 'were running' — 'were' + 'running'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'was running' because it is a form of past continuous, but 'was' is for I/he/she/it — for 'they', use 'were'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'We were playing football when the fire broke out.' Which action was ONGOING (past continuous)?
hints: Which action was happening before and during the interruption?
The ongoing action uses 'was/were + -ing'.
questions.explanation: 'Were playing football' is the ongoing action — it was happening before and during the fire. 'The fire broke out' is the interruption.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the fire broke out' because it is exciting, but that is the interruption — the ongoing action is 'were playing'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She was cooking when the phone rang.' Which action was ONGOING?
hints: Which action was happening before and during the interruption?
The ongoing action uses 'was/were + -ing'.
questions.explanation: 'Was cooking' is the ongoing action — she was cooking before and during the phone call. 'The phone rang' is the interruption.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the phone rang' because it is the interruption, but the ongoing action is 'was cooking'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The children were sleeping when the storm began.' Which action was ONGOING?
hints: Which action was already happening when the other began?
'Were sleeping' is past continuous.
questions.explanation: 'Were sleeping' is the ongoing action — the children were asleep before and during the storm. 'The storm began' is the interruption.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the storm began' because it is the event, but it is the interruption — the ongoing action is 'were sleeping'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'They were walking home when it started to rain.' Which action INTERRUPTED the ongoing action?
hints: Which action came as a surprise?
It is in simple past, not past continuous.
questions.explanation: 'It started to rain' is the interrupting action — it happened during their walk. 'Were walking' is the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'were walking' because it is the longer action, but the question asks for the INTERRUPTION — that is 'it started to rain'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'I was reading when the lights went off.' Which action INTERRUPTED the ongoing action?
hints: Which action is in simple past?
The interrupting action is short and sudden.
questions.explanation: 'The lights went off' is the interrupting action — it happened while I was reading. 'Was reading' is the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'was reading' because it is the main action, but the interrupting action is 'the lights went off'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The pupils were singing when the teacher entered the classroom.' Which action INTERRUPTED the ongoing action?
hints: Which action is in simple past?
It is the sudden action.
questions.explanation: 'The teacher entered the classroom' is the interrupting action — it happened while the pupils were singing. 'Were singing' is the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'were singing' because it is the main action, but the interrupting action is 'the teacher entered'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ dinner when I arrived.'
hints: The ongoing action uses past continuous.
For 'she', use 'was'.
questions.explanation: 'She' takes 'was cooking' — the past continuous for the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cooked' because it is past, but the ongoing action needs past continuous — 'was cooking'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ football when it started to rain.'
hints: The ongoing action uses past continuous.
For 'they', use 'were'.
questions.explanation: 'They' takes 'were playing' — the past continuous for the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'was playing' because it is past continuous, but 'was' is for I/he/she/it — 'they' takes 'were'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ a book when the phone rang.'
hints: The ongoing action uses past continuous.
For 'I', use 'was'.
questions.explanation: 'I' takes 'was reading' — the past continuous for the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'read' because it is past, but the ongoing action needs past continuous — 'was reading'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly pairs past continuous (ongoing) with simple past (interrupting)?
options: We were eating when the power went off.
We ate when the power was going off.
We were eating when the power was going off.
We eat when the power went off.
hints: Ongoing action: past continuous. Interruption: simple past.
The interrupting action is short and sudden.
questions.explanation: 'We were eating' (ongoing) + 'the power went off' (interruption) — the first sentence is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use past continuous for both actions, but the interruption should be simple past — 'went off'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly pairs past continuous (ongoing) with simple past (interrupting)?
options: The baby was sleeping when the doorbell rang.
The baby slept when the doorbell was ringing.
The baby was sleeping when the doorbell was ringing.
The baby sleeps when the doorbell rang.
hints: The ongoing action should be past continuous.
The interrupting action should be simple past.
questions.explanation: 'The baby was sleeping' (ongoing) + 'the doorbell rang' (interruption) — the first sentence is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use past continuous for both actions, but the interruption should be simple past — 'rang'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly pairs past continuous (ongoing) with simple past (interrupting)?
options: Ama was sweeping when Kofi walked in.
Ama swept when Kofi was walking in.
Ama was sweeping when Kofi was walking in.
Ama sweeps when Kofi walked in.
hints: Ongoing action: past continuous. Interruption: simple past.
The shorter action is the interruption.
questions.explanation: 'Ama was sweeping' (ongoing) + 'Kofi walked in' (interruption) — the first sentence is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use past continuous for both actions, but the interruption should be simple past — 'walked in'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG past continuous form?
hints: For 'we', use 'were', not 'was'.
Which sentence uses 'was' with 'we'?
questions.explanation: 'We was playing' is wrong — 'we' takes 'were'. The correct form is 'We were playing football.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'was' with 'we' because both sound natural, but 'we' takes 'were' in standard English.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG past continuous form?
hints: For 'she', use 'was', not 'were'.
Which sentence uses 'were' with 'she'?
questions.explanation: 'She were reading' is wrong — 'she' takes 'was'. The correct form is 'She was reading a book.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'were' with 'she' because it sounds okay, but 'she' takes 'was'.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using past continuous for an ongoing action interrupted by a second action. Use 'when'.
answer: Accept any sentence that correctly uses past continuous (was/were + -ing) for the ongoing action and simple past for the interruption — e.g., 'I was cooking when the phone rang.' Award full marks if both forms are used correctly with 'when'.
hints: Ongoing: was/were + -ing. Interruption: simple past.
Use 'when' to link them.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses past continuous for ongoing action

questions.stem: Write a sentence using past continuous for an ongoing action interrupted by a second action. Use 'while' if possible.
answer: Accept any sentence that correctly uses past continuous for the ongoing action and simple past for the interruption — e.g., 'While I was reading, the lights went off.' Award full marks if both forms are used correctly.
hints: Ongoing: was/were + -ing. Interruption: simple past.
'While' introduces the ongoing action.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses past continuous for ongoing action

questions.stem: Write two sentences, each using past continuous for an ongoing action interrupted by a second action.
answer: Accept any two sentences that correctly pair past continuous (ongoing) with simple past (interruption) — e.g., 'We were eating when the lights went off. She was singing when I arrived.' Award full marks if both sentences are correct.
hints: Each sentence needs one past continuous and one simple past verb.
Use 'when' or 'while'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses past continuous in both sentences

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the imperative forms of verbs to give instructions and directions

skills.description: Identify the imperative verb in a short instruction.
Choose the correct imperative verb to give a given instruction.
Tell an imperative sentence apart from a statement.
Choose the correct imperative verb for a direction.
Choose the correct negative imperative.
Recognise a wrong imperative form.
Write an imperative instruction or direction for a given situation.

questions.stem: Read this instruction: 'Sit down quietly.' Which word is the imperative verb?
hints: The imperative verb comes first in a command.
'Sit' is the action being commanded.
questions.explanation: 'Sit' is the imperative verb — it gives the command. 'Down' is an adverb, 'quietly' is an adverb.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'quietly' because it describes how to sit, but 'quietly' is an adverb — 'Sit' is the imperative verb.

questions.stem: Read this instruction: 'Close the door, please.' Which word is the imperative verb?
hints: The imperative verb is the action word.
'Close' is the command.
questions.explanation: 'Close' is the imperative verb — it gives the command to close the door.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'door' because it is a noun, but the imperative verb is 'Close'.

questions.stem: Read this direction: 'Turn right at the junction.' Which word is the imperative verb?
hints: The imperative verb is the action word.
'Turn' is the command.
questions.explanation: 'Turn' is the imperative verb — it gives the direction. 'Right' is an adverb of direction.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'right' because it tells direction, but 'right' is an adverb — 'Turn' is the verb.

questions.stem: Complete the instruction: '___ on the light.'
hints: The imperative uses the base form of the verb.
Use 'switch', not 'switching' or 'switched'.
questions.explanation: The imperative uses the base form of the verb: 'Switch on the light.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Switching' because it is a verb form, but the imperative is the base verb — 'Switch'.

questions.stem: Complete the instruction: '___ your exercise book to me.'
hints: The imperative uses the base form.
Use 'bring', not 'bringing' or 'brought'.
questions.explanation: The imperative uses the base form: 'Bring your exercise book to me.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Brought' because it is a past form, but the imperative is 'Bring' — base form.

questions.stem: Complete the instruction: '___ the door when you leave.'
hints: The imperative uses the base form.
Use 'close', not 'closing' or 'closed'.
questions.explanation: The imperative uses the base form: 'Close the door when you leave.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Closed' because it is a form of 'close', but the imperative is 'Close'.

questions.stem: Complete the instruction: '___ right at the junction, then walk twenty steps.'
hints: The imperative uses the base form.
Use 'turn', not 'turning' or 'turned'.
questions.explanation: The imperative uses the base form: 'Turn right at the junction, then walk twenty steps.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Turning' because it is a verb form, but the imperative is 'Turn'.

questions.stem: Which of these is an IMPERATIVE sentence?
hints: An imperative gives a command directly.
It starts with the base verb and has no subject.
questions.explanation: 'Stand up straight' is imperative — it gives a direct command with no subject. The others are a statement, a question and a suggestion.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'You should stand up straight' because it involves the same action, but 'should' makes it a suggestion, not an imperative.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an imperative sentence?
hints: An imperative does not have an explicit subject like 'you'.
Which sentence tells someone about an action rather than commanding it?
questions.explanation: 'You are going to school' is a statement, not an imperative — it has a subject ('you') and tells about an action. The others are imperatives.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'Go to school' and 'You are going to school' are the same, but the first is imperative (command) and the second is a statement.

questions.stem: Complete the direction: '___ left at the traffic lights.'
hints: Directions use the imperative — base form.
Use 'Turn', not 'Turning'.
questions.explanation: Directions use the imperative: 'Turn left at the traffic lights.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Turning' because it is a verb form, but the imperative is 'Turn'.

questions.stem: Complete the direction: '___ straight until you reach the water tank.'
hints: Directions use the imperative — base form.
Use 'Walk', not 'Walking'.
questions.explanation: Directions use the imperative: 'Walk straight until you reach the water tank.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Walking' because it is a verb form, but the imperative is 'Walk'.

questions.stem: Complete the direction: '___ at the big mango tree and turn right.'
hints: Directions use the imperative — base form.
Use 'Stop', not 'Stopping'.
questions.explanation: Directions use the imperative: 'Stop at the big mango tree and turn right.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Stopping' because it is a verb form, but the imperative is 'Stop'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct negative imperative: '___ run in the corridor.'
hints: Negative imperative = 'do not' + base verb.
Use 'Do not run' or 'Don't run'.
questions.explanation: The negative imperative is 'Do not run in the corridor' (or 'Don't run'). 'Do not' + base verb is the standard form.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Not run' because it is shorter, but the negative imperative needs 'do not' or 'don't' before the verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct negative imperative: '___ touch the hot pot.'
hints: Negative imperative = 'do not' + base verb.
Use 'Do not touch' or 'Don't touch'.
questions.explanation: The negative imperative is 'Do not touch the hot pot' (or 'Don't touch').
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Not touch' because it is shorter, but the correct form is 'Do not touch'.

questions.stem: Which instruction has the WRONG imperative form?
hints: An imperative does not include 'you' as a subject.
Which sentence has an unnecessary 'you'?
questions.explanation: 'You switch on the light' is wrong — imperatives do not include the subject 'you'. The correct form is 'Switch on the light.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may include 'you' because it feels explicit, but imperatives drop the subject — 'Switch' is enough.

questions.stem: Which instruction has the WRONG imperative form?
hints: An imperative uses the base verb, not the infinitive.
'To sit' is an infinitive, not an imperative.
questions.explanation: 'To sit down' is wrong — the imperative uses the base verb 'sit', not the infinitive 'to sit'. The correct form is 'Sit down, please.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use the infinitive 'to sit' because it names the action, but the imperative is just 'sit'.

questions.stem: Which instruction has the WRONG imperative form?
hints: An imperative uses the base verb, not '-ing'.
'Switching' is a participle, not an imperative.
questions.explanation: 'Switching on the light' is wrong — it uses the -ing form. The imperative uses the base verb: 'Switch on the light.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use the -ing form because it names the action, but the imperative is just 'Switch'.

questions.stem: Write an imperative instruction for a classroom activity.
answer: Accept any sentence using the imperative — e.g., 'Open your books to page 10.' or 'Write your name at the top of the page.' Award full marks if the verb is in the imperative form (base verb, no subject).
hints: Start with the base verb.
Do not include 'you'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses the imperative form (base verb, no subject)

questions.stem: Write an imperative direction for someone to find the school library.
answer: Accept any sentence using the imperative to give directions — e.g., 'Walk straight down this corridor and turn left.' Award full marks if the sentence uses imperative verbs and gives a direction.
hints: Use verbs like 'Walk', 'Turn', 'Stop'.
No 'you' at the start.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a negative imperative instruction to warn someone about a danger.
answer: Accept any sentence using a negative imperative — e.g., 'Do not touch the hot iron.' or 'Don't run near the road.' Award full marks if the sentence uses 'do not' or 'don't' + base verb and warns about a danger.
hints: Use 'Do not' or 'Don't'.
Choose a dangerous action to warn about.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.6.1: Apply the knowledge of different types of adverbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use adverbs to express manner

skills.description: Identify the adverb of manner in a short sentence.
Form an adverb of manner from a given adjective.
Choose the correct adverb of manner to complete a sentence.
Identify which verb an adverb modifies in a given sentence.
Tell an adjective from an adverb and choose the right one in a sentence.
Recognise a wrong form of an adverb of manner.
Write a meaningful sentence using a given adverb of manner.

misconceptions: -ly added to words that don't take -ly
Same form for adjective and adverb not recognised

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Mercy ate slowly.' Which word is the adverb of manner?
hints: An adverb of manner tells HOW something is done.
'Slowly' tells how Mercy ate.
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' is the adverb of manner — it tells how Mercy ate. 'Mercy' is a noun, 'ate' is a verb.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'ate' because it is the action, but the adverb is the word that describes HOW the action was done — 'slowly'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The children ran quickly to the gate.' Which word is the adverb of manner?
hints: Which word tells HOW the children ran?
'Quickly' describes the manner of running.
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' is the adverb of manner — it tells how the children ran. 'Children' is a noun, 'ran' is a verb, 'gate' is a noun.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'ran' because it is the action, but the adverb is 'quickly' — it tells how they ran.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She sang beautifully at the concert.' Which word is the adverb of manner?
hints: Which word tells HOW she sang?
'Beautifully' describes the manner of singing.
questions.explanation: 'Beautifully' is the adverb of manner — it tells how she sang.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sang' because it is the action, but the adverb is 'beautifully'.

questions.stem: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'slow'?
hints: Add -ly to the adjective.
Slow → slowly.
questions.explanation: The adverb form of 'slow' is 'slowly' — add -ly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'slower' because it is a form of the adjective, but 'slower' is comparative — the adverb is 'slowly'.

questions.stem: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'quick'?
hints: Add -ly to the adjective.
Quick → quickly.
questions.explanation: The adverb form of 'quick' is 'quickly' — add -ly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'quicker' because it is a form of the adjective, but the adverb is 'quickly'.

questions.stem: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'happy'?
hints: Change -y to -i before adding -ly.
Happy → happily.
questions.explanation: For adjectives ending in -y, change -y to -i and add -ly: 'happily'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'happyly' with a 'y', but -y changes to -i before -ly.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ate her food ___ .'
hints: We need an adverb of manner to describe HOW she ate.
Use 'slowly', not 'slow'.
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' is the adverb of manner: 'She ate her food slowly.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'slow' because it describes the eating, but 'slow' is an adjective — the adverb is 'slowly'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The boy ran ___ to catch the bus.'
hints: We need an adverb of manner.
Use 'quickly', not 'quick'.
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' is the adverb of manner: 'The boy ran quickly to catch the bus.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'quick' because it describes the running, but 'quick' is an adjective — the adverb is 'quickly'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She smiled ___ when she received the gift.'
hints: We need an adverb of manner.
Use 'happily', not 'happy'.
questions.explanation: 'Happily' is the adverb of manner: 'She smiled happily when she received the gift.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'happy' because it describes the smile, but 'happy' is an adjective — the adverb is 'happily'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The pupils listened carefully to the teacher.' Which verb does the adverb 'carefully' modify?
hints: An adverb of manner modifies a verb.
What action did the pupils do carefully?
questions.explanation: 'Carefully' modifies 'listened' — it tells how the pupils listened.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pupils' because it is closest to the adverb, but 'pupils' is a noun — the adverb modifies the verb 'listened'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The old man walked slowly across the road.' Which verb does the adverb 'slowly' modify?
hints: An adverb of manner modifies a verb.
What action was done slowly?
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' modifies 'walked' — it tells how the old man walked.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'old man' because it is the subject, but the adverb modifies the verb 'walked'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the ADVERB correctly?
hints: An adverb tells HOW she sings.
Use 'beautifully', not 'beautiful'.
questions.explanation: 'She sings beautifully' is correct — 'beautifully' is the adverb of manner. 'Beautiful' is an adjective and cannot describe the verb 'sings'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She sings beautiful' because 'beautiful' sounds nice, but it is an adjective — the adverb is 'beautifully'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the ADJECTIVE correctly?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
'Beautiful' describes 'singer'.
questions.explanation: 'She is a beautiful singer' uses 'beautiful' as an adjective describing the noun 'singer'. The other sentences misuse the adjective.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She sings beautiful' because it sounds similar, but 'beautiful' is an adjective — it cannot modify the verb 'sings'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct word: 'The teacher spoke ___ to the pupils.'
hints: We need an adverb to describe HOW the teacher spoke.
Use 'kindly', not 'kind'.
questions.explanation: 'Kindly' is the adverb: 'The teacher spoke kindly to the pupils.' 'Kind' is an adjective.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'kind' because it describes the speaking, but 'kind' is an adjective — the adverb is 'kindly'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG adverb form?
hints: Which sentence uses an adjective where an adverb is needed?
'Slow' is an adjective, not an adverb.
questions.explanation: 'She ate her food slow' is wrong — it should be 'slowly' because an adverb is needed to describe how she ate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'slow' works as an adverb, but in standard English, 'slowly' is the adverb of manner.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG adverb form?
options: He ran quick to the shop.
He ran quickly to the shop.
hints: Which sentence uses an adjective where an adverb is needed?
'Quick' is an adjective.
questions.explanation: 'He ran quick' is wrong — it should be 'quickly' because an adverb is needed to describe how he ran.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'quick' works as an adverb, but the adverb is 'quickly'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG adverb form?
hints: Which word is misspelt?
Happy → happily, not 'happyly'.
questions.explanation: 'Happyly' is wrong — the adverb of 'happy' is 'happily' (change -y to -i, then add -ly).
questions.misconception: Pupils may keep the 'y' before adding -ly, but -y changes to -i: 'happily'.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the adverb of manner 'slowly'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'slowly' correctly — e.g., 'The tortoise walked slowly.' or 'She ate her food slowly.' Award full marks if 'slowly' is used as an adverb of manner and the sentence makes sense.
hints: Use 'slowly' to describe HOW something was done.
It modifies a verb.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the adverb of manner 'carefully'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'carefully' correctly — e.g., 'She carried the baby carefully.' or 'He read the instructions carefully.' Award full marks if 'carefully' is used as an adverb and the sentence makes sense.
hints: Use 'carefully' to describe HOW something was done.
It modifies a verb.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using an adverb of manner formed from the adjective 'happy'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'happily' correctly — e.g., 'The children played happily in the field.' Award full marks if 'happily' is formed correctly and used as an adverb of manner.
hints: Happy → happily.
Use it to describe HOW something was done.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.7.1: Understand and use idiomatic expressions appropriately in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Identify, explain and use idiomatic expressions correctly

skills.description: Identify the idiomatic expression in a short sentence.
Match an idiom to its correct meaning.
Choose the correct idiom to complete a sentence using context.
Tell the literal meaning of the words apart from the figurative meaning of the idiom.
Interpret an idiom as it is used in a given context.
Write a meaningful sentence using a given idiom.
Recognise a sentence where an idiom is used incorrectly.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Kofi takes after his father — they both have the same smile.' Which phrase is the idiom?
hints: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not literal.
'Takes after' does not mean physically taking something.
questions.explanation: 'Takes after' is the idiom — it means 'resembles' or 'looks like'. It does not mean physically taking something from his father.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'his father' because it is the subject, but 'takes after' is the idiomatic expression.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The trader tried to pull down her rival's business by spreading lies.' Which phrase is the idiom?
hints: Which phrase has a non-literal meaning?
'Pull down' does not mean physically pulling something down.
questions.explanation: 'Pull down' is the idiom — it means to destroy someone's reputation, not to physically pull a building down.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'pull down' means physically pulling something down, but in this sentence it means destroying a reputation.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The exam was a piece of cake — I finished in ten minutes.' Which phrase is the idiom?
hints: Which phrase has a non-literal meaning?
'A piece of cake' does not refer to food here.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' is the idiom — it means something is very easy, not that there was cake in the exam.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'a piece of cake' refers to food, but in this sentence, it means the exam was easy.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'take after' mean?
options: To look or behave like someone
hints: Think of a child who looks like their parent.
'Take after' means to resemble.
questions.explanation: 'Take after' means to look or behave like someone — usually a family member.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'take after' means to physically follow someone, but the idiom means to resemble.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'pull down' mean in the sentence 'He tried to pull down his rival's business'?
options: To destroy someone's reputation or success
To physically pull a building down
To pull something from a shelf
hints: In this sentence, 'pull down' refers to a business.
It means to harm someone's success.
questions.explanation: 'Pull down' means to destroy someone's reputation or success, not to physically pull down a building.
