questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'pull down' means physically demolishing a building, but in the sentence, it refers to destroying a business's reputation.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
hints: Think of a secret being revealed.
The 'cat' is a secret.
questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it literally means freeing a cat, but the idiom means revealing a secret.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'under the weather' mean?
hints: It describes how someone is feeling.
If someone is 'under the weather', they might stay home.
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' means feeling sick or unwell.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it means being outside in bad weather, but it is an idiom for feeling sick.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The maths test was ___ — I finished it in five minutes.'
options: cost an arm and a leg
hints: What does finishing quickly suggest about the test?
'A piece of cake' means something is easy.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' fits the context — the test was easy, so it was finished quickly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'under the weather' because it describes a feeling, but that means feeling sick — not that something is easy.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Ama is not at school today. She is feeling ___ .'
options: the cat out of the bag
hints: What does the sentence say about Ama's health?
She is not at school — she might be sick.
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' fits — it means feeling sick, which explains why Ama is not at school.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'a piece of cake' because it is a common idiom, but it means something is easy — not that someone is sick.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'He ___ when he told everyone about the surprise party before the day.'
options: let the cat out of the bag
hit the nail on the head
hints: What did he do with the surprise?
He revealed it before the day.
questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' fits — it means he revealed a secret (the surprise party).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'hit the nail on the head' because it sounds positive, but that means saying exactly the right thing — it does not fit revealing a secret.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'It was raining cats and dogs.' What is the FIGURATIVE meaning?
options: Cats and dogs were falling from the sky
There were animals in the house
hints: An idiom has a figurative meaning different from literal.
No animals actually fell from the sky.
questions.explanation: Figuratively, 'raining cats and dogs' means it was raining very heavily. Literally, it would mean animals falling — but that is not what the idiom means.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Cats and dogs were falling from the sky' because that is the literal meaning, but the idiom is not literal — it means heavy rain.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The teacher pulled down the pupil's reputation with her harsh words.' What is the FIGURATIVE meaning?
options: The teacher damaged the pupil's reputation
The teacher physically pulled the pupil down
The teacher pulled a building down
The teacher pulled the pupil's clothes
hints: 'Pull down' here refers to reputation.
It does not mean physically pulling something.
questions.explanation: Figuratively, 'pulled down the pupil's reputation' means she damaged it. Literally, it would mean physically pulling something down — but that is not what the sentence says.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'pulled down' means physically pulling, but the sentence is about reputation — it is figurative.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The new phone cost an arm and a leg.' What is the FIGURATIVE meaning?
hints: No one actually paid with body parts.
The idiom is about cost.
questions.explanation: Figuratively, 'cost an arm and a leg' means it was very expensive. Literally, it would mean body parts were paid — which is not true.
questions.misconception: Pupils may take the literal meaning (costing body parts), but the idiom means very expensive.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Ama is very quiet. But when the teacher asked who broke the window, she spoke up and told the truth. She really hit the nail on the head.' What does 'hit the nail on the head' mean here?
options: She said exactly the right thing
She hit the teacher with a nail
hints: What did Ama do when she spoke?
She told the truth about what happened.
questions.explanation: 'Hit the nail on the head' means to say exactly the right thing — in this case, Ama told the truth and identified what happened.
questions.misconception: Pupils may take the literal meaning (hitting a nail), but the idiom means saying exactly the right thing.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Kofi broke the vase and then told his mother a lie about it. When she found out, she said he had really let the cat out of the bag.' What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean here?
options: He revealed the truth about what happened
He put a cat in a bag
hints: What did Kofi try to hide?
The idiom is about secrets being revealed.
questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret. Kofi revealed the truth (that he broke the vase) — he let the secret out.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it means telling a lie, but the idiom means revealing a secret — Kofi revealed that he had lied.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The shop is very expensive. A simple shirt there costs an arm and a leg. But the shop has one special sale every year — only once in a blue moon.' What does 'once in a blue moon' mean here?
hints: What does 'once' mean?
The idiom means something does not happen often.
questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely — the sale happens only once a year, which is rare.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it means monthly because of 'moon', but 'once in a blue moon' means very rarely — not every month.

questions.stem: Write a meaningful sentence using the idiom 'take after'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'take after' correctly — e.g., 'She takes after her mother in looks.' Award full marks if 'take after' is used to mean resemble and the sentence makes sense.
hints: 'Take after' means to resemble someone.
Who does someone in your family resemble?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a meaningful sentence using the idiom 'a piece of cake'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'a piece of cake' correctly — e.g., 'The test was a piece of cake.' Award full marks if 'a piece of cake' means easy and the sentence makes sense.
hints: 'A piece of cake' means something is very easy.
What do you find easy?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiom 'take after' INCORRECTLY?
options: The boy takes after his uncle.
hints: Which sentence has a wrong verb form?
'Take' is irregular — the past form is 'took', not 'taked'.
questions.explanation: 'Taked after' is wrong — the past form of 'take' is 'took'. So the correct sentence would be 'Kofi took after his father.' The other sentences use 'take after' correctly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to 'take' to make 'taked', but 'take' is irregular — the past form is 'took'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an idiom INCORRECTLY?
options: The exam was a piece of cake, so I failed it.
The exam was a piece of cake — I finished in ten minutes.
My phone was very expensive — it cost an arm and a leg.
He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
hints: Which sentence uses an idiom in a way that contradicts its meaning?
'A piece of cake' means easy — so if something is easy, would you fail?
questions.explanation: 'The exam was a piece of cake, so I failed it' is incorrect — 'a piece of cake' means easy, so failing contradicts the idiom. The other sentences use idioms correctly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not notice the contradiction, but 'a piece of cake' means easy — you would not fail an easy exam because it was easy.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.8.1: Apply the knowledge of conjunctions in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Identify and use simple conjunctions – because, since, so, although – to give reasons, link contrasting ideas, show results

skills.description: Identify the conjunction in a short sentence.
Choose the correct conjunction to give a reason (because/since).
Choose the correct conjunction to show a result (so).
Choose the correct conjunction to link contrasting ideas (but/although).
Choose the correct conjunction to show choice or alternative (or/nor).
Join two simple sentences using the correct conjunction from the set.
Recognise a sentence where the wrong conjunction has been used.
Write a meaningful sentence using a given conjunction.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'I stayed home because it was raining.' Which word is the conjunction?
hints: A conjunction joins ideas together.
'Because' introduces the reason.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is the conjunction — it joins the two ideas and gives the reason for staying home.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'raining' because it is the reason, but the conjunction is the word that LINKS the ideas — 'because'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She studied hard, so she passed the exam.' Which word is the conjunction?
hints: A conjunction joins the two parts of the sentence.
'So' shows the result.
questions.explanation: 'So' is the conjunction — it links the studying to the result (passing).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'passed' because it is the result, but the conjunction is 'so' — the word that links.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Although he was tired, he continued working.' Which word is the conjunction?
hints: A conjunction links ideas.
'Although' introduces a contrasting idea.
questions.explanation: 'Although' is the conjunction — it links the idea of being tired to the contrasting idea of continuing to work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'tired' because it is the descriptive word, but the conjunction is 'Although'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'I was late ___ I missed the bus.'
hints: Which conjunction gives a reason?
Why was I late?
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the reason: I was late BECAUSE I missed the bus.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'so' because both connect ideas, but 'so' shows a result, not a reason — the reason is the missed bus.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: '___ it was raining, we stayed indoors.'
hints: Which conjunction gives a reason?
Why did we stay indoors?
questions.explanation: 'Since' gives a reason — it means 'because'. 'Since it was raining, we stayed indoors.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'So' because it connects ideas, but 'so' shows a result — the reason is the rain.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'She passed the exam ___ she studied every day.'
hints: Which conjunction gives a reason for passing?
Why did she pass?
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the reason: she passed BECAUSE she studied every day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'so' because both connect ideas, but 'so' would mean studying was the result of passing — which is the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'It was raining, ___ we stayed indoors.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a result?
What was the result of the rain?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: it was raining, SO we stayed indoors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it connects ideas, but 'because' gives a reason — the rain is the reason, staying indoors is the result.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Kofi studied hard, ___ he passed the exam.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a result?
What was the result of studying hard?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: he studied hard, SO he passed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it is common, but 'because' gives a reason — here, passing is the result of studying.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'The rain was very heavy, ___ the road was flooded.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a result?
What was the result of heavy rain?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: the rain was heavy, SO the road was flooded.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it also connects ideas, but here the flooding is the result of the heavy rain — 'so' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'He was tired, ___ he continued working.'
hints: Which conjunction shows contrast?
The two ideas are opposite — tiredness and continuing to work.
questions.explanation: 'But' shows contrast: he was tired, BUT he continued working (two contrasting ideas).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'so' because both connect ideas, but 'so' would show a result — tiredness would not cause him to continue working.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: '___ she was tired, she continued working.'
hints: Which conjunction shows contrast?
The two ideas are opposite.
questions.explanation: 'Although' shows contrast: ALTHOUGH she was tired, she continued working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because' because it gives a reason, but being tired is the opposite of continuing — the idea is contrast, not cause.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Ama is tall, ___ her sister is short.'
hints: Which conjunction shows contrast?
Tall and short are opposites.
questions.explanation: 'But' shows contrast: Ama is tall, BUT her sister is short (the two facts are opposites).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it connects ideas, but 'because' would suggest being tall causes her sister to be short — clearly wrong.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'You can have rice ___ kenkey for lunch.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a choice between two things?
You are choosing between rice and kenkey.
questions.explanation: 'Or' shows a choice: you can have rice OR kenkey (two options).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'but' because both connect ideas, but 'but' shows contrast — 'or' shows a choice.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'She does not like tea ___ does she like coffee.'
hints: Which conjunction is used with negative alternatives?
'Nor' is used after a negative to add another negative.
questions.explanation: 'Nor' is the correct conjunction for a negative alternative: she does not like tea, NOR does she like coffee.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'or' because it shows choice, but 'or' is used in positive sentences — 'nor' is needed after a negative.

questions.stem: Join these two sentences: 'It was raining.' 'We stayed indoors.' Which is the correct way to join them?
options: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.
It was raining, because we stayed indoors.
It was raining, although we stayed indoors.
It was raining, or we stayed indoors.
hints: What is the relationship between rain and staying indoors?
The rain caused us to stay indoors — that's a result.
questions.explanation: 'So' correctly shows the result: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it links ideas, but 'because' would suggest we stayed indoors CAUSED the rain — which is backwards.

questions.stem: Join these two sentences: 'He was tired.' 'He continued working.' Which is the correct way to join them?
options: Although he was tired, he continued working.
Because he was tired, he continued working.
So he was tired, he continued working.
Or he was tired, he continued working.
hints: What is the relationship? Tiredness and working are opposite.
Use a contrast conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'Although' correctly shows the contrast: Although he was tired, he continued working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because' because it connects ideas, but tiredness does not cause someone to keep working — the ideas are contrasting.

questions.stem: Join these two sentences: 'She studied hard.' 'She passed the exam.' Which is the correct way to join them?
options: She studied hard, so she passed the exam.
She studied hard, because she passed the exam.
She studied hard, although she passed the exam.
She studied hard, or she passed the exam.
hints: What is the relationship between studying and passing?
Studying caused her to pass — that's a result.
questions.explanation: 'So' correctly shows the result: She studied hard, so she passed the exam.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it is common, but 'because' would suggest passing the exam caused her to study — which is backwards.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG conjunction?
options: Because I was late, so I missed the bus.
I was late because I missed the bus.
I missed the bus, so I was late.
Although I was late, I caught the bus.
hints: Which sentence uses BOTH 'because' and 'so'?
You only need one conjunction to link ideas.
questions.explanation: 'Because I was late, so I missed the bus' is wrong — it uses both 'because' and 'so'. Only one conjunction is needed. Correct: 'I was late because I missed the bus.' OR 'I missed the bus, so I was late.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use both 'because' and 'so' to be clear, but using both is redundant and incorrect.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG conjunction?
options: Although he was tired, but he continued working.
Although he was tired, he continued working.
He was tired, but he continued working.
He was tired, so he rested.
hints: Which sentence uses both 'although' and 'but'?
You only need one contrast conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'Although he was tired, but he continued working' is wrong — it uses both 'although' and 'but'. Only one is needed. Correct: 'Although he was tired, he continued working.' OR 'He was tired, but he continued working.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use both 'although' and 'but' to be clear, but using both is redundant and incorrect.

questions.stem: Write a meaningful sentence using the conjunction 'although'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'although' correctly to show contrast — e.g., 'Although it was raining, we went to school.' or 'She passed the exam although she was sick.' Award full marks if 'although' introduces a contrasting idea.
hints: 'Although' shows contrast — two opposing ideas.
Example: Although I was tired, I finished my homework.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B5.3.9.1: Apply the knowledge of modals in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use modals to express a variety of meanings

skills.description: Identify the modal verb in a short sentence.
Choose the correct modal to express ability.
Choose the correct modal for permission or politeness.
Choose the correct modal for obligation or necessity.
Choose the correct modal for possibility.
Choose the correct modal for prediction, intention or determination.
Choose the correct modal for a past activity or event (used to).
Recognise a sentence where the wrong modal has been used for the intended meaning.
Write a sentence using a given modal for a given meaning.

misconceptions: Can for permission and ability confused

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She can swim very well.' Which word is the modal verb?
hints: A modal verb shows ability, permission, obligation or possibility.
'Can' shows ability.
questions.explanation: 'Can' is the modal verb — it shows ability. 'Swim' is the main verb.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'swim' because it is the action, but 'swim' is the main verb — 'can' is the modal.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'You must wear your uniform to school.' Which word is the modal verb?
hints: A modal verb shows obligation or necessity.
'Must' shows a strong obligation.
questions.explanation: 'Must' is the modal verb — it shows obligation. 'Wear' is the main verb.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'wear' because it is the action, but 'wear' is the main verb — 'must' is the modal.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'Kofi ___ swim very fast when he was young.'
hints: 'When he was young' signals past ability.
The past form of 'can' is 'could'.
questions.explanation: 'Could' shows past ability: Kofi could swim very fast when he was young.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'can' because it shows ability, but the sentence is about the past — 'could' is the correct past form.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'She ___ speak three languages.'
hints: Which modal shows ability?
Speaking three languages is an ability.
questions.explanation: 'Can' shows ability: She can speak three languages.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'must' because it sounds strong, but 'must' shows obligation — 'can' is for ability.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: '___ I go out to play, please?'
hints: Which modal asks permission politely?
'May I' is the most polite way to ask permission.
questions.explanation: 'May' is the most polite way to ask permission: 'May I go out to play, please?'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Can' because it is common, but 'may' is more polite and correct for permission.

questions.stem: Complete the response: 'May I borrow your ruler?' 'Yes, you ___ .'
hints: The question uses 'May I' — the response should match.
Answer with the same modal.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, you may' matches the question 'May I...'. The modal in the answer should match the modal in the question.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'can' because it is common, but when the question uses 'may', the polite answer uses 'may' too.

questions.stem: Choose the most polite request: '___ you please help me carry this box?'
hints: Which modal is most polite for a request?
'Could you' is more polite than 'Can you'.
questions.explanation: 'Could you please help me' is the most polite request. 'Could' is more polite than 'can' in requests.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Can' because it is common, but 'could' is more polite — especially with 'please'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'You ___ wear a helmet when riding a bicycle.'
hints: Which modal shows strong obligation or a rule?
Wearing a helmet is a safety rule.
questions.explanation: 'Must' shows strong obligation: You must wear a helmet when riding a bicycle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'may' because it is common, but 'may' shows permission — 'must' is needed for obligation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'I ___ finish my homework before I can play.'
hints: Which modal shows necessity?
Homework is something you need to do before playing.
questions.explanation: 'Have to' shows necessity: I have to finish my homework before I can play.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'might' because it sounds like a plan, but 'might' shows possibility — 'have to' is needed for necessity.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'You ___ see a doctor — you look very sick.'
hints: Which modal gives advice?
Someone who looks sick needs advice, not permission.
questions.explanation: 'Should' gives advice: You should see a doctor — you look very sick.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'can' because it shows ability, but 'can' means 'are able to' — 'should' is needed for advice.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'It ___ rain this afternoon — the sky is dark.'
hints: Which modal shows possibility?
The sky is dark, but it is not certain to rain.
questions.explanation: 'Might' shows possibility: It might rain this afternoon — the sky is dark.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'must' because dark clouds suggest rain, but 'must' shows certainty — 'might' shows possibility.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'She ___ be at the market — she said she was going there.'
hints: Which modal shows possibility?
She said she was going there, so it is possible.
questions.explanation: 'May' shows possibility: She may be at the market — she said she was going there.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'must' because it sounds confident, but 'must' shows certainty — 'may' is for possibility.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'I ___ help you with your homework tomorrow.'
hints: Which modal shows intention or a plan?
'Will' shows intention.
questions.explanation: 'Will' shows intention: I will help you with your homework tomorrow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'may' because it sounds polite, but 'may' shows possibility — 'will' is needed for intention.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'Look at those dark clouds. It ___ rain soon.'
hints: Which modal makes a prediction?
Dark clouds suggest rain is coming.
questions.explanation: 'Will' makes a prediction: It will rain soon (based on the dark clouds).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'may' because rain is not certain, but 'will' is the standard prediction — 'may' would be more tentative.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'I ___ live in Kumasi when I was a child.'
hints: Which expression shows a past activity or state?
'Used to' shows something that happened in the past but does not happen now.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' shows a past activity: I used to live in Kumasi when I was a child.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'use to' because they drop the -d in speech, but the written form is 'used to'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct modal: 'She ___ play the piano, but she stopped last year.'
hints: Which expression shows a past activity that has stopped?
'Used to' shows something done in the past but not now.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' shows a past activity: She used to play the piano, but she stopped last year.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'use to' (missing the -d) or 'is used to' (which means accustomed to), but 'used to' is correct for a past activity.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG modal for the intended meaning?
options: I could swim when I was young.
hints: Which sentence uses 'may' for ability?
'May' shows permission or possibility, not ability.
questions.explanation: 'I may swim very well' is wrong — 'may' shows permission or possibility, not ability. The correct modal is 'can': 'I can swim very well.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'may' can be used for anything, but 'may' shows permission or possibility — ability needs 'can'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG modal for the intended meaning?
options: You should stop at the red light — it is the law.
You must stop at the red light — it is the law.
You can stop at the red light.
You may stop at the red light.
hints: Which sentence uses 'should' for a rule or law?
A law requires 'must', not 'should' — 'should' is advice.
questions.explanation: 'You should stop at the red light — it is the law' is wrong — a law requires 'must', which shows strong obligation. 'Should' is weaker advice, not appropriate for a law.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'should' for any obligation, but laws and rules need 'must' — 'should' is for advice.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the modal 'can' to express ABILITY.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'can' to show ability — e.g., 'She can ride a bicycle.' or 'I can speak two languages.' Award full marks if 'can' shows ability.
hints: Use 'can' to show something someone is able to do.
Example: She can ride a bicycle.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the modal 'must' to express OBLIGATION.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'must' to show obligation — e.g., 'You must wear a helmet when cycling.' or 'Pupils must arrive at school on time.' Award full marks if 'must' shows obligation or necessity.
hints: Use 'must' to show something that is required.
Example: You must wear a helmet when cycling.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.4.10.1: Narrate situations, express feelings and convey point of view about the world/ or fictional world
indicator.objective: Create settings, characters and at least one plot in a narrative text, using appropriate linking words within and across paragraphs to aid cohesion, and using simple literary devices, e.g. direct speech

skills.description: Recognise the elements of a narrative (setting, characters, plot, beginning-middle-ending).
Choose the best setting for a given narrative topic.
Choose a description that brings a character to life rather than just naming them.
Arrange the events of a short narrative in the correct order (beginning, middle, ending).
Recognise the correct punctuation of direct speech.
Choose the correct linking words to connect sentences and paragraphs in a narrative.
Use the 5 Ws (Who? What? When? Where? Why?) to plan a narrative.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short narrative with setting, characters, plot, linking words and direct speech.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short personal narrative (true story from own experience) with the same elements.

questions.stem: Which of these are the main ELEMENTS of a narrative?
hints: A narrative tells a story — what does a story need?
Where, who, and what happens.
questions.explanation: A narrative needs a setting (where/when), characters (who) and a plot (what happens).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Introduction, body, conclusion' because they are parts of a text, but those are for other types of writing — narrative elements are setting, characters and plot.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an element of a narrative?
hints: A list of steps belongs to a different text type.
Which one is not about story elements?
questions.explanation: A list of steps is not a narrative element — it belongs to a process text. Narrative elements are characters, setting and plot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a list of steps is part of a story if it describes events, but a list of steps is a process, not a narrative.

questions.stem: You are writing a narrative titled 'A Day at the Beach'. Which setting is the most appropriate?
options: A sandy shore with waves crashing on the rocks
A busy city street with tall buildings
A dark forest with tall trees
hints: Where does a beach story happen?
It should match the title.
questions.explanation: A sandy shore with waves is the appropriate setting for a beach story — it matches the title.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A quiet classroom' because they know classrooms, but the title says 'At the Beach' — the setting must match.

questions.stem: You are writing a story that begins: 'The children were playing in the field when the sky suddenly turned dark.' Which setting is best?
options: A grassy field under a wide sky, in the afternoon
A small room with no windows
hints: What does the first line describe?
It mentions a field and a sky.
questions.explanation: A grassy field under a wide sky fits the opening line — the children were in a field and the sky changed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A small room' because it feels safe, but the story mentions a field — the setting must match the text.

questions.stem: Which character description brings the character to life?
options: Kofi was a tall boy with a wide smile and a kind heart.
hints: Which description gives details about appearance AND personality?
It uses more than just a name.
questions.explanation: The description with height, smile and kindness gives specific details — this brings the character to life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi was tall' because it gives a detail, but it only covers one feature — a lively description needs more than one detail.

questions.stem: Which character description is the most vivid?
options: Ama had bright, curious eyes and always wore a red ribbon in her hair.
hints: Which description helps you picture Ama clearly?
It uses sensory details and specific features.
questions.explanation: The description with 'bright, curious eyes' and 'a red ribbon in her hair' creates a vivid picture of Ama.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Ama was a student' because it is a fact, but it does not describe what she looks like or is like — vivid descriptions need specific details.

questions.stem: Which character description best brings the character to life in a story?
options: The old man had deep wrinkles, a slow smile, and eyes that seemed to know everything.
The old man lived in a village.
The old man was someone's grandfather.
hints: Which description shows what the character looks like and seems like?
It uses vivid imagery.
questions.explanation: The description with wrinkles, a slow smile and knowing eyes paints a picture — it brings the character to life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The old man was old' because it is true, but it does not help the reader PICTURE the character — vivid descriptions need imagery.

questions.stem:
Arrange these events into a logical story order:
A) She finally found her mother in the market.
B) Ama got separated from her mother.
C) She began to cry.
D) A kind trader helped her look.
hints: What happened first? Ama got separated.
Then she cried, someone helped, then her mother was found.
questions.explanation: Logical order: separated (B) → cried (C) → trader helped (D) → found mother (A). So B, C, D, A.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put finding the mother first because it is the happy ending, but the story must build to the ending.

questions.stem:
Arrange these events into a logical story order:
A) Kofi found a wallet.
B) He took it to the police station.
C) The owner came and thanked him.
D) He felt proud of his honesty.
hints: What happened first? Kofi found the wallet.
Then he took it, the owner came, and he felt proud.
questions.explanation: Logical order: found wallet (A) → took to police (B) → owner thanked him (C) → felt proud (D). So A, B, C, D.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the reward/thanks first because it is the most satisfying part, but the story must follow the chronological order of events.

questions.stem:
Arrange these events into a logical story order:
A) Esi studied hard for the exam.
B) She passed with the highest marks.
C) Her parents were proud of her.
D) She received a prize at assembly.
hints: What happened first? Studying.
Then passing, then pride, then the prize.
questions.explanation: Logical order: studied (A) → passed (B) → parents proud (C) → prize (D). So A, B, C, D.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the prize first because it is the most exciting, but a story builds from the beginning through to the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses CORRECT punctuation for direct speech?
options: Kofi said, "I am going to the market."
Kofi said "I am going to the market."
Kofi said, I am going to the market.
Kofi said, 'I am going to the market.'
hints: Direct speech needs quotation marks around the spoken words.
It also needs a comma before the quotation marks.
questions.explanation: Correct: Kofi said, "I am going to the market." — comma before the quotation, capital letter inside, full stop inside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick the version with single quotes ('...'), but in standard English, direct speech uses double quotation marks ("...").

questions.stem: Which sentence uses CORRECT punctuation for direct speech?
hints: Quotation marks around spoken words, comma before them.
Capital letter after the opening quote.
questions.explanation: Correct: Ama said, "Please help me." — comma before the quotation, capital P inside the quotes, full stop inside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the full stop outside the quotes, but in standard English, the full stop goes INSIDE the closing quotation mark.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses CORRECT punctuation for direct speech?
options: The teacher said, "Sit down quietly, children."
The teacher said, "sit down quietly, children."
The teacher said "Sit down quietly, children."
The teacher said, Sit down quietly, children.
hints: Capital letter at the start of the spoken words.
Comma before the quotation marks.
questions.explanation: Correct: The teacher said, "Sit down quietly, children." — capital S inside the quotes, comma before, full stop inside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may forget the capital letter inside the quotation marks, but direct speech starts with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Choose the correct linking word: 'The children were playing in the field. ___, the sky turned dark.'
hints: The sky turning dark is an unexpected event.
'Suddenly' introduces an unexpected event.
questions.explanation: 'Suddenly' fits — the sky turning dark is a sudden, unexpected event in the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Finally' because it is a common linking word, but 'finally' indicates the end of a sequence — 'suddenly' is better for an unexpected event.

questions.stem: Choose the correct linking word: 'Ama walked to the market. ___, she met her friend Kofi.'
hints: When did she meet Kofi?
It happened while she was walking.
questions.explanation: 'On the way' fits — Ama met her friend while walking to the market.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Finally' because it is a common linking phrase, but 'finally' means at the end — the friend was met during the walk, not at the end.

questions.stem: Plan a narrative using the 5 Ws. Fill in a short answer for each: Who? What? When? Where? Why?
answer: Accept any sensible answers for each of the 5 Ws — e.g., Who: Kofi; What: found a lost dog; When: last Saturday; Where: near the market; Why: to help the dog find its owner. Award full marks if all five are answered coherently and relate to one another.
hints: Who is the main character?
What happens?
When and where does it happen?
Why does it matter?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Plan a narrative about a school event using the 5 Ws. Fill in short answers for each: Who? What? When? Where? Why?
answer: Accept any sensible answers — e.g., Who: the pupils of Basic 5; What: a football match; When: last Friday; Where: the school field; Why: to win the inter-class cup. Award full marks if all five are answered coherently.
hints: Who was involved?
What happened?
When and where?
Why was it important?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short narrative (4-6 sentences) about 'A Day I Will Never Forget'. Include: a clear setting (where and when), at least one character described with detail, a simple plot (beginning, middle, ending), at least two linking words, and one line of direct speech (correctly punctuated).
hints: Start with the setting.
Describe your character with details.
Give events in order.
Use linking words like 'then', 'suddenly', 'finally'.
Add one line of direct speech with quotation marks.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Includes a clear setting (where and when)
Describes at least one character with detail
Has a clear plot (beginning, middle, ending)
Uses at least two linking words
Includes one correctly punctuated line of direct speech

questions.stem: Write a short narrative (4-6 sentences) about 'A Lost Puppy'. Include: a clear setting, at least one named character described with detail, a plot (finding the puppy, helping it, reuniting it with its owner), at least two linking words, and one line of direct speech.
hints: Where does the story take place?
Who finds the puppy?
What happens next?
Use linking words like 'first', 'then', 'finally'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two linking words

questions.stem: Write a short personal narrative (4-6 sentences) about a REAL experience from your own life. It must be a TRUE story, not imagined. Include: setting, yourself as the main character, a plot with a clear sequence, at least two linking words, and one line of direct speech (if appropriate).
hints: Think of a real experience — not a made-up story.
Where were you? When?
What happened first, next, last?
Add linking words like 'then', 'after that', 'finally'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Narrative is personal and true (not fictional)
Has a clear setting and sequence of events
Uses at least two linking words
Includes one correctly punctuated line of direct speech (if appropriate)

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.4.11.1: Create texts
indicator.objective: Write freely on topics of choice on issues in the community

skills.description: Recognise what free writing is.
Choose an appropriate topic on a community issue.
Recognise the stages of the writing process.
Arrange the stages of the writing process in the correct order.
Choose the appropriate audience and purpose for a given free-writing topic.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short free piece on a chosen community issue.
Teacher-assessed written: write a longer free piece on a chosen community issue, following the writing process.
Teacher-assessed written: prepare the piece for publication.

questions.stem: What is 'free writing'?
options: Writing freely on a topic of your choice without strict constraints on form
Copying a passage from a book
Writing only in a specific format
hints: Free = without strict rules.
You choose the topic.
questions.explanation: Free writing is writing freely on a topic of your choice without strict constraints on form — you decide what to say and how to say it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think free writing means no rules at all, but it still needs clear sentences and ideas — it just means the topic and form are free.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of free writing?
options: A short piece about a school event you choose to write about
hints: Which one is freely chosen and free in form?
You pick the topic.
questions.explanation: A short piece about a school event you choose is free writing — you picked the topic and wrote it your own way.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Answering a comprehension question' because it involves writing, but comprehension questions have set answers — free writing is open and creative.

questions.stem: You want to write freely about a community issue. Which topic is suitable?
options: How to keep our market clean
The history of a foreign country
A recipe for a foreign dish
hints: Which topic relates to your community?
It should be about your local area.
questions.explanation: 'How to keep our market clean' is suitable — it is a community issue relevant to your local area.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The history of a foreign country' because it is interesting, but free-writing topics should relate to YOUR community — not a foreign country.

questions.stem: You want to write freely about a school issue. Which topic is suitable?
options: Why we should stop littering in the classroom
The life of a famous singer
How to grow a foreign plant
hints: Which topic is about your SCHOOL?
It should relate to your school environment.
questions.explanation: 'Why we should stop littering in the classroom' is suitable — it is a school issue.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The life of a famous singer' because it is interesting, but it is not a school issue — the topic should relate to your school or community.

questions.stem: Which of these topics is TOO BROAD for a short free-writing piece?
options: Why we should plant trees in our school
How to stop littering in the market
hints: Which topic covers too many things?
A short piece needs a focused topic.
questions.explanation: 'How to improve our community' is too broad — a community has many aspects (cleanliness, safety, health, etc.). The other topics are focused and manageable.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a broad topic gives more to write, but a short free-writing piece needs a FOCUSED topic that can be covered well.

questions.stem: What are the stages of the writing process?
hints: There are five stages.
They start with planning and end with sharing.
questions.explanation: The five stages of the writing process are: pre-writing, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Beginning, middle, ending' because they are used to that structure, but those are parts of a story — the writing process has five stages.

questions.stem: Which stage of the writing process comes AFTER drafting?
hints: After you write the first draft, what do you do?
You improve the ideas.
questions.explanation: After drafting comes revising — you improve the ideas, organisation and clarity of your draft.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Publishing' because it is the next big step they think of, but revising and editing come before publishing.

questions.stem: What is done during the EDITING stage?
hints: Editing is about CORRECTING errors.
It comes after revising.
questions.explanation: During editing, you check spelling, grammar and punctuation — you correct the errors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think editing is about adding new ideas, but editing is about CORRECTING — adding new ideas happens during revising.

questions.stem:
Arrange the writing process stages in the correct order:
A) Drafting
B) Pre-writing
C) Publishing
D) Editing
E) Revising
hints: Start with pre-writing.
Then draft, revise, edit, publish.
questions.explanation: Correct order: Pre-writing (B) → Drafting (A) → Revising (E) → Editing (D) → Publishing (C). So B, A, E, D, C.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put editing before revising because both seem like correcting, but revising comes first (improving ideas), then editing (correcting errors).

questions.stem: Which stage comes right BEFORE publishing?
hints: Publishing is the last stage.
What comes just before the final stage?
questions.explanation: Editing comes right before publishing — you correct all errors, then publish.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Revising' because it also involves improving, but editing (correcting) comes after revising and right before publishing.

questions.stem: You are writing a free piece about 'why pupils should help keep the school clean'. Who is the most appropriate audience?
hints: Who would care about a school issue?
The people who are part of the school.
questions.explanation: Fellow pupils and teachers are the right audience — they are part of the school community and can act on the issue.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Politicians' because they can make changes, but a free-writing piece about a SCHOOL issue is best aimed at the school community.

questions.stem: You are writing a free piece about 'the importance of trees in our community'. What is the most likely purpose?
options: To persuade readers to plant and protect trees
To entertain readers with a funny story
To teach readers how to climb a tree
To describe a tree in detail
hints: What does 'importance of trees' suggest?
It is an issue that needs action.
questions.explanation: The purpose is to persuade readers to plant and protect trees — the topic is about importance and action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'To entertain readers' because free writing can be fun, but the topic is serious — the purpose is persuasion, not entertainment.

questions.stem: Write a short free piece (3-5 sentences) on a community issue of your choice. Choose a focused topic, write clearly, and make sure the ideas relate to your community.
hints: Choose a topic like 'keeping our market clean' or 'why we should plant trees'.
Write 3-5 clear sentences.
Relate the ideas to your community.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short free piece (3-5 sentences) on a school issue of your choice. Choose a focused topic and write clearly.
hints: Choose a topic like 'stopping littering' or 'keeping the classroom clean'.
Write 3-5 clear sentences.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short free piece (3-5 sentences) about 'why we should keep our environment clean'. Choose your focus (school, market, home, street) and write clearly.
hints: Focus on one area: school, market, home or street.
Write 3-5 sentences.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short free piece (3-5 sentences) on a community issue of your choice. Include at least one reason why the issue matters to you personally.
hints: Choose a topic.
Write 3-5 sentences.
Include one personal reason.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a longer free piece (one paragraph, 5-7 sentences) on a community issue of your choice. Follow the writing process: plan, draft, revise, edit, and write a clean final version. Submit your final paragraph.
hints: Plan your ideas first.
Draft the paragraph.
Revise for clarity.
Edit for errors.
Submit the final version.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Final version is clear and organised
Shows evidence of following the writing process

questions.stem: Write a longer free piece (one paragraph, 5-7 sentences) on a school issue of your choice. Follow the writing process and submit the final, clean version.
hints: Plan, draft, revise, edit, publish.
Make your final paragraph clear and neat.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Final version is clear and organised
Shows evidence of following the writing process

questions.stem: Write a longer free piece (one paragraph, 5-7 sentences) on a community issue of your choice. Include at least one specific example to support your idea.
hints: Choose a focused topic.
Write 5-7 sentences.
Include one specific example.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Prepare your free-writing piece for publication: write it in a clean copy, include a title and your name, and make sure it is neat and legible. Submit your publication-ready copy.
hints: Write a neat clean copy.
Add a title.
Add your name.
Make it look ready for the class notice board.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.4.11.1: Create texts
indicator.objective: Write poems and imaginative narrative stories using knowledge of features of poems and imaginative texts

skills.description: Recognise features of poems (lines, stanzas, rhythm, rhyme).
Recognise narrative elements (title, characters, setting, plot, conflict, dialogue).
Recognise features of plays.
Tell a poem apart from a story.
Choose the best title for a given imaginative story or poem.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short poem (4-6 lines) on a given topic, using at least one feature of poems.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short imaginative narrative with setting, characters and at least one conflict.
Teacher-assessed written: prepare the poem or story for publication.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of a poem?
hints: What does a poem look like on the page?
It has short lines grouped together.
questions.explanation: Poems have lines and stanzas (groups of lines) — that is a key feature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a poem must rhyme, but rhyme is optional — lines and stanzas are the defining features.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a feature of a poem?
hints: Poems do not usually have chapters.
Which feature belongs to a novel, not a poem?
questions.explanation: Chapter headings are a feature of novels, not poems. Poems have lines, stanzas and rhythm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think poems can have chapters, but poems are short — they use lines and stanzas, not chapters.

questions.stem: Which of these is an element of an imaginative narrative?
hints: A narrative is a story — what does a story need?
Who and where.
questions.explanation: Characters and setting are narrative elements — who the story is about and where it happens.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Facts and statistics' because they are used in writing, but narrative writing is imaginative — it uses characters and setting, not facts.

questions.stem: Which of these is a CONFLICT in a story?
options: A problem that the character must solve
hints: Conflict = problem.
It creates tension in the story.
questions.explanation: A conflict is a problem that the character must solve — it is the tension in the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think conflict means a fight, but in stories, it means any problem the character faces.

questions.stem: Which of these is a DIALOGUE in a story?
hints: Dialogue = characters speaking.
It appears in quotation marks.
questions.explanation: Dialogue is a conversation between characters — it appears in quotation marks in the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think dialogue is just any writing, but it must be characters SPEAKING to each other.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of a play?
options: Characters speaking to each other on a stage
A narrator telling the whole story
hints: A play is performed on stage.
The characters speak directly.
questions.explanation: In a play, characters speak to each other on stage — dialogue is the main feature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plays have long descriptions, but plays are mostly dialogue and action — descriptions are minimal.

questions.stem: What is a 'stage direction' in a play?
options: Instructions about what characters do (e.g., 'Kofi enters from the left')
hints: Stage directions tell the actors what to do.
They appear in brackets in plays.
questions.explanation: Stage directions are instructions about what characters do — they appear in brackets and guide the actors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a stage direction is a line of dialogue, but it is a direction, not something spoken.

questions.stem: Which of these is a POEM, not a story?
options: 'The rain falls soft upon the roof, / It taps and taps and will not stop.'
'Once upon a time, a girl walked into the forest.'
'Kofi woke up and brushed his teeth.'
hints: Which one has short lines?
Poems are written in lines, not paragraphs.
questions.explanation: The first option is a poem — it is written in short lines. The others are prose sentences from stories.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any text with 'and' is a story, but poems can also use 'and' — the key is the LINE format.

questions.stem: Which of these is a STORY, not a poem?
options: 'Ama walked to the market and bought mangoes. She gave one to her friend.'
'The moon is bright, / It shines at night.'
'Rain, rain, go away, / Come again another day.'
'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, / How I wonder what you are.'
hints: Which one is written as a paragraph of sentences?
Stories are in paragraph form — poems are in lines.
questions.explanation: The first option is a story — it is written in paragraph form. The others are poems, written in lines.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the first is a poem because it is short, but the FORMAT is prose (paragraph) — not lines.

questions.stem: Which is the best title for a story about a boy who finds a lost puppy and returns it to its owner?
hints: The title should capture the main event.
It should not be too broad.
questions.explanation: 'The Lost Puppy' captures the main event of the story — it is specific and interesting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A Boy's Story' because it is about a boy, but it is too general — the title should point to the story's main subject.

questions.stem: Which is the best title for a poem about the harmattan season?
hints: The title should relate to the poem's topic.
It should be specific.
questions.explanation: 'The Harmattan Wind' is specific and captures the poem's topic — the harmattan.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A Poem' because it tells the form, but a title should describe the CONTENT, not just the form.

questions.stem: Which is the best title for an imaginative story about a girl who discovers a magical tree in her village?
hints: The title should capture the magical element.
It should be specific but intriguing.
questions.explanation: 'The Magical Tree' captures the imaginative element — it draws the reader in and points to the story's central feature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'A Girl's Adventure' because the girl is the main character, but the title should focus on what makes the story special — the magical tree.

questions.stem: Write a short poem (4-6 lines) about the rain. Use at least one feature of poems (rhythm, rhyme, or stanzas).
hints: Write 4-6 lines.
Try to make the lines rhyme.
Or create a steady rhythm.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least one feature (rhythm, rhyme, or stanzas)

questions.stem: Write a short poem (4-6 lines) about a friend. Use at least one feature of poems (rhythm, rhyme, or stanzas).
hints: Write 4-6 lines.
Use rhyme or rhythm.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short poem (4-6 lines) about your school. Use at least one feature of poems (rhythm, rhyme, or stanzas).
hints: Write 4-6 lines.
Use rhyme or rhythm.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short poem (5-6 lines) on the topic 'Kindness'. Use at least TWO features of poems (rhythm, rhyme, stanzas) and make sure the poem has a clear message.
hints: Use rhythm AND rhyme (or stanzas).
Make the message clear.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two features of poems

questions.stem: Write a short imaginative narrative (5-7 sentences) about 'A Strange Noise in the Night'. Include a clear setting, at least one named character, and at least one conflict (a problem to solve).
hints: Where does the story happen?
Who is the character?
What is the strange noise?
How does the character solve the problem?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Has at least one named character

hints: Set the scene.
Name your character.
What is the conflict?
How is it resolved?

criteria.description: Has at least one named character

questions.stem: Write a short imaginative narrative (5-7 sentences) about 'A Day the Sun Forgot to Rise'. Include a clear setting, at least one named character, at least one conflict, and at least one line of dialogue.
hints: What would the world be like if the sun forgot to rise?
Who is your character?
What is the conflict?
Include one line of direct speech.

Includes one correctly punctuated line of dialogue

questions.stem: Choose one of your creative pieces (a poem or an imaginative story) and prepare it for publication: write a clean copy, include a title and your name, and make sure it is neat and legible.
hints: Pick your best poem or story.
Write a neat clean copy.
Add a title and your name.
