questions.stem: Which sentence has all words correctly spelt?
options: The children are playing in the garden.
The children are playing in the gardin.
The childen are playing in the garden.
The children are plaing in the garden.
hints: Check each word carefully.
Look for missing letters.
questions.explanation: 'The children are playing in the garden' has all words spelt correctly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may miss 'childen' (missing 'r') or 'plaing' (missing 'y'), but the first sentence is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence has all words correctly spelt?
options: She said she would come to the party.
She sed she would come to the party.
She said she woud come to the party.
She said she would com to the party.
hints: Check tricky words like 'said', 'would', 'come'.
Only one sentence has all correct.
questions.explanation: 'She said she would come to the party' has all words correctly spelt.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'sed' for 'said' or 'woud' for 'would', but the first sentence is correct.

questions.stem: Write the correct spelling for this clue: 'It is a yellow fruit that monkeys like.'
answer: accept: banana
hints: It is long and yellow.
It starts with 'b'.
questions.explanation: The word is 'banana'.

questions.stem: Write the correct spelling for this clue: 'It is the meal you eat in the morning.'
answer: accept: breakfast
hints: It starts with 'break'.
You eat it before school.
questions.explanation: The word is 'breakfast'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.2.1: Show understanding of how punctuations are used appropriately in writing
indicator.objective: Use punctuations: (the comma) to write an address; (the apostrophe) in contraction

skills.description: Place commas correctly when writing an address.
Place the apostrophe correctly in a contraction.
Place a comma after 'Yes' or 'No' at the start of a sentence.
Place a comma after a person's name when directly addressing them.
Identify which punctuation mark is missing or needed in a given sentence.
Punctuate an unpunctuated sentence or short text with the correct commas and apostrophes.

misconceptions: Comma after every word in an address
Apostrophe used for plural instead of contraction
No comma after Yes or No

questions.stem: Which address is correctly punctuated?
options: I live at Adu Street, Adukrom.
I live at Adu Street Adukrom.
I live at Adu, Street, Adukrom.
I live at Adu Street. Adukrom.
hints: In an address, use a comma between the street and the town.
Only one comma is needed here.
questions.explanation: 'I live at Adu Street, Adukrom' is correct — a comma separates the street name from the town.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put a comma after every word, but an address only needs commas between its parts — street, town.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma in the address?
options: My school is at School Road, Cape Coast.
My school is at School Road Cape Coast.
My school is at School, Road, Cape Coast.
My school is at School Road. Cape Coast.
hints: A comma separates the street from the town.
The comma goes after 'Road'.
questions.explanation: 'My school is at School Road, Cape Coast' — the comma separates 'School Road' from 'Cape Coast'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put a full stop instead of a comma, but the address is one idea — use a comma, not a full stop.

questions.stem: Which address is correctly punctuated?
options: She stays at Market Lane, Techiman.
She stays at Market Lane Techiman.
She stays at Market, Lane Techiman.
She stays at Market Lane, Techiman,
hints: One comma is needed between street and town.
No comma is needed at the end of a sentence.
questions.explanation: 'She stays at Market Lane, Techiman' is correct — one comma between street and town, no comma at the end.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add an extra comma at the end, but sentences end with full stops — not commas.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the CORRECT punctuation of the address?
options: I live at 5 Palm Street, Adabraka, Accra.
I live at 5 Palm Street Adabraka Accra.
I live at 5 Palm Street, Adabraka, Accra,
I live at 5, Palm, Street, Adabraka, Accra.
hints: Commas separate the parts of a multi-part address.
No comma after the final full stop.
questions.explanation: 'I live at 5 Palm Street, Adabraka, Accra' — commas separate street, suburb, and city.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put a comma after every word, but commas only go between the meaningful parts of the address.

questions.stem: Which word is correctly punctuated as a contraction?
hints: An apostrophe replaces missing letters.
'Can't' is short for 'cannot'.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'no' from 'cannot'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'cant' without the apostrophe, but contractions need an apostrophe.

questions.stem: Which word is correctly punctuated as a contraction?
hints: Apostrophe replaces the missing 'o'.
'Don't' is short for 'do not'.
questions.explanation: 'Don't' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'o' from 'do not'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'dont' without the apostrophe, but contractions need it.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the CORRECT apostrophe placement?
options: She can't come to school today.
She ca'nt come to school today.
She cant' come to school today.
She cant come to school today.
hints: Apostrophe goes where letters are missing.
In 'can't', the apostrophe replaces 'no'.
questions.explanation: 'She can't come to school today' — the apostrophe in 'can't' is in the right place.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put the apostrophe in the wrong place (ca'nt), but it goes where letters are missing — 'can't'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses contractions correctly?
options: They're going to the market because it's Saturday.
Theyre going to the market because its Saturday.
They're going to the market because its Saturday.
Theyre going to the market because it's Saturday.
hints: 'They're' = they are.
'It's' = it is.
questions.explanation: Both contractions are correct: 'They're' (they are) and 'it's' (it is).
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'its' instead of 'it's' — 'its' shows possession, 'it's' is short for 'it is'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after 'Yes' or 'No'?
options: Yes, I will come to the party.
Yes I will come to the party.
Yes, I, will come to the party.
Yes. I will come to the party.
hints: A comma follows 'Yes' or 'No' at the start of a sentence.
Only one comma is needed here.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, I will come to the party' — a comma follows 'Yes'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may omit the comma after 'Yes', but it is needed to separate the answer from the rest of the sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after 'No'?
hints: A comma follows 'No'.
Only one comma is needed.
questions.explanation: 'No, thank you' — a comma follows 'No'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use a full stop instead of a comma, but the two parts are part of the same response — use a comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated with 'Yes' or 'No'?
options: No, I don't want any more rice.
No I don't want any more rice.
No, I, don't want any more rice.
No. I don't want any more rice.
hints: Comma follows 'No'.
No comma is needed inside the rest of the sentence.
questions.explanation: 'No, I don't want any more rice' — comma after 'No', no extra commas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add a comma after 'I' because it is a pronoun, but 'I' in the middle does not need a comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma for direct address?
hints: When speaking directly to someone, put a comma after their name.
The name comes at the start.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi, can you help me?' — the comma after 'Kofi' shows direct address.
questions.misconception: Pupils may omit the comma after the name, but direct address needs a comma to separate the name from the rest of the sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma for direct address?
hints: A comma follows the name when addressing someone.
The name is at the end here.
questions.explanation: 'Can you help me, Ama?' — the comma before 'Ama' shows direct address.
questions.misconception: Pupils may omit the comma before the name, but direct address needs it.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated for direct address?
options: Esi, please bring me the book.
Esi please bring me the book.
Esi, please, bring me the book.
Esi. please bring me the book.
hints: One comma after the name.
No extra commas inside the sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Esi, please bring me the book' — comma after 'Esi', no extra commas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add a comma after 'please', but 'please' does not need a comma here — only the direct address does.

questions.stem: What punctuation mark is MISSING from this sentence: 'I live at Adu Street Adukrom'?
options: A question mark at the end
hints: The sentence is an address.
Addresses use commas between parts.
questions.explanation: A comma is needed: 'I live at Adu Street, Adukrom.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a full stop is missing, but the sentence ends with an implied full stop — the missing mark is the comma in the address.

questions.stem: What punctuation mark is MISSING from this sentence: 'I cant come to school today'?
options: A question mark at the end
hints: 'Cant' should be a contraction.
Contractions need apostrophes.
questions.explanation: An apostrophe is missing: 'can't' (short for 'cannot').
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on the missing full stop, but the key missing mark is the apostrophe in 'can't' — the sentence also needs a full stop, but the apostrophe is the main focus.

questions.stem: Punctuate this sentence correctly (add commas and apostrophes): 'yes i cant go to the market'
answer: accept: Yes, I can't go to the market.
accept: Yes, I can't go to the market
hints: Comma after 'Yes'.
Apostrophe in 'can't'.
Capital 'I'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Punctuate this sentence correctly (add commas and apostrophes): 'no i dont want to go kofi'
answer: accept: No, I don't want to go, Kofi.
accept: No, I don't want to go, Kofi
hints: Comma after 'No'.
Apostrophe in 'don't'.
Comma before 'Kofi' (direct address).
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Punctuate this short text correctly (add commas and apostrophes): 'ama lives at market lane techiman she cant come to school today'
answer: accept: Ama lives at Market Lane, Techiman. She can't come to school today.
accept: Ama lives at Market Lane, Techiman. She can't come to school today
hints: Add a comma in the address.
Add an apostrophe in 'can't'.
Add a full stop between the two sentences.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Punctuate this short text correctly (add commas and apostrophes): 'yes esi i wont be late she lives at school road cape coast'
answer: accept: Yes, Esi, I won't be late. She lives at School Road, Cape Coast.
accept: Yes, Esi, I won't be late. She lives at School Road, Cape Coast
hints: Comma after 'Yes'.
Comma before 'Esi' (direct address).
Apostrophe in 'won't'.
Comma in the address.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use nouns or noun phrases to refer to quantities or units.

skills.description: Identify the quantity or unit noun phrase in a written sentence.
Choose the correct unit noun for a given noun.
Recognise a wrong unit for a given noun.
Complete a written sentence with the correct quantity or unit phrase.
Write a complete sentence using a given quantity or unit phrase.
Choose the correct verb form when a unit phrase is the subject.
Distinguish a unit from the whole noun.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Please give me a piece of paper.' Which phrase refers to a quantity or unit?
hints: Which phrase tells us how MUCH paper?
It is a unit that measures paper.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of paper' refers to a quantity or unit — it tells us one unit of paper, not the whole stock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'of paper' because it contains 'paper', but the full unit phrase is 'a piece of paper'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She bought a bunch of bananas from the market.' Which phrase refers to a quantity or unit?
hints: Which phrase tells us how MANY bananas?
It is a group unit.
questions.explanation: 'A bunch of bananas' refers to a quantity — a group of bananas held together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the market' because it is a noun, but the market is not a unit — the bunch is.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'He drank a bottle of water.' Which phrase refers to a quantity or unit?
hints: Which phrase tells us how MUCH water?
It is a container unit.
questions.explanation: 'A bottle of water' refers to a quantity — the bottle is the unit that holds the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'of water' because it names water, but the full unit phrase is 'a bottle of water'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of trousers.'
hints: Trousers have two legs — what word do we use?
Trousers come in twos.
questions.explanation: We say 'a pair of trousers' because trousers have two legs. 'Pair' is the correct unit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'piece' because it is common, but we do not say 'a piece of trousers'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of bread.'
hints: What is a whole baked bread called?
It is often cut into slices.
questions.explanation: A whole baked bread is called 'a loaf'. So 'a loaf of bread' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'piece' because we also say 'a piece of bread', but 'a loaf' is the whole bread.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of water.'
hints: What do we keep water in?
It has a lid and holds liquid.
questions.explanation: Water is often kept in a bottle, so 'a bottle of water' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'loaf' because it is a unit, but we do not say 'a loaf of water'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct unit: 'a ___ of keys.'
hints: What do we call a group of keys held together?
It is like a bunch of bananas.
questions.explanation: A group of keys held together is called 'a bunch of keys'. 'Bunch' is the correct unit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pair' because keys can come in pairs, but a group of keys is called a bunch.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'a slice of cake', which word is the UNIT?
hints: Which word tells us how MUCH cake?
It is not the whole cake.
questions.explanation: 'Slice' is the unit — it tells us how much of the cake we have.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cake' because it is a noun, but 'cake' is the whole thing — 'slice' is the unit.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'a bottle of water', which is the WHOLE thing and which is the UNIT?
hints: What is being measured?
What is measuring it?
questions.explanation: Water is the whole thing being measured. The bottle is the unit that holds it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may reverse the two because bottle is a physical object, but it is the measuring unit.

questions.stem: Which of these phrases uses the unit correctly?
hints: Which unit fits its noun?
Cake is cut into slices.
questions.explanation: 'A slice of cake' is correct — slices are units of cake. The others have wrong units.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'a piece of trouser' because we say 'piece', but trousers take 'pair'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Mother bought a ___ of bread from the shop.'
hints: What unit is used for bread?
It is a whole baked bread.
questions.explanation: 'A loaf of bread' is the correct unit for bread.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pair' because it is a common unit, but we do not say 'a pair of bread'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She gave me a ___ of paper to write on.'
hints: What do we call one sheet of paper?
It is a small part of a larger whole.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of paper' is the correct unit — one sheet is one piece.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'pair' because it is a common unit, but we do not say 'a pair of paper'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'Father drank a ___ of tea this morning.'
hints: What do we drink tea from?
It is a small container.
questions.explanation: 'A cup of tea' is the correct unit — tea is drunk from a cup.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'piece' because it is a common unit, but we do not say 'a piece of tea'.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the phrase 'a bunch of bananas'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'a bunch of bananas' correctly, e.g., 'I bought a bunch of bananas from the market.' Award full marks if the phrase is used correctly and the sentence makes sense.
hints: Where do we buy bananas?
What do you do with a bunch of bananas?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the phrase 'a bottle of water'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'a bottle of water' correctly, e.g., 'I drank a bottle of water after football.' Award full marks if the phrase is used correctly.
hints: When do you drink water?
Where would you get a bottle of water?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the phrase 'a pair of shoes'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'a pair of shoes' correctly, e.g., 'I bought a new pair of shoes for school.' Award full marks if the phrase is used correctly.
hints: What do you wear on your feet?
Shoes come in twos.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'A bunch of keys ___ on the table.'
hints: The subject is 'a bunch', not 'keys'.
'A bunch' is singular.
questions.explanation: 'A bunch of keys' is a singular subject — the head noun is 'bunch'. So the verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because 'keys' is plural, but the subject is 'a bunch'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'A pair of trousers ___ on the bed.'
hints: The subject is 'a pair'.
Singular subject takes singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'A pair of trousers' is a singular subject — the head noun is 'pair'. The verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because 'trousers' is plural, but the phrase 'a pair' is the subject.

questions.stem: Which of these uses the unit correctly?
hints: Which unit fits tea?
Tea is drunk from a cup.
questions.explanation: 'A cup of tea' uses the correct unit for tea.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'loaf' works with tea because it is a unit, but loaf is for bread.

questions.stem: Which of these uses the unit correctly?
hints: Bread is cut into slices.
Which unit fits bread?
questions.explanation: 'A slice of bread' is correct — bread is cut into slices.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'glass' works with bread because it is a container, but glass is for liquids.

questions.stem: Which of these uses the unit correctly?
hints: Grapes grow in groups held together.
Which unit fits grapes?
questions.explanation: 'A bunch of grapes' is correct — grapes grow in bunches.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'bottle' works with grapes because grapes can be put in a bottle, but we say 'bunch of grapes' for the natural unit.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use collective nouns to refer to a group of objects and people

skills.description: Identify the collective noun in a written sentence.
Choose the correct collective noun for a group.
Recognise a wrong collective noun.
Choose the singular verb form with a collective noun as subject.
Use a given collective noun in a meaningful written sentence.
Match a collective noun to the group it describes.
Tell a collective noun apart from an ordinary plural.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'A flock of sheep was grazing in the field.' Which word is the collective noun?
hints: Which word names a GROUP?
It is a collective noun for sheep.
questions.explanation: 'Flock' is the collective noun — it names the group of sheep.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sheep' because it is a noun, but 'sheep' is the individual animal.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The team played well and won the match.' Which word is the collective noun?
hints: Which word names a GROUP of players?
It is a collective noun.
questions.explanation: 'Team' is the collective noun — it names the group of players.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'match' because it involves a group, but 'match' is an event.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'A swarm of bees flew over the garden.' Which phrase is the collective noun phrase?
hints: Which phrase names a GROUP of bees?
'Swarm' is the collective.
questions.explanation: 'A swarm of bees' is the collective noun phrase — 'swarm' is the collective noun.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'the garden' because it is a noun, but the garden is not a group.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collective: 'a ___ of sheep.'
hints: What do we call a group of sheep?
It starts with 'f'.
questions.explanation: A group of sheep is called a 'flock'. So 'a flock of sheep' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'herd' because cattle and sheep are both farm animals, but 'herd' is for cattle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collective: 'a ___ of fish.'
hints: What do we call a group of fish?
It starts with 's' — like a place of learning.
questions.explanation: A group of fish is called a 'school'. So 'a school of fish' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'swarm' because fish swim in groups like bees, but the correct term is 'school'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collective: 'a ___ of bees.'
hints: What do we call a group of bees?
It starts with 's'.
questions.explanation: A group of bees is called a 'swarm'. So 'a swarm of bees' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'flock' because bees fly like birds, but the correct term is 'swarm'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collective: 'a ___ of monkeys.'
hints: What do we call a group of monkeys?
It starts with 't'.
questions.explanation: A group of monkeys is called a 'troop'. So 'a troop of monkeys' is correct.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'flock' because monkeys move in groups like birds, but the correct term is 'troop'.

questions.stem: Which of these uses the WRONG collective noun?
hints: Which collective does not fit the animal?
Monkeys do not form flocks.
questions.explanation: 'A flock of monkeys' is wrong — the correct collective for monkeys is 'troop'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'flock' works for any animal group, but each collective noun matches specific animals.

questions.stem: Which of these uses the WRONG collective noun?
hints: Which collective does not fit the animal?
Sheep do not form schools.
questions.explanation: 'A school of sheep' is wrong — the correct collective for sheep is 'flock'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'school' works for many animals, but each collective is specific.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The team ___ playing tomorrow.'
hints: A collective noun takes a singular verb.
'Team' is a single group.
questions.explanation: 'The team' is a singular subject, so it takes the singular verb 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because a team has many players, but the team is treated as one unit.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'A flock of birds ___ flying over the house.'
hints: The subject is 'a flock' — singular.
Birds is just describing the flock.
questions.explanation: 'A flock of birds' — the head noun is 'flock', which is singular. So the verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because birds is plural, but the subject is 'a flock'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The congregation ___ singing a hymn.'
hints: The congregation is one group.
Collective noun takes a singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'The congregation' is a collective noun treated as singular, so the verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because the congregation has many people, but the collective noun takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the collective noun 'flock'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'flock' correctly, e.g., 'A flock of sheep was grazing in the field.' Award full marks if 'flock' is used correctly with a matching group.
hints: What animals form a flock?
Use 'flock of' with the right noun.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the collective noun 'troop'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'troop' correctly, e.g., 'A troop of monkeys swung through the trees.' Award full marks if 'troop' is used correctly.
hints: What animals form a troop?
Use 'troop of' with the right noun.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the collective noun 'team'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'team' correctly, e.g., 'Our team won the match yesterday.' Award full marks if 'team' is used correctly.
hints: What do teams do?
It is a group of players.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: What group does 'congregation' describe?
options: Worshippers in a church or mosque
hints: Where would you see a congregation?
It is a religious group.
questions.explanation: A 'congregation' is a group of worshippers gathered in a church or mosque.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'students in a class' because both are groups, but a congregation is specifically religious.

questions.stem: What group does 'audience' describe?
options: Listeners or viewers at an event
hints: Who watches a performance?
They listen and watch.
questions.explanation: An 'audience' is a group of listeners or viewers watching a performance or event.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'players' because both are at an event, but the audience watches.

questions.stem: What group does 'swarm' describe?
options: A group of bees or insects
hints: Which insects form swarms?
They buzz and fly in large numbers.
questions.explanation: A 'swarm' is a group of bees or other insects flying together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sheep' because sheep also form groups, but the correct collective for sheep is 'flock'.

questions.stem: Which word is a COLLECTIVE noun (not an ordinary plural)?
hints: A collective noun names a group as ONE unit.
'Team' is singular.
questions.explanation: 'Team' is a collective noun — it names a group as one unit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'teams' is the collective because it involves groups, but the collective is the singular form 'team'.

questions.stem: Which word is an ORDINARY PLURAL, not a collective noun?
hints: An ordinary plural just means 'more than one'.
Which word does NOT name a group as one unit?
questions.explanation: 'Books' is an ordinary plural — it just means more than one book.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'flock' because it ends in a consonant, but 'flock' names a group as one unit.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.3.1: Apply knowledge of different types of nouns in communication
indicator.objective: Identify and use abstract nouns to refer to concepts and ideas

skills.description: Identify the abstract noun in a written sentence.
Tell an abstract noun from a concrete noun.
Choose the correct abstract noun to complete a sentence.
Recognise why a noun is abstract.
Use a given abstract noun in a meaningful sentence.
Recognise a concrete noun offered as an abstract noun.
Tell an abstract noun from a verb of the same root.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Her kindness touched everyone.' Which word is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names something you cannot see or touch.
It names a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Kindness' is an abstract noun — it names a quality you cannot see or touch.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'everyone' because it names people, but 'everyone' is a pronoun.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The beauty of the sunset amazed us.' Which word is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a quality or idea.
You can see the sunset, but not 'beauty' itself.
questions.explanation: 'Beauty' is an abstract noun — it names a quality.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sunset' because it is beautiful, but the sunset itself is concrete.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Peace is important for every community.' Which word is an abstract noun?
hints: An abstract noun names a concept.
It is not a physical thing.
questions.explanation: 'Peace' is an abstract noun — it names a concept that cannot be touched.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'community' because it involves people, but 'community' is concrete.

questions.stem: Which word is an ABSTRACT noun?
hints: An abstract noun cannot be seen or touched.
It names a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Honesty' is an abstract noun — a quality.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'flower' because it is pretty (an idea), but the flower itself is concrete.

questions.stem: Which word is a CONCRETE noun?
hints: A concrete noun can be seen or touched.
Which one is a physical object?
questions.explanation: 'Table' is a concrete noun — you can see and touch it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'love' because it is common, but love cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: Which word is an ABSTRACT noun?
hints: An abstract noun cannot be seen or touched.
It names a quality.
questions.explanation: 'Patience' is an abstract noun — a quality.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'shoe' because it is a common word, but you can touch a shoe.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is ABSTRACT and which is CONCRETE? 'The girl showed great courage during the match.'
hints: Courage cannot be seen or touched.
Girl and match are physical things.
questions.explanation: 'Courage' is abstract — a quality. 'Girl' and 'match' are concrete.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'match' is abstract because it is an event, but a match is a physical thing.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct abstract noun: 'She showed great ___ when she waited for her turn.'
hints: What quality do you need when waiting?
It is an abstract noun.
questions.explanation: 'Patience' is the abstract noun that fits — waiting requires patience.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'table' because it is a common noun, but a table is not a quality.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct abstract noun: 'He treated everyone with ___.'
hints: What quality do you show when you treat people well?
It is an abstract noun.
questions.explanation: 'Kindness' is the abstract noun that fits — treating everyone well shows kindness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'book' because it is a common noun, but a book is not a quality.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct abstract noun: 'The soldiers showed great ___ in battle.'
hints: What quality do soldiers need in battle?
It is an abstract noun.
questions.explanation: 'Courage' is the abstract noun that fits — soldiers need courage.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick a physical noun because soldiers use equipment, but the question asks for an abstract noun.

questions.stem: What makes a noun 'abstract'?
options: It names something that cannot be seen, touched or felt
It names a person or place
hints: 'Abstract' means existing as an idea.
Can you touch 'kindness'?
questions.explanation: An abstract noun names something that cannot be seen, touched or felt — a quality, idea or state.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'abstract' means 'complicated', but it refers to concepts you cannot physically touch.

questions.stem: Why is 'peace' an abstract noun?
options: Because it is a state or condition you cannot see or touch
Because it is a long word
Because it is a common noun
hints: Can you see or touch peace?
It is a condition, not a physical thing.
questions.explanation: 'Peace' is abstract because it names a state or condition — you cannot see or touch it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'peace' is concrete because peace happens in real places, but peace itself is a condition.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the abstract noun 'honesty'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'honesty' correctly, e.g., 'Her honesty impressed the teacher.' Award full marks if 'honesty' is used as an abstract noun.
hints: What does honesty mean?
It is the quality of being truthful.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Uses 'honesty' correctly as an abstract noun

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the abstract noun 'patience'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'patience' correctly, e.g., 'You need patience when learning to play the drum.' Award full marks if 'patience' is used correctly.
hints: What does patience mean?
It is the ability to wait calmly.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short sentence using the abstract noun 'courage'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'courage' correctly, e.g., 'It takes courage to speak in front of the class.' Award full marks if 'courage' is used correctly.
hints: What does courage mean?
It is the ability to face fear.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Which of these is a CONCRETE noun, not an abstract noun?
hints: Which one can you see and touch?
A flower grows in the ground.
questions.explanation: 'Flower' is a concrete noun — you can see and touch it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'flower' is abstract because it represents beauty, but the flower itself is physical.

questions.stem: Which of these is a CONCRETE noun?
hints: Which one can you touch?
A table is furniture.
questions.explanation: 'Table' is a concrete noun — you can touch it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'wisdom' because it is a common word, but wisdom cannot be seen or touched.

questions.stem: In 'Her love for her children was strong', what is 'love'?
hints: Look at the word 'her' before it.
'Love' here is the thing she has.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'love' is an abstract noun — the thing she has, not something she does.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'love' is always a verb, but in this sentence it is the abstract noun.

questions.stem: In 'I love my mother', what is 'love'?
hints: Look at the word 'I' before it.
'I' is the subject — 'love' is what I do.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'love' is a verb — the action that 'I' performs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'love' is always an abstract noun, but here it is a verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'beauty' as an ABSTRACT noun?
options: Her beauty was admired by all.
The beauty of the dress was clear.
hints: An abstract noun names a quality.
In which sentence is 'beauty' the quality itself?
questions.explanation: 'Her beauty was admired by all' uses 'beauty' as an abstract noun — the quality she has.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The beauty of the dress' because it looks like a quality, but the clearer abstract-noun use is 'Her beauty was admired'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of verbs in everyday language
indicator.objective: Differentiate between how the simple past and the present perfect tense forms are used in speech and in writing

skills.description: Identify the simple past verb in a short sentence or story.
Identify the present perfect verb (has/have + past participle) in a short sentence.
Form the simple past of a given verb.
Form the present perfect of a given verb.
Choose the correct tense for a given time context.
Recognise a sentence with the wrong tense.
Explain the difference between simple past and present perfect in one sentence.

misconceptions: Present perfect with definite past time

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She walked to school yesterday.' Which word is in the simple past tense?
hints: Simple past shows a finished action in the past.
'Walked' ends in -ed.
questions.explanation: 'Walked' is the simple past verb — it shows a finished action in the past.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'yesterday' because it signals past time, but the verb is 'walked' — 'yesterday' is a time marker.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'They bought mangoes from the market.' Which word is in the simple past tense?
hints: Simple past shows a finished action.
'Bought' is the past of 'buy'.
questions.explanation: 'Bought' is the simple past of 'buy' — a finished action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'mangoes' because it is a noun, but the verb in the past tense is 'bought'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'We visited our grandmother last week.' Which word is in the simple past tense?
hints: Simple past shows a finished action.
'Visited' ends in -ed.
questions.explanation: 'Visited' is the simple past — a finished action.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'week' because it relates to time, but 'week' is a noun — the verb is 'visited'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She has finished her homework.' Which word is in the present perfect tense?
hints: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
Look for 'has finished'.
questions.explanation: 'Has finished' is the present perfect — 'has' + past participle 'finished'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'homework' because it is the object, but the verb phrase is 'has finished'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'They have eaten all the rice.' Which word is in the present perfect tense?
hints: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
Look for 'have eaten'.
questions.explanation: 'Have eaten' is the present perfect — 'have' + past participle 'eaten'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'rice' because it is the object, but the verb phrase is 'have eaten'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'He has gone to the market.' Which word is in the present perfect tense?
hints: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
Look for 'has gone'.
questions.explanation: 'Has gone' is the present perfect — 'has' + past participle 'gone'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'market' because it is the destination, but the verb phrase is 'has gone'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past of 'play'?
hints: Regular verbs add -ed.
Play → played.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'play' is 'played' — add -ed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'play' because it is the base form, but simple past needs -ed: 'played'.

questions.stem: What is the simple past of 'go'?
hints: 'Go' is irregular.
It is not 'goed'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'go' is 'went' — it is irregular.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -ed to make 'goed', but 'go' is irregular — use 'went'.

questions.stem: What is the present perfect of 'play' (with 'she')?
hints: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
With 'she', use 'has'.
questions.explanation: With 'she', the present perfect is 'has played' — 'has' + past participle 'played'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'have played' because it is also present perfect, but 'she' takes 'has'.

questions.stem: What is the present perfect of 'eat' (with 'they')?
hints: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
With 'they', use 'have'.
questions.explanation: With 'they', the present perfect is 'have eaten' — 'have' + past participle 'eaten'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'ate' because it is the past, but present perfect needs 'have' + past participle.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tense: 'I ___ him yesterday.'
hints: 'Yesterday' signals a specific past time.
Present perfect cannot be used with 'yesterday'.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' signals a specific past time, so we use the simple past: 'I saw him yesterday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'have seen' because it is a past form, but 'have seen' (present perfect) cannot be used with 'yesterday' — use simple past.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ in Accra since 2010.'
hints: 'Since' signals an action that started in the past and continues.
Use present perfect with 'since'.
questions.explanation: 'Since 2010' signals an action that started in the past and continues — use present perfect: 'I have lived in Accra since 2010.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'lived' because it is past, but 'since' signals an ongoing action — use 'have lived'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ her homework already.'
hints: 'Already' signals present perfect.
Use 'has' + past participle.
questions.explanation: 'Already' signals present perfect — the action is complete with present relevance: 'She has finished her homework already.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'finished' because it is past, but 'already' signals present perfect — use 'has finished'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ to the market three times this week.'
hints: 'This week' is a time period that is still continuing.
Use present perfect with 'this week'.
questions.explanation: 'This week' is a period still continuing, so use present perfect: 'They have gone to the market three times this week.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'went' because it is past, but 'this week' is still in progress — use 'have gone'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
hints: Which sentence has a past time word with present perfect?
'Yesterday' signals simple past, not present perfect.
questions.explanation: 'I have seen him yesterday' is wrong — 'yesterday' signals past time, so use simple past: 'I saw him yesterday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use present perfect with 'yesterday', but present perfect cannot be used with definite past time words.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
options: I have been here for three years.
hints: Which sentence uses simple past with 'since'?
'Since' signals present perfect.
questions.explanation: 'I lived here since 2010' is wrong — 'since' signals an ongoing action, so use present perfect: 'I have lived here since 2010.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use simple past with 'since', but 'since' requires present perfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
options: She has went to the market.
She has gone to the market.
She is going to the market.
hints: Which sentence uses 'has' with the wrong past participle?
'Gone' is the past participle of 'go'.
questions.explanation: 'She has went' is wrong — the past participle of 'go' is 'gone', not 'went'. Correct: 'She has gone to the market.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'went' as a past participle because it is a past form, but 'gone' is the correct past participle.

questions.stem: What is the difference between simple past and present perfect?
options: Simple past is for finished actions at a definite time; present perfect is for past actions with present relevance or no specific time
Simple past is for the present; present perfect is for the future
Simple past is for actions that continue; present perfect is for finished actions
hints: Simple past: finished, specific time.
Present perfect: past action with present relevance.
questions.explanation: Simple past is used for finished actions at a definite time (e.g., 'I saw him yesterday'). Present perfect is used for past actions with present relevance or without a specific time (e.g., 'I have seen him').
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they mean the same thing because both refer to the past, but they have different uses.

questions.stem: Explain in one or two sentences why 'I saw him yesterday' is correct but 'I have seen him yesterday' is not.
answer: Accept any answer that explains: 'yesterday' is a definite past time, so simple past is used. Present perfect is not used with definite past time words. Award full marks if the answer identifies the time word and the tense rule.
hints: What does 'yesterday' signal?
Which tense goes with definite past time?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Identifies 'yesterday' as a definite past time
Explains that present perfect cannot be used with definite past time

questions.stem: Explain in one or two sentences why 'I have lived here since 2010' is correct but 'I lived here since 2010' is not.
answer: Accept any answer that explains: 'since 2010' signals an action that started in the past and continues — present perfect is needed. Simple past is for finished actions. Award full marks if the answer explains both.
hints: What does 'since 2010' signal?
Is the action finished or ongoing?
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

criteria.description: Explains that present perfect is needed

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of verbs in everyday language
indicator.objective: Use past perfect in speech and in writing

skills.description: Identify the past perfect verb (had + past participle) in a short sentence.
Form the past perfect of a given verb.
Identify which action happened first when past perfect and simple past appear in the same sentence.
Choose the correct tense (past perfect vs simple past) for a given before/after context.
Choose the correct connective to link past perfect and simple past.
Recognise a sentence where past perfect is wrongly used or missing.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short narrative using at least two simple past and two past perfect sentences correctly.

misconceptions: Past perfect for a single past action

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'When I arrived, the bus had left.' Which word is in the past perfect tense?
hints: Past perfect = had + past participle.
Look for 'had left'.
questions.explanation: 'Had left' is the past perfect — 'had' + past participle 'left'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'arrived' because it is past, but that is simple past — past perfect is 'had left'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She had finished her work before the bell rang.' Which word is in the past perfect tense?
hints: Past perfect = had + past participle.
Look for 'had finished'.
questions.explanation: 'Had finished' is the past perfect — 'had' + past participle 'finished'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'rang' because it is past, but that is simple past — past perfect is 'had finished'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'They had eaten before we arrived.' Which word is in the past perfect tense?
hints: Past perfect = had + past participle.
Look for 'had eaten'.
questions.explanation: 'Had eaten' is the past perfect.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'arrived' because it is past, but 'arrived' is simple past — past perfect is 'had eaten'.

questions.stem: What is the past perfect of 'go' (with 'she')?
hints: Past perfect = had + past participle.
Use 'had' + 'gone'.
questions.explanation: The past perfect of 'go' is 'had gone' — 'had' + past participle 'gone'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'has gone' because it is a perfect form, but that is present perfect — past perfect uses 'had'.

questions.stem: What is the past perfect of 'eat' (with 'they')?
hints: Past perfect = had + past participle.
Use 'had' + 'eaten'.
questions.explanation: The past perfect of 'eat' is 'had eaten' — 'had' + past participle 'eaten'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'have eaten' because it is a perfect form, but that is present perfect — past perfect uses 'had'.

questions.stem: What is the past perfect of 'write' (with 'he')?
hints: Past perfect = had + past participle.
The past participle of 'write' is 'written'.
questions.explanation: The past perfect of 'write' is 'had written' — 'had' + past participle 'written'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'wrote' because it is past, but 'wrote' is simple past — past perfect is 'had written'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'When I arrived, the bus had left.' Which action happened FIRST?
options: They happened at the same time
hints: The past perfect action happened first.
'Had left' is past perfect.
questions.explanation: The bus had left (past perfect) BEFORE I arrived (simple past). So the bus leaving happened first.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'arrived' happened first because it appears first in the sentence, but past perfect signals the earlier action.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She had finished her homework before she went to play.' Which action happened FIRST?
options: They happened at the same time
hints: The past perfect action happened first.
'Had finished' is past perfect.
questions.explanation: She had finished her homework (past perfect) BEFORE she went to play (simple past). So finishing homework happened first.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think going to play happened first because it comes later in the sentence, but past perfect signals the earlier action.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'By the time the police arrived, the thief had escaped.' Which action happened FIRST?
options: They happened at the same time
hints: 'By the time' signals the later action.
'Had escaped' is past perfect — the earlier action.
questions.explanation: The thief had escaped (past perfect) BEFORE the police arrived (simple past). So the escape happened first.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the police arriving came first because it is mentioned earlier in the sentence, but past perfect signals the earlier action.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'When we reached the station, the train ___.'
hints: The train left BEFORE we reached the station.
Use past perfect for the earlier action.
questions.explanation: The train left before we arrived — so use past perfect: 'When we reached the station, the train had left.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'left' because it is past, but the earlier action needs past perfect 'had left'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ her work before the bell rang.'
hints: She finished BEFORE the bell rang.
Use past perfect for the earlier action.
questions.explanation: She finished before the bell — so use past perfect: 'She had finished her work before the bell rang.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'finished' because it is past, but the earlier action needs past perfect.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'They ___ the match before it started to rain.'
hints: They won BEFORE the rain started.
Use past perfect for the earlier action.
questions.explanation: They won before the rain — so use past perfect: 'They had won the match before it started to rain.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'won' because it is past, but the earlier action needs past perfect.

questions.stem: Choose the correct connective: 'The bus ___ left ___ I arrived.'
hints: The bus left BEFORE I arrived.
Use past perfect + 'before'.
questions.explanation: The bus had left before I arrived — past perfect + 'before'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'after' because it is a common connective, but the sentence says the bus left BEFORE I arrived — 'before' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct connective: '___ the time we arrived, the film had started.'
hints: Which phrase means 'when we arrived'?
'By the time' is a common phrase with past perfect.
questions.explanation: 'By the time we arrived, the film had started' — 'by the time' is the correct phrase.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'At' because it also relates to time, but 'by the time' is the standard phrase with past perfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
options: When I arrived, the bus left.
When I arrived, the bus had left.
She had finished before the bell rang.
They had eaten before we arrived.
hints: Which sentence is missing past perfect where it is needed?
The bus left BEFORE I arrived — past perfect is needed.
questions.explanation: 'When I arrived, the bus left' is wrong — the bus left BEFORE I arrived, so past perfect is needed: 'the bus had left'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think simple past is fine, but the order of events requires past perfect for the earlier action.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG tense?
options: She had went to the market before it closed.
She had gone to the market before it closed.
She went to the market yesterday.
She has gone to the market.
hints: Which sentence uses 'had' with the wrong past participle?
The past participle of 'go' is 'gone', not 'went'.
questions.explanation: 'She had went' is wrong — the past participle of 'go' is 'gone', not 'went'. Correct: 'She had gone to the market before it closed.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'went' as a past participle because it is a past form, but 'gone' is the correct past participle.

questions.stem: Write a short narrative (3-5 sentences) about a time you missed something. Use at least TWO simple past sentences and TWO past perfect sentences correctly.
hints: Use past perfect for the earlier action.
Use simple past for the later action.
Use connectives like 'when', 'before', 'by the time'.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two simple past verbs
Uses at least two past perfect verbs
Uses past perfect correctly for earlier actions

questions.stem: Write a short narrative (3-5 sentences) about a journey that did not go as planned. Use at least TWO simple past sentences and TWO past perfect sentences.
hints: Past perfect for what happened before.
Simple past for the main events.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two simple past verbs
Uses at least two past perfect verbs
Past perfect is used correctly for earlier actions

questions.stem: Write a short narrative (3-5 sentences) about a school event you attended. Use at least TWO simple past sentences and TWO past perfect sentences.
hints: Use past perfect for events before the main event.
Use simple past for the main event.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two simple past verbs
Uses at least two past perfect verbs
Past perfect is used correctly for earlier actions

questions.stem: Write a short narrative (4-6 sentences) about a time you were late. Use at least TWO simple past sentences and TWO past perfect sentences. Use at least one connective from: when, before, after, by the time.
hints: Use past perfect for what happened first.
Use simple past for the main events.
Use a connective to link them.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two simple past verbs
Uses at least two past perfect verbs

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of verbs in everyday language
indicator.objective: Use singular and plural subjects and the verb forms that go with them.

skills.description: Choose the correct singular verb for a singular subject in simple present, present perfect or past perfect.
Choose the correct plural verb for a plural subject in simple present, present perfect or past perfect.
Choose the correct verb for tricky subjects (collective nouns, indefinite pronouns, compound subjects).
Recognise a sentence with wrong subject-verb agreement.
Identify the multiple tenses used in a short text.
Choose the correct tense form to match a given subject and time context.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short paragraph using at least two different tenses correctly, with all subjects agreeing with their verbs.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boy ___ in the room.'
hints: 'The boy' is singular.
Singular subject → singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'The boy' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because it is a common form of 'be', but 'the boy' is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'She ___ to school every day.'
hints: 'She' is third-person singular.
Add -s to the verb.
questions.explanation: 'She' is third-person singular, so the verb takes -s: 'She walks to school every day.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'walk' because it is the base form, but 'she' needs 'walks'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The cat ___ on the mat.'
hints: 'The cat' is singular.
Add -s to the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'The cat' is singular, so the verb is 'sleeps'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'sleep' because it is the base verb, but singular subjects in simple present take -s.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The girls ___ happy.'
hints: 'The girls' is plural.
Plural subject → plural verb.
questions.explanation: 'The girls' is plural, so the verb is 'are'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because it is common, but 'the girls' is plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boys ___ football every Saturday.'
hints: 'The boys' is plural.
Plural subject → base verb (no -s).
questions.explanation: 'The boys' is plural, so the verb is 'play' (no -s).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'plays' because it looks correct for present tense, but 'plays' is for third-person singular — 'the boys' is plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The pupils ___ in the classroom.'
hints: 'The pupils' is plural.
Plural subject → plural verb.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils' is plural, so the verb is 'are'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because it is short, but 'the pupils' is plural.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The team ___ playing tomorrow.'
hints: A collective noun takes a singular verb.
'Team' is one unit.
questions.explanation: 'The team' is treated as one unit — singular — so the verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because a team has many players, but the team is treated as singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The family ___ going on a trip.'
hints: A collective noun takes a singular verb.
'Family' is one unit.
questions.explanation: 'The family' is treated as one unit — singular — so the verb is 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'are' because a family has many members, but the collective noun is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The boy and the girl ___ here.'
hints: Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural verb.
The boy + the girl = plural.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: 'The boy and the girl are here.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'is' because each subject is singular, but the compound subject is plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence has WRONG subject-verb agreement?
options: The girl with the bags are here.
The girl with the bags is here.
hints: Which sentence has a plural verb with a singular subject?
'The girl' is singular — the verb should be 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'The girl with the bags are here' is wrong — the subject is 'the girl' (singular), so the verb should be 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may agree the verb with 'bags' because it is nearest, but the subject is 'the girl'.

questions.stem: Which sentence has WRONG subject-verb agreement?
hints: Indefinite pronouns like 'everyone' take singular verbs.
'Everyone are' is wrong.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone are happy' is wrong — 'everyone' is singular, so the verb should be 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'everyone' is plural because it means many people, but grammatically it is singular.

questions.stem: Which sentence has WRONG subject-verb agreement?
options: The box of books are heavy.
The box of books is heavy.
hints: The subject is 'the box', not 'the books'.
Singular subject takes singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'The box of books are heavy' is wrong — the subject is 'the box' (singular), so the verb should be 'is'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may agree the verb with 'books' because it is nearest, but the head noun is 'box'.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'Ama woke up early. She has already eaten her breakfast. She is going to school now.' Which tenses are used?
options: Simple past, present perfect, present continuous
hints: Look at 'woke', 'has eaten', 'is going'.
Each verb is a different tense.
questions.explanation: The paragraph uses simple past ('woke'), present perfect ('has eaten') and present continuous ('is going').
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the whole paragraph is past because it starts with 'woke', but the tenses shift appropriately.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'The farmer plants maize every year. Last year, he had a good harvest. He has sold most of the maize.' Which tenses are used?
options: Simple present, simple past, present perfect
hints: Look at 'plants', 'had', 'has sold'.
Each verb is a different tense.
questions.explanation: The paragraph uses simple present ('plants'), simple past ('had') and present perfect ('has sold').
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the paragraph is all present tense because it starts with 'plants', but tenses shift with the time markers.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'She ___ her homework yesterday.'
hints: 'Yesterday' signals simple past.
Use 'finished'.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' signals simple past, so the verb is 'finished'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'has finished' because it is a past form, but 'yesterday' requires simple past.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'They ___ already left when I arrived.'
hints: 'Already left when I arrived' signals past perfect.
Use 'had left'.
questions.explanation: The earlier action (leaving) happened before the later action (arriving) — past perfect is needed: 'They had already left when I arrived.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'have' because it is a perfect form, but past perfect uses 'had'.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences) using at least TWO different tenses correctly. Make sure all subjects agree with their verbs.
hints: Use simple past and present perfect.
Check that singular subjects take singular verbs and plural subjects take plural verbs.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two different tenses
All subjects agree with their verbs

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences) about your school day. Use at least two different tenses correctly, with correct subject-verb agreement.
hints: Use simple past and present perfect.
Check agreement.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two different tenses
All subjects agree with their verbs

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences) about a family member. Use at least two different tenses correctly, with correct subject-verb agreement.
hints: Use simple past and present perfect.
Check agreement.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least two different tenses
All subjects agree with their verbs

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about a trip you have taken. Use at least THREE different tenses correctly, with correct subject-verb agreement.
hints: Use simple present, simple past and present perfect.
Check agreement.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three different tenses
All subjects agree with their verbs

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.5.1: Demonstrate understanding of adjectives in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use comparative forms of regular and irregular adjectives to make comparisons

skills.description: Recognise or use the positive form of an adjective.
Form the comparative of a regular adjective by adding -er.
Form the superlative of a regular adjective by adding -est.
Recognise irregular comparative and superlative forms (good→better→best; bad→worse→worst).
Choose the correct degree for a given context.
Choose the best adjective form to describe family members in a short paragraph.
Recognise a sentence with a wrong adjective form.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short description of a family member using positive, comparative and superlative adjectives correctly.

misconceptions: All three degrees used without context

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the POSITIVE form of an adjective?
options: My mother is kinder than my aunt.
My mother is the kindest person I know.
hints: Positive form is the base adjective — no comparison.
'Kind' is the positive form.
questions.explanation: 'My mother is kind' uses the positive form — no comparison is being made.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'kinder' because it describes the mother, but 'kinder' is comparative — the positive form is just 'kind'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the POSITIVE form of an adjective?
options: The house is bigger than mine.
The house is the biggest in the street.
hints: Positive form = base adjective.
'Big' is the positive form.
questions.explanation: 'The house is big' uses the positive form — no comparison.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'bigger' because it describes the house, but 'bigger' is comparative.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'tall'?
hints: Add -er to the base adjective.
Tall → taller.
questions.explanation: The comparative of 'tall' is 'taller' — add -er.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'tallest' because it is a form of the adjective, but '-est' is superlative — '-er' is comparative.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'big'?
hints: Double the final consonant before adding -er.
Big → bigger.
questions.explanation: For adjectives ending in consonant-vowel-consonant, double the final consonant and add -er: 'bigger'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'biger' with a single 'g', but the consonant doubles: 'bigger'.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'happy'?
hints: Change -y to -i before adding -er.
Happy → happier.
questions.explanation: For adjectives ending in -y, change -y to -i and add -er: 'happier'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'happyer' with a 'y', but -y changes to -i before -er.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'tall'?
hints: Add -est to the base adjective.
Tall → tallest.
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'tall' is 'tallest' — add -est.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'taller' because it is a form of the adjective, but '-er' is comparative — '-est' is superlative.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'happy'?
hints: Change -y to -i before adding -est.
Happy → happiest.
questions.explanation: For adjectives ending in -y, change -y to -i and add -est: 'happiest'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'happyest' or 'most happy', but the correct form is 'happiest'.

questions.stem: What is the comparative form of 'good'?
hints: 'Good' has an irregular comparative.
It is not 'gooder'.
questions.explanation: 'Good' has an irregular comparative: 'better'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -er to make 'gooder', but 'good' is irregular.

questions.stem: What is the superlative form of 'good'?
hints: 'Good' has an irregular superlative.
It is not 'goodest'.
questions.explanation: 'Good' has an irregular superlative: 'best'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add -est to make 'goodest', but the correct form is 'best'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the irregular forms correctly?
options: This book is better than that one, but the other one is the best.
This book is gooder than that one, but the other one is the goodest.
This book is more better than that one, but the other one is the most best.
This book is better than that one, but the other one is the better.
hints: Use 'better' for comparative and 'best' for superlative.
No double comparatives or superlatives.
questions.explanation: 'Better' (comparative) and 'best' (superlative) are the correct irregular forms of 'good'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add 'more' or '-est' to 'better', but that creates a double comparative — just use 'better' and 'best'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Ama is ___ than her sister.'
hints: Comparing two people → use comparative.
Add -er to 'tall'.
questions.explanation: 'Ama is taller than her sister' — comparing two people, so use the comparative 'taller'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'tallest' because it is a form of the adjective, but 'tallest' is for three or more — for two, use 'taller'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Kofi is the ___ boy in the class.'
hints: Comparing three or more → use superlative.
Add -est to 'tall'.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi is the tallest boy in the class' — comparing many boys, so use the superlative 'tallest'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'taller' because it is a form of the adjective, but 'taller' is for two — for many, use 'tallest'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'This is the ___ film I have ever seen.'
hints: Comparing many films → superlative of 'good'.
Good → best.
questions.explanation: 'This is the best film I have ever seen' — comparing many films, so use the superlative 'best'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'better' because it is a form of 'good', but 'better' is comparative — for many, use 'best'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly describes a family member using a comparative adjective?
options: My brother is taller than me.
My brother is tallest than me.
My brother is more taller than me.
hints: Use '-er' + 'than' for comparison.
No double comparatives.
questions.explanation: 'My brother is taller than me' uses the comparative correctly with 'than'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'more taller' because it sounds strong, but 'more' + '-er' is a double comparative.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly describes a family member using a superlative adjective?
options: My grandmother is the kindest person in my family.
My grandmother is the kinder person in my family.
My grandmother is kindest than everyone.
hints: Use 'the' + '-est' for superlative.
No double superlatives.
questions.explanation: 'My grandmother is the kindest person in my family' uses the superlative correctly with 'the'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may omit 'the' before the superlative, but 'the' is needed with superlatives.

questions.stem: Which paragraph correctly uses positive, comparative and superlative adjectives?
options: My sister is kind. My brother is kinder than her. My mother is the kindest of all.
My sister is kind. My brother is more kinder than her. My mother is the most kindest.
My sister is kindest. My brother is kinder. My mother is kind.
My sister is kind. My brother is kind. My mother is kind.
hints: Check that each degree is used correctly.
No double comparatives or superlatives.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph uses 'kind' (positive), 'kinder' (comparative) and 'kindest' (superlative) correctly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may accept 'more kinder' because it sounds emphatic, but it is a double comparative.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG adjective form?
options: She is more taller than her sister.
She is taller than her sister.
She is the tallest in her class.
hints: Which sentence uses both 'more' and '-er'?
'More taller' is a double comparative.
questions.explanation: 'She is more taller' is wrong — it uses both 'more' and '-er'. The correct form is just 'taller'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add 'more' to strengthen a comparative, but that creates a double comparative.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the WRONG adjective form?
options: This is the most best book in the library.
This is the best book in the library.
This book is better than that one.
hints: Which sentence uses both 'most' and '-est'?
'Most best' is a double superlative.
questions.explanation: 'This is the most best book' is wrong — it uses both 'most' and 'best'. The correct form is 'the best'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may add 'most' to strengthen a superlative, but that creates a double superlative.

questions.stem: Write a short description (3-5 sentences) of a family member. Use at least one positive, one comparative and one superlative adjective correctly.
hints: Use the base adjective for positive.
Use '-er' + 'than' for comparative.
Use 'the' + '-est' for superlative.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses a comparative adjective correctly with 'than'
Uses a superlative adjective correctly with 'the'

questions.stem: Write a short description (3-5 sentences) of two family members, comparing them. Use at least one comparative and one superlative adjective correctly.
hints: Compare the two people using '-er' + 'than'.
Use 'the' + '-est' for the superlative.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.6.1: Demonstrate understanding of the use of adverbs in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use adverbs to express manner

skills.description: Identify the adverb of manner in a written sentence.
Form an adverb of manner from a given adjective.
Choose the correct adverb of manner to complete a written sentence using meaning.
Distinguish an adjective from an adverb and choose the right one in a written sentence.
Recognise a sentence with a wrong adverb form.
Write a meaningful sentence using a given adverb of manner.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short paragraph using at least three adverbs of manner correctly.

misconceptions: -ly added to words that don't take -ly
Same form for adjective and adverb not recognised

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The pupils listened carefully to the teacher.' Which word is the adverb of manner?
hints: An adverb of manner tells HOW something was done.
'Carefully' tells how the pupils listened.
questions.explanation: 'Carefully' is the adverb of manner — it tells how the pupils listened.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'listened' because it is the action, but the adverb is 'carefully' — it describes the action.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She spoke softly to the crying baby.' Which word is the adverb of manner?
hints: Which word tells HOW she spoke?
'Softly' describes the manner of speaking.
questions.explanation: 'Softly' is the adverb of manner — it tells how she spoke.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'crying' because it describes the baby, but 'crying' is a verb form — the adverb is 'softly'.

questions.stem: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'slow'?
hints: Add -ly to the adjective.
Slow → slowly.
questions.explanation: The adverb form of 'slow' is 'slowly' — add -ly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'slower' because it is a form of the adjective, but 'slower' is comparative — the adverb is 'slowly'.

questions.stem: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'quick'?
hints: Add -ly to the adjective.
Quick → quickly.
questions.explanation: The adverb form of 'quick' is 'quickly' — add -ly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'quicker' because it is a form of the adjective, but the adverb is 'quickly'.

questions.stem: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'happy'?
hints: Change -y to -i before adding -ly.
Happy → happily.
questions.explanation: For adjectives ending in -y, change -y to -i and add -ly: 'happily'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may write 'happyly' with a 'y', but -y changes to -i before -ly.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She ate her food ___.'
hints: We need an adverb of manner to describe HOW she ate.
Use 'slowly', not 'slow'.
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' is the adverb of manner: 'She ate her food slowly.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'slow' because it describes the eating, but 'slow' is an adjective — the adverb is 'slowly'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'The boy ran ___ to catch the bus.'
hints: We need an adverb of manner.
Use 'quickly', not 'quick'.
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' is the adverb of manner: 'The boy ran quickly to catch the bus.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'quick' because it describes the running, but 'quick' is an adjective.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She smiled ___ when she received the gift.'
hints: We need an adverb of manner.
Use 'happily', not 'happy'.
questions.explanation: 'Happily' is the adverb of manner: 'She smiled happily when she received the gift.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'happy' because it describes the smile, but 'happy' is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the ADVERB correctly?
hints: An adverb tells HOW she sings.
Use 'beautifully', not 'beautiful'.
questions.explanation: 'She sings beautifully' is correct — 'beautifully' is the adverb of manner.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She sings beautiful' because 'beautiful' sounds nice, but it is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the ADJECTIVE correctly?
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
'Beautiful' describes 'singer'.
questions.explanation: 'She is a beautiful singer' uses 'beautiful' as an adjective describing the noun 'singer'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She sings beautiful' because it sounds similar, but 'beautiful' is an adjective.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct word: 'The teacher spoke ___ to the pupils.'
hints: We need an adverb to describe HOW the teacher spoke.
Use 'kindly', not 'kind'.
questions.explanation: 'Kindly' is the adverb: 'The teacher spoke kindly to the pupils.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'kind' because it describes the speaking, but 'kind' is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG adverb form?
hints: Which sentence uses an adjective where an adverb is needed?
'Slow' is an adjective, not an adverb.
questions.explanation: 'She ate her food slow' is wrong — it should be 'slowly' because an adverb is needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'slow' works as an adverb, but in standard English, 'slowly' is the adverb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG adverb form?
options: He ran quick to the shop.
He ran quickly to the shop.
hints: Which sentence uses an adjective where an adverb is needed?
'Quick' is an adjective.
questions.explanation: 'He ran quick' is wrong — it should be 'quickly' because an adverb is needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'quick' works as an adverb, but the adverb is 'quickly'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG adverb form?
hints: Which word is misspelt?
Happy → happily, not 'happyly'.
questions.explanation: 'Happyly' is wrong — the adverb of 'happy' is 'happily' (change -y to -i, then add -ly).
questions.misconception: Pupils may keep the 'y' before adding -ly, but -y changes to -i.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the adverb of manner 'slowly'.
