answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'slowly' correctly, e.g., 'The tortoise walked slowly.' Award full marks if 'slowly' is used as an adverb of manner.
hints: Use 'slowly' to describe HOW something was done.
It modifies a verb.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the adverb of manner 'carefully'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'carefully' correctly, e.g., 'She carried the baby carefully.' Award full marks if 'carefully' is used as an adverb.
hints: Use 'carefully' to describe HOW something was done.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using an adverb of manner formed from the adjective 'happy'.
answer: Accept any sentence that uses 'happily' correctly, e.g., 'The children played happily in the field.' Award full marks if 'happily' is formed correctly and used as an adverb of manner.
hints: Happy → happily.
Use it to describe HOW something was done.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences) about a school event. Use at least THREE adverbs of manner correctly.
hints: Use adverbs like 'quickly', 'carefully', 'happily', 'quietly'.
Each adverb should describe HOW something was done.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three adverbs of manner

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences) about a market day. Use at least THREE adverbs of manner correctly.
hints: Use adverbs like 'busily', 'noisily', 'carefully', 'quickly'.
Each adverb should describe HOW something was done.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three adverbs of manner

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about a journey. Use at least THREE adverbs of manner correctly. Then underline each adverb you used.
hints: Use adverbs like 'slowly', 'carefully', 'quickly'.
Underline each adverb after writing.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three adverbs of manner

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.7.1: Apply the knowledge of prepositions in oral and written communication
indicator.objective: Use prepositions to convey a variety of meanings

skills.description: Choose the correct preposition to show position.
Choose the correct preposition to show direction.
Choose the correct preposition to show time.
Choose the correct preposition to show purpose.
Choose the correct preposition to show possession.
Choose the correct preposition to show comparison.
Choose the correct preposition to show support or opposition.
Recognise a sentence with the wrong preposition.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short paragraph using at least four prepositions correctly with different meanings.

misconceptions: For ambiguous between purpose and possession

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The book is ___ the table.'
hints: Where is the book resting?
It is on top of the table.
questions.explanation: 'On' shows position — the book is on the table.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to' because it is a common preposition, but 'to' shows direction — 'on' shows position.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The cat is hiding ___ the bed.'
hints: Where would a cat hide relative to a bed?
It goes below the bed.
questions.explanation: 'Under' shows position — the cat is below the bed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'towards' because it is a preposition, but 'towards' shows direction — 'under' shows position.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The school is ___ the market.'
hints: Which preposition means 'close to'?
'Near' means close by.
questions.explanation: 'Near' shows position — the school is close to the market.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to' because it is common, but 'to' shows direction — 'near' shows position.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The children ran ___ the playground.'
hints: Which preposition shows movement towards a place?
'Towards' shows direction.
questions.explanation: 'Towards' shows direction — they ran in the direction of the playground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'on' because it is common, but 'on' shows position — 'towards' shows direction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'She walked ___ the room and sat down.'
hints: Which preposition shows movement from outside to inside?
'Into' shows direction into a place.
questions.explanation: 'Into' shows direction — she walked into the room.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'on' because it is common, but 'on' shows position — 'into' shows direction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I was born ___ Monday.'
hints: Use 'on' with days of the week.
'Monday' is a day — use 'on'.
questions.explanation: Use 'on' with days: 'I was born on Monday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'in' because it is common for time, but days take 'on'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'School starts ___ 8 o'clock.'
hints: Use 'at' with specific times.
'8 o'clock' is a specific time.
questions.explanation: Use 'at' with specific times: 'School starts at 8 o'clock.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'on' because they are used to 'on' with days, but specific times take 'at'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'We usually go to the beach ___ December.'
hints: Use 'in' with months.
'December' is a month — use 'in'.
questions.explanation: Use 'in' with months: 'We usually go to the beach in December.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'on' because they are used to 'on' with days, but months take 'in'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'She went to the market ___ some rice.'
hints: Which preposition shows purpose?
'For' means 'in order to get'.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows purpose — she went to the market to get rice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'to' because it is common, but 'to' is followed by a verb — before a noun, use 'for'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'This hoe is ___ weeding the garden.'
hints: Which preposition shows the purpose of the hoe?
The hoe is used for weeding.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows purpose — this hoe is for weeding the garden.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'at' because it is common, but 'at' shows position or time — 'for' shows purpose.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'This shirt is ___ Kofi.'
hints: Which preposition shows that the shirt belongs to Kofi?
'For' can show possession.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows possession here — the shirt is for Kofi (it belongs to him).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'on' because clothes go on a body, but 'for' shows ownership.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The toy is ___ my brother.'
hints: Which preposition shows that the toy belongs to your brother?
'For' can show possession.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows possession — the toy is for my brother.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'in' because it is a common preposition, but 'for' shows ownership.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'She is taller ___ her brother.'
hints: Which preposition is used for comparison?
'Than' is used with comparative adjectives.
questions.explanation: 'Than' is used for comparison: 'She is taller than her brother.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'for' because it is common, but 'for' does not show comparison — 'than' is correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'This bag is heavier ___ that one.'
hints: Which preposition is used with comparative adjectives?
'Heavier than'.
questions.explanation: 'Than' is used for comparison: 'This bag is heavier than that one.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'for' because it is a common preposition, but comparison requires 'than'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I am ___ you — I support your plan.'
hints: Which preposition shows support?
'For' means in support of.
questions.explanation: 'For' shows support: 'I am for you — I support your plan.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'against' because it is the opposite of 'for', but the sentence says 'I support your plan' — that means 'for'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The students were ___ the new rule — they did not like it.'
hints: Which preposition shows opposition?
The students did not like the rule.
questions.explanation: 'Against' shows opposition: 'The students were against the new rule.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'for' because it is common, but 'for' shows support — the sentence shows opposition.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG preposition?
options: We go to the beach in December.
hints: Days of the week take 'on', not 'in'.
Which sentence uses 'in' with a day?
questions.explanation: 'She was born in Monday' is wrong — days of the week take 'on': 'She was born on Monday.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'in' for all time references, but days of the week specifically take 'on'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG preposition?
options: The book is in the table.
The book is on the table.
The cat is under the table.
The bag is beside the table.
hints: Which preposition does not fit the position?
A book rests ON a table, not IN a table.
questions.explanation: 'The book is in the table' is wrong — a book rests ON the table, not IN it. We say 'on the table'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use 'in' because it is common, but 'in' means inside — a book rests on top of a table.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about a journey you made. Use at least FOUR prepositions correctly with different meanings (position, direction, time, purpose).
hints: Use prepositions like 'on', 'towards', 'at', 'for'.
Make sure each preposition conveys a different meaning.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about a school event. Use at least FOUR prepositions correctly with different meanings (position, time, comparison, support/opposition).
hints: Use prepositions like 'near', 'on', 'than', 'for'.
Make sure each preposition conveys a different meaning.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.8.1: Apply the knowledge of conjunctions in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Identify and use conjunctions – because, since, so, although – to give reasons, link contrasting ideas, show results

skills.description: Identify the conjunction in a written sentence or short passage.
Choose the correct conjunction to give a reason (because/since).
Choose the correct conjunction to link contrasting ideas (but/although).
Choose the correct conjunction to show a result (so).
Join two simple sentences into one compound or complex sentence using the correct conjunction.
Recognise and correct a sentence with the wrong conjunction or a double conjunction.
Complete a short paragraph with the correct conjunctions from a given set.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short paragraph using at least three of the target conjunctions correctly.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'I stayed home because it was raining.' Which word is the conjunction?
hints: A conjunction joins ideas together.
'Because' introduces the reason.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is the conjunction — it joins the two ideas and gives the reason for staying home.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'raining' because it is the reason, but the conjunction is the word that LINKS the ideas — 'because'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'She studied hard, so she passed the exam.' Which word is the conjunction?
hints: A conjunction joins the two parts of the sentence.
'So' shows the result.
questions.explanation: 'So' is the conjunction — it links the studying to the result (passing).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'passed' because it is the result, but the conjunction is 'so' — the word that links.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'Although he was tired, he continued working.' Which word is the conjunction?
hints: A conjunction links ideas.
'Although' introduces a contrasting idea.
questions.explanation: 'Although' is the conjunction — it links the idea of being tired to the contrasting idea of continuing to work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'tired' because it is the descriptive word, but the conjunction is 'Although'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'I was late ___ I missed the bus.'
hints: Which conjunction gives a reason?
Why was I late?
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the reason: I was late BECAUSE I missed the bus.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'so' because both connect ideas, but 'so' shows a result, not a reason.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: '___ it was raining, we stayed indoors.'
hints: Which conjunction gives a reason?
Why did we stay indoors?
questions.explanation: 'Since' gives a reason — it means 'because'. 'Since it was raining, we stayed indoors.'
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'So' because it connects ideas, but 'so' shows a result — the reason is the rain.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'She passed the exam ___ she studied every day.'
hints: Which conjunction gives a reason for passing?
Why did she pass?
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the reason: she passed BECAUSE she studied every day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'so' because both connect ideas, but 'so' would mean studying was the result of passing — which is the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'He was tired, ___ he continued working.'
hints: Which conjunction shows contrast?
The two ideas are opposite — tiredness and continuing to work.
questions.explanation: 'But' shows contrast: he was tired, BUT he continued working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'so' because both connect ideas, but 'so' would show a result — tiredness would not cause him to continue working.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: '___ she was tired, she continued working.'
hints: Which conjunction shows contrast?
The two ideas are opposite.
questions.explanation: 'Although' shows contrast: ALTHOUGH she was tired, she continued working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because' because it gives a reason, but being tired is the opposite of continuing — the idea is contrast, not cause.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Ama is tall, ___ her sister is short.'
hints: Which conjunction shows contrast?
Tall and short are opposites.
questions.explanation: 'But' shows contrast: Ama is tall, BUT her sister is short.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it connects ideas, but 'because' would suggest being tall causes her sister to be short — clearly wrong.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'It was raining, ___ we stayed indoors.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a result?
What was the result of the rain?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: it was raining, SO we stayed indoors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it connects ideas, but 'because' gives a reason — the rain is the reason, staying indoors is the result.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Kofi studied hard, ___ he passed the exam.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a result?
What was the result of studying hard?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: he studied hard, SO he passed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it is common, but 'because' gives a reason — here, passing is the result of studying.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'The rain was very heavy, ___ the road was flooded.'
hints: Which conjunction shows a result?
What was the result of heavy rain?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: the rain was heavy, SO the road was flooded.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it also connects ideas, but here the flooding is the result of the heavy rain — 'so' is correct.

questions.stem: Join these two sentences: 'It was raining.' 'We stayed indoors.' Which is the correct way to join them?
options: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.
It was raining, because we stayed indoors.
It was raining, although we stayed indoors.
It was raining, or we stayed indoors.
hints: What is the relationship between rain and staying indoors?
The rain caused us to stay indoors — that's a result.
questions.explanation: 'So' correctly shows the result: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it links ideas, but 'because' would suggest we stayed indoors CAUSED the rain — which is backwards.

questions.stem: Join these two sentences: 'He was tired.' 'He continued working.' Which is the correct way to join them?
options: Although he was tired, he continued working.
Because he was tired, he continued working.
So he was tired, he continued working.
Or he was tired, he continued working.
hints: What is the relationship? Tiredness and working are opposite.
Use a contrast conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'Although' correctly shows the contrast: Although he was tired, he continued working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because' because it connects ideas, but tiredness does not cause someone to keep working — the ideas are contrasting.

questions.stem: Join these two sentences: 'She studied hard.' 'She passed the exam.' Which is the correct way to join them?
options: She studied hard, so she passed the exam.
She studied hard, because she passed the exam.
She studied hard, although she passed the exam.
She studied hard, or she passed the exam.
hints: What is the relationship between studying and passing?
Studying caused her to pass — that's a result.
questions.explanation: 'So' correctly shows the result: She studied hard, so she passed the exam.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'because' because it is common, but 'because' would suggest passing the exam caused her to study — which is backwards.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG conjunction?
options: Because I was late, so I missed the bus.
I was late because I missed the bus.
I missed the bus, so I was late.
Although I was late, I caught the bus.
hints: Which sentence uses BOTH 'because' and 'so'?
You only need one conjunction to link ideas.
questions.explanation: 'Because I was late, so I missed the bus' is wrong — it uses both 'because' and 'so'. Only one conjunction is needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use both 'because' and 'so' to be clear, but using both is redundant and incorrect.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the WRONG conjunction?
options: Although he was tired, but he continued working.
Although he was tired, he continued working.
He was tired, but he continued working.
He was tired, so he rested.
hints: Which sentence uses both 'although' and 'but'?
You only need one contrast conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'Although he was tired, but he continued working' is wrong — it uses both 'although' and 'but'. Only one is needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use both 'although' and 'but' to be clear, but using both is redundant and incorrect.

questions.stem: Complete the paragraph with the correct conjunctions: 'Ama wanted to go to the market. ___ it was raining heavily, she decided to stay home. She was disappointed, ___ she knew it was the right choice.'
hints: First blank gives a reason — 'since' or 'because'.
Second blank shows contrast — 'but' or 'although'.
questions.explanation: 'Since' gives the reason (it was raining), and 'but' shows the contrast (disappointed yet knew it was right).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Although / so' but 'although' would make the first sentence contrast, not reason.

questions.stem: Complete the paragraph with the correct conjunctions: 'Kofi studied very hard for the exam. ___, he passed with the highest marks. His parents were happy, ___ they knew he had worked for it.'
hints: First blank shows result — 'so'.
Second blank gives a reason — 'because'.
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result (he passed), and 'because' gives the reason (he had worked for it).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Because / so' but that reverses the relationship — the passing is the result, not the reason.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-5 sentences) about a time you helped someone. Use at least THREE of these conjunctions correctly: because, since, so, although, but.
hints: Use 'because' or 'since' to give reasons.
Use 'so' to show results.
Use 'although' or 'but' to show contrast.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses at least three target conjunctions

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Using Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
indicator.content_standard: B5.5.9.1: Apply knowledge of grammatical rules to form words, phrases and sentences
indicator.objective: Identify subjects and predicates in compound sentences

skills.description: Tell a simple sentence apart from a compound sentence.
Identify a compound sentence among four options.
Identify the subject of each clause in a compound sentence.
Identify the predicate (verb + object/complement) of each clause.
Identify the two independent clauses and the conjunction between them.
Recognise a compound sentence missing a subject, predicate, or conjunction.
Write a compound sentence on a given topic, correctly joining two independent clauses.
Teacher-assessed written: write a short paragraph about an event using at least two compound sentences with clear subjects and predicates.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence?
options: The boy ran to the market.
The boy ran to the market, and the girl walked home.
The boy ran, and the girl walked.
The boy sang, and the girl danced.
hints: A simple sentence has ONE independent clause.
It has one subject and one verb.
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran to the market' has one subject ('the boy') and one verb ('ran') — it is a simple sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The boy and the girl went to school' because it has 'and', but that is a simple sentence with a compound subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a COMPOUND sentence?
options: The boy ran to the market, and the girl walked home.
The boy ran to the market.
The boy and the girl went to school.
hints: A compound sentence has TWO independent clauses joined by a conjunction.
Each clause needs its own subject and verb.
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran to the market, and the girl walked home' has two independent clauses joined by 'and'. That makes it compound.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The boy and the girl went to school' because it has 'and', but that is a compound subject in one simple sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a COMPOUND sentence?
options: She wanted to go to the party, but she was very tired.
She wanted to go to the party.
She and her sister went to the party.
hints: Two independent clauses joined by a conjunction.
'But' links two complete ideas.
questions.explanation: 'She wanted to go to the party, but she was very tired' has two independent clauses joined by 'but'. That is a compound sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She and her sister went to the party' because it has 'and', but that is one clause with a compound subject.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a compound sentence?
options: The boy ran to the shop.
The boy ran to the shop, and the girl went home.
The boy ran, and the girl walked.
The boy sang, and the girl danced.
hints: Which sentence has only one subject and one verb?
A compound sentence needs TWO independent clauses.
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran to the shop' has only one independent clause — it is a simple sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any sentence with 'and' is compound, but 'and' in a compound subject does not make a compound sentence.

questions.stem: Which of these is a compound sentence?
options: The teacher entered the classroom, and the pupils stood up.
The teacher and the pupils stood up.
hints: Two independent clauses joined by a conjunction.
'And' joins 'the teacher entered...' and 'the pupils stood up'.
Each clause has its own subject and verb.
questions.explanation: 'The teacher entered the classroom, and the pupils stood up' has two independent clauses joined by 'and'. Each clause has its own subject and verb — that is a compound sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The teacher and the pupils stood up' because it has 'and', but that is a simple sentence with a compound subject (only one verb).

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'The boy ran to school, and the girl walked to the market', what are the TWO SUBJECTS?
hints: Who is doing the action in each clause?
The subject is WHO the clause is about.
questions.explanation: The two subjects are 'the boy' (first clause) and 'the girl' (second clause).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'ran / walked' because they are the actions, but those are the VERBS — the subjects are 'the boy' and 'the girl'.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'Ama cooked rice, but Kofi washed the plates', what are the TWO SUBJECTS?
hints: Who is doing each action?
Each clause has its own subject.
questions.explanation: The two subjects are 'Ama' (first clause) and 'Kofi' (second clause).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cooked / washed' because they are the actions, but those are the verbs — the subjects are Ama and Kofi.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'The children sang, and the teachers clapped', what are the TWO SUBJECTS?
hints: Who is doing each action?
Each clause has its own subject.
questions.explanation: The two subjects are 'the children' (first clause) and 'the teachers' (second clause).
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'The children and the teachers' because they are both mentioned, but that would make a compound subject — here, they are subjects of separate clauses.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'Ama cooked rice, but Kofi washed the plates', what are the TWO PREDICATES?
hints: The predicate includes the verb AND what comes after it.
It is what is said about the subject.
questions.explanation: The two predicates are 'cooked rice' (what Ama did) and 'washed the plates' (what Kofi did). Each includes the verb and its object.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'cooked / washed' because they are the verbs, but the predicate includes the whole phrase after the subject.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'The boy ran to school, and the girl walked to the market', what are the TWO PREDICATES?
options: ran to school / walked to the market
hints: The predicate includes the verb and what follows.
It tells what the subject did.
questions.explanation: The two predicates are 'ran to school' and 'walked to the market' — each includes the verb and its destination.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'ran / walked' because they are the verbs, but the full predicate includes the destination.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'The teacher entered the classroom, and the pupils stood up', what are the TWO PREDICATES?
hints: The predicate includes the verb and what follows.
What did each subject do?
questions.explanation: The two predicates are 'entered the classroom' and 'stood up'.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'entered / stood' because they are the verbs, but the predicate is the whole phrase that tells what the subject did.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'She wanted to go, but she was too tired', what are the TWO independent clauses?
options: She wanted to go / she was too tired
hints: Each clause can stand on its own as a sentence.
Look for the two complete ideas joined by 'but'.
questions.explanation: The two independent clauses are 'She wanted to go' and 'she was too tired' — each can stand alone as a sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick part of a clause because they see a familiar phrase, but an independent clause needs its own subject and verb.

questions.stem: In the compound sentence 'The pupils cleaned the classroom, and the teacher praised them', what is the CONJUNCTION?
hints: The conjunction links the two clauses.
Look for the word between the two clauses.
questions.explanation: 'And' is the conjunction that joins the two independent clauses.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'praised' because it is near the conjunction, but 'praised' is a verb — the conjunction is 'and'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT a correct compound sentence?
options: I was hungry I ate the food.
I was hungry, and I ate the food.
I was hungry, so I ate the food.
I was hungry, but I did not eat.
hints: Which sentence is missing a conjunction or punctuation?
Two clauses need to be joined by a conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'I was hungry I ate the food' is a run-on — it is missing the conjunction. The correct form needs 'and' or 'so' between the clauses.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think two clauses next to each other form a compound sentence, but without a conjunction, it is a run-on.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT a correct compound sentence?
options: The boy ran and the girl.
The boy ran, and the girl walked.
The boy sang, and the girl danced.
The boy cooked, but the girl washed.
hints: Which sentence is missing a verb in the second clause?
'The girl' has no verb after it.
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran and the girl' is missing the verb in the second clause — the girl has no action. A compound sentence needs two complete clauses.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sentence is compound because it has 'and', but the second clause is incomplete — no verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT a correct compound sentence?
options: The boy ran, and the girl jumped.
The boy sang, and the girl danced.
The boy cooked, and the girl washed.
hints: Which sentence has only ONE subject with TWO verbs?
A compound sentence needs two independent clauses, each with its own subject.
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran and jumped' has one subject ('the boy') with two verbs ('ran' and 'jumped') — that is a compound predicate, not a compound sentence. It is a simple sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think two verbs with 'and' make a compound sentence, but a compound sentence needs two SUBJECTS and two clauses.

questions.stem: Write ONE compound sentence about a market. Use 'and' or 'but' to join two independent clauses.
answer: Accept any sentence with two independent clauses joined by 'and' or 'but', e.g., 'The traders sold their goods, and the buyers crowded around.' Award full marks if both clauses have a subject and a verb.
hints: Each clause needs its own subject and verb.
Use 'and' or 'but' to join them.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write ONE compound sentence about a school event. Use 'so' or 'but' to join two independent clauses.
answer: Accept any sentence with two independent clauses joined by 'so' or 'but', e.g., 'The pupils practised hard, so they won the match.' Award full marks if both clauses are complete.
hints: Each clause needs its own subject and verb.
Use 'so' or 'but' to join them.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the short-answer rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) about a school event. Include at least TWO compound sentences, with clear subjects and predicates in each clause.
hints: Each compound sentence needs two independent clauses.
Use 'and', 'but', 'or' or 'so' to join them.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Includes at least two compound sentences
Each clause has a clear subject and predicate

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) about an event you attended. Include at least TWO compound sentences and underline the conjunction in each one.
hints: Each compound sentence has two independent clauses.
Underline the conjunction ('and', 'but', 'or', 'so') after writing.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Includes at least two compound sentences
Each clause has a clear subject and predicate

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Building the Love and Culture of Reading
indicator.content_standard: B5.6.1.1: Read widely for pleasure, and to demonstrate independent reading and learning in the literary/content areas
indicator.objective: Read a variety of age- and level appropriate books and present at least a three-paragraph summary of each book read

skills.description: Recognise what a book summary is.
Recognise what makes a book age- and level appropriate.
Recognise the structure of a 3-paragraph summary.
Identify the main idea of a short book blurb or passage.
Pick the key details that belong in a summary.
Teacher-assessed written: write a three-paragraph summary of a book read with beginning/middle/ending structure.
Teacher-assessed observation: read independently during the library period for a sustained time.
Teacher-assessed oral: present the three-paragraph summary to the class or a small group.

questions.stem: What is a book summary?
options: A short restatement of the main ideas of a book in your own words
A copy of the book's first page
A list of every character in the book
A description of the book's cover
hints: A summary is short and in your own words.
It covers the MAIN ideas of the book.
questions.explanation: A book summary is a short restatement of the main ideas of a book in your own words.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a summary is a copy of a page or a list of every detail, but it is a short restatement of main ideas.

questions.stem: Which of these is a GOOD book summary?
options: A short paragraph in your own words that covers the main ideas
A full copy of the book's first chapter
A description of the book's cover colour
A list of every page number in the book
hints: A good summary is short and in your own words.
It covers the MAIN ideas.
questions.explanation: A good book summary is a short paragraph in your own words that covers the main ideas of the book.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think copying a chapter is a good summary, but copying is not summarising — the summary must be in your own words.

questions.stem: What makes a book AGE-APPROPRIATE for a Basic 5 pupil?
options: It has vocabulary, length and themes suitable for a Basic 5 pupil
It is the longest book in the library
hints: Age-appropriate means suitable for the pupil's age and level.
It involves vocabulary, length and themes.
questions.explanation: An age-appropriate book has vocabulary, length and themes suitable for the pupil's level.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick a book because of its cover, but age-appropriate refers to CONTENT — not appearance.

questions.stem: Which book is MOST age-appropriate for a Basic 5 pupil?
options: A short chapter book with simple vocabulary
An adult novel about legal trials
A technical manual for fixing cars
hints: Age-appropriate = suitable for the pupil's level.
Which book has simple vocabulary and suitable length?
questions.explanation: A short chapter book with simple vocabulary is age-appropriate for Basic 5. The others are either too advanced or too young.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick the longest book because they think more text is better, but an adult novel about legal trials is too advanced for Basic 5.

questions.stem: What should the FIRST paragraph of a three-paragraph book summary cover?
options: The title, author and the beginning of the story
The teacher's opinion of the book
hints: The first paragraph sets up the summary.
It should introduce the book and its beginning.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph of a summary should introduce the book (title, author) and describe the beginning of the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may start with the ending because it is exciting, but a summary follows the book's order — beginning, middle, ending.

questions.stem: What should the SECOND paragraph of a three-paragraph book summary cover?
options: The middle of the story — main events and the problem
A list of the book's chapters
hints: The second paragraph develops the summary.
It describes the main events and problem.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph covers the middle of the story — the main events and the problem.
questions.misconception: Pupils may skip the middle and jump to the ending, but the middle paragraph is needed for a full summary.

questions.stem: Read this book blurb: 'Kofi finds a lost puppy in the market. He searches for its owner but meets many difficulties along the way. In the end, Kofi learns about kindness and responsibility.' What is the MAIN IDEA of this book?
options: Kofi finds a lost puppy and learns about kindness through helping it
hints: What is the story mostly about?
It is about finding a puppy and learning something.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Kofi finds a lost puppy and learns about kindness through helping it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'Kofi is a boy' because it is true, but the main idea is about the PUPPY and what Kofi learns.

questions.stem: Read this book blurb: 'Ama and Esi are best friends. When a new girl joins their class, they must learn to share their friendship. The book explores jealousy, kindness and forgiveness.' What is the MAIN IDEA of this book?
options: Two friends learn to share their friendship when a new girl joins their class
Ama and Esi live in Ghana
There is a new girl in the class
hints: What is the story mostly about?
It is about friendship, jealousy and kindness.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that two friends learn to share their friendship when a new girl joins — the book explores jealousy, kindness and forgiveness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'There is a new girl in the class' because it is a detail, but the MAIN IDEA is about friendship and learning.

questions.stem: Book summary plan: 'I want to summarise Kofi and the Lost Puppy. Which detail BELONGS in the summary?'
options: Kofi found the puppy in the market and searched for its owner
hints: Which detail is central to the story?
The main event involves finding the puppy.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi found the puppy in the market and searched for its owner' is a key detail — it is the central event.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick details like 'the market has many stalls' because they set the scene, but a summary needs the MAIN events.

questions.stem: Book summary plan: 'I want to summarise a story about a girl who learns to be brave.' Which detail BELONGS in the summary?
options: She faced her fear of speaking in front of the class
hints: Which detail is central to the story?
The story is about becoming brave.
questions.explanation: 'She faced her fear of speaking in front of the class' is a key detail — it shows how she learned to be brave.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'She wore a red dress' because it is a detail about the character, but it is not central to the theme of bravery.

questions.stem: Write a THREE-PARAGRAPH summary of a book you have read recently. Paragraph 1: introduce the book (title and beginning). Paragraph 2: describe the middle (main events and problem). Paragraph 3: describe the ending. Use your own words.
hints: Start with the title and beginning.
Describe the main events and problem in the middle.
Describe how the story ends.
Use your own words — do not copy.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Includes title and beginning in paragraph 1
Describes main events and problem in paragraph 2

questions.stem: Write a THREE-PARAGRAPH summary of a story book you have read. Include the title and author, main events, and the ending in your own words.
hints: Paragraph 1: title, author, beginning.
Paragraph 2: main events.
Paragraph 3: ending.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a THREE-PARAGRAPH summary of an information book you have read (e.g., about animals, health or the environment). Include the title, the main facts and a conclusion in your own words.
hints: Paragraph 1: title and overview.
Paragraph 2: main facts.
Paragraph 3: conclusion.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a THREE-PARAGRAPH summary of a book you read recently. Include ONE important detail about a character and ONE important detail about the setting. Use your own words.
hints: Character detail: what the character is like or does.
Setting detail: where and when the story happens.
Three paragraphs, own words.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a THREE-PARAGRAPH summary of a book you read. After the summary, add one sentence saying whether you would recommend the book to a friend and why.
hints: Three paragraphs: beginning, middle, ending.
Add one sentence: 'I would/would not recommend this book because...'
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Three paragraphs covering beginning, middle, ending
Includes one recommendation sentence with a reason

questions.stem: Read independently during the library period for 20 minutes. Choose an age- and level-appropriate book from the library.
hints: Choose a book that suits your level.
Read quietly for the full time.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Read independently during the library period for 20 minutes. After reading, write the title of the book you read and one sentence about what happened in it.
hints: Choose a book that suits your level.
Read quietly for the full time.
Write the title and one sentence.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Writes one accurate sentence about the book

questions.stem: Read independently during the library period for 20 minutes. Choose a book you have not read before. Keep a reading log with the date, title, author, and a one-line comment.
hints: Choose a new book.
Read quietly for 20 minutes.
Fill in your reading log.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

questions.stem: Present your three-paragraph summary to a small group. Use your own words, maintain eye contact and speak clearly.
hints: Use your own words.
Look at the group.
Speak clearly and at a good pace.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.

criteria.description: Uses own words (not reading word for word)
Speaks clearly and makes eye contact

questions.stem: Present your three-paragraph summary to the class. After the presentation, answer one question from the audience about the book.
hints: Present clearly.
Be ready to answer a question about the book.
questions.explanation: Teacher assesses using the rubric.
